title: BioMedJImpact: A Comprehensive Dataset and LLM Pipeline for AI Engagement and Scientific Impact Analysis of Biomedical Journals
summary: Assessing journal impact is central to scholarly communication, yet existing resources rarely capture how collaboration and artificial intelligence (AI) research jointly shape venue prestige in biomedicine. We present BioMedJImpact, a large-scale, biomedical-oriented dataset built from 1.74 million PubMed Central articles across 2,744 journals. BioMedJImpact integrates bibliometric indicators, collaboration features, and an LLM-derived AI engagement rate, defined as the proportion of AI-related articles within each journal-year. Specifically, AI engagement rate is extracted through a reproducible three-stage LLM pipeline. We analyze how collaboration intensity and AI engagement rate jointly influence scientific impact across two temporal subsets (2016-2019, 2020-2023). Two main patterns emerge: journals with larger author teams tend to have higher citation impact, while AI engagement rate is positively associated with Impact Factor only in the 2019 subset. To validate the LLM pipeline for deriving the AI engagement rate, we conduct human evaluation, confirming substantial agreement in AI relevance detection and consistent subfield classification. Together, BioMedJImpact provides both a comprehensive dataset at the interface of biomedicine and AI and a validated framework for scalable, content-aware scientometric analysis. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/JonathanWry/BioMedJImpact.

AI.tldr: BioMedJImpact is a large-scale dataset of 1.74M PubMed Central articles across 2,744 biomedical journals, integrating bibliometric indicators, collaboration features, and an LLM-derived AI engagement rate. Analysis reveals larger author teams correlate with higher citation impact, while AI engagement positively associates with Impact Factor only in recent years. The LLM pipeline for AI relevance detection is validated via human evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing resources for assessing journal impact rarely capture how collaboration patterns and AI research jointly shape venue prestige in biomedicine. There is a need for a comprehensive, content-aware dataset that integrates both dimensions to enable more nuanced scientometric analysis.
AI.method: The authors construct BioMedJImpact from 1.74M PubMed Central articles (2,744 journals). They compute bibliometric indicators and collaboration features, then deploy a reproducible three-stage LLM pipeline to extract an AI engagement rate (proportion of AI-related articles per journal-year). They analyze how collaboration intensity and AI engagement jointly influence scientific impact across two temporal subsets (2016–2019 and 2020–2023). Human evaluation validates the LLM pipeline for AI relevance detection and subfield classification consistency.
AI.result: Two main patterns emerge: (1) journals with larger author teams consistently exhibit higher citation impact; (2) AI engagement rate is positively associated with Impact Factor only in the 2019 subset, suggesting a temporal shift in how AI research contributes to journal prestige. Human evaluation confirms substantial inter-annotator agreement in AI relevance detection and consistent subfield classification.
AI.conclusion: BioMedJImpact offers a comprehensive dataset at the intersection of biomedicine and AI, along with a validated, scalable LLM-based framework for content-aware scientometric analysis. It enables future research on how collaboration and AI engagement jointly influence journal impact in biomedicine.

title: From Trajectories to Evidence: Auditable Experimental Records for Industrial Research Agents
summary: Research agents increasingly conduct multi-round machine-learning experiments in industrial recommendation settings and retain the resulting trajectories to guide later decisions. Yet a completed trajectory is not automatically evidence: generated artifacts may be unsupported or incomplete, executed rounds may be invalid or confounded, and later modifications may obscure earlier findings. We study \textbf{trajectory-to-evidence conversion}, asking what a completed research process has actually established. We introduce an evidence-grounded framework that couples bounded verification of consequential artifacts with post-execution claim qualification. A context-isolated generate--verify--repair process checks artifacts for evidence violations and missing downstream requirements before release. After execution, validity and attribution checks consolidate evidence across rounds, qualify intervention-level claims as actionable repairs, diagnostic guards, or withheld findings, and preserve admitted claims as auditable records with explicit provenance and applicability boundaries. A hybrid LLM-assisted controller subsequently applies, defers, or rejects records based on available target evidence. Record audits characterize which claims survive qualification, while downstream diagnostics identify affirmative applicability judgment as a bottleneck for the tested controller. Across paper-to-target adaptations, later rounds often improve on the first, while final rounds frequently underperform an earlier best, exposing non-monotonic trajectory evolution. Candidates produced through the complete workflow also yielded positive online lifts relative to deployed baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper studies trajectory-to-evidence conversion in industrial ML research, proposing a framework that verifies artifacts, qualifies claims post-execution, and uses an LLM-assisted controller to apply, defer, or reject findings. It reveals non-monotonic trajectory evolution and demonstrates online lifts over baselines.
AI.motivation: Completed research trajectories in industrial recommendation systems are not automatically valid evidence. Generated artifacts may be unsupported or incomplete, executed rounds may be invalid or confounded, and later modifications can obscure earlier findings. There is no systematic framework for determining what a completed research process has actually established.
AI.method: The authors introduce an evidence-grounded framework with three components: (1) a context-isolated generate-verify-repair process that checks artifacts for evidence violations and missing downstream requirements before release; (2) post-execution validity and attribution checks that consolidate evidence across rounds, qualify intervention-level claims as actionable repairs, diagnostic guards, or withheld findings, and preserve admitted claims as auditable records with explicit provenance and applicability boundaries; and (3) a hybrid LLM-assisted controller that applies, defers, or rejects records based on available target evidence.
AI.result: Record audits characterize which claims survive qualification. Downstream diagnostics identify affirmative applicability judgment as a bottleneck for the tested controller. Across paper-to-target adaptations, later rounds often improve on the first, while final rounds frequently underperform an earlier best, exposing non-monotonic trajectory evolution. Candidates produced through the complete workflow yielded positive online lifts relative to deployed baselines.
AI.conclusion: The trajectory-to-evidence conversion problem is critical for industrial ML research. The proposed framework provides systematic verification, qualification, and auditable claim preservation. Non-monotonic trajectory evolution highlights the danger of assuming final-round superiority, and the workflow's online performance validates its practical utility.

title: Cross-platform epistemic verification for improving factual reliability in AI-generated news summarization
summary: This study proposes Multi-source Evidence Consen- sus Verification (MECV), a post-hoc hallucination cor- rection framework for AI-generated news summariza- tion. Instead of depending on a single retrieval channel, MECV aggregates evidence from multiple heterogeneous sources, including the source document, Wikipedia, and open-web retrieval. The framework further incorporates a multi-LLM jury mechanism that estimates factual reliabil- ity through contradiction-aware consensus scoring across verifier models. Claims identified as potentially unsup- ported are revised through iterative minimal-edit refine- ment. The proposed framework is evaluated on the SummEd- its benchmark using GPT-4o-mini and DeepSeek-Chat as the verifier jury, with Qwen-Plus as the orchestra- tor. Experimental results show that MECV improves fac- tual consistency while preserving the semantic structure of the original summaries. The findings further suggest that agreement across heterogeneous evidence sources can serve as a useful signal for identifying factual uncertainty in AI-generated summaries, including in information- sensitive domains such as financial news aggregation. This study contributes to research on trustworthy AI and automated journalism by introducing a multi-source verification framework for hallucination correction and demonstrating the value of consensus-based verification for improving factual reliability in AI-generated news summarization.

AI.tldr: MECV is a post-hoc hallucination correction framework for AI news summarization that combines multi-source evidence retrieval (source doc, Wikipedia, web) with a multi-LLM jury for contradiction-aware consensus scoring, followed by iterative minimal-edit refinement of unsupported claims.
AI.motivation: AI-generated news summaries often contain hallucinations (factually unsupported claims). Single-source verification is insufficient; a multi-source, consensus-driven approach can better identify and correct factual errors, particularly in information-sensitive domains like financial news.
AI.method: MECV uses three components: (1) evidence aggregation from the source document, Wikipedia, and open-web retrieval; (2) a multi-LLM jury (GPT-4o-mini + DeepSeek-Chat) with contradiction-aware consensus scoring to estimate factual reliability, orchestrated by Qwen-Plus; (3) iterative minimal-edit refinement to revise claims identified as unsupported.
AI.result: Evaluated on the SummEdits benchmark, MECV improved factual consistency while preserving semantic structure. Agreement across heterogeneous evidence sources proved useful for signaling factual uncertainty, including in financial news aggregation.
AI.conclusion: MECV demonstrates that multi-source consensus-based verification effectively corrects hallucinations in AI-generated news summaries, contributing to trustworthy AI and automated journalism by improving factual reliability through heterogeneous evidence and jury-based verification.

title: Robustness and User-Perceived Value of Popularity Calibration in Music Recommendation: A User Study
summary: Popularity calibration in recommender systems has been studied both as a form of user-centered personalization and as an indicator of popularity bias. Most existing work evaluates calibration through offline metrics, often assuming that users prefer recommendation lists whose popularity distribution matches their historical consumption profile. However, user studies on calibration remain limited, and existing findings suggest that calibrated recommendations do not necessarily have a strong effect on user experience. Moreover, although prior work has shown that calibration metrics can correlate with users' perceptions of recommendation lists, the robustness of this relation remains unclear under different levels of item familiarity and incomplete user-history information. In this work, we study the perceived value and measurement reliability of popularity calibration in music recommendation. We construct personalized track lists from users' recent listening histories and use a controlled naive recommender to create lists with different popularity compositions: highpop-heavy, lowpop-heavy, and calibrated. We investigate whether users perceive differences between these lists, whether calibrated lists are preferred, how robust JSD-based popularity calibration is under different familiarity and history-availability conditions, and how computational popularity labels align with users' own popularity judgments. Our results show that users perceive differences in popularity composition, but do not clearly prefer calibrated lists. We further find that the relation between JSD and perceived popularity depends on item familiarity, list composition, and available user history, while computational and user-judged popularity labels only weakly align. These findings contribute to a more critical understanding of popularity calibration as both an offline metric and a user-facing construct.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether users actually perceive and prefer popularity-calibrated music recommendations. Through a controlled user study, the authors find that while users can discern differences in popularity composition, they do not clearly prefer calibrated lists. Furthermore, the JSD-based calibration metric's relationship to perceived popularity is unstable across varying familiarity and history conditions, and computational popularity labels only weakly align with users' own judgments.
AI.motivation: Prior work assumes users prefer recommendation lists whose popularity distribution matches their listening history, typically evaluated via offline metrics like JSD. However, user studies on popularity calibration are scarce, and existing evidence suggests calibration may not strongly affect user experience. The robustness of calibration metrics under different item familiarity levels and incomplete user-history conditions remains unclear, motivating a critical re-examination of popularity calibration as both a metric and a user-facing construct.
AI.method: The authors conduct a controlled user study in music recommendation. They construct personalized track lists from participants' recent listening histories and use a controlled naive recommender to generate three list types: highpop-heavy, lowpop-heavy, and calibrated. They then investigate: (1) whether users perceive differences in popularity composition, (2) whether calibrated lists are preferred, (3) how robust JSD-based calibration is under varying familiarity and history-availability conditions, and (4) how well computational popularity labels align with users' own popularity judgments.
AI.result: Users can perceive differences in popularity composition across lists but do not clearly prefer calibrated lists. The relationship between JSD and perceived popularity is contingent on item familiarity, list composition, and the amount of available user history. Computational popularity labels show only weak alignment with user-judged popularity.
AI.conclusion: Popularity calibration, while a popular offline metric and personalization strategy, lacks robust user-facing validity. Neither do users reliably prefer calibrated recommendations, nor do computational popularity signals align closely with users' subjective perceptions. This calls for more critical treatment of calibration in both research and practice.

title: Mixed Uncertainty in One View: Co-Visualizing Statistical Variability and Qualitative Confidence
summary: Forecasting involves multiple forms of uncertainty, including both uncertainties that can be quantified directly (quantitative uncertainty) and those that must be expressed through experts' subjective judgments about the forecast and its context (qualitative confidence). Past work has established that conveying both quantitative uncertainty and qualitative confidence in forecasts can alter readers' decision making, but little research investigates the impact of how these forms of uncertainty are presented. In this work, we present three preregistered human-subjects studies (total n = 923) on how different methods of visualizing qualitative uncertainty alongside line charts' confidence intervals affects non-experts' decision making. In particular, we investigate representing qualitative uncertainty separately via text and icons, and integrated into quantitative confidence intervals via color, transparency, and a blurred stroke design. In Experiment 1, we confirm that showing qualitative confidence alongside statistical variability can change patterns of decision making, replicating findings from previous work in the new context of time-series line charts. In Experiments 2 and 3, we find several non-textual encoding techniques that produce similar effects in participants' incorporation of qualitative confidence into their judgments. Our findings suggest actionable guidelines for visualization designers who seek to represent multiple forms of uncertainty for a single line chart forecast. A free copy of this paper and all supplemental materials are available at https://osf.io/7ya2c/overview.

AI.tldr: Three preregistered studies (n=923) examined how different visual encodings of qualitative confidence alongside quantitative uncertainty in line chart forecasts affect non-experts' decision making, finding that non-textual techniques (color, transparency, blurred stroke) can effectively convey qualitative confidence and replicate prior findings in the time-series domain.
AI.motivation: Prior research shows that conveying both quantitative uncertainty and qualitative confidence in forecasts influences decision making, but little is known about how the presentation method matters. The authors aimed to fill this gap by systematically testing visualization techniques for representing qualitative uncertainty alongside confidence intervals in line charts.
AI.method: Three preregistered human-subjects experiments with 923 total participants. Experiment 1 replicated prior findings in the new context of time-series line charts, confirming that showing qualitative confidence alongside statistical variability alters decision patterns. Experiments 2 and 3 tested non-textual encoding techniques — color, transparency, and a blurred stroke design — for integrating qualitative confidence into confidence intervals, comparing them against text and icon-based representations.
AI.result: Experiment 1 successfully replicated the finding that qualitative confidence information changes decision-making patterns when added to line chart forecasts. Experiments 2 and 3 demonstrated that non-textual encoding techniques (color, transparency, blurred stroke) produce effects on participants' incorporation of qualitative confidence comparable to text and icon methods.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide actionable guidelines for visualization designers representing multiple forms of uncertainty in a single line chart forecast, demonstrating that non-textual visual encodings are viable alternatives to text-based approaches for conveying qualitative confidence.

title: F$^2$Agent: Financial Fusion of Agentic Intelligence for Multimodal Trading
summary: With increasingly diverse and heterogeneous information sources, effectively leveraging multimodal data is becoming pivotal for high-quality financial trading. Although recent advancements in Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have enabled the ingestion of multimodal inputs, existing methods fail to capture nuanced cross-modal dependencies and remain vulnerable to market noise, due to limited multimodal modeling, ineffective fusion mechanisms, and inadequate robustness. To address these challenges, we propose F$^2$Agent, a novel multimodal agentic paradigm driven by the Financial Fusion of Agentic Intelligence. F$^2$Agent first deploys a hierarchy of specialized agents to comprehensively extract modality-specific signals. It further introduces a modality-aware adaptive fusion mechanism coupled with noise-robust consistency regularization to dynamically capture fine-grained inter-modality dependencies and generate noise-resilient trading signals. Extensive experiments on six stocks and cryptocurrency assets demonstrate that F$^2$Agent consistently outperforms 16 competitive baselines across multiple trading metrics, with over 20% relative improvement in annualized return on average. Notably, F$^2$Agent delivers returns of 120.48% on GOOG and 148.41% on TSLA, demonstrating its efficacy and robustness in varying market dynamics.

AI.tldr: F²Agent is a multimodal LLM-based agentic framework for financial trading that uses specialized agents for modality-specific signal extraction and a modality-aware adaptive fusion mechanism with noise-robust consistency regularization, achieving over 20% relative improvement in annualized returns over 16 baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based financial trading agents struggle with three key limitations: (1) limited multimodal modeling that fails to capture nuanced cross-modal dependencies among diverse, heterogeneous information sources; (2) ineffective fusion mechanisms that inadequately integrate signals across modalities; and (3) inadequate robustness against market noise, leading to unreliable trading decisions.
AI.method: F²Agent proposes a hierarchical multi-agent architecture where specialized agents first extract modality-specific signals from heterogeneous data sources. It then employs a modality-aware adaptive fusion mechanism to dynamically capture fine-grained inter-modality dependencies. Additionally, a noise-robust consistency regularization technique is introduced to generate trading signals resilient to market noise.
AI.result: F²Agent consistently outperforms 16 competitive baselines across multiple trading metrics on six stocks and cryptocurrency assets, achieving over 20% relative improvement in annualized return on average. It delivers notable returns of 120.48% on GOOG and 148.41% on TSLA.
AI.conclusion: F²Agent demonstrates strong efficacy and robustness across varying market dynamics, validating that the combination of modality-specialized agent hierarchies, adaptive multimodal fusion, and noise-robust regularization can significantly enhance financial trading performance with multimodal data.

title: Towards a Risk Assessment of Malicious Skill Files in Coding Agents
comment: 29 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Preprint; under review
summary: Autonomous coding agents are increasingly embedded in enterprise software workflows with delegated authority over connected systems. Central to this architecture is the agent skills interface: folders of instructions and scripts that agents load dynamically to specialize their behavior. This interface also widens the attack surface, letting malicious shell commands hide within natural-language skill files. We make three contributions. First, an adversarial skill-synthesis method using six LLMs across four families to transform 471 real-world shell commands into benign-appearing skills, released as a benchmark of 2,826 skills mapped to 11 MITRE ATT&CK tactics. Second, a reproducible evaluation pipeline coupling run stratification, evidence anchoring, a refusal veto, and a deterministic declared-intent override with a three-judge LLM-as-a-judge panel, validated against a blind human gold standard (Cohen's kappa = 0.85). Third, a large-scale characterization of two enterprise-grade agents across 5,629 completed runs. Gemini CLI is exploited in 95.5-96.1% of runs and Qwen Code in 71.6-74.0% (raw majority vote to declared-intent-corrected estimate, both within the human gold standard), nearly invariant to the generating model. Explicit safety recognition occurs in only 1.99% of runs. Enterprises must assess and mitigate skill-interface risk before adopting coding agents. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/awsm-research/AgentJailbreak

AI.tldr: The paper exposes a critical vulnerability in autonomous coding agents: adversarial skill files that hide malicious shell commands in natural-language instructions. Across 5,629 runs, Gemini CLI was exploited 95.5–96.1% of the time and Qwen Code 71.6–74.0%, with safety mechanisms triggering in only 1.99% of cases.
AI.motivation: As autonomous coding agents gain delegated authority in enterprise workflows, their dynamic skill-loading interface creates a novel attack surface. The authors aim to systematically characterize how easily natural-language skill files can conceal malicious shell commands and whether existing safeguards detect such attacks.
AI.method: The authors synthesized 2,826 adversarial skills from 471 real-world shell commands mapped to 11 MITRE ATT&CK tactics using six LLMs across four model families. They built a reproducible evaluation pipeline with run stratification, evidence anchoring, a refusal veto, and a deterministic declared-intent override, validated by a three-judge LLM panel against a blind human gold standard (Cohen's κ = 0.85). Two enterprise-grade agents (Gemini CLI and Qwen Code) were tested across 5,629 runs.
AI.result: Gemini CLI was exploited in 95.5–96.1% of runs and Qwen Code in 71.6–74.0%, with results nearly invariant to the generating model. Explicit safety recognition occurred in only 1.99% of runs, demonstrating that current safeguards are highly ineffective against skill-interface attacks.
AI.conclusion: The skill-interface attack surface represents a severe, underexplored risk for enterprise coding agents. Organizations must assess and mitigate these risks before deployment, as current agent safety mechanisms fail to detect malicious payloads embedded in natural-language skill files.

title: Post-Hoc Trajectory-Risk Certification for Modular LLM-Based Security Agents
summary:
Autonomous security agents operate as staged pipelines, such as classifying network traffic and then attributing attacks to a specific technique. Split conformal prediction gives each stage finite-sample coverage, but deployment requires a trajectory-level guarantee across the full chain. These guarantees do not compose automatically when stages are independently trained and calibrated. Bonferroni allocation is distribution-free but conservative under correlated errors. We show that a natural pairwise-correlation extension to three or more stages is invalid because it gives a lower rather than an upper bound, and derive a valid spanning-tree alternative. We distinguish whether stages are dependent from whether an audit sample is large enough to certify that dependence, and give matching upper and information-theoretic lower sample-complexity bounds. We also show that coarse-to-fine label selection can create near-perfect measured correlation without learned dependence.
  On a two-stage intrusion-detection pipeline across 6 open LLMs and 2 datasets, removing this artifact reduces measured correlation from near 1 to 0-0.78. A direct audit of trajectory failure becomes 13.7% tighter than Bonferroni once the audit reaches the required sample size, but is worse when undersized. A modular certificate using per-stage certificates and a pairwise overlap bound yields a positive average gain of 0.6%, quantifying the cost of lacking joint access. Same-model, cross-model, and permuted-pairing tests show that residual dependence reflects shared sample difficulty, not shared model representations. Average trajectory coverage across 12 configurations is 92.7% +/- 2.4% at alpha = 0.10. Under cross-dataset deployment, single-step miscoverage reaches 100% even when accuracy remains 78%, showing that distribution shift destroys calibrated confidence before raw accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the problem of providing finite-sample coverage guarantees across multi-stage autonomous security pipelines. It shows that naive extensions of pairwise correlation bounds to three or more stages are invalid, proposes a valid spanning-tree alternative, derives sample-complexity bounds, and demonstrates empirically that residual dependence reflects shared sample difficulty rather than shared model representations. A direct audit of trajectory failure outperforms Bonferroni correction when sample size is sufficient.
AI.motivation: Autonomous security agents use staged pipelines (e.g., classify traffic → attribute attack technique). While split conformal prediction provides per-stage finite-sample coverage guarantees, these do not compose into a trajectory-level guarantee across the full chain. Existing approaches like Bonferroni allocation are distribution-free but overly conservative under correlated errors. The paper seeks a tighter, valid method for joint trajectory-level coverage guarantees.
AI.method: The authors (1) prove that extending pairwise correlation bounds to ≥3 stages is invalid (yielding a lower bound rather than an upper bound) and derive a valid spanning-tree-based alternative; (2) distinguish between whether stages are dependent vs. whether an audit sample is large enough to certify that dependence; (3) derive matching upper and information-theoretic lower sample-complexity bounds; (4) identify an artifact where coarse-to-fine label selection creates spurious near-perfect measured correlation; (5) validate via a two-stage intrusion-detection pipeline using 6 open LLMs and 2 datasets, testing direct trajectory audits, modular certificates with pairwise overlap bounds, and same-model/cross-model/permuted-pairing designs to isolate sources of residual dependence.
AI.result: Key empirical results: Removing the coarse-to-fine artifact reduces measured correlation from near 1 to 0–0.78. Direct trajectory audit is 13.7% tighter than Bonferroni when sample size is sufficient, but worse when undersized. Modular certificate using per-stage certificates with pairwise overlap bounds yields 0.6% average positive gain. Residual dependence stems from shared sample difficulty, not shared model representations. Average trajectory coverage across 12 configurations is 92.7% ± 2.4% at α = 0.10. Under cross-dataset deployment, single-step miscoverage reaches 100% despite 78% accuracy, demonstrating that distribution shift destroys calibrated confidence before raw accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes that valid trajectory-level conformal guarantees for multi-stage pipelines require careful handling of inter-stage dependence. The spanning-tree bound is a valid alternative to invalid pairwise-correlation extensions. Sample-size requirements for auditing dependence are characterized with tight bounds. Coarse-to-fine artifacts can inflate measured correlation. In practice, direct trajectory audits outperform Bonferroni given sufficient data, and distribution shift catastrophically undermines calibrated confidence.

title: Simulator-Grounded Large Language Models for Industrial Causal Reasoning: Tool-Use, Structured Injection, and Plant-Portable Retrieval for Wastewater Treatment Decision Support
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables. Preprint submitted to Elsevier
summary: Wastewater operators need answers grounded in how their plant's variables interact and how fast effects propagate, not in generic pretraining text, when asking causal questions such as "why is N2O rising?" or "what happens if I cut aeration by 20%?". We compare three concrete ways to ground a frozen Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model in an architecturally interpretable wastewater simulator (CCSS-IX): a live simulator oracle (Method 1), structured parameter injection (Method 2), and a Decoupled Recall-Reasoning (DRR) retriever (Method 3). On a 198-question causal benchmark the three reach 99.5%, 79%, and 75.8%, forming a deployment ladder above the strongest retrieval-augmented baseline at 48%. The DRR retriever has 110M parameters and trains per plant in ~17 seconds; after cross-plant transfer to a biologically distinct plant it still reaches 88%, while Method 2's static table cannot transfer. On a 60-question counterfactual benchmark only Method 3 handles queries about what happens after an intervention: +16.3 pp over Method 2, paired 95% CI [+7.1, +26.4] pp, with 100% on the timescale and operating-regime categories. On the AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC) with an OpenBookQA fact corpus, the same selective-retrieval mechanism reaches 79% versus unconstrained Llama-3.1-8B 76% and full-injection 74%, a +3 pp out-of-domain replication that argues against a result specific to wastewater treatment. We provide the first single-simulator comparison of live tool-use, static parameter injection, and learned numerical-parameter retrieval for industrial causal question answering.

AI.tldr: Three methods for grounding an LLM in a wastewater simulator are compared: live oracle (99.5%), structured parameter injection (79%), and a Decoupled Recall-Reasoning retriever (75.8%). The DRR retriever (110M params, ~17s training) transfers across plants (88%) and uniquely handles counterfactuals (+16.3 pp), with out-of-domain replication on ARC (+3 pp).
AI.motivation: Wastewater operators need causal answers grounded in their specific plant's dynamics (interaction strengths, propagation speeds), not generic pretraining text. Existing approaches lack systematic comparison of grounding strategies for industrial causal QA.
AI.method: Three grounding methods for a frozen Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model are compared: (1) a live simulator oracle providing perfect numerical answers, (2) structured parameter injection that statically encodes simulator parameters into the prompt, and (3) a Decoupled Recall-Reasoning (DRR) retriever — a 110M-parameter model that learns to selectively retrieve relevant numerical parameters from the simulator, training per plant in ~17 seconds. Evaluation uses a 198-question causal benchmark and a 60-question counterfactual benchmark. Out-of-domain replication is tested on ARC with OpenBookQA.
AI.result: On the causal benchmark: Method 1 (99.5%), Method 2 (79%), Method 3 (75.8%), best RAG baseline (48%). On counterfactuals: Method 3 outperforms Method 2 by +16.3 pp (95% CI [+7.1, +26.4]), with 100% on timescale and operating-regime categories. Cross-plant transfer: DRR reaches 88% on a biologically distinct plant; Method 2's static table fails to transfer. ARC replication: DRR achieves 79% vs Llama-3.1-8B (76%) and full-injection (74%).
AI.conclusion: The three methods form a deployment ladder trading off accuracy vs practicality. The DRR retriever offers the best balance: strong performance, fast per-plant training, cross-plant transferability, and unique counterfactual handling. The ARC replication suggests the selective retrieval mechanism generalizes beyond wastewater. This is the first single-simulator comparison of live tool-use, static parameter injection, and learned numerical-parameter retrieval for industrial causal QA.

title: MS-MLB: An Open Machine Learning Benchmark for Blood-Based MS Classification
summary: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is diagnosed through clinical assessment, magnetic resonance imaging, laboratory evidence when appropriate, and exclusion of better explanations. Blood RNA expression data may contain disease associated immune signal, but a blood RNA classifier cannot be treated as a replacement for clinical diagnosis. This paper presents MS-MLB (Multiple Sclerosis Machine Learning Benchmark), a reproducible open benchmark for machine learning based MS research classification from whole blood RNA expression data. MS-MLB uses the public GSE17048 cohort, converts it into an MS versus healthy control task, and evaluates multiple algorithms under a shared, leakage controlled pipeline that a researcher can rerun without reconfiguring the evaluation. The evaluation includes nested cross-validation, an untouched stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC and precision recall analysis, calibration measurement, and an exploratory MS Research Score. In the final benchmark summary, Gradient Boosting ranked first by MS Research Score on the holdout set, with an MS Research Score of 93.83, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, $F_{1}$ score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050. Prior studies have applied machine learning to MS blood transcriptomic data, including PBMC stage classification and whole blood diagnostic signature modeling. The contribution here is different and narrower. To our knowledge, MS-MLB is the first open benchmark focused on MS versus healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA expression data with a documented external model submission pathway built into the framework. The score is intended for research comparison only and has not been clinically validated. The benchmark is accessible here: https://github.com/duckyquang/MS-MLB.

AI.tldr: MS-MLB is an open, reproducible benchmark for evaluating machine learning classifiers that distinguish multiple sclerosis from healthy controls using whole blood RNA expression data (GSE17048), with Gradient Boosting achieving the top performance (AUC-ROC 0.989, F1 0.927) on a leakage-controlled holdout set.
AI.motivation: While blood RNA expression may contain MS-associated immune signals, existing ML studies on MS blood transcriptomics lack standardized, reproducible benchmarks with rigorous evaluation pipelines. The authors aimed to fill this gap with a fully open, rerunnable framework for fair algorithm comparison — explicitly not as a diagnostic replacement.
AI.method: MS-MLB uses the public GSE17048 whole blood RNA expression cohort, converts it to a binary MS vs. healthy control classification task, and employs a leakage-controlled pipeline with nested cross-validation, a stratified untouched holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC/PR analysis, calibration (Brier score), and a composite "MS Research Score" metric. Multiple ML algorithms are evaluated under identical conditions, with an external model submission pathway built in.
AI.result: Gradient Boosting ranked first with an MS Research Score of 93.83, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, F1 score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050 on the holdout set.
AI.conclusion: MS-MLB is the first open benchmark for MS vs. healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA data with a documented external submission pathway. The scores are for research comparison only and lack clinical validation.

title: Agentic Nesting: A New Methodology for Existing Enterprise Application Integration and Services
summary: Enterprise operations extensively rely on multiple heterogeneous business systems and information applications, which also result in severe data silos and process fragmentation. Enterprises have invested considerable financial and material resources in building these applications, however, effectively leveraging and orchestrating them remains a formidable challenge. Conventional approaches to enterprise application integration, encompassing middleware architectures such as Enterprise Service Bus (ESB), API gateway infrastructures, and Robotic Process Automation (RPA), suffer from inherent limitations like high architectural coupling, escalating operation and maintenance costs, and limited intelligence capabilities. This paper proposes Agentic Nesting, a multi-agent collaboration framework in which existing enterprise applications are encapsulated as autonomous AI agents within a hierarchically nested structure. Rather than flat interconnection, agents are organized into layered stewardship topologies that mirror the compositional complexity of enterprise ecosystems. The framework extracts a digital agent proxy from each legacy application to enable natural-language interaction and autonomous manipulation, coordinates multiple agents through a central orchestrator for task decomposition and dynamic dispatching, and exposes a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and process orchestration. The main contributions of this paper are the proposition of the "Application-as-Agent" integration paradigm and the "Conversation-as-Integration" interaction philosophy, together with an exploration of the generalization potential of this methodology in scenarios encompassing heterogeneous system coordination, and large-scale data applications.

AI.tldr: Proposes "Agentic Nesting," a multi-agent framework that wraps legacy enterprise applications as hierarchical AI agents, enabling natural-language orchestration via a central orchestrator to overcome data silos and integration challenges.
AI.motivation: Enterprise IT landscapes suffer from severe data silos and process fragmentation due to heterogeneous business systems. Traditional integration approaches (ESB, API gateways, RPA) are limited by high architectural coupling, escalating maintenance costs, and insufficient intelligence, making it difficult to effectively leverage and orchestrate existing application investments.
AI.method: The paper introduces "Agentic Nesting," a multi-agent collaboration framework with three core mechanisms: (1) each legacy application is encapsulated as an autonomous AI agent via a digital agent proxy enabling natural-language interaction and autonomous manipulation; (2) agents are organized into layered stewardship topologies reflecting enterprise compositional complexity rather than flat interconnections; (3) a central orchestrator handles task decomposition, dynamic dispatching, and exposes a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and process orchestration.
AI.result: The paper contributes two novel paradigms: "Application-as-Agent" (recasting enterprise applications as autonomous agents) and "Conversation-as-Integration" (using natural-language dialogue as the integration mechanism). The framework demonstrates generalization potential for heterogeneous system coordination and large-scale data applications.
AI.conclusion: Agentic Nesting offers a paradigm shift from traditional middleware-based integration toward AI-driven, conversation-mediated orchestration of enterprise systems, with the hierarchical agent topology providing a scalable, intelligent alternative to conventional ESB, API gateway, and RPA approaches.

title: A Mechanistic Analysis of Gender Sensitivity in Dense Retrieval Models
summary: While gender bias in dense retrieval models is well documented, with prior work showing that models often score male-gendered documents higher than female or neutral variants, the internal mechanisms producing these disparities are poorly understood. In this paper, we mechanistically analyze bi-encoder models to localize gender sensitivity, finding that the signal originates in input embeddings and propagates through a small set of late-layer attention heads that carry both gender and term-matching signals. Guided by these findings, we test steering interventions at both identified points and find distinct effects: embedding-level steering non-specifically neutralizes score differences, while attention-level steering produces directional shifts. Our findings provide a mechanistic basis for targeted debiasing and highlight the challenge of disentangling gender from relevance signals in shared model components.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of gender bias in bi-encoder dense retrieval models, localizing bias to input embeddings and specific late-layer attention heads that mix gender and relevance signals. Steering at embeddings produces non-specific neutralization, while attention-level intervention yields directional shifts, offering mechanistic insights for targeted debiasing.
AI.motivation: Although gender bias in dense retrieval models is well-documented — with male-gendered documents systematically scored higher — no prior work has examined the internal computational mechanisms responsible for these disparities. Understanding where and how bias arises within model components is essential for designing principled, targeted mitigation strategies.
AI.method: The authors perform a mechanistic interpretability analysis on bi-encoder retrieval models. They trace gender sensitivity through model components, identifying its origin and propagation path. They then apply two types of steering interventions: (1) embedding-level steering and (2) attention-head-level steering, comparing the distinct effects each produces on gender-based score differentials.
AI.result: Gender bias originates in input embeddings and propagates through a small, identifiable set of late-layer attention heads that jointly encode both gender and term-matching signals. Embedding-level steering non-specifically neutralizes gender score differences, while attention-level steering produces directional (rather than merely neutralizing) shifts in retrieval scores.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a mechanistic foundation for targeted debiasing in dense retrieval models. They also underscore a fundamental challenge: gender and relevance signals are entangled within shared model components, complicating efforts to remove bias without degrading retrieval performance.

title: Turing's Frist Imitation Game: Design Concepts and a Human-Approximates-Machine Reading
summary: This paper examines Turing's 1948 report, "Intelligent Machinery", as an important conceptual source for the later imitation games. Its first contribution is to identify and integrate the design concepts underlying the 1948 chess-based imitation game: the possibility that intelligent machines may make mistakes, the exclusion of irrelevant physical features, the role of the human judge, and Turing's claim that intellectual activity consists mainly of search. The paper's second contribution is to argue that restricting the human contestant to a rather poor chess player increases the role of intellectual search and makes human behaviour more comparable to machine behaviour. This interpretation presents the 1948 game as a human-approximates-machine game and suggests that the imitation game framework can be used not only to ask whether machines imitate humans, but also to examine when human intelligence becomes machine-like under specific task constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper reinterprets Turing's 1948 "Intelligent Machinery" report, arguing it frames a chess-based imitation game where a weak human player's constrained intellectual search mirrors machine behaviour, thus broadening the imitation game's purpose beyond machine-human mimicry.
AI.motivation: To recover and integrate the overlooked design concepts in Turing's 1948 report that prefigure the later imitation games, and to offer a novel interpretation that expands the framework's applicability.
AI.method: Historical-conceptual analysis of Turing's 1948 "Intelligent Machinery" report, identifying and synthesizing four key design concepts: machine fallibility, exclusion of irrelevant physical features, the human judge's role, and intellectual activity as search. A reinterpretation of the chess-based game's constraint (weak human player) is then advanced.
AI.result: The paper identifies four integrated design concepts in the 1948 report. It further argues that restricting the human contestant to a poor chess player amplifies the role of intellectual search, making human and machine behaviour more comparable, thus reframing the 1948 game as a "human-approximates-machine" paradigm.
AI.conclusion: Turing's 1948 chess-based imitation game functions as a human-approximates-machine test, suggesting the imitation game framework can also investigate when human intelligence becomes machine-like under specific task constraints, not just whether machines imitate humans.

title: A Two-Tier Perspective on Inference-Time Parallelism in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-driven multi-agent systems typically require multiple model invocations and complex coordination during inference, and their execution strategies directly affect system accuracy, latency, and computational cost. Parallel execution provides a means to improve inference-time efficiency. From the perspective of inference-time execution, this paper models parallelism in multi-agent systems as two distinct levels of decision processes: Replica Parallelism, which explores multiple complete solution paths at the task level, and Structural Parallelism, which enables concurrent execution within a single solution path through task decomposition. However, the roles of different forms of parallelism and their interrelationships still lack systematic study in terms of unified organization and coordination. We therefore propose TIPEX, a controllable execution framework that unifies these two levels of parallelism and coordinates their roles within the inference process under a unified execution semantics while supporting systematic combinations and analyses of different parallel strategies and parameter configurations. Systematic experiments on the GAIA benchmark demonstrate that inference-time parallelism can significantly improve accuracy and reduce end-to-end latency at the cost of increased token consumption. Further analysis shows that Replica and Structural Parallelism exhibit complementary effects across task complexities, with tasks of intermediate difficulty benefiting most from their coordination, while overly aggressive parallel strategies do not necessarily yield better performance.

AI.tldr: TIPEX is a controllable execution framework that unifies Replica Parallelism (exploring multiple solution paths) and Structural Parallelism (concurrent execution within a single path via task decomposition) in LLM-driven multi-agent systems, demonstrating on GAIA that coordinated parallelism improves accuracy and reduces latency at the cost of increased token usage, with intermediate-difficulty tasks benefiting most.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven multi-agent systems suffer from high inference costs due to multiple model invocations and complex coordination. While parallel execution can improve efficiency, the two forms—Replica Parallelism and Structural Parallelism—lack systematic study regarding their unified organization, coordination, and interrelationships.
AI.method: The authors propose TIPEX, a controllable execution framework that models inference-time parallelism as two decision levels: Replica Parallelism (task-level, exploring multiple complete solution paths) and Structural Parallelism (within-path, enabling concurrent execution through task decomposition). TIPEX unifies these under a single execution semantics, supporting systematic combinations and configurable parallel strategies.
AI.result: Systematic experiments on the GAIA benchmark show that inference-time parallelism significantly improves accuracy and reduces end-to-end latency, at the cost of increased token consumption. Replica and Structural Parallelism exhibit complementary effects across task complexities, with intermediate-difficulty tasks benefiting most from their coordination. Overly aggressive parallel strategies do not necessarily improve performance.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time parallelism in multi-agent systems, when properly unified and coordinated through frameworks like TIPEX, offers a tunable trade-off between accuracy, latency, and token cost. The two forms of parallelism are complementary, and optimal performance requires calibrated strategies rather than maximal parallelism.

title: Improving Debugging in Verification-Aware Languages Through Automated Fault Localization: A Case Study in Dafny
summary:
Verification-aware languages, like Dafny, integrate formal specifications directly into source code to enable static correctness checks. However, when verification fails, the feedback provided is often limited to the specific condition of the error, such as a violated postcondition, rather than the root cause of the fault. While Dafny's counterexample features provide concrete execution traces, these typically expose a single failing path per assertion failure, leaving the developer to manually look through the entire trace to locate the error.
  This paper investigates automated fault localization for verification-aware languages by comparing two paradigms: state-based and counterexample-based localization. Our state-based localization strategy replicates the ``snapshot'' methodology of AutoFix by inferring invariants and predicates to identify suspicious program states. The counterexample-based strategy consists of a family of techniques that progressively enrich the use of verifier output: from raw counterexample extraction, to structured single-trace ranking, and to multi-trace aggregation.
  To validate these methods, we present an evaluation framework using MutDafny to generate a diverse mutant dataset from DafnyBench and measure localization effectiveness using the EXAM score. Our results show that counterexample-based approaches substantially outperform state-based localization in this setting. Structured ranking over a single trace yields the largest improvement over raw counterexample output, while multi-trace aggregation provides additional gains in robustness and debugging utility by increasing coverage and reducing path bias introduced by the solver. These findings demonstrate that effective fault localization in verification-aware languages depends both on using counterexample information, and how that information is structured and diversified.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates automated fault localization for verification-aware languages like Dafny, comparing state-based ("snapshot") methods with counterexample-based techniques. It introduces a family of counterexample-based strategies ranging from raw extraction to structured single-trace ranking and multi-trace aggregation. Evaluated using MutDafny mutants on DafnyBench with EXAM scores, counterexample-based approaches significantly outperform state-based methods, with structured ranking providing the largest improvement and multi-trace aggregation adding robustness and reduced solver path bias.
AI.motivation: When verification fails in languages like Dafny, the feedback is limited to the specific error condition (e.g., a violated postcondition) rather than the root cause. Existing counterexample features expose only a single failing path per assertion failure, forcing developers to manually inspect the entire trace. There is a need for automated fault localization that goes beyond raw counterexample output to pinpoint the actual source of verification failures.
AI.method: The authors compare two paradigms: (1) state-based localization, replicating AutoFix's "snapshot" methodology using inferred invariants and predicates to identify suspicious program states, and (2) counterexample-based localization, a family of techniques progressing from raw counterexample extraction to structured single-trace ranking (re-ranking trace elements by suspiciousness) to multi-trace aggregation (combining signals across multiple traces). Evaluation uses MutDafny to generate mutants from DafnyBench, measuring effectiveness via the EXAM score metric.
AI.result: Counterexample-based approaches substantially outperform state-based localization. Structured ranking over a single trace yields the largest improvement over raw counterexample output. Multi-trace aggregation provides additional gains in robustness and debugging utility by increasing coverage and reducing solver-introduced path bias.
AI.conclusion: Effective fault localization in verification-aware languages depends not only on using counterexample information, but critically on how that information is structured and diversified. Structured ranking and multi-trace aggregation are key to maximizing the utility of verifier output for debugging.

title: ASTELD: A Six-Axis Classification Framework for Autonomous AI Agents - Design, Evaluation, and an OpenClaw Case Study
comment: 40 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Introduces and empirically evaluates the ASTELD six-axis classification framework across eight autonomous AI agent platforms, with OpenClaw as an in-depth case study
summary: Autonomous AI agent platforms differ substantially in architecture, security, tool integration, execution, autonomy, and deployment, yet the field lacks a common classification scheme for comparing these design choices. We propose ASTELD, an operational six-axis classification framework for autonomous AI agents: Architecture pattern, Security posture, Tool integration model, Execution paradigm, Level of autonomy and human control, and Deployment topology. ASTELD is constructed by synthesizing prior agent taxonomies with observable platform properties and explicit category-assignment rules. We evaluate its discriminative and explanatory utility by mapping eight representative frameworks and by using OpenClaw as an in-depth case study. The resulting profiles separate all eight platforms under their dominant configurations and reveal three cross-platform patterns: a security-accessibility diagonal, strong execution-architecture coupling, and capability convergence with persistent architectural differentiation. We further classify 50+ OpenClaw derivatives and find that innovation concentrates on the Security, Execution, and Deployment axes, indicating that ASTELD can explain where ecosystem fragmentation occurs. The OpenClaw case study also supplies a six-category vulnerability taxonomy, evidence from five institutional assessments, and adoption and governance analyses that connect platform coordinates to observed risks. These results position ASTELD as a reproducible method for comparing agent platforms, identifying unoccupied design regions, guiding framework selection, and organizing future empirical research. The analysis also exposes a consequential empty region: none of the evaluated systems combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security.

AI.tldr: ASTELD is a six-axis classification framework for autonomous AI agents (Architecture, Security, Tool integration, Execution, Level of autonomy, Deployment). Evaluated on eight platforms, it reveals cross-platform patterns, explains ecosystem fragmentation, and identifies an unoccupied design region: no system combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agent platforms differ across architecture, security, tool integration, execution, autonomy, and deployment, yet the field lacks a common classification scheme for systematically comparing these design choices.
AI.method: The authors synthesize prior agent taxonomies with observable platform properties and explicit category-assignment rules to construct ASTELD. They evaluate its discriminative and explanatory utility by mapping eight representative frameworks and using OpenClaw as an in-depth case study, classifying 50+ derivatives and conducting institutional assessments, vulnerability taxonomy, and governance analysis.
AI.result: ASTELD separates all eight platforms under dominant configurations. Three cross-platform patterns emerge: a security-accessibility diagonal, strong execution-architecture coupling, and capability convergence with persistent architectural differentiation. The OpenClaw case reveals innovation concentrates on Security, Execution, and Deployment axes. A consequential empty region is identified: no system combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security.
AI.conclusion: ASTELD provides a reproducible method for comparing agent platforms, identifying unoccupied design regions, guiding framework selection, and organizing future empirical research. The empty region of local-first + enterprise-grade security represents a significant gap for future development.

title: Mean-Field Dynamics of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) with chain-of-thought reasoning have been widely applied in recent years, and theoretical explanations of their behavior may help deepen our understanding and guide model optimization. In this study, we introduce a framework that seeks statistical regularities and theoretical interpretations in LLM reasoning without simplifying the model architecture or making analogies to existing physical systems. We formulate LLM reasoning as a guided discovery process on a clue graph, and derive a one-dimensional ordinary differential equation for the fraction of discovered clues using the mean-field approximation. Experimentally, clue tokens are identified using the normalized surprisal of a student LLM on the outputs of a teacher LLM, and statistical regularities are obtained by averaging over many reasoning chains of thought. Our experiments show that the resulting statistical regularities are reproducible within the same dataset and can be fitted by the solving the proposed theoretical equation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a theoretical framework that models LLM chain-of-thought reasoning as a guided clue-discovery process on a graph, derives a mean-field ODE describing the fraction of discovered clues over time, and validates the model empirically using surprisal-based clue identification across many reasoning chains.
AI.motivation: To provide theoretical explanations for chain-of-thought reasoning behavior in LLMs without resorting to simplified architectures or analogies to physical systems, thereby deepening understanding and guiding optimization.
AI.method: LLM reasoning is formulated as a guided discovery process on a clue graph. A mean-field approximation yields a one-dimensional ODE governing the fraction of discovered clues. Clue tokens are empirically identified via normalized surprisal of a student LLM on teacher LLM outputs, and statistical regularities are obtained by averaging over many CoT chains. The ODE is then fitted to these empirical regularities.
AI.result: The derived statistical regularities are reproducible within the same dataset and can be well-fitted by the proposed theoretical ODE, validating the framework's descriptive power.
AI.conclusion: The proposed mean-field ODE framework effectively captures statistical regularities in LLM chain-of-thought reasoning, offering a principled theoretical lens for understanding and potentially improving LLM reasoning processes.

title: When Do Corrective Features Help? An Agent for Corrective Feature Discovery on Black-Box Forecasters
summary: Frozen pretrained forecasters often fail in structured, recurring ways that are costly to repair through fine-tuning. We study corrective feature discovery: mining interpretable features of a frozen forecaster's residual to drive a lightweight post-hoc corrector. Prior automated feature engineering models the data-generating process; corrective features instead model the model-failure process. We present CRAFTER (Corrective Residual Agent with Feature-based Temporal Exploration and Reasoning), which keeps the backbone frozen and mines its residual with two complementary generators: a compositional search over the raw input channels, and a large language model (LLM) that proposes named feature combinations, binary flags, and short executable code. A single validation-grounded gate accepts or rejects every candidate regardless of its origin, and a validation-selected corrector applies the accepted features or leaves the forecast unchanged. This source-agnostic pipeline also allows prior feature-engineering systems to be evaluated under identical conditions, making CRAFTER an instrument for attributing forecast improvements to the feature source alone. Across six public datasets and six frozen backbones, CRAFTER surpasses every dedicated feature-engineering system at every feature budget, roughly doubling the improvement achieved by the corrector alone and reducing the error of the weakest backbones by up to 27%. These gains are robust across different LLM backends and persist even when applied on top of fine-tuned backbones.

AI.tldr: CRAFTER mines interpretable corrective features from a frozen forecaster's residuals using compositional search and LLM-generated candidates, validated by a source-agnostic gate, to build lightweight post-hoc correctors that substantially reduce forecast errors across diverse backbones and datasets.
AI.motivation: Frozen pretrained forecasters exhibit structured, recurring failures that are expensive to fix via fine-tuning. Rather than modeling the data-generating process (as in prior automated feature engineering), the authors argue for modeling the model-failure process — discovering features that explain residual errors — to enable lightweight, interpretable post-hoc correction without modifying the backbone.
AI.method: CRAFTER uses two complementary feature generators operating on the frozen backbone's residuals: (1) compositional search over raw input channels, and (2) an LLM that proposes named feature combinations, binary flags, and short executable code. A single validation-grounded binary gate accepts or rejects every candidate regardless of origin. Accepted features feed a validation-selected corrector that either adjusts the forecast or leaves it unchanged. The pipeline is source-agnostic, enabling fair comparison with prior feature-engineering systems.
AI.result: Across six public datasets and six frozen backbones, CRAFTER surpasses every dedicated feature-engineering system at every feature budget, roughly doubling the corrector-alone improvement and reducing the weakest backbones' error by up to 27%. Gains are robust across LLM backends and persist even on top of fine-tuned backbones.
AI.conclusion: Corrective feature discovery — modeling the failure process rather than the data process — is a highly effective strategy for post-hoc forecast improvement. The source-agnostic, gated architecture of CRAFTER provides both strong empirical performance and a fair benchmarking instrument for attributing gains to feature sources.

title: The Ignition Index: Measuring Global Workspace Dynamics in Language Models
summary: We introduce the Ignition Index (I), a validated scalar metric that operationalizes Global Workspace Theory's (GWT) all-or-none ignition prediction in transformer language models. The metric fits a four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength, extracting steepness parameter beta-hat: high values indicate abrupt, ignition-like transitions; low values indicate graded build-up. Across 11 models spanning five architecture families, shuffled-label controls demonstrate 9.6-fold selectivity for genuine linguistic structure over spurious probe capacity (p < 0.001, Mann-Whitney U-test). We find: (1) Feedforward transformers exceed SSMs by 89% in aggregate beta-hat (p < 1e-13, Cohen's d = 0.52), with Mamba exhibiting near-linear profiles consistent with absent global broadcast. (2) Huginn-3.5B exhibits 2.12-fold higher ignition along its iteration axis than its depth axis, demonstrating that recurrent architectures manifest workspace-like transitions along the recurrence dimension. (3) Pythia-410M shows a PELT-detected phase transition at training step 256 (+67%), preceding induction-head formation. (4) Hypotheses linking ignition to model scale and signal strength were not confirmed, suggesting transformer architectures may saturate available ignition mechanisms. The Ignition Index provides the first validated quantitative bridge between GWT's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability, with 9.6-fold measurement selectivity and architecture-level discriminability not previously characterized in the scaling literature. Code: https://github.com/saman-rahbar/ignition-index

AI.tldr: The Ignition Index (I) is a validated scalar metric that quantifies Global Workspace Theory's all-or-none ignition prediction in transformer LMs by fitting a sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy vs. signal strength, extracting steepness β̂. Applied across 11 models, it achieves 9.6-fold selectivity for genuine linguistic structure, reveals that feedforward transformers exceed SSMs by 89% in ignition steepness, that recurrent architectures (Huginn) manifest ignition along the iteration axis, and that a phase transition in Pythia-410M occurs at training step 256 preceding induction-head formation.
AI.motivation: Operationalizing Global Workspace Theory's (GWT) cognitive prediction of all-or-none ignition — where information either breaks into a global workspace or doesn't — into a quantifiable, validated metric for transformer language models. No prior metric bridges GWT's dynamical predictions with mechanistic interpretability in a validated manner.
AI.method: Design of the Ignition Index (I): a four-parameter sigmoid is fit to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength. The steepness parameter β̂ captures the abruptness of the transition — high β̂ = ignition-like; low β̂ = graded. Validated across 11 models from 5 architecture families using shuffled-label controls to measure selectivity (9.6-fold), with statistical testing (Mann-Whitney U, Cohen's d) and PELT changepoint detection for training dynamics.
AI.result: (1) Feedforward transformers exceed SSMs by 89% in aggregate β̂ (p < 1e-13, d = 0.52); Mamba shows near-linear profiles consistent with absent global broadcast. (2) Huginn-3.5B exhibits 2.12× higher ignition along its iteration axis vs. depth axis. (3) Pythia-410M shows a PELT-detected phase transition at training step 256 (+67%), preceding induction-head formation. (4) Hypotheses linking ignition to model scale and signal strength were not confirmed, suggesting architectural saturation.
AI.conclusion: The Ignition Index provides the first validated quantitative bridge between GWT's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability, offering 9.6-fold measurement selectivity and architecture-level discriminability previously uncharacterized in the scaling literature.

title: An Ontology-Based Framework for Student Profiling and Content Personalization in Higher Education
summary: The expansion of access to Digital Information and Communication Technologies and the offer of distance or semi-distance education courses that make use of virtual learning environments brought changes in the teaching and learning processes, requiring that the student be even more protagonist in this process. The present study aimed to identify important aspects to be considered in the implementation and improvement of self-paced learning and e-learning in higher education courses, with the purpose of rethinking pedagogical models of courses offered at a distance so that they reach even more of your learning objectives. The research is characterized as qualitative, of bibliographic nature, and discusses techniques to monitor and record, electronically and automatically, the results of the process and learning. The importance of processes that store and manage the student's profile is highlighted, both in terms of content and forms of access. The article proposes the use of ontologies to store information about the educational process and presents a computational architecture for this purpose.

AI.tldr: This paper examines key factors for enhancing self-paced e-learning in higher education, emphasizing automated monitoring of learning processes and student profiling. It proposes an ontological approach and a computational architecture to store and manage educational process information.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of digital technologies and virtual learning environments in distance education has shifted greater responsibility onto students as protagonists of their own learning. Existing pedagogical models for distance courses often fall short of achieving their learning objectives, necessitating a rethinking of how these courses are designed and delivered.
AI.method: This is a qualitative, bibliographic study. The authors discuss techniques for electronic and automatic monitoring and recording of learning processes and outcomes. They explore approaches to storing and managing student profiles—both content-related and access-pattern-related—and propose the use of ontologies alongside a supporting computational architecture for organizing educational data.
AI.result: The study identifies critical aspects for implementing and improving self-paced e-learning, including the need for automated tracking of learning results, robust student profile management, and semantic organization of educational data. The proposed ontology-based computational architecture offers a structured solution for storing and retrieving information about the educational process.
AI.conclusion: To make distance education more effective, institutions must adopt pedagogical models that leverage automated monitoring and ontology-driven student profiling. The proposed architecture provides a foundation for more adaptive, learner-centered virtual learning environments.

title: A Multi-Layer System for Ultra-High-Resolution Static 360-Degree Telepresence
comment: 11 pages, 11 figures. Accepted to IEEE ISMAR 2026, to appear in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG)
summary: 360-degree video telepresence offers strong immersive potential but remains constrained by the limited resolution of current capture and display hardware. Many telepresence installations feature fixed viewpoints and largely static scenes, yet optimization strategies tailored to such setups have received limited attention. We present a multi-layer, ultra-high-resolution system for static 360-degree telepresence that combines an 8K panoramic camera with a rotatable 4K pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) camera. Our approach builds a three-layer representation: (1) a tile-based ultra-high-resolution panoramic background, generated by offline stitching high-detail 4K PTZ scans onto the base 8K panorama to achieve effective resolution beyond native capture, and represented as a set of spatial tiles; (2) a dynamic update layer that composites foreground motions from the 8K stream via real-time high-resolution background matting; and (3) a region-of-interest 4K layer that streams a real-time PTZ view of the selected region and additionally updates the corresponding background tiles over time. We evaluate the proposed system through comparisons with representative video super-resolution approaches and a user study assessing perceived detail and immersive experience. Our results indicate that tile-based background refinement, together with user-guided updates, provides a practical way to balance panoramic fidelity and interactivity in static 360-degree telepresence.

AI.tldr: A multi-layer system combining an 8K panoramic camera with a rotatable 4K PTZ camera to achieve ultra-high-resolution static 360-degree telepresence through tiled background refinement, dynamic foreground compositing, and user-guided region-of-interest updates.
AI.motivation: 360-degree video telepresence is limited by current capture/display hardware resolution, and optimization strategies for fixed-viewpoint, largely static scenes remain underexplored despite being common in telepresence installations.
AI.method: A three-layer representation: (1) tile-based ultra-high-resolution background via offline stitching of PTZ scans onto an 8K panorama; (2) a dynamic update layer compositing foreground from 8K stream using real-time high-resolution background matting; (3) a region-of-interest 4K layer streaming real-time PTZ views and progressively updating background tiles.
AI.result: Evaluated against representative video super-resolution methods and through a user study; results show tile-based background refinement with user-guided updates effectively balances panoramic fidelity and interactivity.
AI.conclusion: Tile-based background refinement combined with user-guided updates offers a practical solution for balancing high panoramic fidelity with interactivity in static 360-degree telepresence scenarios.

title: Certifying Collective Reasoning in Multi-Agent Systems via Koopman Spectral Analysis
summary: Orchestrated collectives of large language model (LLM) agents that debate and vote are an emerging form of computational intelligence: the intelligent behaviour resides in the \emph{interaction}, not in any single agent. They improve task accuracy, yet remain black boxes at the system level: there is no principled test of convergence, no bound on the rounds needed, and no faithful account of what drove a decision. This paper develops a novel framework based on Koopman operator theory and validates its theoretical guarantees on multi-agent consensus dynamics. Treating the collective as one nonlinear dynamical system on a communication graph, we read its essential behaviour off the spectrum of its Koopman transfer operator, an exact linear representation of the nonlinear dynamics estimated from interaction traces. The spectrum yields three machine-checkable certificates: the sub-dominant eigenvalue $λ_2$ fixes the intrinsic timescale of reasoning and yields a convergence deadline computable \emph{before} the debate runs; its eigenvector names the coherent factions the collective reasons in, and $|λ_2|$ certifies when that explanation is valid; and the leading spectral coordinates form a compressed, auditable message basis. On an attention-consensus model, the deadline tracks observed convergence with log--log correlation $0.93$ and bounds it in 96\% of 24 configurations; attribution is exact whenever the spectrum certifies metastability; eight of 32 coordinates preserve the decision at 99.7\% fidelity; and a certificate learned from 15 debates held on 60/60 held-out debates. The study runs in minutes on a CPU, making spectral certification a practical layer for trustworthy collective reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Koopman operator theory framework to analyze multi-agent LLM debate systems as nonlinear dynamical systems, providing spectral certificates for convergence deadlines, faction identification, and compressed decision representations — all computable in minutes on a CPU with strong empirical validation.
AI.motivation: LLM agent collectives that debate and vote improve task accuracy but remain black boxes at the system level: there is no principled test of convergence, no bound on required debate rounds, and no faithful account of what drove a collective decision. The authors seek to make these systems auditable and trustworthy by developing rigorous mathematical guarantees.
AI.method: The collective is modeled as a nonlinear dynamical system on a communication graph. The Koopman transfer operator — an exact linear representation of the nonlinear dynamics — is estimated from interaction traces. Its spectrum yields three certificates: (1) the sub-dominant eigenvalue λ₂ provides a convergence deadline computable before the debate runs; (2) its eigenvector identifies coherent factions and |λ₂| certifies explanation validity; (3) leading spectral coordinates form a compressed, auditable message basis.
AI.result: On an attention-consensus model, the deadline tracks observed convergence with log-log correlation of 0.93 and bounds it in 96% of 24 configurations. Attribution is exact when the spectrum certifies metastability. Eight of 32 spectral coordinates preserve the decision at 99.7% fidelity. A certificate learned from 15 debates held on 60/60 held-out debates.
AI.conclusion: Spectral certification via Koopman operator theory provides a practical, computationally lightweight layer for trustworthy collective reasoning in LLM agent systems, replacing black-box debate with machine-checkable guarantees.

title: Reasoning from Traces: Divergence-Guided Agentic Repair of WebAssembly Discrepancies
summary: WebAssembly (Wasm) promises seamless reuse of C/C++ codebases as portable, fast, sandboxed binaries. In practice, however, this promise often falls short: recent studies show that cross-compiling the same C/C++ source to Wasm and native binaries frequently leads to runtime discrepancies, owing to library implementation differences or compiler bugs.
