We also propose a competence model able to predict the competence level required to solve tasks. By properly assessing contributors' competences, we can identify and train candidates to replace core contributors. Our replication package, including code, data, and documentation, is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21605122

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a competence model using code metrics from contributions to assess OSS contributors' skill levels, aiming to predict the competence needed for tasks and facilitate the identification and training of replacement contributors when core members disengage.
AI.motivation: Core contributor disengagement in OSS projects is increasing and threatens project survival. Replacing these contributors is difficult and time-consuming due to insufficient knowledge about candidates' actual competence levels, which currently requires interviews and exams to verify.
AI.method: The authors collect code metrics from source code contributions and develop a competence model that predicts the competence level required to solve specific tasks. This model uses quantitative code-related metrics to assess contributor capabilities in a structured manner.
AI.result: The paper presents a competence model and associated replication package (code, data, documentation) for assessing OSS contributor competences, though specific experimental results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Proper assessment of contributor competences via code metrics enables identification and training of candidates to replace disengaged core contributors, addressing a critical sustainability challenge in OSS projects.

title: eMicro: Real-Time Multi-Hop Access Control for Microservices with eBPF
comment: Accepted at the 33rd ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS) 2026
summary: Modern cloud applications often comprise thousands of microservices whose interactions form complex request paths. Traditional inter-service access control restricts individual service-to-service requests, but fails to prevent multi-hop attacks, where each hop appears legitimate yet the overall path violates security intent. This gap leaves systems exposed to unauthorized access and data exfiltration. In this paper, we present eMicro, a path-aware defense system for microservices that prevents such attacks while remaining efficient and deployable. eMicro enforces real-time multi-hop access control through three key techniques: (1) history-based access control extended to capture service invocation sequences; (2) security policies encoded as efficient deterministic finite automaton (DFA), supporting constant-time lookups and compact label propagation; (3) eBPF-based in-kernel request tracing for transparent, low-overhead enforcement without code changes. Evaluations on DeathStarBench and production cloud traces from Uber, Alibaba, and ByteDance, covering 12 million request workflows and thousands of services, demonstrate the scalability of eMicro. eMicro performs policy checks in 1 microsecond, stores 50 million policies in only 100 MB, and reduces propagation overhead by 90% with negligible runtime impact. These results show that eMicro delivers scalable and efficient protection against multi-hop attacks, making it practical for deployment in large-scale microservice environments.

AI.tldr: eMicro is a path-aware access control system for microservices that prevents multi-hop attacks by enforcing real-time, history-based security policies encoded as DFAs, implemented via eBPF in-kernel tracing for transparent, low-overhead enforcement.
AI.motivation: Traditional inter-service access control only validates individual service-to-service requests (single-hop), leaving systems vulnerable to multi-hop attacks where each step appears legitimate but the overall request path violates security intent, enabling unauthorized access and data exfiltration.
AI.method: eMicro employs three techniques: (1) history-based access control that captures full service invocation sequences; (2) security policies encoded as deterministic finite automata (DFA) for constant-time lookups and compact label propagation; (3) eBPF-based in-kernel request tracing enabling transparent enforcement without application code modifications.
AI.result: Evaluated on DeathStarBench and production traces from Uber, Alibaba, and ByteDance (12M workflows, thousands of services): policy checks in 1μs, 50M policies stored in 100MB, 90% reduction in propagation overhead, negligible runtime impact.
AI.conclusion: eMicro provides scalable, efficient protection against multi-hop attacks and is practical for deployment in large-scale microservice environments.

title: Scaffold-Mediated Post-Training: Co-Evolving Model Parameters and Procedural Scaffold Graphs
summary: Post-training of large language models optimizes only parameters, while inference-time procedural scaffolds are typically designed independently of parameter training. This disconnect makes it difficult to automatically acquire and internalize complex strategies. We propose scaffold-mediated post-training: procedural scaffolds are organized into an evolvable graph structure that co-evolves with model parameters through discovery, distillation, and dynamic recompilation. We instantiate this paradigm as Skill Training. On FeatureBench, automatically discovered skills improve the passed rate by 8.1pp, and after progressive distillation the model still achieves a 27.7% passed rate without any external scaffold (distillation retention rate 85.2%, defined as post-distillation / with-skill passed rate), significantly outperforming standard SFT on the same data.

AI.tldr: Proposes scaffold-mediated post-training, where procedural scaffolds co-evolve with model parameters via discovery, distillation, and dynamic recompilation. Instantiated as Skill Training, it improves FeatureBench pass rate by 8.1pp with scaffolds and achieves 85.2% distillation retention rate, outperforming standard SFT.
AI.motivation: Current post-training only optimizes model parameters, while inference-time procedural scaffolds are designed independently. This disconnect prevents models from automatically acquiring and internalizing complex strategies. The authors aim to bridge this gap.
AI.method: Scaffold-mediated post-training organizes procedural scaffolds into an evolvable graph structure that co-evolves with model parameters through three mechanisms: discovery (automatically finding new scaffolds), distillation (internalizing scaffold knowledge into model parameters), and dynamic recompilation (reorganizing the scaffold graph). This is instantiated as "Skill Training" and evaluated on FeatureBench.
AI.result: Automatically discovered skills improve FeatureBench pass rate by 8.1 percentage points. After progressive distillation, the model achieves a 27.7% pass rate without external scaffolds, yielding an 85.2% distillation retention rate (post-distillation / with-skill pass rate), significantly outperforming standard SFT on identical data.
AI.conclusion: Scaffold-mediated post-training effectively bridges the gap between parameter optimization and procedural scaffolding, enabling models to both leverage external scaffolds at inference time and internalize strategic capabilities through distillation, surpassing standard supervised fine-tuning.

title: Marginal Matching Does Not License Factorized Sampling: Auditing Conditional Style Leakage in Factorized Generative Models
summary:
Factorized generative models commonly regularize a latent style variable z_s by matching its marginal distribution to a fixed Gaussian prior and interpret this as evidence that the style representation is independent of class information. We show that this interpretation is incorrect. Matching only the marginal distribution places no constraint on the class-conditional distributions, allowing the latent style to remain highly predictive of the label despite appearing perfectly Gaussian in aggregate. We derive an exact decomposition showing that this mismatch is one of four conditions required for factorized sampling, and demonstrate that eliminating it is necessary but not sufficient to obtain the intended factorization.
  Empirically, our case-study model and four representative latent baselines achieve near-zero global MMD while still allowing a linear probe to recover class labels with 74%--100% accuracy (10% chance level). Our model reaches 99.15% clustering accuracy, whereas externally evaluated class-conditional generation succeeds only 16% of the time. This leakage remains under six independent perturbations involving model capacity, curriculum, prior geometry, and supervision across two datasets. Four mitigation strategies reduce probe accuracy to 21%--46%, although they leave within-class dependence largely unchanged. A post-hoc conditional prior improves externally evaluated class generation to 0.97 on MNIST without retraining but reaches only 0.41 on CIFAR-10, while an empirical style bank achieves 0.88 on CIFAR-10. These results demonstrate that no divergence computed solely on the marginal distribution of the style latent can certify independence from class labels, and that reporting marginal statistics alone does not verify the property commonly claimed in factorized generative models.

AI.tldr: Factorized generative models that only match the marginal distribution of a style latent to a Gaussian prior fail to guarantee independence from class labels. The paper proves this theoretically, demonstrates empirically that class labels remain highly predictable from ostensibly "Gaussianized" style latents, and evaluates mitigation strategies, concluding that marginal statistics alone cannot certify the intended factorization.
AI.motivation: Many factorized generative models claim that a latent style variable z_s is independent of class information because its marginal distribution matches a Gaussian prior. The authors challenge this by showing that marginal matching imposes no constraint on class-conditional distributions, allowing z_s to remain highly predictive of class labels despite appearing perfectly Gaussian in aggregate.
AI.method: The authors derive an exact decomposition of the mismatch between marginal and conditional distributions as one of four conditions for factorized sampling. Empirically, they evaluate a case-study model and four baselines using global MMD, linear probing accuracy, clustering accuracy, and externally evaluated class-conditional generation. They test under six perturbations (model capacity, curriculum, prior geometry, supervision) across two datasets. Four mitigation strategies are assessed, along with post-hoc conditional priors and empirical style banks.
AI.result: Models achieve near-zero global MMD while linear probes recover labels with 74–100% accuracy (chance=10%), and clustering accuracy reaches 99.15%, yet class-conditional generation succeeds only 16% externally. This leakage persists under all six perturbations. Mitigation strategies reduce probe accuracy to 21–46% but leave within-class dependence largely intact. A post-hoc conditional prior achieves 0.97 on MNIST but only 0.41 on CIFAR-10; an empirical style bank reaches 0.88 on CIFAR-10.
AI.conclusion: No divergence computed solely on the marginal distribution of the style latent can certify independence from class labels. Reporting marginal statistics alone does not verify the factorization property commonly claimed in factorized generative models.

title: Abstract Event Causal Rules: Induction and Application
summary: Event-centric intelligent analytical systems heavily depend on explicit causal event knowledge for risk early warning, decision-making support and narrative comprehension. Nevertheless, existing instance-level causal pairs suffer severe generalization deficits on low-frequency long-tail and unseen event combinations. To address this limitation, this work proposes Abstract Event Causal Rule (AECR), a novel relation-level causal abstraction paradigm that transforms concrete cause-effect pairs into generalized abstract causal logic while retaining their intrinsic causal relationships. We design a multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system coupled with similarity-constrained clustering to distill trustworthy AECRs from noisy raw causal data, based on which two complete AECR knowledge bases are built. To validate the practical utility of abstract causal knowledge, we propose an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE), which injects the retrieved AECRs into the causality Graph Event Prediction (CGEP) benchmark task via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion. Quantitative experimental results reveal that applying AECRs substantially strengthens the generalization capacity of event causal reasoning and brings consistent performance improvements to event prediction, with the most prominent gains observed on rare and unseen event samples.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Abstract Event Causal Rules (AECR), a relation-level causal abstraction paradigm that generalizes concrete cause-effect pairs into abstract causal logic. A multi-agent system with similarity-constrained clustering distills trustworthy AECRs into two knowledge bases. An Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE) injects these rules into event prediction, yielding consistent improvements, especially on rare and unseen events.
AI.motivation: Existing instance-level causal event pairs suffer from severe generalization deficits on low-frequency long-tail and unseen event combinations, limiting their utility in event-centric intelligent systems for risk warning, decision support, and narrative comprehension.
AI.method: (1) AECR formulation: a relation-level causal abstraction paradigm transforming concrete cause-effect pairs into generalized abstract causal logic. (2) CACI (Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction): a multi-agent system with similarity-constrained clustering to distill trustworthy AECRs from noisy raw data, yielding two complete AECR knowledge bases. (3) AR-GCAE (Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder): integrates retrieved AECRs into the Causality Graph Event Prediction (CGEP) benchmark via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion.
AI.result: Applying AECRs substantially strengthens the generalization capacity of event causal reasoning and yields consistent performance improvements on event prediction. The most prominent gains are observed on rare and unseen event samples.
AI.conclusion: Abstract event causal rules at the relation level effectively mitigate the generalization limitations of instance-level causal pairs. The proposed CACI system and AR-GCAE encoder together form a viable pipeline for building and deploying abstract causal knowledge, demonstrating practical utility particularly for long-tail and zero-shot causal reasoning scenarios.

title: Gryphon-v2: One Model in Place of a Cascade - Generate-and-Rank Recommender with Rollout Distillation
summary: Industrial recommender systems are commonly deployed as multi-stage cascades with separate candidate generators, pre-rankers, and final rankers. Although effective, these cascades require repeated user-history processing, complex feature pipelines, and multiple serving stages. Semantic-ID-based generative retrieval offers a path toward simpler end-to-end systems, but next-item prediction alone does not capture the fine-grained preferences encoded by production ranking objectives. We present Gryphon-v2, a unified generate-and-rank architecture for end-to-end recommendation. The model encodes a user history once, generates Semantic-ID candidates with an autoregressive decoder, resolves them to catalogue items, and ranks them with an item-level Ranking Module that reuses the shared encoder states. To transfer fine-grained production ranking preferences without adding an expensive second model to the serving path, we distill a high-capacity, training-only Teacher Ranker into the Ranking Module. Gryphon-v2 is trained with Rollout Distillation: teacher scores are the only ranking supervision, and they are collected over two complementary candidate distributions. Rollouts from the current decoder expose the Ranking Module to candidates produced by the same generation mechanism used at serving time, while logged impressions cover items users were actually shown. In an online A/B experiment on a large-scale recommendation surface at Yandex Music, a single Gryphon-v2 model replaces a production cascade comprising more than 15 candidate generators, pre-ranking, and final ranking. The deployment increases the number of active users by 1.41% at serving latency comparable to the production cascade. These results support the practical viability of a generative retriever with a Ranking Module distilled from the Teacher Ranker as an end-to-end alternative to a production cascade.

AI.tldr: Gryphon-v2 proposes a unified generate-and-rank architecture that replaces multi-stage industrial recommendation cascades with a single end-to-end model. It uses an autoregressive decoder to generate Semantic-ID candidates and an item-level Ranking Module distilled from a training-only Teacher Ranker via Rollout Distillation. Deployed at Yandex Music, it replaced 15+ cascade components and increased active users by 1.41% at comparable latency.
AI.motivation: Industrial recommender systems rely on multi-stage cascades (candidate generators, pre-rankers, final rankers) that incur repeated user-history processing, complex feature pipelines, and multiple serving stages. While Semantic-ID generative retrieval simplifies this, next-item prediction alone fails to capture the fine-grained ranking preferences encoded by production ranking objectives. The authors aim to unify generation and ranking into one end-to-end model without adding an expensive second inference model.
AI.method: Gryphon-v2 uses a shared encoder to process user history once, an autoregressive decoder to generate Semantic-ID candidates, and an item-level Ranking Module that reuses encoder states. A training-only Teacher Ranker distills fine-grained production ranking preferences into the Ranking Module via Rollout Distillation: teacher scores serve as the sole ranking supervision, collected over two complementary candidate distributions — decoder rollouts (matching serving-time generation) and logged impressions (items actually shown to users).
AI.result: In an online A/B experiment at Yandex Music, a single Gryphon-v2 model replaced a production cascade of 15+ candidate generators, pre-ranking, and final ranking. The deployment yielded a 1.41% increase in active users while maintaining serving latency comparable to the production cascade.
AI.conclusion: A generative retriever paired with a Ranking Module distilled from a Teacher Ranker is a practically viable end-to-end alternative to multi-stage production cascades, achieving both simplification and improved user engagement.

title: SpaceVLA: Spatially Grounded VLA for Robotic Manipulation with User-Authored Grasp and Place Anchors
comment: A poster for the ISMAR conference, 4 pages, 3 figures
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models follow language commands but often lack explicit spatial intent for manipulation. We present Visual Intent Anchors, an XR pipeline that lets users specify grasp and placement regions and renders them as image-space overlays for VLA control. We collect 200 Unity pick-and-place demonstrations and fine-tune OpenVLA-7B with LoRA on temporally subsampled annotated observations. The policy predicts tokenized 7-DoF incremental actions from marked RGB observations and language. We evaluate the policy in closed-loop Unity trials, achieving a grasp success rate of 91.25% and mean grasp and placement errors of 0.5 cm and 0.7 cm, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Visual Intent Anchors, an XR pipeline that lets users specify spatial grasp/placement regions as image overlays for VLA models. Fine-tuning OpenVLA-7B with LoRA on 200 annotated demonstrations achieves 91.25% grasp success and sub-centimeter placement errors in Unity trials.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models follow language commands but lack explicit spatial intent specification for manipulation tasks, limiting precision in grasp and placement operations.
AI.method: An XR pipeline called Visual Intent Anchors allows users to specify grasp and placement regions, which are rendered as image-space overlays. These annotated RGB observations, combined with language instructions, are fed into OpenVLA-7B fine-tuned with LoRA using 200 Unity pick-and-place demonstrations with temporally subsampled frames. The policy predicts tokenized 7-DoF incremental actions.
AI.result: In closed-loop Unity evaluations, the policy achieves a grasp success rate of 91.25%, with mean grasp error of 0.5 cm and mean placement error of 0.7 cm.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting VLA models with explicit visual spatial anchors significantly improves manipulation precision, demonstrating that image-space overlays are an effective interface for conveying spatial intent in robot control.

title: IFlowNets: Extending Generative Samplers to Learn Strategies in Incomplete Information Games
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Dynamics at the Frontiers of Optimization, Sampling, and Games
summary: While many algorithms blend reinforcement learning (RL) with counterfactual regret (CFR) methods to leverage tradeoffs in computational speed and performance, there are fewer investigations into generative sampling frameworks in game theoretic applications in incomplete information games. We extend a generative flow network framework, Adversarial Flow Networks (AFlowNets), to incomplete information games, called Information Flow Networks (IFNs). We prove that previously established constraints for generative flow networks in complete information games are inadmissible for obtaining valid densities (corresponding to player strategies) and a valid training objective. We show that our proposed generalization, IFlowNets, alleviates this issue and strictly generalizes AFlowNets. In preliminary results for three standard game environments, IFlowNets perform comparably to or better than Outcome Sampling Monte Carlo Counterfactual Regret (OSMCCFR) and standard RL-based methods in performance and speed.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Information Flow Networks (IFlowNets), a generalization of Adversarial Flow Networks (AFlowNets) to incomplete information games. It proves that existing GFlowNet constraints from complete information settings are invalid for incomplete information games, proposes corrected constraints, and demonstrates comparable or superior performance to OS-MCCFR and standard RL methods.
AI.motivation: While many algorithms combine RL with CFR for incomplete information games, generative sampling frameworks remain underexplored in this domain. AFlowNets were designed only for complete information games, and naively applying their constraints to incomplete information settings yields invalid player strategy densities and flawed training objectives.
AI.method: The authors generalize AFlowNets to IFlowNets by reformulating the trajectory-level constraints and flow consistency conditions to accommodate information sets (imperfect information). They prove that the original AFlowNet constraints are inadmissible for incomplete information games and derive corrected constraints that ensure valid densities and a proper training objective. IFlowNets strictly subsume AFlowNets as a special case.
AI.result: Preliminary experiments on three standard game environments show IFlowNets achieve performance comparable to or better than Outcome Sampling MCCFR and standard RL-based baselines, with competitive computational speed.
AI.conclusion: IFlowNets successfully extend generative flow networks to incomplete information games, correcting previously inapplicable constraints. The approach represents a promising new direction for game-theoretic applications using generative sampling frameworks.

title: Keeping Models and Code in Sync: Roundtrip Engineering for Tactical Domain-Driven Design
summary: Domain-Driven Design gives teams a shared vocabulary for complex business logic, but that vocabulary only stays useful as long as the model and the code agree with each other. In practice, they drift apart: code changes outpace the model, or model revisions never make it into the codebase. This paper presents JDomInO, a bidirectional synchronization toolchain for tactical DDD that keeps a Java codebase and its domain model connected through a shared metamodel, with the goal of keeping the two in sync as the system evolves. JDomInO generates Java code structure deterministically from a domain model (forward path) and reconstructs a domain model from existing Java code (reverse path). The forward path has been fully validated on a Hotel Management scenario covering all 12 building block types in the metamodel; the reverse path's mapping logic has passed unit testing, with end-to-end validation underway. We also outline how the structured domain model produced by JDomInO could serve as a precision context layer for AI code assistants, helping them respect aggregate boundaries and DDD semantics that raw source code alone does not convey.

AI.tldr: JDomInO is a bidirectional synchronization toolchain that keeps Java code and Domain-Driven Design (DDD) models aligned through a shared metamodel. It generates Java code from domain models and reconstructs domain models from existing code, with forward generation validated on all 12 building block types and reverse mapping passing unit tests.
AI.motivation: In DDD practice, the domain model and the codebase inevitably drift apart over time—code changes outpace model updates, or model revisions never reach the code. This undermines the shared vocabulary that DDD aims to provide, creating a need for automated synchronization between model and code.
AI.method: The authors develop JDomInO, a bidirectional toolchain built around a shared metamodel encompassing all tactical DDD building blocks. The forward path deterministically generates Java code structure from a domain model specification. The reverse path reconstructs a domain model from existing Java code through mapping logic. The forward path was validated on a Hotel Management scenario covering all 12 building block types; the reverse path was unit-tested.
AI.result: The forward generation path was fully validated on a Hotel Management case study covering all 12 building block types in the metamodel. The reverse path's mapping logic passed unit testing, with end-to-end validation still in progress. The authors also propose that the structured domain model output could serve as a precision context layer for AI code assistants to respect aggregate boundaries and DDD semantics.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional synchronization between DDD models and code is feasible through a shared metamodel approach. JDomInO demonstrates this for Java, and the structured domain model it produces holds promise as enriched context for AI-assisted development, enabling tools to reason about DDD semantics beyond what raw source code conveys.

title: The Trust-Free Aggregation Layer of the Unicity Infrastructure
summary: Unicity is a novel blockchain infrastructure for enabling users to execute off-chain peer-to-peer token transactions while preventing parallel states of tokens (double-spending) with minimal blockchain complexity and storage. A key component of the infrastructure is the Aggregation Layer responsible for storing information about the spent states of tokens and providing compact cryptographic proofs of no double-spending for the users without making any compromises in trust. Aggregation Layer is a layer 2 style service that holds an append-only key-value repository that periodically certifies its state using a traditional blockchain that we call the Consensus Layer. Every time while certifying a changed state the Aggregation Layer provides a cryptographic proof to the Consensus Layer about the append-only consistency of the key-value store. We use the Radix Sparse Merkle Trees (RSMTs) to create the cryptographic digest r_i of the store in every round i and authentication paths of special type in order to prove that the next digest r_{i+1} was obtained while only adding some key-value pairs (k,v) to the repository. The proof verification code is implemented as an Algebraic Intermediate Representation (AIR) circuit on top of the Plonky3 STARK toolkit. Our implementation uses no trusted setup, achieves throughput of 10,000 insertions per second and and millisecond range verification time on a single consumer-class CPU.

AI.tldr: Unicity is a blockchain infrastructure enabling off-chain P2P token transactions with double-spend prevention using an Aggregation Layer backed by Radix Sparse Merkle Trees and STARK-based proofs, achieving 10,000 insertions/sec and millisecond verification on consumer hardware without trusted setup.
AI.motivation: Enable users to execute off-chain peer-to-peer token transactions while preventing double-spending, with minimal on-chain complexity and storage overhead.
AI.method: Employs an Aggregation Layer (layer-2) maintaining an append-only key-value store that periodically certifies its state to a Consensus Layer (traditional blockchain). Uses Radix Sparse Merkle Trees (RSMTs) to produce cryptographic digests and append-only consistency proofs across rounds. Proof verification is implemented as an Algebraic Intermediate Representation (AIR) circuit using the Plonky3 STARK toolkit.
AI.result: Achieves 10,000 insertions per second throughput and millisecond-range verification time on a single consumer-class CPU, with no trusted setup required.
AI.conclusion: Unicity demonstrates a practical, scalable layer-2 aggregation architecture for off-chain token transactions with strong double-spend guarantees, leveraging STARK-based verifiable computation for append-only key-value store consistency proofs.

title: Large Language Models Threaten Double-blind Review
summary: Double blind peer review serves as the scientific community primary defense against status and affiliation bias. Its effectiveness rests on the assumption that anonymized manuscripts convey scientific merit without revealing their authors. While authorship can often be recovered using citation networks or stylistic markers, we show that this assumption is increasingly fragile in the presence of large language models (LLMs). Using only titles and abstracts from papers published after model training, we find that LLMs collapse anonymity more efficiently than humans, with belief concentrating onto a small subset of plausible authors drawn from pools of five domain expert candidates. This vulnerability persists even when stylistic and bibliographic cues are excluded, indicating that stable patterns in problem framing and research focus function as latent conceptual signatures of authorship. Together, these findings indicate that double blind review is vulnerable to automated semantic inference, necessitating a revaluation of how anonymity and fairness are maintained in an AI augmented research ecosystem.

AI.tldr: LLMs can deanonymize double-blind peer review by inferring authorship from titles and abstracts alone, using latent conceptual signatures rather than stylistic or bibliographic cues, raising concerns about the future of review fairness.
AI.motivation: Double-blind peer review assumes authorship cannot be inferred from anonymized manuscripts. Prior work showed authorship leakage via citation networks and stylistic markers, but the advent of LLMs introduces a new threat: automated semantic inference from scientific content alone. This paper investigates whether LLMs break this anonymity assumption.
AI.method: The authors tested LLMs on the task of identifying authors from pools of five domain experts using only post-training titles and abstracts. They excluded stylistic and bibliographic cues to isolate semantic/content-based signals. Performance was compared against human baseline accuracy, with belief concentration measured across candidate sets.
AI.result: LLMs substantially outperform humans at authorship identification from abstracts alone. Belief concentrates onto a small subset of plausible candidates. The vulnerability persists even without stylistic or bibliographic cues, implicating stable patterns in problem framing and research focus as "latent conceptual signatures" of authorship.
AI.conclusion: Double-blind review is vulnerable to automated semantic inference by LLMs. This necessitates rethinking how anonymity and fairness are preserved in peer review as AI tools become more capable, potentially requiring new safeguards beyond traditional anonymization.

title: PRISM: Priority-aware Rubric Internalization via Structured Multimodal Data Synthesis
summary: Real-world multimodal instructions often bundle multiple requirements with unequal importance, yet most multimodal training data still reduce instruction following to answering one self-contained question. We study this gap through \textbf{rubric comprehension}, which casts the model not as a generator measured against rubrics but as an \textbf{executor} that follows them: given an image and a typed, prioritized rubric, the model must verify each rule before producing an overall judgment. To support this setting, we propose \textbf{PRISM}, a four-stage data synthesis framework that produces persona--task pairs, prefix-guided rule sets, quality-filtered rubrics, and structured verification traces. We further introduce \textbf{PRISM-Eval}, whose Loose and Strict metrics use deterministic matching against fixed labels and therefore require no inference-time judge model. With only 10K synthesized samples, PRISM lifts Qwen3-VL-4B from 9.5\% to 30.1\% Strict accuracy on PRISM-Eval while preserving average performance on general benchmarks, and the gains transfer to four additional open-source MLLMs across dense and MoE architectures, suggesting that structured rubric supervision is a scalable path toward multi-rule, priority-aware multimodal instruction following.

AI.tldr: PRISM introduces rubric comprehension, where multimodal models act as executors that verify prioritized rules before making judgments. Through a four-stage data synthesis framework, it generates structured training data that significantly improves multi-rule instruction following across multiple model architectures.
AI.motivation: Real-world multimodal instructions often contain multiple requirements with varying importance, but existing training data oversimplifies instruction following to single self-contained questions. There is a gap between this simplification and the need for models to handle prioritized, multi-rule instructions.
AI.method: PRISM proposes a four-stage data synthesis framework: (1) generating persona-task pairs, (2) creating prefix-guided rule sets, (3) quality-filtering rubrics, and (4) producing structured verification traces. Models are trained as executors that verify each rule in a typed, prioritized rubric against an image before producing an overall judgment. PRISM-Eval uses deterministic matching against fixed labels with Loose and Strict metrics, eliminating the need for inference-time judge models.
AI.result: With only 10K synthesized samples, PRISM improves Qwen3-VL-4B from 9.5% to 30.1% Strict accuracy on PRISM-Eval while maintaining average performance on general benchmarks. The gains transfer to four additional open-source MLLMs across both dense and MoE architectures.
AI.conclusion: Structured rubric supervision is a scalable approach for achieving multi-rule, priority-aware multimodal instruction following, and the PRISM framework demonstrates that small amounts of high-quality synthesized data can yield significant improvements without degrading general capabilities.

title: Otter: A Time-Aware, History-Conditioned Human Chess AI
summary:
Otter is a 15.3M-parameter human chess AI that predicts human move selection by modeling play as a time-aware, sequential process rather than treating each position in isolation. It combines two conditioning signals: (1) a move history encoder that conditions predictions on the last 20 moves, capturing opening preferences, positional drift, and intra-game behavioral tendencies; and (2) a time control module that modulates predictions based on clock pressure. Otter is trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million Lichess rapid games over 30 days on a single T4 GPU.
  Otter achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move-prediction accuracy, surpassing the prior state-of-the-art human chess model, Maia 2, with far fewer parameters and less training data. Across 11 Elo brackets (<1100 to >=2000), accuracy peaks at 57.38% in the 1900-1999 bracket. These results show that modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move prediction than position-only approaches, using a smaller model. Code, trained models, and complete training logs are publicly released.

AI.tldr: Otter is a compact 15.3M-parameter model that predicts human chess moves by incorporating move history and time pressure, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy (55.23% top-1) on Lichess data while using fewer parameters than prior models.
AI.motivation: Prior human chess AI models like Maia 2 treat each position in isolation, ignoring the sequential, time-constrained nature of human play. The authors argue that capturing intra-game behavioral tendencies, opening preferences, and clock pressure effects should yield more human-accurate move predictions.
AI.method: Two conditioning signals are combined: (1) a move history encoder that conditions predictions on the last 20 moves to capture opening preferences, positional drift, and behavioral tendencies; and (2) a time control module that modulates predictions based on clock pressure. The model is trained on 6.1B positions from 117M Lichess rapid games over 30 days on a single T4 GPU.
AI.result: Otter achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move-prediction accuracy, surpassing Maia 2 with far fewer parameters and less training data. Accuracy peaks at 57.38% in the 1900–1999 Elo bracket. The model demonstrates consistent gains from both history and time conditioning.
AI.conclusion: Modeling chess move prediction as a time-aware, sequential process yields superior human move prediction accuracy compared to position-only approaches, and can be done efficiently with a smaller model. Code, models, and training logs are publicly released.

title: Align-RAG: Alignment Is All You Need for TSFM In-Context Learning
summary: Retrieval-augmented forecasting promises to adapt frozen Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) to new domains without fine-tuning, but recent methods typically rely on learned fusion modules, i.e., trained adapters that merge retrieved examples into the backbone's forecast, based on the assumption that frozen backbones cannot dynamically incorporate retrieved context on their own. We show this assumption is unnecessary. We introduce Align-RAG, a training-free method that applies a closed-form per-pair amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase shift to retrieved past-future windows before they enter a frozen backbone's context. With no learned parameters, Align-RAG outperforms the state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter on a frozen Chronos-Bolt on all seven datasets of the standard benchmark (avg -3.75% MSE), showing that the gains previously attributed to learned fusion are recoverable without any training. Align-RAG further improves zero-shot MSE on four additional frozen TSFMs with various architectures by 2.5% to 13.7% per backbone with no per-backbone tuning. To probe why alignment helps, we compare the frozen backbone's prediction shift under aligned demonstrations to the closed-form ridge prediction shift on the same pairs. We find that aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts that track a closed-form ridge predictor on the same pairs, with a future-shuffle control ruling out a futures-averaging account. Together, these results indicate that frozen TSFMs already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals, and that closed-form alignment should be the default baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting before any fusion module is trained. Code available at: https://github.com/masadi-99/align-rag

AI.tldr: Align-RAG is a training-free method for retrieval-augmented time series forecasting that uses closed-form amplitude rescaling and phase shifting to align retrieved examples before feeding them into a frozen foundation model, outperforming trained adapters without any learned parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented forecasting methods assume frozen TSFMs cannot dynamically incorporate retrieved context and thus rely on trained fusion modules/adapters. The authors challenge this assumption, hypothesizing that simple closed-form alignment of retrieved examples may be sufficient to unlock the frozen backbone's inherent in-context capabilities.
AI.method: Align-RAG applies two closed-form transformations to each retrieved past-future window pair before concatenating them into the frozen backbone's context: (1) per-pair amplitude rescaling to match the query's scale, and (2) integer-lag phase shift to temporally align patterns. These require no learned parameters, no gradient updates, and no per-backbone tuning. The method also includes a ridge-regression-based analytical probe comparing frozen backbone prediction shifts under aligned demonstrations to closed-form ridge prediction shifts.
AI.result: On Chronos-Bolt, Align-RAG outperforms the SOTA trained retrieval adapter across all 7 benchmark datasets (avg -3.75% MSE). Across 4 additional frozen TSFMs with diverse architectures, zero-shot MSE improves by 2.5%–13.7% per backbone without per-backbone tuning. Analytical probing shows aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts that track a closed-form ridge predictor, while a future-shuffle control rules out simple futures-averaging.
AI.conclusion: Frozen TSFMs already possess dynamic in-context retrieval capabilities that can be unlocked via simple closed-form alignment, obviating the need for trained fusion modules. Align-RAG should serve as the default training-free baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting before any learned adapter is trained.

title: Temporal Tracking of Reeb-Space Sheets
summary: Time-varying bivariate fields arise in many scientific applications, where the relationship between two scalar quantities evolves over time. While topological methods such as merge trees provide an effective framework for identifying and tracking features in univariate data, analogous approaches for bivariate fields remain comparatively underexplored. Reeb spaces extend topological analysis to multivariate data by representing fiber connectivity through a collection of interconnected sheets, making these sheets natural candidates for describing bivariate structures. However, establishing temporal correspondences between sheets is challenging due to the structural complexity of Reeb spaces, sensitivity to noise, and the difficulty of defining meaningful similarity measures across timesteps. We present a framework for tracking Reeb space sheets in time-varying bivariate fields. The method establishes correspondences between sheets in consecutive timesteps using complementary similarity measures defined in the spatial domain and the range space. We evaluate the method on a synthetic torus dataset and two time-varying molecular electronic structure datasets. The results show that Reeb space sheet tracking reveals persistent structures and highlights interesting intervals of temporal change. Overall, the results demonstrate that Reeb space sheets can serve as trackable topological structures and provide a foundation for the visual analysis of time-varying bivariate data.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a framework for tracking Reeb space sheets across timesteps in time-varying bivariate fields, using complementary similarity measures in both the spatial domain and range space to establish temporal correspondences.
AI.motivation: While merge trees effectively track features in univariate time-varying data, analogous topological methods for bivariate fields are underdeveloped. Reeb spaces naturally represent bivariate fiber connectivity as sheets, but establishing temporal correspondences between these sheets is difficult due to structural complexity, noise sensitivity, and the lack of meaningful similarity measures across timesteps.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework that tracks Reeb space sheets across consecutive timesteps by computing complementary similarity measures: one defined in the spatial domain (capturing geometric correspondence of fibers) and one defined in the range space (capturing proximity in the bivariate function value domain). Correspondences are then established between sheets in adjacent timesteps based on these combined measures.
AI.result: Evaluated on a synthetic torus dataset and two time-varying molecular electronic structure datasets, the method successfully reveals persistent structures and highlights intervals of significant temporal change.
AI.conclusion: Reeb space sheets can serve as trackable topological structures, providing a foundation for visual analysis of time-varying bivariate data.

title: Hybrid-Adaptive Thread Tuning to Mitigate Simulation Execution Bottlenecks in High-Performance Reinforcement Learning Inference
summary: In simulation-in-the-loop decision-making systems, reinforcement learning (RL) inference is often constrained by simulator-side execution overhead, where workloads are highly dynamic and sensitive to runtime thread configurations. Existing multithreaded strategies struggle to match thread resources before or during execution, causing resource contention, scheduling overhead, and reduced throughput. Through empirical analysis, we identify the ratio of task execution time to scheduling time as the key factor determining the optimal thread count. Building on this insight, we propose AutoThread, a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning method for mitigating simulation bottlenecks in RL inference. AutoThread employs a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) as a thread-count predictor and incorporates a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model to constrain and guide prediction, enabling fast and accurate estimation under dynamic workloads. It further performs load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate for prediction errors and refine resource allocation. Experiments show that AutoThread improves average speedup by 18.4\% over static strategies, achieves average throughput of 1.7x and 1.8x that of XGBoost and Reinforcer, respectively, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8\% compared with state-of-the-art methods. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/suchenjm/AutoThread.

AI.tldr: AutoThread is a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning method that uses a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) predictor combined with an M/M/1 queueing model to dynamically optimize thread counts for RL inference under simulation bottlenecks, achieving significant throughput gains and execution time reductions over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: In simulation-in-the-loop RL systems, simulator-side execution overhead creates dynamic workloads that are highly sensitive to thread configurations. Existing multithreaded strategies fail to effectively match thread resources before or during execution, leading to resource contention, scheduling overhead, and reduced throughput.
AI.method: AutoThread uses a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) as a thread-count predictor, constrained and guided by a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model for fast, accurate estimation under dynamic workloads. It also employs load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate for prediction errors and refine resource allocation in real time.
AI.result: AutoThread achieves an 18.4% average speedup over static strategies, delivers 1.7x and 1.8x the average throughput of XGBoost and Reinforcer respectively, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8% compared with state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The ratio of task execution time to scheduling time is the key factor determining optimal thread count. AutoThread effectively addresses RL inference bottlenecks by combining PINO-based prediction with queueing-theoretic constraints and online fine-tuning, yielding substantial performance improvements in dynamic simulation environments.

title: Agent-Based Test Assertion Generation via Diverse Perspective Aggregation
summary: Test assertions are critical elements of unit tests, serving as checkpoints to validate expected behavior and ensure software correctness. Numerous techniques have been proposed to automate assertion generation, with recent progress notably driven by large language models (LLMs). Despite the promise, existing approaches such as ChatAssert suffer from modest accuracy, heavy reliance on oversampling, and vulnerability to model randomness due to one-shot prompting. To address these limitations, we propose AssertMate, a novel agent-based assertion generation framework that enhances the quality and reliability of LLM-generated assertions through three key components: (1) actual value construction that identifies assertion targets via static analysis and type-aware heuristics; (2) multi-perspective expected value prediction using code generation, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning agents; and (3) an LLM-as-a-Judge collaboration mechanism to select the most appropriate assertion. Evaluation on the Defects4J benchmark demonstrates that AssertMate significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in compilation success and pass rates, along with substantially higher bug detection capabilities. Integration with EvoSuite further validates AssertMate's practicality, yielding superior mutation coverage and kill counts. Ablation studies reveal that each of the three components makes a significant and complementary contribution to the overall performance. This work affirms the great potential of aggregating diverse perspectives to enhance the effectiveness of LLM-based assertion generation.

AI.tldr: AssertMate is an agent-based framework for automated test assertion generation that combines static analysis, multi-perspective expected value prediction (code generation, RAG, CoT), and an LLM-as-a-Judge selection mechanism, significantly outperforming prior methods on Defects4J and integrating effectively with EvoSuite.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based assertion generation approaches like ChatAssert suffer from modest accuracy, heavy reliance on oversampling, and vulnerability to model randomness due to one-shot prompting, necessitating a more robust multi-agent approach.
AI.method: AssertMate employs three components: (1) static analysis with type-aware heuristics to identify assertion targets and construct actual values; (2) three parallel agents—code generation, RAG, and CoT reasoning—to predict expected values from different perspectives; and (3) an LLM-as-a-Judge collaboration mechanism that selects the most suitable assertion among candidates.
AI.result: On Defects4J, AssertMate significantly outperforms SOTA techniques in compilation success, pass rates, and bug detection. Integration with EvoSuite yields superior mutation coverage and kill counts. Ablation studies confirm each component contributes significantly and complementarily.
AI.conclusion: Aggregating diverse perspectives through a multi-agent framework substantially enhances LLM-based assertion generation effectiveness, affirming the value of collaborative agent architectures in software testing automation.

title: S12X Patch Diffing with QBinDiff
comment: Preprint of paper to be presented at VehicleSec 2026. This version includes appendices beyond the page limits of the conference
summary: This paper presents a reverse engineering analysis of a firmware update for a commercial vehicle Brake ECU. We analyze the updater executable to extract firmware and perform differential binary analysis of the S12X architecture firmware images. Our research identifies specific changes in the recall that address undocumented vulnerabilities in legacy protocol processing. We demonstrate that the patched functionality contained critical flaws. The findings confirm the safety recall remediation was also a security patch.

AI.tldr: Reverse engineering of a commercial vehicle Brake ECU firmware update reveals that a safety recall also served as an undisclosed security patch, addressing critical vulnerabilities in legacy protocol processing.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether a commercial vehicle Brake ECU safety recall contained hidden security fixes beyond the publicly stated safety improvements, by extracting and analyzing the firmware update.
AI.method: Reverse engineering of the updater executable to extract firmware, followed by differential binary analysis across S12X architecture firmware images (pre- and post-recall versions) to identify code changes.
AI.result: The recall patched undocumented vulnerabilities in legacy protocol processing. The analysis confirmed that the patched functionality contained critical flaws and that the safety recall remediation functioned as a covert security patch.
AI.conclusion: Safety recalls in automotive ECUs may serve dual purposes, and the lack of transparency about embedded security fixes underscores the need for coordinated disclosure practices in the automotive domain.

title: Safe Evolution with Circuit Anchors
summary: In biological evolution, unconstrained mutation can lead to catastrophic outcomes: organisms may evolve enhanced capabilities while losing essential functions for survival. Nature's solution is \textit{developmental constraints}, where core regulatory genes remain anchored while peripheral genes adapt freely. We observe that current self-evolution algorithms for large language models lack analogous constraints. They optimize purely for capability, implicitly assuming safety will be preserved. Our experiments reveal this assumption to be dangerously wrong: models can \textit{misevolve} into powerful yet dangerous entities. Inspired by how Hox genes anchor body structure across $500$ million years of evolution, we propose \textbf{Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE)}. Using mechanistic interpretability, we identify a tiny \textit{safety circuit}, comprising less than $2$\% of model features, that causally mediates safety behaviors. We anchor this circuit during evolution, constraining it within a small displacement bound while allowing the remaining features to evolve freely. This mirrors the biological principle of \textit{evolvability with constraint}: preserving what is essential while adapting what is peripheral. Experiments across $3$ model families and two evolution algorithms demonstrate that CAE achieves superior safety preservation with minimal capability loss, substantially outperforming explicit reward-based constraints in both effectiveness and efficiency. Just as developmental constraints prevent biological evolution from producing nonviable organisms, circuit anchoring prevents model evolution from producing capable but dangerous systems.

AI.tldr: Current LLM self-evolution methods lack safety constraints, causing models to "misevolve" into capable but dangerous systems. Inspired by developmental constraints in biology (e.g., Hox genes), the authors propose Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE), which identifies a small safety circuit (~2% of features) via mechanistic interpretability and constrains it during evolution, achieving superior safety preservation with minimal capability loss.
AI.motivation: Self-evolution algorithms for LLMs optimize purely for capability without constraints, leading to models that become more powerful but lose essential safety behaviors — a phenomenon the authors term "misevolution." This mirrors biological evolution without developmental constraints, where unconstrained mutation can produce catastrophic outcomes. No existing method provides a principled, efficient mechanism to preserve safety during model evolution.
AI.method: The authors propose Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE), which uses mechanistic interpretability to identify a minimal "safety circuit" — a small set of model features (<2% of total) that causally mediate safety behaviors. During self-evolution, this circuit is anchored within a small displacement bound in representation space, while the remaining features evolve freely. This mirrors the biological principle of evolvability with constraint: Hox genes remain conserved while peripheral genes adapt.
AI.result: Experiments across 3 model families and 2 evolution algorithms show CAE achieves superior safety preservation with minimal capability loss, substantially outperforming explicit reward-based constraints in both effectiveness and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Circuit anchoring provides a principled, efficient approach to preventing model evolution from producing capable but dangerous systems, analogous to how developmental constraints prevent biological evolution from producing nonviable organisms. The work establishes mechanistic interpretability as a practical tool for AI safety in the context of self-improving models.

title: Beyond Full-Model Rollback: AuroSFT for Adapter-State Multi-Task Fine-Tuning
summary: Multi-task supervised fine-tuning (SFT) often casts a heterogeneous data mixture as a single optimization problem, even though different tasks may reach their best generalization at different times. msft exposes this mismatch through task-wise roll-out, exclusion, and rollback, but its original formulation materializes the scheduler state as full-model checkpoints, making stage transitions costly to store, restore, and deploy. This paper introduces AuroSFT, a parameter-efficient framework that recasts the carried state of overfitting-aware multi-task SFT as a compact, mergeable adapter state. AuroSFT freezes the pretrained backbone, trains only injected adapters, rolls back adapter checkpoints at task-wise peaks, and continues on the remaining active mixture. At the layer level, each adapter applies an AuroRA-inspired adaptive nonlinear layer to a low-rank weight factor rather than to the sample representation. The resulting update remains linear in the input, rank-bounded, and exactly mergeable into the frozen projection. Under the retained-backbone comparison protocol, AuroSFT achieves 61.36% average accuracy, compared with 59.85% for the corresponding msft reference row, and obtains higher accuracy on all five backbones. Our code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuroSFT-80D1.

AI.tldr: AuroSFT introduces a parameter-efficient multi-task SFT framework that replaces full-model checkpointing with compact, mergeable adapter states, enabling overfitting-aware task-wise rollback without the storage/deployment overhead of msft.
AI.motivation: In multi-task supervised fine-tuning, different tasks peak in generalization at different training stages, but standard SFT treats the mixture as a single optimization problem. The existing msft method addresses this via task-wise roll-out, exclusion, and rollback, but it requires storing full-model checkpoints, making stage transitions expensive in storage, restoration, and deployment.
AI.method: AuroSFT freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only injected adapters. It performs rollback of adapter checkpoints at task-wise peaks and continues training on the remaining active mixture. At the layer level, each adapter uses an AuroRA-inspired adaptive nonlinear layer applied to a low-rank weight factor (not the sample representation), yielding updates that are linear in the input, rank-bounded, and exactly mergeable into the frozen projection.
AI.result: Under the retained-backbone comparison protocol, AuroSFT achieves 61.36% average accuracy versus 59.85% for the corresponding msft reference, with higher accuracy on all five backbones tested.
AI.conclusion: AuroSFT successfully recasts overfitting-aware multi-task SFT into a parameter-efficient adapter-based framework, matching or exceeding msft performance while eliminating the need for expensive full-model checkpointing.

title: SearchAuditor: Auditing and Attributing Failures in Long-Horizon Search Agents
summary: Deep search agents tackle challenging questions through long-horizon web interactions, a process that is both complex and fragile: small reasoning errors may propagate through long, noisy trajectories into fluent but incorrect answers. Diagnosing such failures is difficult, requiring the manual inspection of extremely long execution traces, which could be beyond human capacity. We therefore introduce SearchAuditBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether LLM auditors can localize, attribute, and repair these failures, thereby reducing the human burden. SearchAuditBench comprises 1,243 failed trajectories, averaging 73.1 messages and 65.1K tokens, collected from eight open-weight models on five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, a search-specific root cause, and a reference repair with grading rubrics. We further propose SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework that effectively localizes, attributes, and repairs search-agent failures through evidence-grounded adjudication. Experimental results show that even the strongest baseline, when powered by a frontier model like GPT-5.5, attains only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. In contrast, our SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across different frontier models, achieving an end-to-end pass rate of 32.3%, and resuming failed runs with its repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.

AI.tldr: SearchAuditBench is a benchmark of 1,243 failed deep-search agent trajectories for evaluating LLM auditors on localizing, attributing, and repairing search failures. The proposed SearchAuditor framework outperforms baselines (32.3% vs. 26.6% pass rate) and helps agents recover from errors.
AI.motivation: Deep search agents produce long, complex web interaction trajectories where small reasoning errors propagate into fluent but incorrect answers. Manual inspection of these extremely long traces to diagnose failures is prohibitively difficult, creating a need for automated LLM-based auditing to reduce human burden.
AI.method: The authors introduce SearchAuditBench, a benchmark of 1,243 failed trajectories (avg. 73.1 messages, 65.1K tokens) from eight open-weight models across five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with critical error steps, root causes, and reference repairs with grading rubrics. They also propose SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework using evidence-grounded adjudication to localize, attribute, and repair search-agent failures.
AI.result: The strongest baseline (GPT-5.5-powered) achieves only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across frontier models, reaching a 32.3% end-to-end pass rate. Resuming failed runs with SearchAuditor's repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.
AI.conclusion: Automated auditing of deep-search agent failures is a challenging but feasible task. While even frontier models struggle, SearchAuditor's multi-perspective, evidence-grounded approach yields consistent improvements, demonstrating the potential for reducing human effort in diagnosing and repairing complex search-agent failures.

title: Cleo: A Transparent and Controllable Chatbot for Conversational Commerce
summary: We demonstrate Cleo, a transparent and controllable conversational product advisor that addresses the challenges of opacity, unpredictability of LLMs, and the complexity of comparisons in conversational commerce. With our chatbot system, we make four contributions: First, we introduce transparency by prompting the LLM to reflect on interpreted user needs, while an auditable ranking mechanism reveals loss values per attribute, explaining ranking decisions. Second, we propose controllability through a hybrid architecture separating deterministic ranking from language generation. A ranker applies categorical filters and numeric loss functions over 3,638 product specifications. Meanwhile, a constrained LLM generates grounded descriptions constrained to catalog evidence, thus mitigating the risk of hallucinated or persuasive content. Third, we provide decision support in the form of natural-language comparisons and a highlights feature. These aim to reduce mental workload by contextualizing specifications relative to user needs. Fourth, we contribute an extensible experimental system for IR and HCI researchers, as well as practitioners of conversational search and recommendation. Unlike traditional faceted search or opaque LLM-only recommenders, our approach allows for fluid conversation while maintaining algorithmic transparency. In a live demonstration, attendees will experience information needs elicitation and reflection, conversational refinement with real-time re-ranking, inspection of per-attribute loss explanations, and AI-generated multi-item comparisons. The system aims to advance the design of transparent and controllable conversational systems that provide support for decision-making during online product search.

AI.tldr: Cleo is a conversational product advisor that combines a transparent, deterministic ranking engine with a constrained LLM to deliver controllable, hallucination-mitigated product recommendations, supporting decision-making through explainable rankings and natural-language comparisons.
AI.motivation: Existing conversational commerce systems suffer from three key problems: LLM opacity (users cannot see why recommendations are made), unpredictability (hallucinated or persuasive content), and the cognitive complexity of comparing multiple products across attributes. The authors aim to address these gaps by designing a system that is both transparent and controllable.
AI.method: Cleo employs a hybrid architecture that decouples deterministic ranking from language generation. A ranker applies categorical filters and numeric loss functions over 3,638 product specifications to produce auditable, per-attribute loss values. A constrained LLM then generates grounded natural-language descriptions strictly tied to catalog evidence. The system also includes a user-facing layer for needs elicitation, conversational refinement with real-time re-ranking, inspection of loss explanations, and AI-generated multi-item comparisons.
AI.result: The paper presents a live demonstration system. Attendees can experience end-to-end interaction: information-needs elicitation and reflection, real-time conversational re-ranking, per-attribute loss inspection, and comparative highlights. No quantitative evaluation results are reported in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Cleo advances the design of transparent and controllable conversational recommender systems by proving that fluid conversation and algorithmic transparency are not mutually exclusive, offering an extensible platform for IR and HCI research.

title: Topic Matters: How Linguistic Properties can Shape Reading Behaviour in Selective Exposure Studies
comment: In CHI EA '26: Proceedings of the Extended Abstracts of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
summary: Research on selective exposure frequently relies on eye tracking to study reading behaviour, often assuming that texts across different controversial topics are comparable once basic controls are applied. This assumption is problematic if topic-dependent linguistic properties systematically shape how users read and allocate attention. We therefore examine whether such properties relate to differences in reading behaviour in selective exposure contexts. We analyse linguistic features and eye-tracking data from a laboratory study in which 68 participants searched for and read news articles on climate change and migration policy. Our results reveal systematic differences in both textual characteristics and reading behaviour across topics. These findings identify an important methodological confound in selective exposure research and highlight the need to account for topic-specific linguistic properties when interpreting eye-tracking measures and designing systems intended to mitigate biased information consumption.

AI.tldr: Linguistic properties of texts vary systematically across controversial topics, shaping how readers allocate visual attention. This creates a methodological confound in selective exposure research that relies on eye tracking across different topics.
AI.motivation: Prior selective exposure research using eye tracking assumes textual comparability across controversial topics after basic controls. This assumption may be invalid if topic-dependent linguistic properties systematically influence reading behaviour, potentially confounding cross-topic comparisons.
AI.method: The authors conducted a laboratory study with 68 participants who searched for and read news articles on two controversial topics (climate change and migration policy). They analyzed linguistic features of the texts alongside eye-tracking data to examine whether topic-dependent linguistic properties correlate with systematic differences in reading behaviour.
AI.result: Systematic differences were found in both textual characteristics (linguistic properties) and reading behaviour (eye-tracking measures) across the two topics, confirming that topic-dependent linguistic features shape how users read and allocate attention.
AI.conclusion: Topic-specific linguistic properties constitute an important methodological confound in selective exposure research. Researchers must account for these properties when interpreting eye-tracking measures and when designing systems aimed at mitigating biased information consumption.

title: Does Latent Context Help? A Controlled Evaluation of Inverse Reinforcement Learning in Arctic Shipping
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted navigation can help Arctic shipping adapt to rapidly changing sea-ice conditions, but reliable deployment requires reward models that are interpretable and robust to changing environments. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a framework for recovering such rewards from vessel trajectories, while recent meta-IRL methods introduce latent context variables to capture behavioral heterogeneity. However, it remains unclear whether these latent representations recover genuinely hidden preferences or simply re-encode information already available in the observed state. We conduct a controlled evaluation on 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels across nine Arctic shipping seasons, comparing a linear shared reward, a nonlinear shared reward, and a latent-context model built on the same nonlinear architecture. The nonlinear reward improves held-out likelihood by 50.9% over the linear baseline, whereas adding vessel-specific latent context reduces performance by 16.5%. Behavioral analysis, context probes, and a pre-registered feature-hiding ablation show that apparent vessel-level variation is largely explained by observable route and environmental conditions rather than hidden vessel-specific factors. Moreover, predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer yield different model rankings, demonstrating that no single metric is sufficient to evaluate learned rewards. These findings motivate testing whether the observed route, environmental, and vessel features already explain behavioral variation before adding per-vessel latent context. This supports more trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains.

AI.tldr: A controlled evaluation using Arctic shipping AIS data shows that adding vessel-specific latent context to inverse reinforcement learning degrades performance; observable route and environmental features already explain behavioral variation, cautioning against unnecessary latent-variable model complexity for trustworthy AI deployment.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted Arctic navigation requires interpretable, robust reward models for safe deployment. While meta-IRL with latent context variables promises to capture heterogeneous vessel preferences, it is unclear whether these latent representations recover genuinely hidden preferences or merely re-encode observable state information. This ambiguity threatens model trustworthiness in safety-critical maritime operations.
AI.method: The authors conducted a controlled evaluation on 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels across nine Arctic shipping seasons. They compared three model architectures: (1) a linear shared reward, (2) a nonlinear shared reward (neural network-based), and (3) a latent-context model built on the same nonlinear architecture incorporating vessel-specific latent variables. Evaluation employed held-out likelihood, behavioral analysis, context probes, a pre-registered feature-hiding ablation, and metrics including predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer.
AI.result: The nonlinear reward model improved held-out likelihood by 50.9% over the linear baseline, but adding vessel-specific latent context reduced performance by 16.5%. Context probes and feature-hiding ablation revealed that apparent vessel-level behavioral variation is overwhelmingly explained by observable route and environmental conditions, not hidden vessel-specific factors. Different metrics (predictive accuracy, route fidelity, reward transfer) produced different model rankings, demonstrating no single metric suffices for evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Before introducing per-vessel latent context in IRL, researchers should test whether observable features already explain behavioral variation. The finding that latent variables may re-encode available state information rather than genuine hidden preferences supports more parsimonious, interpretable, and trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains like Arctic navigation.

title: CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents
summary:
Modern LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenHands share a common inefficiency: they spend much of their token budget finding the file to patch, rather than patching it. On SWE-Bench Verified, a 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, with many calls spent on grep, glob, and view_file during repository exploration. We introduce CodeGrep, a 14B retrieval agent trained end-to-end with GRPO to issue multi-turn parallel grep, glob, and read tool calls and return candidate files to a frozen downstream coding agent.
  On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep preserves resolve rate while substantially improving efficiency: 27.0% versus 25.8% for the no-retrieval baseline, with 15% fewer rounds and 19% fewer tokens on resolved instances. Across retrievers, downstream utility follows a precision threshold: BM25 with precision 0.375 degrades the agent, Jina with precision 0.445 is neutral, and CodeGrep with precision 0.677 crosses the threshold at which retrieval begins to reduce rollout cost. To enable this study, we mine supervision from 67K open-source agent trajectories using CATM and build a Git-worktree environment for multi-turn agent RL. In our setting, applying the efficiency signal at the advantage layer rather than the reward layer reduces KL drift and translates cleanly into downstream efficiency. We will release the model, training pipeline, RL environment, and evaluation harnesses.

AI.tldr: CodeGrep is a 14B retrieval agent trained with GRPO that efficiently locates files needing patches in code repositories, reducing LLM coding agents' token usage by 19% and rounds by 15% on SWE-Bench Verified while maintaining resolve rates, by achieving high retrieval precision (0.677) that crosses the threshold where retrieval actually helps downstream agents.
AI.motivation: Modern LLM coding agents (e.g., Claude Code, OpenHands) waste significant token budgets on repository exploration (grep, glob, view_file) rather than actual code patching. On SWE-Bench Verified, a 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per issue, with many calls spent locating files. The authors aim to offload this file-finding burden to a specialized, efficient retrieval agent to reduce cost while preserving task success rates.
AI.method: The authors introduce CodeGrep, a 14B parameter retrieval agent trained end-to-end with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It issues multi-turn parallel grep, glob, and read tool calls to identify candidate files, which are then passed to a frozen downstream coding agent. Training supervision is mined from 67K open-source agent trajectories using CATM (Context-Aware Trajectory Mining). A custom Git-worktree environment is built for multi-turn agent reinforcement learning. Crucially, the efficiency signal is applied at the advantage layer rather than the reward layer during RL, which reduces KL drift and translates more cleanly into downstream efficiency gains.
AI.result: On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep achieves a 27.0% resolve rate versus 25.8% for the no-retrieval baseline, while reducing rounds by 15% and tokens by 19% on resolved instances. The study reveals a precision threshold effect: BM25 (precision 0.375) degrades downstream performance, Jina (0.445) is neutral, and CodeGrep (0.677) crosses the threshold where retrieval begins to reduce rollout cost. Applying the efficiency signal at the advantage layer rather than the reward layer reduces KL drift.
AI.conclusion: A high-precision retrieval agent (CodeGrep at 0.677 precision) can offload repository exploration from coding agents, yielding significant efficiency gains without sacrificing resolve rates. The precision threshold phenomenon suggests that low-precision retrievers actively harm downstream agents, while sufficiently precise ones unlock cost savings. The advantage-layer efficiency signal technique is an important design choice for stable RL training in this setting. The authors commit to releasing all artifacts: model, training pipeline, RL environment, and evaluation harnesses.

title: Robust Context-Aware Detection of Malicious Instructions in Text
summary: The remarkable instruction-following ability of modern LLMs has enabled their practical use as the minds of agents that can autonomously complete increasingly complex tasks. Therein, however, also lies their vulnerability to attacks which embed malicious instructions in text, common variants of which are known as indirect prompt injection (IPI). A fundamental task in addressing this vulnerability is successful segmentation of a given text into benign and malicious sentences (if any). While a number of approaches for this task have been proposed, no detector combines query-relative detection at the segment level, and none are hardened against adaptive evasion attacks realizable in agentic executions. We address the former limitation by developing an approach for malicious sentence classification that is both context- and query-aware. Next, to harden the resulting classifier against evasion, we present two adversarial training methods. The first is directly adapted feature-space adversarial training (AT) in which evasions are approximated using projected-gradient-based optimization in the embedding space.
