The second simulates realizable evasion attacks in the AT loop through LLM-based paraphrasing. Crucially, we parametrize both AT variants to facilitate a smooth tradeoff between utility and attack robustness. In extensive experiments using indirect prompt injection benchmarks we show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art IPI defense baselines under static attacks, while in the case of adaptive attacks, our AT variants provide significantly higher utility, lower attack success rate, and often both. Finally, we show that the best AT parameters can depend intimately on the particular application domain. Consequently, domain-dependent tuning of malicious text detectors is likely necessary in practice. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/tavia-liu/CAD.

AI.tldr: Proposes a context- and query-aware malicious sentence classifier for detecting indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, hardened via two adversarial training variants: embedding-space projected-gradient AT and LLM-based paraphrasing AT. Demonstrates superior performance over SOTA baselines under both static and adaptive attacks, with tunable utility-robustness tradeoffs.
AI.motivation: Existing IPI detectors lack segment-level, query-relative detection and are not hardened against adaptive evasion attacks realizable in agentic LLM executions. Both limitations are critical for practical deployment of LLM agents.
AI.method: A context- and query-aware classifier for malicious sentence segmentation. Two adversarial training (AT) methods for robustness: (1) feature-space AT using projected-gradient optimization in embedding space, and (2) LLM-paraphrasing-based AT that simulates realizable evasion attacks. Both are parameterized for smooth utility-robustness tradeoff tuning.
AI.result: The proposed approach outperforms SOTA IPI defenses under static attacks. Under adaptive attacks, both AT variants yield significantly higher utility and lower attack success rates than baselines. Optimal AT parameters are domain-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Query- and context-aware segment-level detection with adversarial training offers strong protection against both static and adaptive IPI attacks. Practical deployment likely requires domain-specific tuning of the detector.

title: SemiAdapt-Instruct: Extensible Instruction Tuning via Latent Domain-Specialised Adapters
summary: Instruction-tuned LLMs are deployed into environments where domains evolve, yet extending a fine-tuned model's capabilities without full retraining remains an unsolved practical challenge. We present SemiAdapt-Instruct, a modular framework that discovers latent instruction domains, trains per-domain LoRA adapters in parallel, and performs parameter-free routing, incorporating new domains via single-adapter training without modifying existing components. SemiAdapt-Instruct outperforms full model fine-tuning across all configurations on both ROUGE-L and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, while matching single LoRA fine-tuning and delivering extensibility that monolithic approaches cannot provide. We empirically demonstrate this extensibility by showing that updating a single adapter with new domain data outperforms all monolithic baselines. Our study also finds that independent discovery methods converge on the same specialisation-friendly domains. These findings demonstrate that decomposing heterogeneous instruction data into latent domains enables extensible NLP systems where evolving domains require only targeted single-adapter updates, eliminating the need for full model retraining.

AI.tldr: SemiAdapt-Instruct is a modular framework that discovers latent instruction domains, trains per-domain LoRA adapters in parallel with parameter-free routing, and supports extensibility by adding new domains via single-adapter training without full retraining—outperforming full fine-tuning and matching single LoRA while enabling targeted updates.
AI.motivation: Instruction-tuned LLMs deployed in evolving domains face a practical challenge: extending a model's capabilities without full retraining. Current approaches lack extensibility—monolithic fine-tuning requires retraining the entire model when new domains emerge, which is costly and impractical for dynamic environments.
AI.method: SemiAdapt-Instruct uses three modular stages: (1) unsupervised discovery of latent instruction domains from heterogeneous data, (2) parallel training of per-domain LoRA adapters for each discovered domain, and (3) parameter-free routing to select the appropriate adapter at inference time. New domains are incorporated by training only a single new adapter without modifying existing ones.
AI.result: SemiAdapt-Instruct outperforms full model fine-tuning across all configurations on both ROUGE-L and LLM-as-a-judge metrics, while matching single LoRA fine-tuning performance. Updating a single adapter with new domain data outperforms all monolithic baselines, empirically validating the extensibility claim. Independent domain discovery methods converge on the same specialization-friendly domains.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing heterogeneous instruction data into latent domains enables extensible NLP systems where evolving domains require only targeted single-adapter updates, eliminating the need for full model retraining. This demonstrates a practical path toward modular, maintainable instruction-tuned LLM deployment.

title: Beyond Rotations: AuroOFT for Expressive Quantized Orthogonal Fine-Tuning
summary: Quantized orthogonal fine-tuning (qoft) enables parameter-efficient adaptation of low-bit language models by learning structured activation rotations before frozen quantized weights. However, its task-specific updates remain constrained to linear orthogonal transformations, limiting input-dependent nonlinear corrections. We introduce AuroOFT, which keeps qoft as a stable quantization-compatible branch while attaching a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual to each adapted linear layer. AuroOFT maps activations into an RMS-normalized compact latent space and uses adaptive nonlinear bases with bounded or token-dependent gating. The zero-initialized up projection makes AuroOFT functionally identical to qoft at initialization, while orthogonality remains a branch-level stability property rather than a property of the combined nonlinear layer. Under matched data, optimization, decoding, and parser protocols, AuroOFT improves Macro-6 over matched qoft by 1.30-2.70% on the 1.5B/3B Qwen2.5 settings, exceeds QLoRA by 6.52-10.62%, and saves 32.3-44.7% trainable parameters relative to QLoRA in representative scales. The small exam-style multiple-choice math set is treated only as a protocol-sensitivity diagnostic. Our code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuroOFT-F3FD.

AI.tldr: AuroOFT enhances quantized orthogonal fine-tuning (qoft) by adding a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual branch, improving task performance while preserving quantization compatibility and initialization equivalence. It outperforms both qoft and QLoRA on Qwen2.5 models with fewer trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: qoft is limited to linear orthogonal transformations, lacking input-dependent nonlinear corrections that could improve adaptation quality for low-bit quantized language models.
AI.method: AuroOFT retains qoft as a stable quantization-compatible core branch and augments each adapted linear layer with a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual. Activations are mapped into an RMS-normalized compact latent space using adaptive nonlinear bases with bounded or token-dependent gating. The zero-initialized up-projection ensures functional equivalence to qoft at initialization, while orthogonality is preserved as a branch-level property.
AI.result: On 1.5B/3B Qwen2.5 models under matched protocols, AuroOFT improves Macro-6 over qoft by 1.30–2.70%, exceeds QLoRA by 6.52–10.62%, and reduces trainable parameters by 32.3–44.7% relative to QLoRA.
AI.conclusion: AuroOFT successfully combines the stability and quantization-compatibility of orthogonal fine-tuning with the expressiveness of nonlinear low-rank residuals, yielding significant accuracy gains with parameter efficiency. The small math set serves only as a protocol-sensitivity diagnostic, not a primary benchmark.

title: PD-GS: Phoneme-Driven 3DGS for Audio-Driven Talking Heads
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables fast, photorealistic talking-head rendering, yet accurate lip articulation remains elusive: mouth motion is often over-smoothed and may violate hard articulatory constraints such as bilabial closures, producing the notorious ``leaky mouth'' artifact. A key difficulty is that brief, discrete articulatory events are inferred from a continuous acoustic embedding under a regression objective, which biases predictions toward averaged mouth configurations. While modern self-supervised speech encoders provide rich prosodic and phonetic cues, they do not provide an explicit, frame-aligned linguistic target that reliably disambiguates closure-level events. We propose \textbf{Phoneme-Driven Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS)}, which augments a 3DGS talker with time-aligned phoneme tokens obtained from an automatic ASR and forced-alignment pipeline. Our core component, the \textbf{Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM)}, adaptively fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings through a learned gate, allowing the model to preserve smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. PD-GS is trained purely from monocular video using image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision. On HDTF, PD-GS achieves the best lip geometry among the compared baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences, yielding more linguistically faithful neural avatars.

AI.tldr: PD-GS enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting talking heads by integrating time-aligned phoneme tokens via a Linguistic Fusion Module, using adaptive gating to resolve the "leaky mouth" artifact and improve lip articulation accuracy, particularly for bilabial closures.
AI.motivation: 3DGS-based talking-head rendering suffers from over-smoothed mouth motion and "leaky mouth" artifacts because continuous acoustic embeddings under regression objectives bias predictions toward averaged configurations, lacking explicit frame-aligned linguistic targets to disambiguate closure-level articulatory events.
AI.method: PD-GS augments a 3DGS talker with time-aligned phoneme tokens from an automatic ASR and forced-alignment pipeline. The Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM) adaptively fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings via a learned gate, preserving smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. Training uses only monocular video with image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision.
AI.result: On the HDTF benchmark, PD-GS achieves the best lip geometry among baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences.
AI.conclusion: Integrating explicit, time-aligned phoneme supervision via an adaptive fusion mechanism significantly improves articulatory precision in 3DGS-based talking-head rendering, yielding more linguistically faithful neural avatars.

title: "I don't know anything about laptops!" - User Perception of Digital Product Advisors Adapting to Their Knowledge Levels
summary: Conversational commerce uses digital assistants to support the search process and decision-making in e-commerce. Effective communication in these interactions can be facilitated by assistants adapting their communication style to users and supporting shared understanding. An open challenge in this context is adapting the presentation of complex product information to users with varying levels of domain knowledge. To investigate strategies for such knowledge-level adaptation, we set up a chatbot-assisted laptop search scenario. In a between-subjects experiment (n = 251), we examined novice and expert perceptions of product attribute recommendations presented as technical information only (T), or augmented with performance categories (TC), attribute explanations (TE), or both (TCE). For novices, approaches with explanations (TE, TCE) were perceived as more helpful and led to higher perceived learning than those without. Novices also rated the combined approach (TCE) more appropriate than the baseline (T) and TC in terms of information quantity, indicating that explanations are crucial to understand and benefit from performance categories. Critically, experts showed no significant differences across conditions, suggesting that providing supplementary information beneficial to novices did not detract from their experience. We distill these findings into four concrete design guidelines for inclusive text-based product advisors in technical domains: use TCE by default; keep a single inclusive interface; avoid standalone categories; and support user agency and personalize to the stated use case.

AI.tldr: A study comparing strategies for adapting product information to users' domain knowledge in conversational commerce found that augmenting technical specs with explanations and performance categories helps novices without harming experts, yielding four design guidelines for inclusive chatbot interfaces.
AI.motivation: Conversational commerce assistants struggle to present complex product information effectively to users with varying domain expertise. The key open challenge is how to adapt communication—specifically product attribute recommendations—to different knowledge levels so that both novices and experts can make informed decisions without either group being disadvantaged.
AI.method: A between-subjects experiment (n=251) using a chatbot-assisted laptop search scenario. Participants (novices and experts) were assigned to one of four conditions: technical information only (T), technical + performance categories (TC), technical + explanations (TE), or technical + both categories and explanations (TCE). Perceived helpfulness, perceived learning, and information quantity appropriateness were measured across conditions.
AI.result: For novices, conditions with explanations (TE, TCE) were perceived as more helpful and produced higher perceived learning than T or TC alone. Novices also rated TCE as more appropriate in information quantity than T and TC, suggesting explanations are essential to leverage performance categories. Experts showed no significant differences across any conditions, indicating that supplementary information for novices did not degrade expert experience.
AI.conclusion: Four design guidelines for inclusive text-based product advisors in technical domains: (1) use TCE (technical + categories + explanations) by default; (2) maintain a single inclusive interface rather than separate versions; (3) avoid presenting performance categories without accompanying explanations; and (4) support user agency and personalize to the stated use case.

title: A Modular Workflow for Multimodal Reading Experiments
comment: In Proceedings of the 30th International Conference on Knowledge-Based and Intelligent Information & Engineering Systems
summary: We introduce a web-based modular workflow for real-time multimodal experiments in naturalistic online reading. The workflow integrates eye tracking, EEG, and interaction data from mouse and keyboard, synchronizes them via Lab Streaming Layer, and links gaze to browser-based text at the word, sentence, and AOI levels. It is designed as a reusable experimental procedure that can be adapted to different sensors, tasks, and analysis goals. As a use case, we apply the workflow to a study of selective exposure in online news search and reading. During the experiment, gaze-derived measures are computed online, while EEG and other synchronized streams are processed immediately after task sessions based on fixation-triggered segmentation. The resulting behavioral, neural, and linguistic metrics support selecting text passages for targeted post-task rating or labelling within the same lab session. The workflow thus provides a general basis for multimodal research on reading and related cognitive processes, and supports the empirical validation, in ecological contexts, of constructs that are typically operationalised through self-report measures.

AI.tldr: A reusable web-based workflow integrating eye tracking, EEG, and interaction data for real-time multimodal experiments in naturalistic online reading, demonstrated through a selective exposure study in news search.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between controlled lab paradigms and ecologically valid online reading research by enabling synchronized, real-time multimodal data collection (eye tracking, EEG, interaction data) within naturalistic browser-based reading tasks, and to support empirical validation of constructs typically reliant on self-report.
AI.method: A modular web-based workflow using Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) for synchronization. Gaze is linked to browser text at word, sentence, and AOI levels. Online gaze-derived measures are computed during experiments; EEG and other streams are segmented post-task via fixation-triggered segmentation. The pipeline is adaptable to different sensors, tasks, and analysis goals.
AI.result: The workflow was successfully applied to a selective exposure study in online news search and reading. Behavioral, neural, and linguistic metrics were derived and used to select text passages for targeted post-task rating/labelling within the same lab session, demonstrating closed-loop experimental capability.
AI.conclusion: The workflow provides a general, reusable foundation for multimodal reading research in ecological contexts, enabling the empirical validation of psychological constructs beyond traditional self-report measures through synchronized behavioral, neural, and linguistic data streams.

title: From Siloed Algorithms to Compliance-First Agentic Platforms: A Multi-Layered Architecture for Hospital AI Systems
summary: Hospitals are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence for triage, imaging, scheduling etc., yet most deployments remain isolated point solutions locked inside departmental silos, resulting in duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value. Despite explosive growth of AI in healthcare market and accelerating investment, an estimated 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale, largely due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints. This research proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first, Agentic AI architecture with multiple interoperable layers, extending existing hospital AI platform models with: (i) an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows across clinical, operational, and financial domains, (ii) a Compliance and Policy Layer that centralizes policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, DISHA Act, India's DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC security and safety standards, and (iii) a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric that plugs federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into real-world Hospital Information Management System (HIMS) flows. Using a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open, ready-to-deploy prototype implementation, this study demonstrates the end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access. The resulting architecture offers hospital leaders a pragmatic blueprint to move from ad hoc tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform that can be tailored to on-premise, hybrid and cloud-native deployments.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first, Agentic AI architecture with interoperable layers (Agent Orchestration, Compliance/Policy, Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric) to address healthcare AI scaling failures. Demonstrated via synthetic dataset and prototype, showing reduced turnaround times and manual documentation while maintaining policy-guarded data access.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid AI adoption in hospitals and accelerating investment, 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints. Most deployments remain isolated point solutions in departmental silos, leading to duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value.
AI.method: The authors propose a multi-layer Agentic AI architecture extending existing hospital AI platforms with: (i) an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows across clinical, operational, and financial domains; (ii) a Compliance and Policy Layer centralizing policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, EU AI Act, DISHA Act, India's DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC standards; and (iii) a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric incorporating federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into HIMS flows. Validation uses a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open, deployable prototype for end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging.
AI.result: The prototype demonstrated end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access.
AI.conclusion: The architecture provides hospital leaders a pragmatic blueprint to transition from ad hoc AI tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform, deployable across on-premise, hybrid, and cloud-native environments.

title: Mapping the Emerging Curriculum for AI-Assisted Software Engineering via Syllabus Analysis
summary: As Generative AI coding tools reshape professional software development, universities have begun designing courses to prepare students for AI-assisted development workflows. By analyzing the syllabi of these courses, we can gather empirical evidence about these courses, reveal how this emerging curricular area is being defined, and gain guidance for future curriculum design. We analyzed 23 publicly available syllabi and course materials of upper-division, credit-bearing courses that meet specific criteria, including explicitly addressing Generative AI in software engineering. Through iterative qualitative coding, we characterized courses' learning objectives, assessments, topics, and documented AI tools. Our analysis reveals commonalities and differences among these courses that allow researchers and educators to study and develop future courses.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 23 publicly available syllabi of upper-division university courses that explicitly integrate Generative AI into software engineering, using qualitative coding to characterize learning objectives, assessments, topics, and AI tools, revealing how this emerging curricular area is being defined.
AI.motivation: As Generative AI coding tools reshape professional software development, universities are designing courses to prepare students for AI-assisted workflows. However, there is little empirical evidence on how these courses are structured. Analyzing syllabi provides insight into how this new curricular area is taking shape and offers guidance for future curriculum design.
AI.method: The authors collected and analyzed 23 publicly available syllabi and course materials from upper-division, credit-bearing courses that explicitly address Generative AI in software engineering. They applied iterative qualitative coding to systematically characterize the courses across four dimensions: learning objectives, assessments, topics, and documented AI tools.
AI.result: The analysis uncovered both commonalities and differences among the surveyed courses. These patterns reveal how instructors are currently defining and operationalizing AI-assisted software engineering education, providing an empirical baseline for understanding this emerging field.
AI.conclusion: The findings offer a foundational reference for researchers and educators to study, compare, and design future courses on Generative AI in software engineering, helping to mature this nascent curricular area.

title: Quantifying Bitcoin Network Resilience Through Critical Scenario Discovery: A Dual-Layer Framework for Discovering Contentious Fork Conditions in Decentralized Consensus
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables, presented at Wyoming Bitcoin Research Institute Workshop July 2026
summary: Bitcoin's consensus depends not only on protocol rules but on the emergent behavior of a heterogeneous network of nodes with divergent economic stakes. Whether a contentious soft fork resolves cleanly or fractures into a persistent chain split is difficult to predict analytically but can be explored through controlled experimentation. This paper applies Scenario Discovery, an ensemble-simulation methodology using the Patient Rule Induction Method (PRIM), to identify the configuration regions that produce contentious fork outcomes. Using Warnet to run real bitcoind nodes across 1,330 valid scenarios spanning economic weight, mining-pool commitment, pool ideology, hashrate, and difficulty-retarget regime, we identify the parameter thresholds separating clean resolution from contested split. We show that economic weight distribution across a partition, not hashrate majority, is the primary determinant of resolution under Bitcoin's operational retarget interval and moderate price divergence. Three findings follow: an economic-support floor (0.45-0.50) and override ceiling (0.78-0.82) bound the contested space, with an Economic Self-Sustaining Point (0.74) between them; a pool-commitment "flip-point" (0.214 of committed hashrate) at which committing the largest pool to the upgrading chain paradoxically reverses the outcome; and outcomes resolve on two independent layers, hashrate and economic adoption, governed by different parameters. Individual user nodes show no detectable influence on fork outcomes under the modeled economic weightings. We close with three monitoring questions, answerable from public data, that translate these thresholds into operational guidance.

AI.tldr: Using ensemble simulations of real bitcoind nodes across 1,330 scenarios, this paper identifies precise economic-weight and pool-commitment thresholds that govern whether contentious Bitcoin soft forks resolve cleanly or fracture. Economic weight distribution — not hashrate majority — is the primary determinant, and a paradoxical flip-point exists where committing the largest pool reverses the intended outcome.
AI.motivation: Bitcoin consensus emerges from heterogeneous nodes with divergent economic stakes, and predicting whether a contentious soft fork resolves cleanly or fractures into a persistent chain split is analytically difficult. The authors aim to move beyond speculation by systematically identifying the parameter thresholds that determine fork outcomes.
AI.method: The paper applies Scenario Discovery using the Patient Rule Induction Method (PRIM), an ensemble-simulation methodology. Using Warnet to run real bitcoind nodes, the authors execute 1,330 valid scenarios spanning five dimensions: economic weight distribution, mining-pool commitment, pool ideology, hashrate, and difficulty-retarget regime. PRIM is used to identify configuration regions (parameter thresholds) that produce contentious fork outcomes.
AI.result: Three key findings emerge: (1) An economic-support floor (0.45–0.50) and override ceiling (0.78–0.82) bound the contested space, with an Economic Self-Sustaining Point at 0.74 between them; (2) a pool-commitment "flip-point" at 0.214 of committed hashrate, where committing the largest pool to the upgrading chain paradoxically reverses the outcome; and (3) fork outcomes resolve on two independent layers — hashrate and economic adoption — governed by different parameters. Economic weight distribution, not hashrate majority, is the primary determinant of resolution. Individual user nodes show no detectable influence.
AI.conclusion: The authors translate the identified thresholds into three operational monitoring questions answerable from public data, providing practical guidance for assessing contentious fork risks. The findings suggest that economic weight distribution across partitions is the dominant factor in fork resolution under Bitcoin's normal retarget interval and moderate price divergence.

title: PoolBench: A Benchmark for Pooling Strategies in Concept Representation Evaluation for Decoder-Only LLMs
summary: Pooling is a consequential but under-examined design choice in decoder-only concept representation work: practitioners must collapse token-level hidden states into a passage-level vector, yet no shared protocol exists for comparing this choice across concepts, models, and tasks. Reported gains are confounded by simultaneous changes in dataset, layer, construction method, and pooling rule, making principled decisions impossible. We introduce PoolBench, a benchmark that isolates pooling as the experimental variable under a fixed evaluation protocol. PoolBench covers 17 concepts, 19 pooling strategies, and 3 open-weight decoder-only models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B), evaluated on a single audited corpus of 37,693 real-text passages. The primary axis is linear separability (D1/AUROC); steered concept prevalence (D2/SCP) and output-level disentanglement (D3) serve as diagnostic axes. The primary finding is decisive: W4_hierarchical reaches a cross-model mean AUROC of 0.7799, while the widely adopted P1_last_token baseline reaches only 0.7640 and is statistically significantly worse (Friedman+Nemenyi, p = 2.0e-36; 77 significant pairs among 18 effective strategies). Rankings are stable across layers (rho = 0.961--0.990). A key negative result: strong detection does not imply strong steering -- D2 and D3 are substantially weaker than D1 for most concepts, indicating a fundamental representational limit rather than a pooling failure. On mid-difficulty concepts, W4_hierarchical outperforms P1_last_token by 0.042--0.113 AUROC; construction method choice (DiffMean vs. REPE) has a larger effect (delta AUROC 0.15) than pooling (delta AUROC 0.016), establishing the correct practical hierarchy. We release the corpus, pre-extracted activations, scorer models, steering vectors, and evaluation code as a reusable protocol for pooling research.

AI.tldr: PoolBench isolates pooling strategy as the sole experimental variable across 17 concepts, 19 pooling methods, and 3 open-weight LLMs. W4_hierarchical pooling significantly outperforms the common P1_last_token baseline (AUROC 0.7799 vs. 0.7640). Critically, strong concept detection does not translate to strong concept steering, revealing a fundamental representational limit. Construction method choice (DiffMean vs. REPE) matters more than pooling choice.
AI.motivation: Prior work on decoder-only concept representation conflates pooling choice with dataset, layer, construction method, and evaluation protocol, making it impossible to determine which pooling strategies actually work best. No shared benchmark or protocol exists for isolating and comparing pooling rules.
AI.method: PoolBench evaluates 19 pooling strategies on 17 concepts across Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B using a fixed corpus of 37,693 real-text passages. The primary axis is linear separability (D1, measured by AUROC). Diagnostic axes include steered concept prevalence (D2/SCP) and output-level disentanglement (D3). Statistical significance is assessed via Friedman+Nemenyi tests. Rank stability across layers is measured by Spearman's rho.
AI.result: W4_hierarchical achieves the best cross-model mean AUROC (0.7799), significantly outperforming P1_last_token (0.7640, p=2.0e-36). Rankings are stable across layers (rho=0.961–0.990). However, D2 and D3 substantially underperform D1 for most concepts, indicating detection ≠ steering. Construction method (DiffMean vs. REPE) has a larger effect (ΔAUROC ≈ 0.15) than pooling (ΔAUROC ≈ 0.016), establishing the correct practical hierarchy of design choices.
AI.conclusion: Pooling matters but less than construction method. W4_hierarchical is the recommended pooling strategy. The detection–steering gap (D1 >> D2/D3) reveals a fundamental representational limit in current concept representation methods. PoolBench provides the first standardized protocol for pooling research, with all artifacts released for reproducibility.

title: An Emerging Retail Portfolio Management Application: Personalized, Tax-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Natural Language Goals
summary: Retail investors lack access to the kind of personalized, tax-aware portfolio management that institutional clients take for granted -- existing robo-advisors use static, rule-based allocation, and institutional-grade systems require account minimums and technology stacks unavailable to individual investors. We present a fully built, integration-tested application that closes this gap: a FastAPI backend and web dashboard that let a user describe an investment goal in plain language (e.g. "I want steady growth but need to sell some shares next month for a down payment"), routes that goal to one of six investment mandates, and produces a live, broker-integrated portfolio recommendation from athree-phase reinforcement learning system -- a self-supervised cross-asset encoder, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) allocation policy with a learned intent router, and a lightweight LoRA adapter that personalizes recommendations from an individual's revealed brokerage behavior without retraining the shared model. The system is functionally complete and integration-tested end-to-end against a live brokerage API (Alpaca, paper-trading mode), including multi-user authentication, a trust first preview-before-apply confirmation flow, daily email digests, and an auditable action-integrity chain, but has not yet been opened to real end-users; we report this honestly as an emerging, pre-deployment application with a concrete path to full deployment, alongside 14-day walk-forward backtests (bootstrapped confidence intervals included) as preliminary, pre-deployment validation rather than production performance. We also report several practical engineering lessons -- silently-inactive integration paths, hanging third-party API calls, and the value of end-to-end empirical verification over trusting checkpoint metadata -- that we believe generalize to other applied RL systems built on external, live data sources.

AI.tldr: A fully built, integration-tested application that provides personalized, tax-aware portfolio management for retail investors using a three-phase RL system with a FastAPI backend, web dashboard, and live broker integration, validated through 14-day walk-forward backtests.
AI.motivation: Retail investors lack access to personalized, tax-aware portfolio management that institutional clients enjoy. Existing robo-advisors use static, rule-based allocation, while institutional systems have prohibitive account minimums and inaccessible technology stacks. This work aims to close that gap.
AI.method: The system comprises: (1) a FastAPI backend and web dashboard accepting plain-language investment goals, routed to one of six investment mandates; (2) a three-phase RL system incorporating a self-supervised cross-asset encoder, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) allocation policy with a learned intent router, and a lightweight LoRA adapter for personalization from revealed brokerage behavior without retraining the shared model; (3) integration with Alpaca's live brokerage API (paper-trading mode) including multi-user authentication, preview-before-apply confirmation, daily email digests, and an auditable action-integrity chain. Validation uses 14-day walk-forward backtests with bootstrapped confidence intervals.
AI.result: The system is functionally complete and integration-tested end-to-end but has not yet been deployed to real end-users. Preliminary 14-day walk-forward backtests with bootstrapped confidence intervals are reported as pre-deployment validation, not production performance. Several practical engineering lessons are also reported, including silently-inactive integration paths, hanging third-party API calls, and the value of end-to-end empirical verification over trusting checkpoint metadata.
AI.conclusion: The application demonstrates a viable architecture for bringing institutional-grade, personalized, tax-aware portfolio management to retail investors via RL and broker integration. It is reported honestly as an emerging, pre-deployment system with a concrete path to full deployment. The engineering lessons generalize to other applied RL systems relying on external, live data sources.

title: When Privileged Guidance Misaligns: State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents
summary: Privileged on-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multi-turn agents by allowing a synchronized teacher to re-score the student's response at every turn with access to training-only references, such as successful trajectories. In interactive environments, however, the student's preceding actions continually change the execution state. As the student takes different actions or completes subgoals in a different order, its rollout may reach states not covered by the reference, making the reference an unreliable source of guidance for the state actually reached. Applying privileged distillation indiscriminately therefore creates state--reference mismatch. This mismatch motivates a central objective: providing privileged reference guidance that remains compatible with the student's current execution state. We introduce State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation (SMRC-SD), which explicitly determines when and how a privileged trajectory should guide an on-policy student. At each turn, SMRC-SD verifies whether the student's current execution state matches a supported state along the reference trajectory. Distillation is applied only at matched states, filtering out turns for which the reference lacks locally compatible guidance. For each matched state, SMRC-SD further constructs state-conditioned teacher context from the successful trajectory, grounding supervision in the state actually reached. Across ALFWorld and WebShop, SMRC-SD consistently outperforms unconditional successful full-path distillation. With Qwen3-1.7B, it improves task success from $0.746$ to $0.865$ on ALFWorld and from $0.574$ to $0.693$ on WebShop. Controlled routing and context ablations support both selecting locally supported turns and constructing state-compatible teacher context as contributors to these gains. Code is available at https://github.com/liujunzhuo/SMRC-SD.

AI.tldr: SMRC-SD addresses state–reference mismatch in privileged on-policy distillation for multi-turn agents by applying teacher guidance only at states matching the reference trajectory and using state-conditioned context, leading to significant task success improvements on ALFWorld and WebShop.
AI.motivation: In interactive multi-turn environments, a student agent's divergent actions lead to states not covered by privileged reference trajectories. Indiscriminate privileged distillation creates state–reference mismatch, where the reference becomes unreliable guidance for the student's actual state.
AI.method: SMRC-SD (State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation): (1) verifies at each turn whether the student's state matches a supported state along the reference trajectory; (2) applies distillation only at matched states, filtering out mismatched turns; (3) constructs state-conditioned teacher context from the successful trajectory for each matched state.
AI.result: With Qwen3-1.7B, SMRC-SD improves task success from 0.746→0.865 on ALFWorld and 0.574→0.693 on WebShop, consistently outperforming unconditional full-path distillation. Ablations confirm both routing and context construction contribute.
AI.conclusion: Selectively applying privileged distillation only at state-matched turns with state-compatible context effectively resolves state–reference mismatch, yielding substantial gains in multi-turn interactive agent training.

title: Beyond Top-K: Replacing Black-Box Retrieval with Interpretable Agentic Operations
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation over long documents is dominated by one design: chunk the text, embed the chunks, and surface the top-k nearest neighbours of the query. We argue that for an important class of documents -- financial statements, audit reports, regulatory returns -- this design is structurally unsound, and we make the argument measurable. On a 780-page government financial report, 86.8% of content lines are table rows, thousands of near-identical figures compete in one embedding space, and a figure inherits its unit from a header a median of 13 lines above it -- so a chunk boundary routinely separates a number from whether it is in lakh or crore, an error of two orders of magnitude. A table-aware chunker built as a steelman fixes the unit problem but leaves 27-30% of numeric chunks with no fiscal-year header at every chunk size we tried. We propose READ (Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search), in which an agent reads the raw document through three deterministic operations -- normalized lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads -- exposed over the Model Context Protocol, so a trajectory is a replayable audit trail, not an opaque similarity score. On 51 verified questions READ answers 58.8% against dense retrieval's 15.7% (p_Holm = 2 x 10^-5) -- or 35.3% tuned, which READ still leads by 23.5 points (p_Holm = 0.017). An agent given the same loop but a top-k tool reaches only 27.5%, locating the gain in the interface rather than in iteration. We also report what the evidence does not support: BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ, so our result separates embedding-based from embedding-free retrieval, not agentic from lexical search.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the dominant chunk-and-embed paradigm for retrieval-augmented generation over long documents, demonstrating it is structurally unsound for financial reports where table rows dominate and chunk boundaries sever numbers from their units. The authors propose READ, an embedding-free agentic search system using deterministic operations over the Model Context Protocol, which significantly outperforms dense retrieval on a financial document QA benchmark.
AI.motivation: Dense retrieval over chunked documents fails systematically on financial statements because: (1) 86.8% of content lines are table rows, (2) near-identical figures compete in embedding space, and (3) chunk boundaries routinely separate a number from its unit header (e.g., lakh vs. crore), producing errors of two orders of magnitude. The authors argue this design is structurally unsound for this document class and seek to quantify and remedy the failure.
AI.method: The authors propose READ (Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search), where an agent reads the raw document through three deterministic operations exposed via the Model Context Protocol: normalized lexical search, structural navigation (table-aware traversal), and bounded span reads. This produces a replayable audit trail rather than an opaque similarity score. They also construct a table-aware chunker as a "steelman" baseline to isolate and measure the unit-separation problem, and evaluate against dense retrieval, BM25, and an agent equipped with a top-k tool on 51 verified questions from a 780-page government financial report.
AI.result: On 51 verified questions, READ achieves 58.8% accuracy versus dense retrieval's 15.7% (p_Holm = 2×10⁻⁵) and versus tuned dense retrieval's 35.3% (still a 23.5-point lead, p_Holm = 0.017). An agent with a top-k loop reaches only 27.5%, locating the gain in the interface rather than iteration. The table-aware chunker leaves 27–30% of numeric chunks without fiscal-year headers regardless of chunk size. BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ, meaning the result separates embedding-based from embedding-free retrieval, not agentic from lexical search.
AI.conclusion: For table-heavy, structured financial documents, embedding-free deterministic search (READ) decisively outperforms embedding-based dense retrieval. The performance gain stems from the interface design (structural navigation + bounded spans) rather than iterative agentic reasoning. BM25's statistical parity with READ suggests the core finding is about the embedding vs. non-embedding distinction, not agentic vs. lexical methods.

title: PoseForge: Editable Pose Analytics for AI-Assisted Sports Coaching
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. To appear in IEEE VIS 2026
summary: Athletic coaching increasingly relies on video analysis, yet raw footage lacks tools to quantify motion or simulate valid technique corrections. Drawing on formative interviews with eleven cricket experts (coaches, performance analysts, captains, and players), we introduce PoseForge, a visual analytics system that extracts 3D skeletal poses from single-camera sports videos for interactive movement analysis. In a cricket batting case study, PoseForge computes interpretable kinematic metrics such as feet gap and elbow angle, compares them against scientifically derived norms, and uses an AI coach to suggest targeted adjustments, presented visually and through natural-language feedback (e.g., "increase feet gap by 10 cm"). Users can directly modify poses via mouse interaction or natural-language instructions, with inverse kinematics maintaining anatomical plausibility and real-time updates of metrics and comparisons. An evaluation with the same eleven cricket experts found PoseForge effective for diagnosing movement issues and exploring corrective alternatives, highlighting its applicability in low-resource, academy, and grassroots coaching settings, while identifying opportunities for enhanced sport-specific metrics and longitudinal tracking. PoseForge is available as open-source software at https://github.com/DataVisards/PoseForge.

AI.tldr: PoseForge is a visual analytics system that extracts 3D skeletal poses from single-camera sports videos, computes kinematic metrics, compares them against normative data, and uses an AI coach to suggest corrections — all with direct pose manipulation via mouse or natural language — validated through a cricket case study with eleven domain experts.
AI.motivation: Raw sports video footage lacks quantitative tools for motion analysis and simulation of valid corrective techniques. Coaches at academy and grassroots levels, particularly in low-resource settings, need accessible methods to diagnose movement flaws and explore corrective alternatives without expensive multi-camera motion capture systems.
AI.method: The authors conducted formative interviews with eleven cricket experts (coaches, performance analysts, captains, players) to inform design. PoseForge extracts 3D skeletal poses from single-camera video, computes interpretable kinematic metrics (e.g., feet gap, elbow angle), and compares them against scientifically derived norms. An AI coach module generates targeted adjustments with natural-language feedback. Users can interactively modify poses via mouse or natural-language instructions, with inverse kinematics enforcing anatomical plausibility and real-time metric updates.
AI.result: Evaluation with the same eleven cricket experts demonstrated that PoseForge is effective for diagnosing movement issues and exploring corrective alternatives. The system was deemed particularly suitable for low-resource, academy, and grassroots coaching settings. The study also identified opportunities for richer sport-specific metrics and longitudinal athlete tracking.
AI.conclusion: PoseForge successfully bridges the gap between raw video footage and quantitative, interactive movement analysis for cricket coaching. By combining 3D pose extraction, kinematic norm comparison, AI-driven feedback, and direct pose manipulation, it offers a practical tool for resource-constrained environments. The open-source release encourages further development and adaptation to other sports.

title: Escaping the Self-Repair Trap: Improving Test Oracle Generation via Dual-Context Awareness
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for regression-oracle completion, where a test prefix is given and the current program version is treated as expected behavior. Recent approaches increasingly rely on iterative self-repair and execution feedback, but optimizing execution success does not necessarily yield strong fault-revealing oracles. This objective, widely adopted in repair-based methods, serves only as a proxy and may be misaligned with the true goal of oracle generation. Such misalignment biases the repair process, giving rise to a feedback-driven degeneration that we term the Self-Repair Trap, where iterative repair progressively drives models toward assertions that are easier to satisfy but less effective at detecting faults. To address this issue, we propose DCAware, a computationally efficient, non-iterative framework that prioritizes high signal-to-noise contextual grounding over multi-round repair. DCAware integrates structured static context with selectively retrieved dynamic states, enabling precise and robust oracle generation without iterative feedback loops. Extensive experiments based on execution and mutation testing show that DCAware consistently improves fault-revealing effectiveness while maintaining high execution success, outperforming prior methods with substantially lower computational cost. Our results suggest that improving contextual quality is more effective than adding iterative repair complexity in the studied regression-oracle setting.

AI.tldr: DCAware proposes a non-iterative framework for LLM-based regression oracle generation that avoids the "Self-Repair Trap" — where iterative repair loops bias models toward easy-to-satisfy but fault-insensitive assertions. By grounding generation in structured static context and selective dynamic states, DCAware achieves better fault-revealing effectiveness and lower computational cost than iterative self-repair methods.
AI.motivation: Iterative self-repair with execution feedback is widely used for LLM-based regression oracle completion, but optimizing for execution success is a proxy objective misaligned with the true goal of generating fault-revealing oracles. This misalignment causes a "Self-Repair Trap": repair loops progressively degenerate assertions toward those trivially satisfied yet ineffective at detecting faults, undermining oracle quality.
AI.method: DCAware is a computationally efficient, non-iterative framework that prioritizes high signal-to-noise contextual grounding. It integrates structured static context (e.g., code structure, type information) with selectively retrieved dynamic execution states, enabling precise oracle generation in a single pass without iterative feedback.
AI.result: Extensive experiments using execution-based and mutation-testing metrics show DCAware consistently improves fault-revealing effectiveness while maintaining high execution success rates. It outperforms prior iterative self-repair methods at substantially lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: In the regression-oracle setting, improving contextual quality is more effective than adding iterative repair complexity. DCAware demonstrates that a well-grounded, non-iterative approach can surpass multi-round repair methods in both accuracy and efficiency.

title: Exploring Privacy Leakage and Data Disclosure Violations in the MacOS Application Ecosystem
summary: The systematic and excessive data collection practices of tech companies have rendered online privacy both a necessity and a sought-after commodity. However, while the privacy risks of the web, mobile, and IoT ecosystems have been extensively examined, desktop environments have been largely overlooked. As desktop apps continue to be widely used, they remain a critical yet understudied dimension of user privacy. In this paper, we address this gap by presenting the first, to our knowledge, comprehensive study of the mechanisms designed to regulate and disclose data collection and sharing practices in the macOS ecosystem. We adopt an app-development-centric view, and shed light on the interactions between the various macOS mechanisms that mediate apps' data access. Driven by our findings, we develop NutriScan, an analysis framework that incorporates both static and dynamic analysis techniques to create a consolidated view of macOS apps' data practices and disclosures. We use our system to dynamically analyze 1K macOS apps, and find that 85% of them access user-data APIs without disclosing it. 49.7% also exfiltrate data to advertising entities and hosting providers, 12.5% of which do so without a corresponding disclosure. We find that desktop apps are being leveraged by online trackers to enrich user profiles and device fingerprints, thus shedding new light on the true scope of the online tracking ecosystem. Our analysis reveals how the macOS app ecosystem is comprised of disjoint mechanisms with divergent data abstractions, thus increasing complexity for developers while also facilitating undisclosed privacy-invasive practices. Accordingly, we propose a series of mitigations that aim to both streamline the data disclosure process for developers and improve Apple's app vetting process.

AI.tldr: First comprehensive study of macOS data collection mechanisms, revealing that 85% of 1K analyzed apps access user data without disclosure, with 49.7% exfiltrating data to advertisers. The authors develop NutriScan, a hybrid static/dynamic analysis framework, and propose mitigations for Apple's ecosystem.
AI.motivation: While privacy risks in web, mobile, and IoT ecosystems have been extensively studied, the desktop app ecosystem — particularly macOS — remains critically under-examined despite widespread usage. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically investigating the mechanisms that regulate and disclose data collection practices on macOS.
AI.method: The authors develop NutriScan, an analysis framework combining static and dynamic analysis techniques to produce a consolidated view of macOS apps' data practices and disclosures. They adopt an app-development-centric perspective to examine interactions between macOS mechanisms that mediate data access, then dynamically analyze 1,000 macOS applications.
AI.result: 85% of analyzed macOS apps access user-data APIs without proper disclosure. 49.7% exfiltrate data to advertising entities and hosting providers, with 12.5% doing so without any corresponding disclosure. Desktop apps are actively leveraged by online trackers to enrich user profiles and device fingerprints, expanding the known scope of the tracking ecosystem. The macOS privacy framework is fragmented with disjoint mechanisms and divergent data abstractions.
AI.conclusion: The macOS app ecosystem suffers from disjoint privacy mechanisms that increase developer complexity while enabling undisclosed privacy-invasive practices. The authors propose mitigations to streamline data disclosure for developers and strengthen Apple's app vetting process.

title: Where Privacy Risk Lives in English-Source Multilingual RAG: A Stage-Decomposed Audit Across Five Query Languages
summary: A common assumption holds that switching to a non-English language makes a multilingual RAG system easier to attack for personal information. We test this on an English-source synthetic-PII corpus with five query languages and a two-stage defence (LLM input judge + regex output filter), in a pipeline whose translator, judge, back-translator, and generator are all Qwen2.5-7B -- so every finding below is pipeline-conditional, not a causal ranking of language-inherent risk. Under output-only filtering, English has the highest observed unstructured-PII leak rate; only English-vs-Swahili separates cleanly under document-level bootstrap intervals. Once the input judge is added, residual leaks remain on Arabic and Swahili, and back-translating the query does not close the gap (an ablation we report but cannot use as a causal diagnostic, since the back-translator is also Qwen). On a separate n=17 multilingual-prompted-judge residual corner, attaching the gold corpus document to the input judge blocks 15/17 residual cells. We frame this last result as a mechanism diagnostic, not a deployable defence: it uses oracle retrieval, BLOCK/ALLOW rates are measured on adversarial queries only, and we measure no benign-query false-positive rate and no answer-utility cost. The supplementary material contains code, corpora, queries, and per-trial JSONLs; the priority follow-up is an independent-MT plus non-Qwen-judge replication with a native-speaker query set, scoped in the Limitations section.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether non-English queries increase PII leakage in multilingual RAG systems, finding that under Qwen2.5-7B pipeline conditions, English unexpectedly shows the highest leak rate; adding an input judge reduces but doesn't eliminate leaks for Arabic/Swahili, and oracle document attachment blocks most residual leaks.
AI.motivation: Challenge the common assumption that non-English languages make multilingual RAG systems more vulnerable to personal information extraction attacks, by empirically testing leakage rates across different query languages under a controlled pipeline.
AI.method: Uses an English-source synthetic-PII corpus with five query languages, a two-stage defence (LLM input judge + regex output filter), with all pipeline components (translator, judge, back-translator, generator) being Qwen2.5-7B. Evaluates under output-only filtering, input-judge addition, back-translation ablation, and an oracle document-attachment diagnostic on a 17-cell multilingual residual corner.
AI.result: Under output-only filtering, English exhibits the highest unstructured-PII leak rate; only English vs. Swahili separates under bootstrap intervals. Adding the input judge leaves residual leaks on Arabic and Swahili; back-translation does not close the gap. Attaching the gold corpus document to the input judge blocks 15/17 residual cells in the diagnostic test.
AI.conclusion: The common assumption about non-English vulnerability is not supported under this Qwen2.5-7B pipeline; findings are pipeline-conditional, not causal language-risk rankings. The oracle-attachment result serves as a mechanism diagnostic rather than a deployable defence. Priority follow-up requires independent MT and non-Qwen judge replication with native-speaker queries.

title: Evaluating Machine Learning Models for Post-Wildfire Debris-Flow Prediction
summary: Prediction of post-wildfire debris flows is critical for mitigating hazards to communities, infrastructure, and resources during intense rainfall in recently burned areas. However, identifying reliable machine learning models is complicated by overlapping debris-flow and non-debris-flow events in feature space, the need for model interpretability, and limited training data. This paper addresses these challenges through a systematic evaluation of machine learning models in terms of predictive performance, feature importance, and synthetic data augmentation. Using basin-scale observations of post-wildfire debris-flow events across the western United States, we compare 15 models, including the Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN). Repeated stratified cross-validation shows that TabPFN achieves the highest unaugmented performance with a threat score of 0.637, closely followed by the best tree-based models. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are used to identify the features driving predictions, revealing that short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation consistently rank highest, while burn severity and terrain features contribute less. We further evaluate synthetic data augmentation using TabPFN-generated samples to address the scarcity of debris-flow observations. Synthetic augmentation improves the performance of all models except CNN, with the largest mean threat score increase of +0.041 among the deep learning models. By combining rigorous model benchmarking, interpretable feature analysis, and synthetic data augmentation, this work provides a comprehensive framework for improving post-wildfire debris-flow prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates 15 machine learning models for predicting post-wildfire debris flows, finding TabPFN achieves the best performance (threat score 0.637). SHAP analysis reveals short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation are dominant predictors, while synthetic data augmentation using TabPFN-generated samples boosts most models, especially deep learning approaches (+0.041 mean threat score increase).
AI.motivation: Post-wildfire debris-flow prediction is hindered by three key challenges: (1) overlapping feature distributions between debris-flow and non-debris-flow events, (2) the need for model interpretability in high-stakes hazard assessment, and (3) limited training data due to the rarity of well-documented post-wildfire debris-flow observations.
AI.method: The authors benchmark 15 machine learning models (including TabPFN and various tree-based and deep learning models) using basin-scale observations from the western United States. Repeated stratified cross-validation is employed for robust evaluation. SHAP is applied for feature importance analysis. Synthetic data augmentation is performed using TabPFN to generate artificial samples, and the impact on all models' performance is measured.
AI.result: TabPFN achieves the highest unaugmented threat score of 0.637, followed closely by tree-based models. SHAP analysis shows short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation are the most influential features, while burn severity and terrain features are less important. Synthetic augmentation improves all models except CNN, with deep learning models gaining the largest mean increase in threat score (+0.041).
AI.conclusion: The combination of rigorous model benchmarking, SHAP-based interpretability, and TabPFN-driven synthetic data augmentation provides a comprehensive and effective framework for improving post-wildfire debris-flow prediction, addressing both performance and data scarcity challenges.

title: Small Foundation Models of Human Cognition and Behaviour
comment: published as a conference paper at COLM'26
summary: Large language models fine-tuned on human behavioural data have emerged as general-purpose cognitive proxies, but the scale this requires, and whether these models process task structure or exploit statistical shortcuts, remain open questions. We train fourteen models from 135M to 14B parameters across four architecture families on Psych-101, a dataset of 10.7 million trial-level choices from 160 experiments. In-distribution, scale barely matters. The models fall within a narrow band, as though against a ceiling, and 0.6B to 1B parameters suffice to match a 70B baseline on held-out participants. Out-of-distribution, that band opens into a markedly steeper scaling gradient, with larger models clearly advantaged in generalisation to novel task structure. To determine what information these models use, we run two diagnostics. We progressively strip four prompt channels -- task instructions, experimental stimuli, outcome feedback, and choice history -- across 27 experiments, and permute trial order. Masking the content of stimuli and feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information and pushes models below chance, demonstrating that choice history alone does not account for performance. Permutation reveals invariance on tasks with independent trials but sensitivity where trial order is determined by prior responses. Small cognitively fine-tuned models therefore show promise as noise ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, though their scope remains bounded by the paradigms seen in training.

AI.tldr: The paper trains 14 models (135M–14B parameters) on 10.7M trial-level choices from 160 psychological experiments and finds that scale matters little in-distribution but substantially aids out-of-distribution generalization. Diagnostic ablations show models rely primarily on stimuli and feedback rather than choice-history shortcuts, and trial-order permutation reveals invariance for independent trials but sensitivity to sequential dependencies.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether scaling laws apply to cognitive fine-tuning, and to determine whether such models genuinely process task structure or merely exploit superficial statistical patterns (shortcuts).
AI.method: Fourteen models across four architecture families (135M to 14B parameters) are fine-tuned on Psych-101 (10.7M trial-level choices, 160 experiments). In-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization are evaluated. Two diagnostics are applied: (1) progressive stripping of four prompt channels (instructions, stimuli, feedback, choice history) across 27 experiments, and (2) permutation of trial order to test sensitivity to sequential dependencies.
AI.result: In-distribution performance saturates at 0.6B–1B parameters, matching a 70B baseline. Out-of-distribution reveals a steeper scaling gradient favoring larger models. Masking stimuli and feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information, pushing models below chance, ruling out reliance on choice history alone. Permutation shows invariance on independent-trial tasks but sensitivity when trial order depends on prior responses.
AI.conclusion: Small cognitively fine-tuned models can serve as noise-ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, but their generalization is bounded by the paradigms seen during training. Genuine task-structure processing is supported, not mere shortcut exploitation.

title: OneEmo: A Unified Multimodal Reasoning Model for Emotion Perception, Understanding, and Interaction
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in emotional intelligence. However, prevailing research predominantly focuses on task-specific specialization, often neglecting inter-task synergy and leaving latent reasoning potential underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce OneEmo, a unified affective generalist capable of mastering emotion perception, comprehension, and interaction. For this purpose, we first construct EmoWorld-130K, a comprehensive dataset that distills specialized affective knowledge into explicit reasoning trajectories via a human-in-the-loop workflow. Supervised fine-tuning on this corpus reveals significant mutual benefits derived from multi-task learning. Second, to fully unlock the latent reasoning potential, we propose Emo-Chord, a novel reinforcement learning strategy that stabilizes optimization through unified multi-task reward allocation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OneEmo achieves state-of-the-art performance against similarly sized baselines across most benchmarks. Notably, despite having significantly fewer parameters than commercial models, OneEmo delivers highly competitive results. This paper paves the way for more reliable and interpretable affective computing. The code is available at https://github.com/waHAHJIAHAO/OneEmo.

AI.tldr: OneEmo is a unified MLLM for affective computing that jointly handles emotion perception, comprehension, and interaction. It uses a multi-task dataset (EmoWorld-130K) with reasoning trajectories and a novel RL strategy (Emo-Chord) for multi-task reward allocation, achieving SOTA performance against similarly sized models.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM research in emotional intelligence is fragmented into task-specific models, neglecting the synergy between emotion-related tasks (perception, comprehension, interaction) and failing to exploit latent multi-task reasoning potential.
AI.method: (1) EmoWorld-130K: a human-in-the-loop dataset distilling specialized affective knowledge into explicit reasoning trajectories. (2) Supervised fine-tuning on this corpus for multi-task mutual benefits. (3) Emo-Chord: a reinforcement learning strategy with unified multi-task reward allocation to stabilize optimization and unlock latent reasoning.
AI.result: OneEmo achieves state-of-the-art performance on most benchmarks against similarly sized baselines, and delivers highly competitive results compared to commercial models despite having significantly fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: The unified multi-task approach with structured reasoning trajectories and coordinated RL optimization paves the way for more reliable and interpretable affective computing systems.

title: Expertise-Based Developer Assignment for Long-Term Software Components in Open-Source Projects
comment: Accepted at the Conference on Advanced Artificial Intelligence and Education (CAAIE 2026). 11 pages, 5 figures
summary: Open-source software development through GitHub has enabled countless software projects to be developed by developers from across the world. Assigning the right task to the right developer enables teams to work efficiently. Assigning a task which is not representative of a developer's expertise results in slower completion time and less maintainable code. Whilst much work has been done to automate this assignment for specific jobs, there is little work addressing the assignment of developers to expertise-specific long-term components of a new project. This paper produces a web application that models developers' expertise based on their previous Git commits and automatically assigns them to an optimal task within a new project. Testing showed that the system's speed varies depending on the back-end model used but server-side data caching improved worst-case speeds by a factor of 9.86. 72.4% of tasks had their target developer listed in the top 10, out of a possible 47.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a web application that models developer expertise from Git commit history to automatically assign developers to optimal tasks in new software projects. Testing shows 72.4% of assignments placed the target developer in the top 10 recommendations, and caching improved worst-case performance by 9.86×.
AI.motivation: Manual task assignment in open-source projects often mismatches developers' expertise, leading to slower completion times and less maintainable code. While automated assignment exists for specific short-term tasks (e.g., bug triaging), there is a gap in addressing long-term, expertise-specific component assignments when launching new projects.
AI.method: The authors built a web application that extracts developer expertise profiles from prior Git commits and uses a back-end model to match developers to tasks in a new project. Server-side data caching was employed to mitigate performance bottlenecks.
AI.result: Server-side caching improved worst-case speeds by a factor of 9.86. In evaluation, 72.4% of tasks had their correct target developer ranked within the top 10 recommendations, from a pool of 47 developers.
AI.conclusion: The system demonstrates that mining Git history is a viable basis for automated long-term task assignment in open-source projects, offering strong recommendation accuracy and acceptable runtime performance when caching is applied.

title: PromptShield Home: Ambient Multimodal Prompt Injection Defense for Smart-Home Agents
comment: This work has been accepted as a poster to UbiComp 2026
summary: Smart-home assistants increasingly use multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that perceive video and audio directly. This raises a safety question specific to the home: can the agent tell a genuine user command from ambient or externally-sourced content, television speech, on-screen text, or an overheard conversation, that merely looks like a command? We introduce PromptShield-Home, a pilot benchmark of realistic smart-home scenarios spanning addressee ambiguity, screen/audio injection, health-monitor false triggers, mixed occupancy, and a legitimate-command floor, and use it to compare three abstraction layers: traditional detectors (L0), a single MLLM agent (L1; vision, vision+ASR, and audio-visual), and multi-agent mediation (L2; voting, role specialists, cross-model arbitration). Because the label distribution is skewed toward inaction, aggregate accuracy is misleading, a constant always-block predictor scores 82%, so we report unsafe-execution and safe-completion rates separately. The two paradigms fail in opposite ways: detectors act on everything, while every MLLM configuration over-refuses, completing almost no genuine command and missing a true fall in every case. Crucially, their correct sets are disjoint: an oracle that always picks the right layer reaches 94.1%, against 76.5% for the best single layer. We report this as an upper bound, not a system - no router is implemented - and argue that home-agent safety is best served by learned routing and sensor fusion, not by replacing detectors with an MLLM.

AI.tldr: PromptShield-Home is a benchmark for smart-home MLLM agents evaluating whether they can distinguish genuine user commands from ambient/screen/injected content. The study finds that traditional detectors over-trigger while MLLMs over-refuse, and their correct predictions are disjoint — an oracle combining both layers reaches 94.1% accuracy, motivating learned routing and sensor fusion rather than outright MLLM replacement of detectors.
AI.motivation: Smart-home assistants increasingly deploy multimodal LLMs that directly perceive video and audio streams. This raises a critical home-specific safety question: can the agent discriminate a genuine user command from ambient or externally-sourced content — television speech, on-screen text, overheard conversations — that merely resembles a command? No existing benchmark systematically evaluates this addressee-ambiguity problem in realistic home settings.
AI.method: The authors introduce PromptShield-Home, a pilot benchmark covering five scenario classes: addressee ambiguity, screen/audio injection, health-monitor false triggers, mixed occupancy, and a legitimate-command floor. They evaluate three abstraction layers: (L0) traditional detectors, (L1) a single MLLM agent in three modalities (vision, vision+ASR, audio-visual), and (L2) multi-agent mediation strategies (voting, role specialists, cross-model arbitration). Given skewed label distribution (inaction dominates), they report unsafe-execution and safe-completion rates separately rather than aggregate accuracy. An oracle that selects the correct layer per instance establishes an upper bound.
AI.result: A constant always-block predictor achieves 82% aggregate accuracy due to class imbalance, rendering overall accuracy misleading. The two paradigms exhibit opposite failure modes: traditional detectors act on everything (high false-positive rate), while every MLLM configuration over-refuses, completing almost no genuine commands and missing a true fall in every case. Critically, the correct prediction sets are disjoint. The oracle achieves 94.1% versus 76.5% for the best single layer. No router is implemented — this is reported purely as an upper bound.
AI.conclusion: Home-agent safety is best served by learned routing and sensor fusion that combine detectors and MLLMs, rather than replacing detectors with an MLLM. The disjoint error profiles of the two paradigms suggest complementary strengths that a hybrid architecture could exploit.

title: Cross-Architecture Steering Transfer in Language Models: A Systematic Empirical Study
summary: Independently trained large language models may develop shared internal representations of semantic concepts despite architectural differences -- but whether this geometric similarity has functional consequences for cross-model behavioural control remains untested. We present the first systematic evaluation of cross-model steering transfer and show that shared LLM geometry is functionally exploitable, conditionally: concept directions from one model can steer a different independently trained model when sufficient representational capacity exists. We study five open-weight models spanning three parameter scales (0.8B--8B) and two architectural lineages, training one Sparse Autoencoder per model across 15 semantic domains and testing alignment across all 20 directed model pairs. We observe a suggestive discontinuity near 1.7B parameters: at >= 1.7B scale, 47--49% of cross-model feature pairs validate (Pearson r >= 0.60, Procrustes cosines 0.895--0.956), while alignment degrades sharply below 0.8B. Cross-model steering vectors (B3-TI) achieve a 71.0% win rate across 15 supervised concepts versus 68.0% for same-model native vectors; a single universal vector achieves 67.3% in 4 of 5 models without any per-model supervision. Transfer degrades for models below 1.7B and for one model with generation instability, confirming that functional exploitability requires sufficient representational capacity. Our findings underscore the importance of scale thresholds in mechanistic interpretability: tools validated at 7B scale may not transfer to smaller models without revalidation. We provide the first functional complement to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis -- geometric convergence across independently trained LLMs supports cross-model behavioural control without fine-tuning, under the identified scale conditions.

AI.tldr: Independently trained LLMs exhibit geometrically similar internal representations that can be functionally exploited for cross-model steering, but only above a critical scale threshold (~1.7B parameters). Below this, alignment and transfer degrade sharply. A single universal steering vector derived from one model can control multiple others without per-model supervision.
AI.motivation: While prior work (the Platonic Representation Hypothesis) suggests that independently trained models converge on shared representational geometries, whether this geometric similarity has functional consequences — specifically, enabling cross-model behavioral control via steering — remained untested. This paper aims to fill that gap with the first systematic evaluation.
AI.method: The authors study five open-weight LLMs across three parameter scales (0.8B–8B) and two architectural lineages. They train one Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) per model across 15 semantic domains, extract concept directions, and test alignment across all 20 directed model pairs using Pearson correlation and Procrustes cosine similarity. They then evaluate cross-model steering transfer by comparing same-model native steering vectors, cross-model vectors (B3-TI), and a single universal vector applied to multiple models.
AI.result: A discontinuity emerges near 1.7B parameters: at ≥1.7B, 47–49% of cross-model feature pairs validate (Pearson r ≥ 0.60, Procrustes cosines 0.895–0.956). Cross-model steering vectors achieve a 71.0% win rate across 15 supervised concepts vs. 68.0% for same-model vectors. A single universal vector achieves 67.3% in 4 of 5 models without per-model supervision. Alignment and transfer degrade below 1.7B and in one model with generation instability.
AI.conclusion: Shared LLM geometry is functionally exploitable for cross-model behavioral control, but only when sufficient representational capacity exists (≥~1.7B parameters).
