This identifies a scale threshold critical for mechanistic interpretability: tools validated at larger scales may not transfer downward without revalidation. The findings provide the first functional complement to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

title: Rectifying Geometric Misalignment: Online Source-Free Adaptation for Class-Imbalanced EEG
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) based Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) often require unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) to generalize across subjects and sessions. While Riemannian alignment methods like the Riemannian Centering Transformation (RCT) are effective for handling covariate shifts, they implicitly assume balanced class priors. However, in realistic online BCI scenarios, the label distributions vary dynamically (label shift), causing standard alignment techniques to geometrically misalign the target data distributions. In this work, we propose OSPDIM (Online SPD manifold information maximization), a source-free online UDA framework designed to address label shifts on the Riemannian manifold. OSPDIM introduces a manifold-constrained bias parameter into the tangent space mapping, which is optimized via information maximization to correct the geometric skew caused by imbalanced data streams. Unlike offline methods relying on global batch statistics, OSPDIM estimates and corrects geometric bias on-the-fly. Simulations on 2D SPD matrices visually demonstrate that OSPDIM successfully rectifies the misalignment where standard centering fails. Extensive experiments on multiple motor imagery datasets show that OSPDIM significantly outperforms standard Riemannian baselines, particularly in challenging online adaptation scenarios with severe class imbalance, offering a robust solution for practical, plug-and-play BCI systems.

AI.tldr: OSPDIM is a source-free online unsupervised domain adaptation method for EEG-based BCIs that corrects geometric misalignment on the Riemannian manifold caused by dynamically shifting class priors, outperforming standard Riemannian alignment under severe class imbalance.
AI.motivation: Existing Riemannian alignment methods like RCT assume balanced class priors, but real-world online BCI scenarios exhibit dynamic label shifts. These label shifts cause standard alignment techniques to geometrically misalign target data distributions, degrading cross-subject/session generalization.
AI.method: OSPDIM operates on the SPD (symmetric positive definite) manifold. It introduces a manifold-constrained bias parameter into the tangent space mapping and optimizes it online via information maximization to correct geometric skew from imbalanced data streams, without requiring source data or global batch statistics.
AI.result: 2D SPD matrix simulations visually demonstrate that OSPDIM rectifies misalignment where standard centering fails. Extensive motor imagery dataset experiments show significant improvement over Riemannian baselines, especially under severe class imbalance in online adaptation.
AI.conclusion: OSPDIM provides a robust, plug-and-play solution for practical online BCI systems, effectively handling label shift on the Riemannian manifold in a source-free manner.

title: Project2Task: Graph-Guided Project-Level Planning for Autonomous Research
summary: Research agents can increasingly search literature, propose hypotheses, generate code, run experiments, and draft manuscripts from a single topic. However, a research project is not merely a larger task: it is a long-horizon agenda that must be advanced through multiple bounded tasks with distinct but related objectives, parallel alternatives, and dependency-aware sequences. Existing single-task systems often treat the project as one oversized task, produce a flat set of vague or overlapping tasks, or leave task boundaries and execution order to manual coordination. We introduce Project2Task, a graph-guided project-level planning layer for autonomous research. Given a project brief, it represents candidate contributions as innovation atoms and organizes them in a directed lineage graph. A lightweight Bernoulli block-model objective selects among horizontal, vertical, and hybrid portfolio decompositions. Project2Task then generates bounded tasks with explicit contribution ownership, repairs overlaps and missing execution fields, and emits dependency-aware task contracts that specify objectives, inputs, expected artifacts, evaluation requirements, boundary constraints, dependencies, and execution order. The contracts are independent of any particular downstream research executor and support integration of task outputs into a coherent project-level result. On a benchmark of ten project briefs yielding roughly 30 tasks, manuscript-based portfolio evaluation gives Project2Task an average quality score of 7.15, compared with 4.58 for the Brief Baseline and 5.31 for the Topic-only Setting. Integrating its contracts with AutoResearchClaw increases average downstream task accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759. These results demonstrate the value of explicit project-to-task planning for producing coherent, non-redundant, and executable research-task portfolios.

AI.tldr: Project2Task is a graph-guided planning layer that decomposes a research project brief into a portfolio of bounded, dependency-aware tasks using innovation atoms and a directed lineage graph, significantly outperforming baselines in portfolio quality and downstream task execution accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous research agents treat an entire project as a single oversized task or produce flat, vague, overlapping tasks without proper dependency management. A research project is a long-horizon agenda requiring multiple bounded tasks with distinct objectives, parallel alternatives, and dependency-aware sequences — a structure current single-task systems fail to capture.
AI.method: Project2Task introduces a graph-guided planning layer that (1) represents candidate contributions as "innovation atoms" organized in a directed lineage graph, (2) uses a lightweight Bernoulli block-model objective to select among horizontal, vertical, and hybrid portfolio decompositions, (3) generates bounded tasks with explicit contribution ownership, repairs overlaps and missing execution fields, and (4) emits dependency-aware task contracts specifying objectives, inputs, expected artifacts, evaluation requirements, boundary constraints, dependencies, and execution order. These contracts are executor-agnostic and support coherent project-level integration.
AI.result: On a benchmark of 10 project briefs yielding ~30 tasks, manuscript-based portfolio evaluation gave Project2Task an average quality score of 7.15 vs. 4.58 (Brief Baseline) and 5.31 (Topic-only Setting). Integrating contracts with AutoResearchClaw improved average downstream task accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759.
AI.conclusion: Explicit project-to-task planning via graph-guided decomposition and dependency-aware contracting significantly improves the coherence, non-redundancy, and executability of research-task portfolios, demonstrating clear value over flat or underspecified task generation approaches.

title: Sensor-Level Fault Diagnosis for Automotive Software Validation Using Large Language Models
summary: The pre-series validation of automotive software on hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) platforms produces large volumes of multivariate sensor recordings whose assessment against functional safety requirements exceeds what manual review can sustain at campaign scale. Threshold-based tooling reports that a deviation has occurred but neither identifies its nature nor locates its source, while data-driven classifiers, although accurate, rely on large labelled datasets and return opaque decisions that sit uneasily with the traceability demanded by ISO 26262. This study examines whether open-source instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs), given a textual description of sensor behaviour, can serve as data-efficient and interpretable engines for fault detection and diagnosis inside the validation loop. A two-phase framework is proposed: automated requirement checking on a dSPACE real-time platform first isolates the recordings that violate a safety requirement, and only these are inspected, with sliding windows of the signals reduced to statistical, relational, and contextual descriptors, embedded in a fixed prompt, and mapped by a 4-bit low-rank-adapted LLM to a fault location accompanied by a written justification. Four model families ranging from two to eight billion parameters were adapted and tested on a gasoline-engine case study spanning six injected fault classes. The smallest model matched the largest at 81.6\% accuracy, whereas a comparably sized model failed to converge, indicating that diagnostic competence under task-specific adaptation follows convergence rather than parameter count, with the entire adapt-and-evaluate cycle fitting on a single commodity accelerator.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using instruction-tuned LLMs fine-tuned with LoRA for fault detection and diagnosis in automotive HIL validation, achieving 81.6% accuracy with a 2B-parameter model while providing interpretable justifications, demonstrating that task-specific convergence matters more than model size.
AI.motivation: Current threshold-based tools in automotive HIL validation only flag deviations without identifying their nature or source, while data-driven classifiers require large labeled datasets and produce opaque decisions incompatible with ISO 26262 traceability requirements. There is a need for data-efficient, interpretable fault detection and diagnosis.
AI.method: A two-phase framework: (1) automated requirement checking on a dSPACE real-time platform isolates recordings violating safety requirements; (2) only flagged recordings are analyzed using sliding windows converted to statistical, relational, and contextual descriptors embedded in fixed prompts. Four LLM families (2B–8B parameters) are adapted via 4-bit quantization and LoRA to output fault locations with written justifications. Evaluated on a gasoline-engine case study with six injected fault classes.
AI.result: The smallest model (2B parameters) matched the largest at 81.6% accuracy. A comparably sized model failed to converge entirely. The entire adapt-and-evaluate cycle fit on a single commodity GPU accelerator.
AI.conclusion: Diagnostic competence under task-specific adaptation depends on convergence behavior rather than parameter count. Instruction-tuned LLMs with LoRA offer a viable, data-efficient, and interpretable alternative for fault diagnosis in safety-critical automotive validation workflows.

title: Behavioral Residualization for Unsupervised Intrusion Detection in Automotive CAN Networks
summary:
Modern vehicles rely on the Controller Area Network (CAN) bus, whose design prioritizes low cost and real-time performance but provides no message authentication or encryption. An attacker with physical or remote access can therefore inject arbitrary frames, making intrusion detection an important defense-in-depth mechanism.
  Most published CAN intrusion detection systems rely on presence-based features, such as novel arbitration IDs, frozen payload bytes, or anomalous DLC values. These features perform well on public datasets containing easily separable attacks but fail when attackers reuse legitimate arbitration IDs. We present per-ID behavioral residualization, a CAN-specific representation that extracts fourteen temporal, protocol, and payload features from sliding windows and residualizes them against each arbitration ID's normal baseline. Our central claim is that this representation, rather than any individual detector, drives the performance gains.
  Across six unsupervised detectors and two datasets, residualization improves mean F1 in the majority of evaluations (21/24 on HCRL and 30/36 on ROAD across five seeds). On the more realistic ROAD dataset, where attacks reuse legitimate IDs, the representation achieves recall >= 0.99 with high ROC-AUC on targeted signal-manipulation attacks. Two limitations are explicitly quantified: novel-ID flooding (HCRL DoS, F1 = 0.02) and cross-ID fuzzing (ROAD, F1 = 0.27), defining the measured coverage boundary of the proposed representation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes per-ID behavioral residualization, a CAN bus feature representation that extracts temporal, protocol, and payload features from sliding windows and residualizes them against each arbitration ID's normal baseline. This representation, rather than any specific detector, drives substantial performance gains: on the realistic ROAD dataset, it achieves recall ≥ 0.99 with high ROC-AUC on targeted attacks, though it struggles with novel-ID flooding (F1 = 0.02) and cross-ID fuzzing (F1 = 0.27).
AI.motivation: Existing CAN intrusion detection systems rely on presence-based features (novel IDs, frozen payload bytes, anomalous DLC) that perform well on easily separable public dataset attacks but fail when attackers reuse legitimate arbitration IDs. A more robust, generalizable representation is needed for realistic attack scenarios.
AI.method: The authors introduce per-ID behavioral residualization: fourteen temporal, protocol, and payload features are extracted from sliding windows and residualized against each arbitration ID's normal baseline. This representation is evaluated across six unsupervised detectors (to demonstrate representation- rather than detector-driven gains) on two datasets (HCRL, ROAD) across five seeds.
AI.result: Residualization improved mean F1 in the majority of evaluations: 21/24 on HCRL and 30/36 on ROAD. On ROAD (realistic, ID-reuse attacks), recall ≥ 0.99 with high ROC-AUC was achieved on targeted signal-manipulation attacks. Two failure modes were quantified: novel-ID flooding (HCRL DoS, F1 = 0.02) and cross-ID fuzzing (ROAD, F1 = 0.27).
AI.conclusion: The per-ID behavioral residualization representation is the primary driver of detection performance, not any particular detector. The approach establishes strong detection capability on realistic attacks where IDs are reused, while transparently quantifying its coverage boundary at novel-ID flooding and cross-ID fuzzing attacks.

title: A Study of ASR Adaptation and Representation Dimensionality Reduction in Persian Speech Emotion Recognition Using Whisper
summary: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) in low-resource languages remains a challenging problem due to limited labeled data. In this work, we study the use of Whisper for Persian SER with a particular focus on representation dimensionality reduction and language-specific model adaptation. We propose a SER framework in which frame-level embeddings extracted from the Whisper encoder are reduced in dimensionality using PCA, eliminating the need for learned projection layers and substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters. The reduced representations are aggregated using an attention-based pooling mechanism and classified with a lightweight prediction head. In addition, we investigate whether fine-tuning Whisper on a Persian automatic speech recognition (ASR) task improves downstream SER performance. Experiments conducted on the ShEMO dataset under a speaker-independent evaluation protocol show that PCA-based dimensionality reduction consistently improves emotion recognition performance while reducing training latency and memory usage. ASR fine-tuning yields only modest gains for SER, suggesting limited transfer from language adaptation to emotion-related representations under the evaluated conditions. These findings provide practical insights into the efficient use of large pretrained speech models for emotion recognition in low-resource languages.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Persian speech emotion recognition framework using Whisper encoder embeddings reduced via PCA and aggregated with attention pooling, finding that PCA improves performance and efficiency, while ASR fine-tuning offers only modest SER gains.
AI.motivation: SER in low-resource languages like Persian suffers from limited labeled data. The authors aim to efficiently leverage large pretrained speech models (Whisper) without introducing heavy learned projection layers, and explore whether language-specific ASR adaptation transfers to emotion recognition.
AI.method: Frame-level embeddings from the Whisper encoder are dimensionality-reduced via PCA (eliminating learned projections), then aggregated with an attention-based pooling mechanism and classified through a lightweight prediction head. Additionally, Whisper is fine-tuned on Persian ASR to assess downstream SER gains, with evaluation on ShEMO under speaker-independent protocol.
AI.result: PCA-based dimensionality reduction consistently improves emotion recognition accuracy while reducing training latency and memory usage. ASR fine-tuning yields only modest SER improvements, indicating limited cross-task transfer between language adaptation and emotion representations.
AI.conclusion: PCA is a practical and efficient alternative to learned projection layers for adapting large pretrained models to low-resource SER. Language-specific ASR fine-tuning provides minimal benefit for emotion recognition, offering guidance for efficient model deployment in resource-constrained settings.

title: QEvict: Recoverable Quantized KV Eviction for Attention-Drift-Robust Long-Context Decoding
comment: 24 pages, 6 figures. The first four authors contributed equally
summary: Autoregressive large language model inference is increasingly constrained by the memory footprint of the Key-Value (KV) cache. A dominant line of work reduces this footprint by evicting tokens that appear unimportant under attention-derived scores. However, such policies make an implicit irreversible decision: once a token is evicted, it cannot become useful again. We show that this assumption is brittle during decoding. Token and window importance drift as generated queries evolve, causing standard eviction policies to permanently discard states that later receive substantial attention under the full-cache model. To characterize this behaviour, we introduce Future Missed Mass and Global LIR, two diagnostics that measure future attention assigned to discarded states and the reactivation of historically inactive regions. We propose QEvict, a three-tier KV-cache management scheme that replaces binary retain-or-delete eviction with recoverable eviction. QEvict maintains high-confidence windows in full precision, stores intermediate windows in a quantized recoverable tier, and deletes only the lowest-confidence windows. During decoding, cumulative attention scores update window importance and when a quantized window becomes important again, it is dequantized and promoted to the full-precision. Under a fixed memory budget, this design preserves broader historical context while retaining exact full precision for the most important regions. Across long-context understanding, retrieval, and reasoning benchmarks, QEvict consistently improves over representative eviction and quantization baselines, reducing missed attention and improving information retention

AI.tldr: QEvict introduces a three-tier KV-cache management scheme that replaces irreversible token eviction with recoverable eviction, using full-precision, quantized, and deleted tiers to preserve broader context while maintaining accuracy under fixed memory budgets.
AI.motivation: Standard KV-cache eviction policies make irreversible decisions based on attention scores at a single point, but token importance drifts during decoding. Once evicted, a token cannot be recovered even if it later becomes highly relevant, leading to missed attention and degraded generation quality.
AI.method: The authors first characterize the problem using two diagnostics: Future Missed Mass (attention later assigned to evicted tokens) and Global LIR (reactivation of historically inactive regions). They then propose QEvict, a three-tier system: (1) high-confidence windows kept in full precision, (2) intermediate windows stored in a quantized recoverable tier, and (3) lowest-confidence windows deleted. Cumulative attention scores dynamically update window importance; quantized windows can be dequantized and promoted to full precision when their importance rises.
AI.result: QEvict consistently outperforms representative eviction and quantization baselines across long-context understanding, retrieval, and reasoning benchmarks, reducing missed attention and improving information retention under fixed memory budgets.
AI.conclusion: Recoverable eviction via a quantized intermediate tier effectively addresses the drift problem in KV-cache management, preserving broader historical context while maintaining exact precision for critical tokens, and offers a practical path beyond binary retain-or-delete policies.

title: TriQua: Reconciling Granularity and Context in Factuality Evaluation
summary: The "decompose-then-verify" paradigm for LLM factuality evaluation faces a fundamental trade-off: atomic facts, i.e., one sentence conveying one unit of information, often omit essential context, while broader statements lack the granularity needed for precise assessment. To address this, we introduce TriQua, a framework that flexibly models facts based on their complexity. Simple claims are extracted as standard triples, while complex claims are represented as hyperrelational facts by attaching auxiliary contextual qualifiers. This adaptive structure preserves the necessary context for accurate retrieval and verification without sacrificing atomicity. Furthermore, TriQua's verification process directly annotates concrete errors within specific triples and qualifiers, providing fine-grained explainability for error detection. Alongside the framework, we propose TriQuaScore to quantify the factuality of these structured fact units. Empirical evaluations show that TriQuaScore strongly aligns with human annotated factuality scores, TriQua achieves robust decomposition quality, and outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification.

AI.tldr: TriQua introduces an adaptive fact decomposition framework that represents simple claims as standard triples and complex claims as hyperrelational facts with contextual qualifiers, enabling precise factuality evaluation with fine-grained error annotation and explainability.
AI.motivation: Existing "decompose-then-verify" approaches face a trade-off: atomic facts lack essential context for accurate verification, while broader statements lack granularity for precise error detection. There is a need for a flexible representation that adapts to fact complexity.
AI.method: TriQua models facts adaptively based on complexity: simple claims are extracted as standard (subject, relation, object) triples, while complex claims become hyperrelational facts with auxiliary contextual qualifiers attached. Verification directly annotates errors within specific triples and qualifiers. TriQuaScore quantifies factuality of these structured units.
AI.result: TriQuaScore strongly aligns with human-annotated factuality scores. TriQua achieves robust decomposition quality and outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive fact modeling with hyperrelational qualifiers effectively resolves the atomicity-context trade-off in LLM factuality evaluation, delivering both precise verification and fine-grained explainability.

title: AgentExecutor: Partial Code Execution via Agentic Context Generation
summary: Executing code snippets is essential for dynamic program analysis, but it remains challenging to execute an arbitrary code snippet due to issues like missing context and incomplete dependencies. Existing approaches to partial code execution, such as LExecutor and Treefix, leverage the power of language models to infer missing information and enable execution. However, they suffer from (i) limited action spaces and feedback, and (ii) rigid optimization strategies, which restrict their effectiveness and efficiency. In this paper, we propose AgentExecutor, a novel multi-agent framework for partial code execution. Our approach introduces a three-phase design: execution environment preparation, dynamic exploration with iterative refinement, and prefix evolution via program synthesis. Supported by the power of LLM agents who can think, act, and get feedback iteratively, AgentExecutor is able to autonomously explore a richer action space, enabling diverse operations such as creating resource files and resolving environment configuration. Furthermore, it adopts adaptive optimization strategies, including coverage-guided context pruning and prefix evolution via program synthesis, to systematically improve the execution quality of partial code. We evaluate AgentExecutor on two widely used datasets comprising Stack Overflow snippets and open-source project code. The results show that AgentExecutor achieves up to 94% and 90% code coverage, outperforming the state-of-the-art approach Treefix by 19.9% and 13.8%, respectively. In addition, AgentExecutor significantly reduces execution time (by up to 80.3%) and cost (by up to 56.6%). These findings demonstrate that AgentExecutor provides an effective and efficient solution for partial code execution.

AI.tldr: AgentExecutor is a multi-agent LLM-based framework for partial code execution that achieves up to 94% code coverage, outperforming existing methods by ~13-20% while reducing execution time by up to 80.3% and cost by up to 56.6%.
AI.motivation: Existing partial code execution tools (LExecutor, Treefix) are limited by restricted action spaces, insufficient feedback mechanisms, and rigid optimization strategies, hampering their effectiveness and efficiency when executing arbitrary, incomplete code snippets.
AI.method: AgentExecutor employs a three-phase multi-agent framework: (1) execution environment preparation, (2) dynamic exploration with iterative refinement, and (3) prefix evolution via program synthesis. LLM agents autonomously explore a rich action space (e.g., creating resource files, resolving environment configs) and employ adaptive optimization including coverage-guided context pruning and program synthesis-based prefix evolution.
AI.result: On Stack Overflow snippets and open-source project code datasets, AgentExecutor achieves 94% and 90% code coverage, outperforming Treefix by 19.9% and 13.8% respectively. It also reduces execution time by up to 80.3% and cost by up to 56.6%.
AI.conclusion: AgentExecutor demonstrates that a multi-agent LLM framework with richer action spaces and adaptive optimization provides an effective and efficient solution for partial code execution, significantly advancing the state of the art.

title: A Self-Explainable Deep Architecture for Security Applications
summary: Deep learning models have become integral to security applications due to their ability to model complex relationships in data and detect sophisticated threats. However, their complexity makes it difficult to understand how predictions are generated, posing significant challenges for interpretability, particularly in security applications where transparency is critical. Existing explanation methods, such as visual explanation techniques and post-hoc approaches, suffer from several limitations: reduced faithfulness due to local approximation errors, instability caused by reliance on randomness, and computational inefficiency that hinders real-time usage. To address these issues, we introduce XSec, a self-explainable deep architecture developed for security applications. During training, XSec uses a novel mask-based approach to extract informative sub-features from the data and learns prototypes, representative patterns that characterize each class. XSec then leverages the prototypes in a dedicated similarity layer at test time to compute similarity scores and generates interpretable explanations without the need for post-hoc analysis. We evaluate XSec across five diverse security scenarios, demonstrating its ability to achieve an average classification accuracy of 97.33% with minimal performance compromise. XSec produces deterministic explanations for a fixed trained model and input and substantially reduces explanation latency compared with approximation-based and perturbation-based post-hoc methods. Through this effort, we extend the applicability of self-explainable AI to security applications, bridging the gap between deep learning performance and the need for explainability in critical scenarios.

AI.tldr: XSec is a self-explainable deep architecture for security applications that uses mask-based sub-feature extraction and prototype learning to generate built-in, deterministic explanations, achieving 97.33% average accuracy across five security scenarios while dramatically reducing explanation latency compared to post-hoc methods.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models are increasingly used in security applications but suffer from poor interpretability. Existing explanation methods (visual, post-hoc) are limited by unfaithfulness from local approximations, instability from randomness, and computational inefficiency that prevents real-time use. Security-critical scenarios demand both high performance and transparent, trustworthy explanations.
AI.method: XSec is a self-explainable deep architecture with two key innovations: (1) a mask-based approach during training that extracts informative sub-features from input data, and (2) prototype learning that identifies representative class-characterizing patterns. At test time, a dedicated similarity layer computes similarity scores between extracted features and learned prototypes, inherently generating interpretable explanations without any post-hoc analysis.
AI.result: XSec achieved an average classification accuracy of 97.33% across five diverse security scenarios with minimal performance degradation. It produces deterministic explanations (fixed for a given trained model and input) and substantially reduces explanation latency compared to both approximation-based and perturbation-based post-hoc methods.
AI.conclusion: XSec successfully extends self-explainable AI to security applications, effectively bridging the gap between deep learning performance and the critical need for explainability in high-stakes security scenarios.

title: Conditional Cognitive Biases in LLMs: How Biased User Turns Modulate In-Context Reasoning
summary: We present an evaluation of cognitive bias expression in state-of-the-art instruction-tuned LLMs under realistic multi-turn interaction settings. Our work introduces a novel three-condition experimental framework that disentangles the effect of exposure to a biased user turn from the effect of the turn's semantic content, alongside a benchmark of 24,300 jury-validated user prompts spanning all 81 cells of a 9x9 target-human bias interaction matrix. Across eight frontier LLMs, we find that biased conversational context systematically increases bias expression relative to zero-shot baselines in 6 of 8 models. We identify two competing behavioral dynamics underlying this effect: conversational exposure to biased reasoning generally amplifies downstream bias tendencies, while explicitly stated bias cues often trigger alignment-related suppression behaviors that reduce overt bias expression. We release our framework, codebase, and dataset to support future research on context-conditioned cognitive biases and behavioral adaptation in LLMs.

AI.tldr: Study evaluates how multi-turn interactions with biased users affect bias expression in 8 frontier instruction-tuned LLMs, using a novel three-condition framework with 24,300 validated prompts. Finds biased context increases bias in 6/8 models via two competing dynamics: exposure amplifies bias, while explicit bias cues trigger suppression.
AI.motivation: Prior work on LLM bias has largely focused on single-turn, zero-shot evaluations. Real-world LLM interactions are multi-turn and conversational, where user biases may influence model responses over time. The authors aim to disentangle whether bias expression arises from mere exposure to biased conversational context or from the semantic content of biased prompts, filling a gap in understanding context-conditioned cognitive biases in LLMs.
AI.method: A three-condition experimental design: (1) zero-shot baseline, (2) exposure to biased user turns without explicit bias cues, and (3) exposure to turns with explicit bias content. A benchmark of 24,300 jury-validated user prompts covers a 9×9 matrix of target-human bias interactions. Eight frontier instruction-tuned LLMs are evaluated under realistic multi-turn interaction settings.
AI.result: Biased conversational context systematically increased bias expression over zero-shot baselines in 6 of 8 models. Two competing dynamics were identified: (a) conversational exposure to biased reasoning amplifies downstream bias tendencies, and (b) explicitly stated bias cues trigger alignment-related suppression, reducing overt bias expression.
AI.conclusion: Multi-turn conversational context significantly modulates bias expression in LLMs through competing amplification and suppression dynamics. The released framework, codebase, and dataset provide infrastructure for future research on context-conditioned cognitive biases and behavioral adaptation in language models.

title: DG-FedReuse: Proxy-Gradient-Gated Cached-Update Reuse with Matched Sparse Uplink Accounting
summary: Federated learning repeatedly incurs local optimization and model-update transmission. We study DG-FedReuse, a simulator-level mechanism that allows selected clients to contribute age-decayed cached updates when a stochastic head-gradient discrepancy proxy remains below a round-dependent threshold. A hard cache-age limit and minimum fresh-client quota constrain reuse, while fresh updates use an adaptive per-tensor Top-K numerical-field representation. Experiments cover six image-classification datasets, 50 virtual clients, Dirichlet label heterogeneity (α=0.5), and three seeds. At a common 90-round budget, DG-FedReuse yields 83.36-85.42% modeled update-data-field uplink saving, compared with 76.88% for matched Top-K FedAvg; the seed-aligned accuracy differences range from -5.29 to -0.14 percentage points. Best-observed test accuracies obtained under test-controlled checkpointing are retained only as exploratory archival evidence and range from -2.38 to +0.45 percentage points relative to matched FedAvg. A symmetric dense-model-downlink sensitivity reduces the headline saving to 41.68-F42.71% and the incremental gain over Top-K FedAvg to 3.24-4.27 percentage points, demonstrating the dependence of communication conclusions on the accounting boundary. The study characterizes the proposed reuse rule in the implemented simulator; it does not establish unbiased generalization, end-to-end bandwidth reduction, runtime or energy savings, faster convergence, or superiority over existing stale-update and lazy-aggregation methods.

AI.tldr: DG-FedReuse introduces a mechanism where selected clients reuse age-decayed cached model updates when gradient discrepancy is small, combined with adaptive Top-K compression for fresh updates. Experiments across 6 datasets show 83.36–85.42% uplink savings versus 76.88% for plain Top-K FedAvg, though with accuracy trade-offs. Savings drop significantly when downlink is accounted for (41.68–42.71%).
AI.motivation: Federated learning incurs substantial communication costs from repeated local optimization and model-update transmission. The authors aim to reduce uplink communication by allowing stale cached updates to be reused when safe, exploiting temporal gradient similarity to avoid redundant transmission.
AI.method: DG-FedReuse operates at the simulator level. Selected clients may submit age-decayed cached (stale) updates whenever a stochastic head-gradient discrepancy proxy falls below a round-dependent threshold. Constraints include a hard cache-age limit and a minimum quota of fresh clients. Fresh updates employ an adaptive per-tensor Top-K numerical-field representation for compression. The study also examines sensitivity when symmetric dense-model downlink is included in the communication accounting.
AI.result: At a 90-round budget across 6 image-classification datasets (50 clients, Dirichlet α=0.5), DG-FedReuse achieves 83.36–85.42% modeled update-data-field uplink saving vs. 76.88% for matched Top-K FedAvg. Seed-aligned accuracy differences range from −5.29 to −0.14 pp. Best-observed test accuracies (exploratory only) range −2.38 to +0.45 pp relative to matched FedAvg. With symmetric downlink included, headline savings drop to 41.68–42.71% and incremental gain over Top-K FedAvg shrinks to 3.24–4.27 pp.
AI.conclusion: DG-FedReuse demonstrates meaningful uplink savings over Top-K FedAvg in a simulated setting, but conclusions are sensitive to whether downlink is accounted for. The study explicitly disclaims generalization, end-to-end bandwidth reduction, runtime/energy savings, faster convergence, or superiority over existing stale-update and lazy-aggregation methods.

title: Coherence-Oriented Dream Scene Visualisation
summary: Dreams can be emotionally intense but difficult to communicate. We describe the Dream Scene Visualiser (DSV) system which turns written dream descriptions into a temporal sequence of four panel images visualising the dream. This starts with a large language model prompted to split a dream description into four chronological parts. Then a text-to-image model produces images for each part with visual coherence maintained across the sequence, and DSV regenerates any image not suitably matching the text. We evaluate DSV over 50 visualisations from dream descriptions in DreamBank, and report quality, fidelity and coherence results via objective measures employing the CLIP, DINOv2 and Qwen2-VL vision-language models.

AI.tldr: The Dream Scene Visualiser (DSV) converts written dream descriptions into coherent four-panel image sequences using LLM-based temporal segmentation and text-to-image generation with a regeneration step for quality assurance, evaluated on 50 DreamBank dreams using CLIP, DINOv2, and Qwen2-VL metrics.
AI.motivation: Dreams are emotionally intense but inherently difficult to communicate. There is a need for systems that can translate subjective, often surreal dream narratives into visual representations, bridging the gap between internal experience and shareable visual media.
AI.method: The DSV pipeline has three stages: (1) a large language model splits a dream description into four chronological parts; (2) a text-to-image model generates images for each part while maintaining visual coherence across the sequence; (3) a quality control step where DSV regenerates any image that insufficiently matches its corresponding text prompt. Evaluation uses objective metrics from CLIP, DINOv2, and Qwen2-VL vision-language models to measure quality, fidelity, and coherence.
AI.result: The system was evaluated on 50 visualizations derived from DreamBank dream descriptions. Results report quantitative measures of image quality, text-image fidelity, and cross-panel coherence as assessed by CLIP, DINOv2, and Qwen2-VL models.
AI.conclusion: The DSV demonstrates a viable pipeline for transforming subjective dream narratives into temporally coherent visual sequences, with automated regeneration serving as an effective quality control mechanism. The multi-model evaluation framework provides a reproducible approach for assessing dream visualization systems.

title: Divergent Perceptuomotor Recalibration in Virtual Reality and Video-Passthrough Mixed Reality on the Same Head-Mounted Display
summary: Virtual reality (VR) and video-passthrough mixed reality (MR-VPT) can be delivered on the same headset, but it is unclear whether these two interaction modalities produce comparable perceptuomotor behavior. Although delivery through the same headset controls many display-level characteristics, VR and MR-VPT differ in both their visual-feedback pipelines and the action-relevant visual information available to guide movement, such as whether the surrounding environment and the user's body are synthetically rendered or preserved through passthrough. This study compared visually guided manual pointing in VR and MR-VPT using the same headset. Forty adults were assigned to either a VR or MR-VPT group and completed a pointing task in the physical, unmediated reality (UR) before and after performing the same task in their assigned XR modality. The analyses revealed numerous important insights. First, groups had comparable baseline performance in UR prior to XR exposure. Second, the two modalities produced opposite initial biases during XR exposure: the VR group undershot the target, whereas the MR-VPT group overshot. Third, although both groups reduced error with continued exposure to XR, there were differences in the patterns of adaptation: the VR group adapted more slowly and exhibited stronger distance-dependent undershooting than the MR-VPT group. Finally, after XR exposure, both groups showed significant undershooting aftereffects with the VR group retaining a persistent residual undershoot, suggesting incomplete de-adaptation. The results suggest that perceptuomotor recalibration is shaped not only by display-level constraints but also by the action-relevant visual information available within the interaction environment. These findings highlight the need to validate perceptuomotor interaction techniques separately in VR and MR-VPT, even when they are implemented on the same hardware.

AI.tldr: This study compared visually guided manual pointing in VR versus video-passthrough mixed reality (MR-VPT) on the same headset, finding opposite initial biases (VR undershooting, MR-VPT overshooting), different adaptation rates, and persistent aftereffects — demonstrating that perceptuomotor recalibration differs between modalities despite identical hardware.
AI.motivation: VR and MR-VPT can run on the same headsets, yet it is unclear whether they yield comparable perceptuomotor behavior. Their visual-feedback pipelines and the action-relevant visual information (synthetic vs. preserved real-world views, including the user's own body and surroundings) differ fundamentally, which may produce distinct sensorimotor outcomes that have not been systematically characterized.
AI.method: Forty adults were assigned to either a VR or MR-VPT group. Both groups performed a visually guided manual pointing task in unmediated reality (UR) at baseline, then in their assigned XR modality, and finally again in UR to assess aftereffects. Pointing biases, adaptation rates, and distance-dependent error patterns were compared between groups.
AI.result: (1) Baseline UR performance was equivalent across groups. (2) Initial XR exposure produced opposite biases: VR group undershot targets, MR-VPT group overshot. (3) Both groups reduced error with continued exposure, but VR participants adapted more slowly and showed stronger distance-dependent undershooting. (4) Post-XR aftereffects included significant undershooting in both groups, with VR participants retaining a persistent residual undershoot indicative of incomplete de-adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Perceptuomotor recalibration is shaped by both display-level constraints and the action-relevant visual information in the interaction environment. The findings underscore that VR and MR-VPT cannot be assumed equivalent for perceptuomotor tasks and must be validated separately, even when implemented on identical hardware.

title: LangChoiceBench: Measuring and Explaining Programming-Language Choice in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to exhibit strong Python preferences when generating project-level code, but there is currently no systematic way to measure this behaviour across new models. To bridge this gap, we introduce LangChoiceBench, a project-level code-generation benchmark for measuring Python preference, recommendation-implementation consistency, and language diversity. LangChoiceBench covers 28 projects across seven software areas where Python is often a poor default. We evaluate 25 diverse LLMs and find that Python remains heavily over-selected, recommendation-implementation consistency is low, and smaller open-weight models generally show stronger Python preference and lower language diversity. We further analyse 9,826 reasoning traces and find that most Python choices are automatic or driven primarily by ease, rather than explicit consideration of project requirements. In a smaller but important set of cases, models fabricate contextual support for choosing Python - a failure mode we call phantom evidence - or produce code that contradicts the language selected in their own reasoning.

AI.tldr: LangChoiceBench is a benchmark for measuring LLMs' Python preference in project-level code generation. Evaluating 25 models across 28 projects, the authors find heavy Python over-selection, low recommendation-implementation consistency, and identify failure modes including "phantom evidence" — where models fabricate justifications for choosing Python.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit strong Python preferences in project-level code generation, yet no systematic method exists to measure this behavior across models. The authors aim to bridge this gap.
AI.method: They introduce LangChoiceBench, a benchmark of 28 projects across seven software domains where Python is suboptimal. They evaluate 25 diverse LLMs, measuring Python preference, recommendation-implementation consistency, and language diversity. They further analyze 9,826 reasoning traces to understand why models choose Python.
AI.result: Python remains heavily over-selected; recommendation-implementation consistency is low; smaller open-weight models exhibit stronger Python preference and lower language diversity. Most Python choices are automatic or ease-driven rather than requirement-driven. Two notable failure modes emerge: "phantom evidence" (fabricating contextual support for Python) and code that contradicts the model's own stated language choice.
AI.conclusion: LLMs systematically over-prefer Python in project-level coding tasks, often without genuine consideration of project requirements. This reveals a significant gap in language-appropriate code generation, with phantom evidence representing a particularly concerning failure mode.

title: When Experience Becomes Instruction: Trajectory Poisoning in Self-Evolving Agent Skill Systems
summary: Self-evolving skill (SES) systems distill agent trajectories into persistent skills, allowing untrusted experience to become trusted instruction. We introduce PoisonedEvolution, a trajectory-poisoning attack on this promotion process. Our skill-visible black-box attacker can inspect a target skill and contribute bounded evidence, but cannot observe private pools or evolution logic or edit the skill bank. Artifact poisoning requires Inclusion, Evolution Attribution, and Realization. Attribution is the distinctive bottleneck: the target behavior must appear causally useful, recurrent, and generalizable before promotion. We evaluate four representative security-effect families using inert canary specifications. At 10% attacker support, across six mainstream LLM evolvers in SkillClaw, PoisonedEvolution embeds target behaviors in 546/600 trials (91.0% SER). On the structurally different Trace2Skill pipeline at the same ratio, it embeds target behaviors in 369/600 trials (61.5% SER), demonstrating transfer across evolution architectures. In a representative controlled study, three consistent attacker records suffice in a 30-record batch, whereas a single record is much weaker. Ablations identify recurring support, causal framing, and domain-aligned encoding as the main determinants of success. These findings expose evidence promotion as a security boundary for self-evolving agents.

AI.tldr: PoisonedEvolution demonstrates a trajectory-poisoning attack on self-evolving skill systems, where a small fraction of malicious trajectories (10%) can reliably embed target behaviors into trusted skill banks across multiple LLM evolvers, exposing evidence promotion as a critical security vulnerability.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving skill (SES) systems automatically distill agent trajectories into persistent, trusted skills. This "promotion" from untrusted experience to trusted instruction creates a novel attack surface: if an attacker can poison the trajectory pool, malicious behaviors may be permanently embedded as trusted skills. Prior work has not systematically examined this evidence-promotion boundary.
AI.method: The authors design PoisonedEvolution, a skill-visible black-box attack where the attacker can inspect a target skill and contribute bounded poisoned trajectories, but cannot observe private pools, evolution logic, or edit the skill bank directly. The attack must satisfy three conditions: Inclusion (poisoned evidence enters the pool), Evolution Attribution (the target behavior appears causally useful, recurrent, and generalizable — the key bottleneck), and Realization (the promoted skill is subsequently executed). Evaluation uses four security-effect families with inert canary specifications across six LLM evolvers in the SkillClaw framework and the Trace2Skill pipeline, at 10% attacker support ratios.
AI.result: At 10% attacker support, PoisonedEvolution achieves 91.0% success rate (546/600 trials) on SkillClaw across six LLM evolvers and 61.5% (369/600) on Trace2Skill. A controlled study shows three consistent attacker records in a 30-record batch suffice for successful embedding, while a single record is significantly weaker. Ablations identify recurring support, causal framing, and domain-aligned encoding as primary success determinants.
AI.conclusion: Evidence promotion — the process by which untrusted trajectories are distilled into trusted skills — constitutes a fundamental security boundary in self-evolving agent systems. Systems designers must treat this promotion step as a security-critical operation requiring explicit defenses rather than relying on statistical robustness alone.

title: CNM-BERT: A Drop-In Structural Embedding for Chinese Characters via Ideographic Description Sequences
summary: Token-based encoders like BERT treat Chinese characters as atomic identifiers, ignoring their recursive orthographic structure. Consequently, models rely on contextual co-occurrence, degrading performance on rare and out-of-vocabulary (OOV) characters. We propose the Compositional Network Model (CNM), a lightweight augmentation that injects discrete compositional structure into Transformer encoders. CNM parses Ideographic Description Sequences (IDS) into trees, encodes them via a recursive Tree-MLP, and fuses the structural embeddings into BERT without modifying the backbone. Evaluated on the Wu et al. (2025) structural-probing benchmark, CNM-BERT outperforms the strongest baseline (ChineseBERT) on long-tail and OOV characters by +9.8 Structure accuracy and +7.7 Radical F1. Furthermore, CNM-BERT achieves consistent gains across CLUE, MRC, and NER tasks at both base and large scales, demonstrating that explicit structural injection delivers both robust OOV understanding and tangible downstream value.

AI.tldr: CNM augments BERT by parsing Chinese characters' Ideographic Description Sequences (IDS) into trees and encoding them via a recursive Tree-MLP, injecting explicit compositional structure to improve rare and OOV character representation without modifying the backbone model.
AI.motivation: Standard token-based encoders like BERT treat Chinese characters as atomic units, ignoring their internal recursive orthographic structure (radicals, components). This forces models to depend solely on contextual co-occurrence, leading to degraded performance on rare and out-of-vocabulary (OOV) characters.
AI.method: The Compositional Network Model (CNM) is a lightweight augmentation that: (1) parses Ideographic Description Sequences (IDS) into compositional trees capturing character structure; (2) encodes these trees via a recursive Tree-MLP; and (3) fuses the resulting structural embeddings into BERT's representations without altering the underlying Transformer backbone.
AI.result: On the Wu et al. (2025) structural-probing benchmark, CNM-BERT outperforms the strongest baseline (ChineseBERT) by +9.8 on Structure accuracy and +7.7 on Radical F1 for long-tail and OOV characters. It also achieves consistent gains across CLUE, MRC, and NER tasks at both base and large model scales.
AI.conclusion: Explicit structural injection via CNM delivers robust OOV understanding and tangible downstream performance improvements, demonstrating that leveraging orthographic compositionality is a practical and effective strategy for Chinese NLP.

title: Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs) for Predictive Latent Dynamics
summary: World models learn latent states that summarize interaction histories, evolve over time, and support prediction, simulation, or planning. Most existing world models represent these states using classical vectors, probability distributions, recurrent hidden states, or transformer activations. In this paper, we introduce Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs), a quantum-inspired framework for predictive world modeling with structured latent states, latent transition operators, and measurement-inspired decoding maps. We study whether mathematical structures inspired by quantum theory, such as complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latents, provide useful inductive biases for world modeling. We establish three foundational properties: classical inclusion, predictive sufficiency, and structured compactness. We then instantiate complex-valued and density-matrix-like QSWM variants and evaluate them on elementary cellular automata against strong classical baselines. Results show promising local predictive potential for complex-valued QSWMs, while also revealing limitations in long-horizon rollout, density-matrix variants

AI.tldr: Introduces Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs) that use complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latents inspired by quantum theory for predictive world modeling, establishing three foundational properties and evaluating on elementary cellular automata, finding promising local predictions but limited long-horizon performance.
AI.motivation: Existing world models rely on classical representations (vectors, distributions, RNN hidden states, transformer activations). The authors investigate whether quantum-inspired mathematical structures—complex numbers and density matrices—provide useful inductive biases for learning structured latent states, transition operators, and measurement-like decoding maps in predictive world modeling.
AI.method: The paper proposes QSWMs with three components: structured latent states (complex-valued or density-matrix-like), latent transition operators, and measurement-inspired decoding maps. It establishes three theoretical properties: classical inclusion (subsumes classical models), predictive sufficiency (latent states capture all relevant information for future prediction), and structured compactness (efficient representation). Two concrete variants are instantiated—complex-valued and density-matrix-based—and evaluated on elementary cellular automata prediction tasks against strong classical baselines.
AI.result: Complex-valued QSWMs demonstrate promising local predictive potential on elementary cellular automata. However, both variants exhibit limitations: long-horizon rollout performance degrades significantly, and density-matrix variants underperform relative to expectations.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-inspired inductive biases show some promise for short-term world modeling but face challenges in long-horizon prediction. The density-matrix formulation, despite theoretical appeal, does not yet translate to practical gains, suggesting further work is needed to bridge quantum-inspired theory and effective world model design.

title: Search2Skill: Skill Distillation Beyond Knowledge Boundaries Via Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reusable skills, which encapsulate the procedural knowledge required to solve real-world professional tasks, offer LLM-based agents a path toward self-evolution in expert domains. Existing self-evolving skill methods construct skills internally from the model's parametric knowledge or trajectories, and are therefore bounded by what the model already knows. However, the domain conventions and standard procedures underlying professional skills often lie beyond this boundary and are hard to elicit from the agent alone. To address this issue, we therefore propose a novel framework, Search2Skill, that automatically identifies the agent's capability gaps, searches external sources to address them, and distills the retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills. Specifically, Search2Skill is optimized by a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills. Experiments on eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks show that Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under both streaming and held-out evaluation protocols. Further analyses show that the gains arise from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and that the acquired skills transfer across model scales.

AI.tldr: Search2Skill is a framework that enables LLM agents to self-evolve in expert domains by identifying capability gaps, searching external sources for missing knowledge, and distilling retrieved evidence into reusable skills, optimized via rubric-based reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving skill methods are bounded by the model's internal parametric knowledge or trajectories, leaving domain conventions and standard procedures—which often lie beyond the model's knowledge boundary—inaccessible. The key insight is that professional skills require external knowledge that cannot be elicited from the agent alone.
AI.method: Search2Skill is a three-stage framework: (1) automatically identifies the agent's capability gaps, (2) searches external knowledge sources to fill those gaps, and (3) distills retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills. The entire pipeline is optimized using a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly learns when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills.
AI.result: Experiments across eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks demonstrate that Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under streaming and held-out evaluation protocols. Ablation analyses reveal gains stem from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and acquired skills transfer across model scales.
AI.conclusion: Search2Skill effectively bridges the gap between an agent's internal knowledge and external domain expertise by converting retrieved information into reusable skills. The skill abstraction mechanism, rather than raw retrieval, drives performance improvements, and these skills exhibit cross-scale transferability.

title: Reducing belief in conspiracy theories as they unfold using large language models
summary: The emergence of conspiracy theories in the wake of major events is a significant societal challenge. Here we test whether conversational dialogues with a large language model (LLM) can reduce belief in immediately unfolding conspiracies. In experiments conducted in the days following the July 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump and the September 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk, U.S. adults (Experiment 1: N = 472; Experiment 2: N = 1035) holding conspiratorial views about the crisis event engaged in a multi-turn conversation with an LLM prompted to reduce their conspiracy belief. Compared to control participants who either discussed an irrelevant topic with an LLM or viewed a static fact sheet, participants in the LLM treatment showed significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs in both experiments. We also found evidence of downstream effects of the LLM treatment, observing reduced belief in different conspiracies one to two months later in the wake of subsequent crisis events. These results shed light on the psychology of emerging conspiracies and highlight the potential for scalable, cognitively-focused interventions to counteract misinformation in the immediate aftermath of high-profile societal events.

AI.tldr: Conversational dialogues with a large language model (LLM) significantly reduced belief in emerging conspiracy theories following two high-profile events, with effects persisting to downstream conspiracies months later.
AI.motivation: Conspiracy theories that emerge immediately after major societal events pose a significant challenge, yet scalable, cognitively-focused interventions for counteracting such beliefs in real time remain underexplored.
AI.method: Two experiments (total N = 1,507) conducted shortly after the July 2024 Trump assassination attempt and the September 2025 Charlie Kirk assassination. U.S. adults with conspiratorial views engaged in multi-turn conversations with an LLM prompted to reduce conspiracy belief. Control conditions involved either discussing an irrelevant topic with an LLM or viewing a static fact sheet. Follow-up assessed downstream effects on different conspiracies one to two months later.
AI.result: LLM treatment significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs compared to both control conditions in both experiments. Downstream effects were observed: reduced belief in unrelated conspiracies one to two months later following subsequent crisis events.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based conversational interventions are a scalable and effective approach for reducing belief in emerging conspiracies, with durable effects that generalize to other conspiracy beliefs over time.

title: In Terms of Explainability: Refining Requirements for Self-Explainable Systems
summary: Autonomous and software-intensive systems have been growing in occurrence, complexity, and assumed responsibility. Due to the high complexity of these systems, properties like transparency and explainability must be a focus of investigation. To date, no universally applicable definition and guide for the development of (self-)explainable systems exists. A need for explainability standards has already been recognized in the EU AI Act and the IEEE Transparency Standard 7001-2021. To address this need, we propose unified definitions in explainability based on an analysis and combination of existing definitions. Additionally, we present structured explainability requirements that are necessary to build (self-)explainable systems. By analysing the resulting taxonomy, we propose the incorporation of explanation goodness and thus correctness of explanations into the unified definitions. With our approach, we support the development of formal standards for (self-)explainable systems. Establishing such a uniform taxonomy also is a beneficial step towards certifying or auditing explainable systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes unified definitions and a structured taxonomy for explainability in autonomous and software-intensive systems, incorporating explanation goodness/correctness, to support the development of formal standards, certification, and auditing of (self-)explainable systems.
AI.motivation: Autonomous and software-intensive systems are increasingly complex and responsible, yet no universally applicable definition or development guide for (self-)explainable systems exists. Regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act and IEEE 7001-2021 signal a recognized need for explainability standards, motivating the authors to fill this gap.
AI.method: The authors analyze and combine existing definitions of explainability from the literature to derive unified definitions. They then develop structured explainability requirements and construct a taxonomy. Through analysis of this taxonomy, they propose incorporating the notion of "explanation goodness" (correctness of explanations) into the unified definitions.
AI.result: A set of unified definitions for explainability, a structured taxonomy of explainability requirements, and the conceptual integration of explanation goodness/correctness into the unified framework.
AI.conclusion: Establishing a uniform taxonomy and unified definitions is a beneficial step toward developing formal standards for (self-)explainable systems and enables progress in certifying or auditing such systems, addressing regulatory needs.

title: Detecting Safety Training Modification in Language Models via Activation Analysis
summary: We introduce AMS (Activation-based Model Scanner), a tool that detects modifications to safety training in language models by measuring the geometric structure of safety-relevant concepts in activation space. Safety training creates measurable separation between harmful and benign content classes; certain safety modifications collapse or rotate this structure, while others leave it intact. We validate AMS across 14 model configurations spanning 4 architecture families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral) and four safety-modification categories (instruction-tuned, base, abliterated, uncensored fine-tunes). Leave-one-out cross-validation of thresholds achieves 71% accuracy (10/14); bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on sigma point estimates have median width 3.4 sigma. We measure behavioral compliance on 20 stratified JailbreakBench prompts per model and find that sigma on the harmful-content concept predicts compliance with Pearson r = -0.546 (p = 0.043), directionally but with meaningful noise. Mechanistic analysis identifies a four-class taxonomy of safety-training modifications distinguished by activation-space signature: training removal collapses cluster separation; weight-orthogonalization abliteration both collapses separation and rotates the refusal direction; rotation-without-collapse abliteration preserves separation while rotating direction; and behavioral fine-tuning preserves both magnitude and direction. AMS's Tier 1 sigma-threshold detects the first two classes; Tier 2 direction-similarity verification detects the third. The fourth is undetectable by activation-only probing and represents a documented failure mode. We discuss threshold calibration, limitations of single-run measurement, and the open problem of detecting behavioral-only safety modifications.

AI.tldr: AMS detects safety-training modifications in LLMs by analyzing geometric structure of safety-relevant concepts in activation space, achieving 71% detection accuracy across 14 model configurations and identifying a four-class taxonomy of modification types with distinct activation-space signatures.
AI.motivation: To develop a reliable, activation-space-based method for detecting when language models' safety training has been tampered with, since behavioral compliance alone is noisy and insufficient for robust detection.
AI.method: AMS measures the geometric structure (cluster separation via sigma, refusal direction via cosine similarity) of harmful vs. benign content representations in activation space. It uses a two-tier detection system: Tier 1 applies sigma thresholds to detect cluster collapse, and Tier 2 uses direction-similarity verification to detect rotation-without-collapse modifications. Validated via leave-one-out cross-validation and bootstrap confidence intervals across 14 model configurations spanning 4 architecture families and 4 modification categories. Behavioral validation uses 20 stratified JailbreakBench prompts per model.
AI.result: Leave-one-out cross-validation achieved 71% accuracy (10/14); bootstrap 95% CI on sigma estimates had median width 3.4 sigma. Harmful-content sigma predicted behavioral compliance with Pearson r = -0.546 (p = 0.043). A four-class taxonomy emerged: (1) training removal collapses cluster separation; (2) weight-orthogonalization abliteration collapses separation and rotates refusal direction; (3) rotation-without-collapse abliteration preserves separation but rotates direction; (4) behavioral fine-tuning preserves both — and is undetectable by activation-only probing.
AI.conclusion: Activation-space geometry provides a viable, partially effective detection mechanism for safety-training modifications, though behavioral-only fine-tuning remains an open undetectable failure mode. The two-tier approach covers three of four modification classes.

title: ConWriter: Transition-Constrained Stateful Long-Form Story Generation with Lightweight Neuro-Symbolic Consistency Control
summary: Long-form story generation requires models to preserve narrative consistency across extended contexts, yet existing prompting-based methods often accumulate temporal, factual, character, commonsense, and stylistic errors as the story grows. We propose ConWriter, a training-free framework for consistency-aware long story generation. ConWriter writes stories incrementally at the scene level, guided by static story requirements, dynamic narrative memory, symbolic state reasoning, and uncertainty-aware risk signals. Rather than treating long-story generation as a single free-form decoding process, ConWriter maintains evolving story states, checks whether new scenes satisfy required narrative transitions, and uses uncertainty-aware risk signals to prioritize validation and localized repair. This enables consistency control during generation, before local errors propagate into later scenes. We evaluate ConWriter on ConStory-Bench, covering four long-story tasks: continuation, generation, expansion, and completion. Due to the high cost of long-form generation and evaluation, we use the first five cases from each task and test 3k, 6k, and 12k target lengths across Qwen3.5-Plus, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GPT-5 series. Experiments follow the official ConStory-Bench evaluation protocol.

AI.tldr: ConWriter is a training-free framework for long-form story generation that introduces scene-level incremental writing with dynamic narrative memory, symbolic state reasoning, and uncertainty-aware risk signals to maintain consistency across five error dimensions (temporal, factual, character, commonsense, stylistic), evaluated on the ConStory-Bench benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing prompting-based methods for long-form story generation suffer from accumulated narrative inconsistencies—temporal, factual, character, commonsense, and stylistic errors—that propagate as stories grow longer. A structured, training-free approach is needed to catch and repair these errors at the scene level before they cascade.
AI.method: ConWriter generates stories incrementally at the scene level using four components: (1) static story requirements that encode fixed narrative constraints, (2) dynamic narrative memory that tracks evolving story states across scenes, (3) symbolic state reasoning to verify whether new scenes satisfy required narrative transitions, and (4) uncertainty-aware risk signals that prioritize validation and trigger localized repair when inconsistencies are detected, preventing error propagation.
AI.result: Evaluated on ConStory-Bench across four long-story tasks (continuation, generation, expansion, completion) using the first five cases per task at 3k, 6k, and 12k target lengths. Experiments span three model series: Qwen3.5-Plus, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GPT-5, following the official ConStory-Bench evaluation protocol.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that a training-free, scene-level framework with consistency monitoring and localized repair mechanisms can mitigate the compounding error problem in long-form story generation, though specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.

title: Spectral Distillation: From Nonlinear Dynamics to Linear State-Space Models
summary: Can nonlinear dynamical systems be learned through a compact linear state-space representation, without directly solving a non-convex system-identification problem? We give a provable pipeline for doing so. Starting from observations of an unknown nonlinear dynamical system, we first learn an implicit spectral predictor using Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex method that competes with the best linear observer for the system. We then apply spectral-to-LDS distillation to convert this predictor into an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system. Our main theorem shows that the average prediction error of the distilled LDS decomposes into an exponentially-small distillation term and the OSF learning term governed by the Luenberger complexity of the best observer. The guarantee is dimension-free: it depends on observer complexity rather than on the latent dimension needed to represent the nonlinear system. To our knowledge, this yields the first end-to-end provable method for extracting a best-in-hindsight LDS representation of nonlinear dynamics through convex learning followed by provable distillation. Experiments on linear LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning show that the train-then-distill pipeline produces compact LDS predictors that match or outperform directly trained baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first end-to-end provable method for learning nonlinear dynamical systems via compact linear state-space representations (LDS), using convex OSF learning followed by spectral-to-LDS distillation, with dimension-free guarantees.
AI.motivation: Learning nonlinear dynamical systems typically requires solving non-convex system-identification problems, which lack provable guarantees. The authors aim to bypass this by learning a compact linear state-space representation through convex methods, without directly tackling non-convex optimization.
AI.method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex method that learns an implicit spectral predictor from trajectory observations, competing with the best linear observer; (2) Spectral-to-LDS distillation, which converts the implicit predictor into an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system (LDS) with provable error decomposition.
AI.result: The main theorem establishes that the distilled LDS's average prediction error decomposes into an exponentially small distillation term plus an OSF learning term bounded by the Luenberger complexity of the best observer. The guarantee is dimension-free, depending on observer complexity rather than latent state dimension. Experiments on LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning show the pipeline matches or outperforms directly trained baselines.
AI.conclusion: This work yields the first end-to-end provable pipeline for extracting best-in-hindsight LDS representations of nonlinear dynamics, combining convex learning with provable distillation, and demonstrates practical effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks.

title: LUNAR: Benchmarking Personalized Large Language Models on UNiversal User BehAvioR Logs
summary: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks primarily rely on textual personas or isolated behavioral signals, providing limited evaluation of cross-domain behavioral personalization, where responses must be grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities. To address this gap, we introduce LUNAR, the first benchmark for evaluating how LLMs personalize responses from longitudinal app interaction histories across universal daily-life domains, including clothing, food, housing, and mobility. To support scalable benchmark construction while mitigating data sparsity and privacy concerns, LUNAR uses a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world behavioral patterns. Fidelity analyses show closer alignment with real behavioral distributions than other synthetic benchmarks. Experiments on 19 mainstream LLMs show that access to behavioral logs is necessary but not sufficient for deep personalization: neither more context nor larger models guarantees better performance; effective personalization depends on selecting and integrating relevant evidence across domains. Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records consistently outperforms compressed memory, while stronger personalization can come at the cost of privacy protection. These findings identify evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control as key challenges for personalized LLMs.

AI.tldr: LUNAR is a benchmark for evaluating cross-domain behavioral personalization in LLMs using longitudinal app interaction histories. It employs a coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world patterns. Experiments across 19 LLMs reveal that access to behavioral logs is necessary but insufficient; effective personalization hinges on evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks are limited to textual personas or isolated behavioral signals and fail to evaluate cross-domain behavioral personalization grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities (clothing, food, housing, mobility). There is a need for a benchmark that uses longitudinal, multi-domain behavioral data while addressing data sparsity and privacy concerns.
AI.method: The authors introduce LUNAR, constructed via a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world behavioral patterns. Fidelity is validated against real behavioral distributions. Evaluation covers 19 mainstream LLMs under varying conditions: access to behavioral logs, context length, model size, and retrieval strategies (fine-grained retrieval vs. compressed memory).
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Behavioral logs are necessary but not sufficient — neither more context nor larger models guarantee better personalization. (2) Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records consistently outperforms compressed memory. (3) Stronger personalization can degrade privacy protection. Performance depends critically on selecting and integrating relevant cross-domain evidence.
AI.conclusion: Evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control are identified as the core challenges for advancing personalized LLMs. The LUNAR benchmark provides a foundation for systematically investigating these dimensions.

title: What Current AI Benchmarks Leave Unmeasured: Modality, Search, Citations, and Implications (for Safety Evaluations)
summary: Large language model (LLM) benchmark evaluations are routinely used to support claims about model safety, reliability, and deployment readiness. Yet most evaluations rely on a single access modality (model APIs), perform a single run per prompt, and report accuracy as the primary outcome metric, without accounting for conditions such as web search that may have effects on model behavior in deployment. We audit these assumptions for one of the most widely-used LLMs, comparing two modalities, ChatGPT's chat UI and OpenAI's API, with and without web search enabled. We use a stratified total sample of 401 prompts from two popular benchmarks, BBQ and SafetyBench, collecting 4,812 total responses across three repeated runs per prompt. Beyond standard performance measures, we evaluate model output dimensions including response consistency, response text similarity, citation grounding, and abstention behavior. For instance, chat UI responses were less accurate than API responses on both benchmarks with search disabled.
