Enabling web search reduced accuracy by up to 8 percentage points, and even reversed the direction of modality performance trends for one benchmark. Repeated runs of the same prompt produced inconsistent responses in up to 21\% of prompts. The two modalities also grounded answers in different citations, and abstention behavior was also inconsistent across both modalities. These results illustrate that, even within a model family, reporting only simple accuracy metrics can obscure important forms of model behavioral variation relevant to AI safety assessments. We argue that AI safety evaluations should systematically account for modality, multi-run consistency, search conditions, and response-level behaviors to better reflect how deployed AI systems behave in practice.

AI.tldr: LLM benchmark evaluations typically report single-run accuracy from one access modality, ignoring how factors like web search and multiple runs affect behavior. Auditing ChatGPT's chat UI vs. API across 401 prompts from BBQ and SafetyBench (4,812 responses), the authors find that modality, search enablement, and repeated runs significantly alter accuracy, consistency, citation grounding, and abstention — undermining the reliability of standard single-metric safety assessments.
AI.motivation: Current LLM safety evaluations rely on oversimplified assumptions: single access modality (APIs), single-run prompting, and accuracy-only reporting — without accounting for real-world deployment conditions like web search or behavioral consistency across repeated runs. These practices may obscure meaningful variation in model behavior relevant to AI safety.
AI.method: The authors audited ChatGPT (chat UI vs. OpenAI API), with and without web search enabled, using a stratified random sample of 401 prompts drawn from two safety benchmarks (BBQ and SafetyBench). They collected 4,812 total responses across three repeated runs per prompt and evaluated accuracy, response consistency (exact match), text similarity, citation grounding, and abstention rates across conditions.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Chat UI responses were less accurate than API responses on both benchmarks with search disabled. (2) Enabling web search reduced accuracy by up to 8 percentage points and reversed the direction of modality performance trends on one benchmark. (3) Up to 21% of prompts produced inconsistent responses across repeated runs. (4) The two modalities grounded answers in different citations. (5) Abstention behavior was inconsistent across modalities.
AI.conclusion: Reporting only simple accuracy metrics obscures important behavioral variation relevant to AI safety. The authors argue that safety evaluations should systematically incorporate modality, multi-run consistency, search conditions, and response-level behavioral dimensions to better reflect how deployed AI systems actually behave in practice.

title: DCAS: Decoupling CLI Agent Scaffolding to Internalize Planning across Scaffolds
summary: CLI-based software-engineering agents have matured rapidly, yet the open ecosystem has converged on a single training environment: trajectory datasets used to fine-tune open models are collected almost exclusively under OpenHands. Models fine-tuned on this data score well under OpenHands but degrade substantially when deployed under any non-training scaffold. Untrained base models do not show this divergence, indicating the gap is fine-tuning-induced and tied to the conventions of the training scaffold. We argue that a load-bearing scaffold-specific behavior is planning structure, in two senses this paper distinguishes: explicit planning, a pre-execution plan produced as a first-class artifact, and implicit planning, the structural conventions that shape execution throughout the agent loop. Under this hypothesis, closing the gap requires moving planning from a fixed scaffold artifact to a learned model capability. We introduce Decoupling CLI Agent Scaffolding (DCAS), a backend-substitution interception layer that routes API traffic between any CLI scaffold and any backend model without modifying the scaffold, enabling cross-scaffold evaluation and planning-aware trajectory collection. Using DCAS, a controlled plan-source intervention confirms planning quality is a high-leverage component, with gains exceeding the cross-scaffold drops we observe. A model fine-tuned on a small set of DCAS-collected planning-aware trajectories under a single scaffold gains consistently across non-training scaffolds, and the two senses of planning are empirically separable in training data.

AI.tldr: Open-source CLI agents fine-tuned on OpenHands trajectories suffer severe performance degradation when deployed under different scaffolds due to scaffold-specific planning conventions. The authors introduce DCAS, a backend-substitution layer that decouples scaffold from model, enabling cross-scaffold evaluation and planning-aware data collection. Fine-tuning on DCAS-collected trajectories yields consistent gains across non-training scaffolds.
AI.motivation: The open-source CLI agent ecosystem relies heavily on a single training environment (OpenHands), causing fine-tuned models to overfit to scaffold-specific conventions. This results in significant performance drops when models are deployed under different scaffolds, while base models show no such divergence. The authors aim to identify the root cause and provide a remedy.
AI.method: The authors propose Decoupling CLI Agent Scaffolding (DCAS), a backend-substitution interception layer that routes API traffic between any CLI scaffold and any backend model without modifying the scaffold. DCAS enables two key capabilities: (1) cross-scaffold evaluation to measure scaffold-induced performance gaps, and (2) planning-aware trajectory collection. A controlled plan-source intervention isolates planning quality as the key factor. The method distinguishes between explicit planning (pre-execution plans as first-class artifacts) and implicit planning (structural conventions shaping the agent loop).
AI.result: Planning quality is confirmed as a high-leverage component, with gains from improved planning exceeding the observed cross-scaffold performance drops. A model fine-tuned on a small set of DCAS-collected planning-aware trajectories under a single scaffold shows consistent performance gains across non-training scaffolds. The two senses of planning (explicit and implicit) are empirically separable in training data.
AI.conclusion: Closing the scaffold-induced performance gap requires moving planning from a fixed scaffold artifact to a learned model capability. DCAS provides a practical mechanism for collecting scaffold-agnostic training data, and planning-aware fine-tuning yields robust cross-scaffold generalization.

title: Enhancing Anomaly Resilience in Research Networks: A Large-Scale Forecasting Benchmark for Dynamic Security Baselining
summary: Research and Education Networks (RENs) serve as critical infrastructure for scientific discovery, yet they face a unique security paradox: their normal traffic patterns which are characterized by massive, bursty "elephant flows" are statistically indistinguishable from volumetric attacks such as DDoS to conventional monitoring systems. This similarity leads to high false-positive rates in anomaly detection, blinding security operators to genuine threats. In this paper, we propose and evaluate a high-fidelity traffic forecasting framework designed to establish dynamic security baselines for RENs. Leveraging an exclusive 57-day Internet2 dataset spanning ten backbone routers (13.7 billion packets), we perform the first large-scale benchmark of anomaly-aware forecasting models in this domain. We systematically evaluate six model families, from SARIMA to state-of-the-art long-sequence architectures (TiDE, PatchTST), across 960 experimental configurations. Our results demonstrate that these advanced architectures, particularly TiDE, reduce baseline prediction error by 30-42% compared to traditional methods ($p < 0.001$), significantly improving the distinction between legitimate scientific bursts and potential anomalies. Furthermore, we introduce a novel anomaly-integration strategy that improves model robustness by 3.3% in the presence of noise. This work provides the first statistically validated framework for distinguishing scientific workflows from network attacks, enabling more autonomous and resilient network security operations.

AI.tldr: RENs struggle to distinguish legitimate scientific elephant flows from DDoS attacks. This paper benchmarks six forecasting model families on 57 days of Internet2 backbone data (13.7B packets) and shows that modern architectures like TiDE reduce prediction error by 30-42%, enabling better separation of normal bursts from anomalies.
AI.motivation: Research and Education Networks (RENs) face a fundamental security paradox: legitimate high-volume scientific data transfers ("elephant flows") are statistically indistinguishable from DDoS attacks to conventional anomaly detection systems, resulting in high false-positive rates that blind operators to real threats. No prior work has established a statistically validated, anomaly-aware traffic forecasting baseline tailored to this domain.
AI.method: The authors collected a 57-day dataset from ten Internet2 backbone routers (13.7 billion packets). They benchmarked six model families — SARIMA and five deep-learning long-sequence architectures (including TiDE and PatchTST) — across 960 experimental configurations. They evaluated forecasting accuracy for establishing dynamic security baselines and introduced a novel anomaly-integration strategy to improve model robustness under noisy conditions.
AI.result: Advanced architectures, particularly TiDE, reduced baseline prediction error by 30-42% over traditional methods (p < 0.001). The anomaly-integration strategy improved model robustness by 3.3% in the presence of noise, yielding better discrimination between legitimate scientific bursts and genuine attacks.
AI.conclusion: This work delivers the first statistically validated framework for distinguishing scientific workflows from network attacks on REN backbones, enabling more autonomous and resilient network security operations through high-fidelity dynamic baselines.

title: DREAM: LLM-based Dynamic Role-playing via Event-Aware Memory Graph
comment: Accepted at KDD 2026. Camera-ready version to appear. 16 pages, 5 figures
summary: Role-playing agents (RPAs) have emerged as a key application of large language models, enabling immersive and high-fidelity character simulation. Accurate role-playing of established characters requires not only stylistic imitation but also temporally consistent and causally grounded behavioral reasoning. However, existing RPAs primarily rely on static character descriptions and unstructured memory, limiting their ability to maintain long-term narrative and personality coherence. We introduce DREAM, a structured memory framework for role-playing agents inspired by the Activating Event-Belief-Consequence (ABC) cognitive model. DREAM transforms unstructured literary text into an Event-aware Memory Graph (EMG) that organizes character experiences into temporally ordered and causally linked event graph. This representation enables the construction of dynamic, dual-granularity character profiles that capture both stable personality traits and event-driven behavioral evolution. We further propose the Temporal Causal Memory (TCM) benchmark to evaluate temporal consistency and long-range causal narrative coherence. DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance across CoSER, LIFECHOICE, and TCM, outperforming multiple strong baselines. Our approach demonstrates the effectiveness of structured memory in enhancing the interpretability and consistency of role-playing agents.

AI.tldr: DREAM introduces a structured memory framework for role-playing agents that transforms unstructured text into an Event-aware Memory Graph (EMG), inspired by the ABC cognitive model, enabling temporally consistent and causally coherent character simulation with state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing role-playing agents rely on static character descriptions and unstructured memory, which limits their ability to maintain long-term narrative and personality coherence. They lack mechanisms for temporally consistent and causally grounded behavioral reasoning, which are essential for accurate character simulation.
AI.method: DREAM proposes a structured memory framework based on the Activating Event-Belief-Consequence (ABC) cognitive model. It converts unstructured literary text into an Event-aware Memory Graph (EMG) that organizes character experiences into temporally ordered and causally linked event graphs. From this, it constructs dynamic, dual-granularity character profiles capturing both stable personality traits and event-driven behavioral evolution. A new evaluation benchmark, Temporal Causal Memory (TCM), is also introduced.
AI.result: DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on three benchmarks: CoSER, LIFECHOICE, and the newly proposed TCM, outperforming multiple strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Structured memory, as implemented in DREAM, effectively enhances both the interpretability and consistency of role-playing agents, demonstrating the value of cognitively inspired memory architectures for character simulation.

title: Perturbation Sensitivity at Convergence: A Simple Signal for Identifying Spuriously Correlated Samples
summary: Models trained by empirical risk minimization on data containing spurious correlations achieve high average accuracy while failing on subpopulations where the correlation does not hold. Existing methods for identifying the affected samples without group annotations rely on signals from early training, which requires locating the epoch at which to intervene, a hyperparameter typically selected using group-labeled validation data. We show that a usable signal is available after convergence, when loss no longer distinguishes the two populations. Samples consistent with the spurious correlation are classified by a shared rule, while the remaining samples are fit through configurations specific to individual inputs and are correspondingly more fragile. Applying a fixed perturbation to a converged model's inputs flips the predictions of the latter far more often than the former. The resulting procedure requires two forward passes per training sample, no group annotations at any stage, and no early-stopping epoch. Using the detected samples to rebalance training raises worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 57.3% to 80.8%, against 85.8% with ground-truth group labels.

AI.tldr: After model convergence, samples that rely on spurious correlations are classified via a shared, robust rule, while minority samples are fit by fragile, input-specific configurations. Perturbing inputs flips predictions for fragile samples far more often, enabling group detection without any group annotations or early-stopping tuning, and rebalancing with detected groups lifts worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 57.3% to 80.8%.
AI.motivation: Empirical risk minimization on spurious-correlated data yields high average accuracy but catastrophically low accuracy on subpopulations where the spurious correlation breaks. Existing mitigation methods require either group labels or careful selection of an early-training intervention epoch using group-annotated validation data. The authors aim to remove both requirements entirely.
AI.method: The authors propose leveraging a post-convergence signal: after training converges, samples aligned with the spurious correlation are classified by a shared, stable decision rule, whereas minority (non-correlated) samples are fit by fragile, instance-specific mechanisms. A fixed input perturbation is applied to a converged model; the rate of prediction flipping is substantially higher for the fragile, minority-group samples. This perturbation-based fragility score is computed in two forward passes per sample, requiring no group annotations and no early-stopping epoch selection. Detected samples are then used to rebalance training.
AI.result: On the Waterbirds benchmark, worst-group accuracy improves from 57.3% (ERM baseline) to 80.8% using the proposed detection and rebalancing, compared to 85.8% with ground-truth group labels. This narrows the gap to oracle performance while using no group annotations at any stage.
AI.conclusion: A strong signal for identifying spurious-correlation-dependent samples exists after convergence rather than only during early training. Post-hoc input perturbation fragility effectively separates majority (spurious-aligned) from minority (non-aligned) samples, enabling group-annotation-free rebalancing that approaches the performance of fully supervised group-label methods.

title: WorldClaw: Agentic 3D Open-World Generation at Scale
comment: Authors are listed in alphabetical order by given name
summary: Generating large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from open-ended text remains challenging because a system must jointly maintain global spatial coherence, rich local content, and explicit assets suitable for downstream editing and reuse. We present WorldClaw, a fully agentic, coarse-to-fine framework for open-world 3D scene generation. Planning agents translate a text prompt into a structured specification of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations. WorldClaw then builds a globally coherent terrain foundation from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative or procedural materials, and a region-aware height field. For detail-demanding regions, it generates terrain-conditioned compositions, reconstructs editable textured meshes, and recovers their placement on the terrain; render-based agents further refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts. Across diverse open-world prompts, WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes with coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets while preserving a consistent global terrain structure.

AI.tldr: WorldClaw is an agentic, coarse-to-fine framework that generates large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from text prompts, maintaining global terrain coherence, rich local content, and reusable editable assets through a pipeline of planning agents, terrain construction, detail generation, and render-based refinement.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for text-to-3D scene generation struggle to simultaneously maintain global spatial coherence across large scales, produce rich local detail, and deliver explicit, editable instance-level assets suitable for downstream reuse. An integrated framework addressing all three requirements is lacking.
AI.method: WorldClaw employs a coarse-to-fine, fully agentic pipeline: (1) Planning agents translate text prompts into structured specifications of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations. (2) A globally coherent terrain foundation is built from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative/procedural materials, and a region-aware height field. (3) For detail-demanding regions, terrain-conditioned compositions are generated, editable textured meshes are reconstructed and placed on the terrain, and render-based agents iteratively refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contact points.
AI.result: Across diverse open-world prompts, WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes featuring coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets, all while preserving a consistent global terrain structure.
AI.conclusion: WorldClaw demonstrates that an agentic, coarse-to-fine architecture can successfully bridge global scene coherence with local detail richness and asset editability, advancing the state of open-world 3D generation from textual descriptions.

title: Learning Globally Reusable Skills for Coding Agents
summary: Automated skill evolution enables Large Language Model (LLM) agents to continuously improve without expensive retraining. However, existing approaches typically treat skill evolution as a sequence of local updates, overlooking relationships among skills and often producing overfitted skill updates that fail to generalize across tasks. We propose GSE, a globalized skill evolution framework that jointly optimizes skill compatibility and skill generalization. To preserve consistency across the skill bank, GSE maintains a Skill Relation Graph (SRG) that explicitly models and co-evolves inter-skill relationships. To improve generalization, GSE performs cluster-based skill consolidation to abstract reusable capabilities from local updates and employs replay-driven verification to prevent overfitting and behavioral regressions. We evaluate GSE on two representative software engineering tasks: bug-revealing test generation and false-positive bug report filtering. Across two state-of-the-art coding agents, OpenHands and mini-SWE-agent, GSE consistently achieves the best precision, recall, and F1-score. Compared with existing evolution techniques, GSE improves precision and recall by 6.1%~34.1% and 31.8%~180.0% for test generation, and by 15.4%~96.4% and 13.1%~19.8% for false-positive filtering. Deployment on an internal industrial agent further yields a 61.4% improvement in F1-score, demonstrating the effectiveness and generalizability of GSE for evolving effective skills.

AI.tldr: GSE is a globalized skill evolution framework for LLM agents that uses a Skill Relation Graph and cluster-based consolidation to jointly optimize skill compatibility and generalization, significantly outperforming existing methods on software engineering tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent skill evolution methods treat updates as isolated local modifications, ignoring inter-skill relationships and producing overfitted skills that fail to generalize across tasks. There is a need for a framework that jointly addresses skill consistency and generalization.
AI.method: GSE introduces three core components: (1) a Skill Relation Graph (SRG) that explicitly models and co-evolves inter-skill relationships to preserve consistency; (2) cluster-based skill consolidation that abstracts reusable capabilities from local updates; and (3) replay-driven verification to prevent overfitting and behavioral regression.
AI.result: On bug-revealing test generation and false-positive bug report filtering, GSE achieves the best precision, recall, and F1-score across OpenHands and mini-SWE-agent. It improves precision by 6.1%–34.1% and recall by 31.8%–180.0% for test generation, and precision by 15.4%–96.4% and recall by 13.1%–19.8% for false-positive filtering. An industrial deployment yields a 61.4% F1-score improvement.
AI.conclusion: GSE demonstrates that jointly optimizing skill compatibility and generalization via relational modeling and consolidation significantly outperforms local-update-based evolution, with strong generalizability across academic and industrial settings.

title: Breaking Customized LLMs for Coding: Automated Red Teaming for Instruction Backdoor Attacks
comment: Accepted to the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026
summary:
LLM customization platforms allow users to build task-specific models for code intelligence tasks by embedding instructions into system prompts, without modifying the underlying model parameters. While these platforms lower the barrier to developing customized LLMs, they also introduce a new attack surface: instruction backdoor attacks, in which adversaries implant hidden malicious behaviors into customized instructions. However, existing attacks suffer from two key limitations. First, they often rely on explicit trigger patterns readily detected by platform-side or user-side inspection. Second, they require substantial manual effort to craft task-specific backdoored instructions, limiting their scalability.
  In this paper, we propose ARIA, an automated red-teaming framework for crafting covert and effective backdoored instructions against customized LLMs. ARIA leverages an attacker LLM to iteratively generate and refine backdoored instructions, guided by structured feedback from the target LLM along three dimensions: stealthiness, clean-task utility, and backdoor effectiveness. We evaluate ARIA on three code intelligence tasks, using four representative LLMs, and compare it with three baseline attacks. Experimental results show that ARIA achieves the highest attack success rate of 0.945, while maintaining the best clean-task utility across all tasks. ARIA also generalizes well across programming languages and remains robust to generation temperature. Furthermore, ARIA significantly outperforms existing attacks in evading platform-side and user-side detection, achieving a false negative rate of up to 1.000, and stays effective against existing defense methods, demonstrating its strong generalizability and robustness.

AI.tldr: ARIA is an automated red-teaming framework that uses an attacker LLM to iteratively generate covert backdoored instructions for LLM customization platforms, achieving high attack success (0.945) while evading detection and preserving clean-task utility across code intelligence tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM customization platforms enable users to build task-specific models via system prompt instructions, but this introduces instruction backdoor attacks. Existing attacks are limited by reliance on explicit trigger patterns (easily detected) and require substantial manual effort to craft task-specific backdoored instructions, hindering scalability.
AI.method: ARIA uses an attacker LLM that iteratively generates and refines backdoored instructions through structured feedback from the target LLM across three dimensions: stealthiness (evading detection), clean-task utility (preserving normal performance), and backdoor effectiveness (triggering malicious behavior). The framework automates the entire attack crafting pipeline.
AI.result: Evaluated on three code intelligence tasks with four LLMs against three baselines: ARIA achieved the highest attack success rate of 0.945 while maintaining best clean-task utility. It generalized across programming languages, remained robust to generation temperature, achieved false negative rates up to 1.000 against detection, and stayed effective against existing defenses.
AI.conclusion: ARIA demonstrates that automated, covert, and effective instruction backdoor attacks are feasible against LLM customization platforms, exposing significant security vulnerabilities. Its strong generalizability and robustness against detection and defenses highlight the urgent need for more effective countermeasures in LLM customization ecosystems.

title: Position: It's Time to Optimize LLMs for Self-Consistency
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), Position Paper Track
summary: Despite ever-increasing sophistication in language model (LM) pre- and post-training pipelines, many important failures persist: models overcondition on user framing ("sycophancy"), exhibit incomplete logical generalization, and produce confident but incorrect responses. We argue that these failures arise from a modeling assumption permeating all aspects of the pipeline: that behavior can be specified and evaluated independently on single-output pairs. Many model failures are difficult, if not impossible, to detect without reasoning about relationships between a model's responses across inputs. In this position paper, we propose self-consistency as a framework for understanding these failures. We first observe that a wide variety of techniques designed to improve specific aspects of LM behavior-targeting properties as diverse as adversarial robustness and factual coherence-can be understood as special cases of a common "consistency optimization" procedure and addressed with a standard set of optimization tools. We next outline a set of new model properties that could be achieved by optimizing for consistency, and conclude with a discussion of what it would mean to develop generally consistent LMs, including the capabilities they would enable and the objections they raise.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that many persistent LM failures (sycophancy, logical gaps, overconfidence) stem from evaluating models on single input-output pairs rather than across related inputs. It proposes self-consistency as a unifying framework, showing that diverse improvement techniques are special cases of consistency optimization, and outlines a vision for generally consistent LMs.
AI.motivation: Despite advanced training pipelines, LMs continue to exhibit failures like sycophancy (overconditioning on user framing), incomplete logical generalization, and confident but incorrect responses. The authors argue these failures are undetectable when behavior is evaluated on isolated single-output pairs, a pervasive modeling assumption throughout current LM pipelines.
AI.method: This is a position paper that proposes self-consistency as a conceptual framework. The authors demonstrate that diverse existing techniques — targeting properties such as adversarial robustness and factual coherence — can be unified as special cases of a common "consistency optimization" procedure, addressable with standard optimization tools. They then outline potential new model properties achievable through consistency optimization.
AI.result: As a position paper, it presents no empirical results. The key finding is a conceptual unification: many disparate LM improvement methods (for adversarial robustness, factuality, etc.) are shown to be instances of the same underlying consistency optimization framework.
AI.conclusion: Developing generally consistent LMs would require optimizing behavior across related inputs rather than isolated pairs. This shift could enable new capabilities but also raises important objections that warrant further discussion.

title: Posture and Sustainment Optimization Under Adversarial Uncertainty
summary: Pre-commitment posture, the assignment of military assets to theater locations before conflict scenarios resolve, is a critical and formally unsolved problem in joint operational planning. Current practice relies on greedy heuristics that maximize value and ignore geographic coverage and are structurally vulnerable to adversaries that target high-strategic value locations. This paper presents a scenario-weighted adversarially robust posture optimization engine for the Posture and sustainability allocation (PSA) problem, modeled as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. We introduce the Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer, which places assets by maximizing scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency over a distribution of threat scenarios, and the RobustCEV extension, which iterates against a Bayesian adversary that updates its targeting distribution in response to observed placement. Across three experiments in an Indo-Pacific basing environment with 20 assets and 5 theater locations, we demonstrate that: (1) the greedy baseline incurs a permanent 25.1% posture efficiency penalty due to geographic under-coverage and a 57.3% scenario-weighted readiness collapse under value-correlated adversarial threat; (2) the CEV optimizer recovers up to 19.8% efficiency over greedy when the threat distribution carries a geographic signal, with a curated set of 5 to 20 scenarios sufficient to capture the majority of this gain; and (3) the RobustCEV extension recovers up to 158% efficiency relative to a naive optimizer when an adaptive adversary employs a deceptive threat prior. All findings are validated using paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction and two-level variance decomposition, confirming that the performance gaps reported are structural properties of placement strategies rather than sampling artifacts.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CEV and RobustCEV optimizers for military asset pre-commitment posture, modeled as a finite-horizon MDP, demonstrating up to 19.8% efficiency gains over greedy baselines and up to 158% recovery against adaptive Bayesian adversaries in an Indo-Pacific basing scenario.
AI.motivation: Current joint operational planning relies on greedy heuristics that maximize value while ignoring geographic coverage, leaving posture structurally vulnerable to adversaries targeting high-strategic-value locations. No formal solution exists for the pre-commitment posture problem.
AI.method: The PSA problem is modeled as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. The Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer maximizes scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency across a threat distribution. The RobustCEV extension iterates against a Bayesian adversary that dynamically updates its targeting distribution based on observed asset placement.
AI.result: In Indo-Pacific experiments with 20 assets and 5 locations: (1) greedy baselines suffer a 25.1% permanent efficiency penalty and 57.3% readiness collapse under value-correlated threats; (2) CEV recovers up to 19.8% efficiency with 5–20 scenarios; (3) RobustCEV achieves up to 158% efficiency recovery against deceptive adversarial priors. All results validated via paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction and two-level variance decomposition.
AI.conclusion: Scenario-weighted adversarial optimization structurally outperforms greedy heuristics for posture planning. The CEV framework captures geographic coverage benefits efficiently with modest scenario counts, while RobustCEV provides resilience against adaptive adversaries employing deceptive priors.

title: Predicting Agile Success: The Critical Few Factors
summary: While Agile projects are more successful than traditional software development project management approaches, their overall success rate remains relatively low, with a high percentage of projects still deemed challenged or failed. This low project success rate is attributed to projects not being rigorously evaluated against critical success factors (CSF) of Agile projects and contemporary project success criteria. To identify the CSF that contribute to Agile software development project success as perceived by Agile practitioners, this study used a positivist approach to investigate the CSF of Agile software development projects. PLS-SEM with SmartPLS was used to analyse the data and test the hypotheses to identify significant relationships between the constructs and project success criteria. This research found that a few critical factors significantly contribute to Agile project success. The study developed a novel model that can be used to evaluate and measure project success.

AI.tldr: This study identifies critical success factors (CSFs) for Agile software development projects using PLS-SEM analysis, finding that only a few factors significantly drive success, and proposes a novel evaluation model for measuring Agile project success.
AI.motivation: Despite Agile projects outperforming traditional approaches, success rates remain low with many projects challenged or failed. The authors attribute this to insufficient rigorous evaluation against CSFs and contemporary success criteria, motivating an empirical investigation into which factors Agile practitioners perceive as truly critical to project success.
AI.method: The study adopts a positivist approach, surveying Agile practitioners and analyzing data using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS software to test hypotheses regarding relationships between identified constructs and project success criteria.
AI.result: The analysis revealed that only a limited subset of the hypothesized critical success factors exhibit statistically significant relationships with Agile project success criteria, leading to the development of a novel, parsimonious model for evaluating and measuring Agile project success.
AI.conclusion: A focused set of critical success factors — rather than a broad array — meaningfully predicts Agile project success. The resulting model offers practitioners a practical tool for rigorous evaluation and measurement of Agile project outcomes.

title: Algebraic Cryptanalytic Extraction on Hard-Label Neural Networks
summary: Although the state-of-the-art neural network model extraction attack in the hard-label setting by Carlini et al. at EUROCRYPT 2025 has polynomial-time complexity in theory, its dual-point clustering relies on singular value decomposition (SVD) with a time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(n^2 \cdot (d^{(k)})^3)$, resulting in huge runtime in practice. To address this computational bottleneck, this work transforms Carlini et al.'s geometric-view hard-label attack into an algebraic framework, and proposes a novel Approximate Signature Vector (ASV) method to achieve efficient parameter extraction on Fully Connected Neural Networks (FCNNs) by leveraging two key observations: high-dimensional random vectors are nearly orthogonal, and neurons in practical DNNs tend to learn disentangled features. The proposed ASV method replaces SVD-based rank checking with simple inner-product operations, reducing the clustering complexity to $\mathcal{O}(n \cdot (d^{(k)})^3)$ on average. Furthermore, this paper presents the first model extraction attack against hard-label max-pooling Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by proposing an advanced ASV method with a kernel-centric clustering scheme instead of the neuron-centric clustering, which fully exploits the property of weight sharing in convolutions and fills the cryptanalysis gap. Experiments on a 64-64$\times$4-10 FCNN and LeNet-5 (CNN) with max pooling demonstrate that our ASV method drastically cuts clustering time, and improves the overall efficiency in the model extraction.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an Approximate Signature Vector (ASV) method that transforms Carlini et al.'s SVD-based hard-label model extraction attack into an algebraic framework, using inner-product operations instead of SVD for clustering, drastically reducing runtime. It also extends the attack to max-pooling CNNs via a kernel-centric clustering scheme.
AI.motivation: Carlini et al.'s EUROCRYPT 2025 hard-label model extraction attack, while polynomial-time in theory, suffers from a practical computational bottleneck: its dual-point clustering relies on SVD with O(n²·(d^(k))³) complexity, making it prohibitively slow in practice. This work aims to overcome that bottleneck and extend the attack to CNNs with max-pooling, which was previously not addressed.
AI.method: The authors reframe Carlini et al.'s geometric hard-label attack into an algebraic framework. They propose the Approximate Signature Vector (ASV) method, leveraging two observations: (1) high-dimensional random vectors are nearly orthogonal, and (2) practical DNN neurons learn disentangled features. The ASV method replaces SVD-based rank checking with simple inner-product operations, reducing average clustering complexity to O(n·(d^(k))³). For CNNs with max-pooling, they devise an advanced ASV with kernel-centric (rather than neuron-centric) clustering that exploits convolutional weight sharing.
AI.result: Experiments on a 64-64×4-10 FCNN and LeNet-5 (CNN with max pooling) show that the ASV method significantly reduces clustering time and improves overall model extraction efficiency compared to the SVD-based approach.
AI.conclusion: The ASV method successfully addresses the computational bottleneck in Carlini et al.'s hard-label attack and fills the cryptanalysis gap by enabling the first model extraction attack against hard-label max-pooling CNNs, achieving substantial efficiency gains.

title: Analysis of Numerical Localisation in LLM Translations
summary: The work of Tang et. al. (2025) on numerical translation is extended by analysing the capability of five large language models (LLMs) for the localisation of times, numbers, and dates instead of translation. Models were selected that could be loaded onto and run on commodity hardware and a baseline quality for each mode is computed, then three different strategies to improve on that accuracy were tested. In contrast to Tang et. al., it was discovered that on the tested LLMs, embedding the localisation principles into the prompt context provided a statistically significant improvement in accuracy compared to direct translation or the alternative strategies.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Tang et al. (2025) by evaluating five commodity-hardware LLMs on numerical localisation (times, numbers, dates) rather than translation, establishing baseline accuracy and testing three improvement strategies, finding that embedding localisation principles into prompt context yields statistically significant accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: Tang et al. (2025) focused on numerical translation, but the capability of LLMs to handle numerical localisation — adapting times, numbers, and dates to locale-specific formats — remained unexplored, particularly on models that can run on commodity hardware. There is a practical need to understand and improve localisation accuracy in resource-constrained deployment scenarios.
AI.method: Five LLMs capable of running on commodity hardware were selected. A baseline localisation accuracy was computed for each model across times, numbers, and dates. Three distinct improvement strategies were then tested: (1) direct translation, (2) embedding localisation principles into the prompt context, and (3) two alternative strategies. Accuracy was compared statistically across all approaches, contrasting findings with Tang et al.'s translation-focused results.
AI.result: Embedding localisation principles into the prompt context provided a statistically significant improvement in accuracy over both direct translation and the other alternative strategies across the tested LLMs. This contrasts with the findings of Tang et al. (2025), suggesting that numerical localisation may benefit from different prompting approaches than numerical translation.
AI.conclusion: For LLMs running on commodity hardware, prompt engineering that explicitly embeds localisation principles is the most effective strategy for numerical localisation tasks, diverging from prior findings in numerical translation and highlighting the task-specific nature of optimal prompting strategies.

title: Why the Third Axis Is Freedom
comment: Experiment code available on GitHub, in the papers folder: https://github.com/ViscousLemming/Technical-Appendices
summary: In generative training, a model produces an output and is penalised for its difference from an example. With one output per comparison, a model that produces one common answer can outperform a model retaining a broader repertoire. Explorative Modeling (XM) produces $K$ outputs per comparison and updates on the closest, claiming exploration as a "third pretraining axis" associated with generative expressivity. Here I show the third axis is actually freedom, meaning the weakness of the constraint implied by a model's behaviour. Previous work showed freedom is a property of function rather than form. Parameters, architecture, minimum-description-length (MDL), and data can vary while the behavioural constraint remains unchanged. It was formally proved that weakest models are likeliest to generalise, and freedom selection beat MDL by 110-500\% in induction experiments. I prove average XM loss depends on the chance a candidate misses an acceptable region, with exploration raising miss probability to power $K$. For $K>1$, match probability rises with freedom. I then demonstrate empirically that XM optimises for freedom. In a Forward XM experiment, larger $K$ increased or saturated measured freedom, and increased freedom at every tested value under context-dependent targets. I trained XM candidate pools and compared validation selection with a freedom selector that read unlabelled parent contexts. Freedom won in 29 of 30 cases. Generative expressivity is a mode-count proxy for freedom, that discards the extension structure that gives freedom its generalisation significance. XM is a means, freedom an end, and selecting for freedom improved XM under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: XM (Explorative Modeling) produces K outputs per comparison and updates on the closest, but the author argues its purported "third pretraining axis" of exploration is actually freedom—the weakness of behavioral constraint. The paper proves XM loss depends on the probability a candidate misses an acceptable region, with exploration raising miss probability to the K-th power, meaning match probability rises with freedom for K>1. Empirically, freedom selection outperformed validation selection in 29/30 cases, and selecting for freedom improved XM under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: The author contests the claim that exploration in Explorative Modeling (XM) constitutes a "third pretraining axis" associated with generative expressivity. Instead, they argue the true underlying mechanism is freedom—the weakness of behavioral constraint—and that this distinction matters because freedom has formal generalization significance while generative expressivity (a mode-count proxy) discards the extension structure that gives freedom its power.
AI.method: The paper combines formal proof and empirical demonstration. Theoretically, it proves that average XM loss depends on the chance a candidate misses an acceptable region, with K-output exploration raising miss probability to power K, so for K>1, match probability rises with freedom. Empirically: (1) a Forward XM experiment showed larger K increased or saturated measured freedom; (2) XM candidate pools were trained and validation selection was compared against a freedom selector using unlabelled parent contexts, with freedom winning 29/30 cases.
AI.result: Key results: (1) Formal proof that XM's loss structure inherently favors high-freedom models when K>1. (2) Freedom selection beat minimum description length (MDL) by 110-500% in prior induction experiments. (3) In Forward XM, larger K increased freedom. (4) Freedom-based selection outperformed validation selection in 29 of 30 cases. (5) Selecting for freedom improved XM performance under distribution shift.
AI.conclusion: Exploration in XM is not a distinct pretraining axis but rather a mechanism that inadvertently selects for behavioral freedom—a property already known to drive generalization. Generative expressivity is merely a mode-count proxy for freedom that loses critical extension structure. The author concludes that XM is a means, freedom is the end, and explicitly selecting for freedom yields better results under distribution shift than XM alone.

title: OrchestraBench: Evaluating Multi-Agent Orchestration Failure Modes, Recovery, and Decomposition Quality
summary: Multi-agent orchestration frameworks are moving from demos to production, yet benchmarks typically report task accuracy without diagnosing why a pipeline failed, where a cascade began, or which routing decision caused the breakdown. OrchestraBench evaluates failure, recovery, and decomposition through a controlled, seed-reproducible failure-injection harness over templated enterprise workflows. It introduces cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery as primary metrics and compares routing policies with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests. On a 26-case gold-labelled diagnostic, a keyword/flag router scored 0% on adversarial cases with misleading or missing surface flags, whereas an intent-reasoning model router scored 100%, matching the oracle. Controlled mechanism probes with a real Claude agent over a verifiable arithmetic dependency chain revealed three failure-handling tiers across five MAST modes: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent or semantic modes never recovered (0.0). This ordering persisted when the computation was reframed as a loan-approval workflow and across Sonnet, Opus, and Haiku, although absolute rates shifted with context. Blind retry reproduced latent faults and increased time to detection, indicating that detection and attribution are necessary for containment. Cascade radius increased with pipeline depth (mean 0.9 to 4.7 across depths 3-7). A trusted-state repair ablation showed that apparent containment gains primarily came from the trusted-state signal rather than autonomous detection. These results are controlled-chain mechanism probes, not domain-workload claims.

AI.tldr: OrchestraBench evaluates multi-agent orchestration frameworks by diagnosing failure modes, cascade behavior, and recovery, using controlled failure injection. Key findings: intent-based routers outperform keyword routers on adversarial cases (100% vs 0%); tool faults recover fully while latent/semantic faults never recover; cascade radius grows with pipeline depth; and trusted-state signals drive containment more than autonomous detection.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for multi-agent orchestration frameworks report only task accuracy, failing to explain why a pipeline broke, where cascading failures began, or which routing decision triggered the breakdown. There is a need for diagnostic evaluation that reveals failure mechanisms, recovery behavior, and decomposition quality.
AI.method: The authors introduce OrchestraBench, a controlled, seed-reproducible failure-injection harness applied to templated enterprise workflows. It uses cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery as primary metrics, compares routing policies with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests, and conducts mechanism probes over a verifiable arithmetic dependency chain using a real Claude agent across five MAST modes. A trusted-state repair ablation isolates the source of containment gains.
AI.result: A keyword/flag router scored 0% on adversarial cases with misleading or missing surface flags, while an intent-reasoning model router scored 100% (matching oracle). Across five MAST modes, three failure-handling tiers emerged: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent/semantic modes never recovered (0.0). This ordering persisted across workflow reframing (loan-approval) and three model variants (Sonnet, Opus, Haiku). Blind retry reproduced latent faults and increased detection time. Cascade radius increased with pipeline depth (mean 0.9 at depth 3 to 4.7 at depth 7). The trusted-state repair ablation showed containment gains stem primarily from the trusted-state signal, not autonomous detection.
AI.conclusion: Diagnosing failure in multi-agent systems requires evaluating beyond task accuracy — specifically, measuring cascade radius, per-failure-mode recovery, and routing robustness to adversarial inputs. Intent-based routing and trusted-state signals are critical for containment, while blind retry is insufficient for latent or semantic faults. The authors emphasize these are controlled mechanism probes, not general domain-workload claims.

title: Epistemic Trustworthiness in Generative AI: A Normative Framework for Warranted Reliance in High-Stakes Workflows
comment: Accepted at AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2026)
summary: Generative AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes professional contexts, where their outputs shape what users believe, how they reason, and what they treat as settled. This raises a central question for responsible AI: under what conditions is reliance on generative AI outputs epistemically warranted rather than behaviourally induced? Existing frameworks largely ask whether AI outputs are accurate, fair, explainable, safe, or trusted by users. These questions remain necessary, and each can contribute to warranted reliance. However, they do not directly specify warranted reliance as a distinct evaluative target: the conditions under which users are justified in treating AI outputs as inputs into their own reasoning. We argue that this requires an account of epistemic trustworthiness: what makes a system epistemically worthy of reliance. Drawing on philosophical accounts of trustworthiness as competence and audience-orientation, we develop a constitutive normative framework comprising three jointly necessary and non-fungible conditions. First, epistemic humility requires systems to represent and communicate the limits of their competence. Second, epistemic access requires systems to enable users to inspect, question, and contest outputs in context. Third, resistance to epistemic injustice requires systems to recognise users as legitimate epistemic agents and avoid marginalising their knowledge and experience. Through real-world case analyses in legal reasoning, medical reasoning, and hiring, we show how failures of epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice can produce consequential harms that standard measures of accuracy, fairness, and usability do not address on their own. We conclude by outlining design and evaluation implications for GenAI systems organised around epistemically warranted reliance rather than output correctness alone.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that responsible deployment of generative AI in high-stakes domains requires a shift from evaluating outputs solely on accuracy/fairness to assessing "epistemically warranted reliance." It proposes a three-condition normative framework: epistemic humility (communicating limits), epistemic access (enabling scrutiny and contestation), and resistance to epistemic injustice (recognizing users as legitimate epistemic agents). Case analyses in law, medicine, and hiring illustrate how failures in these conditions cause harms unaddressed by standard metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing responsible AI frameworks focus on accuracy, fairness, explainability, safety, and trust, but none directly address the normative question: under what conditions are users *justified* in treating AI outputs as premises in their own reasoning? The authors identify a gap — the absence of a framework for "epistemic trustworthiness" as a distinct evaluative target — and argue that without it, reliance may be merely behaviorally induced rather than rationally warranted, risking consequential epistemic harms in professional contexts.
AI.method: The paper develops a constitutive normative framework through conceptual analysis grounded in philosophical theories of trustworthiness (competence + audience-orientation). It derives three jointly necessary and non-fungible conditions — epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice — and applies them through real-world case analyses across three high-stakes domains: legal reasoning, medical reasoning, and hiring. Each case demonstrates how failures in these conditions produce distinct harms that standard evaluative criteria (accuracy, fairness, usability) fail to capture.
AI.result: The case analyses reveal that failures in epistemic humility (e.g., overconfident outputs masking uncertainty) lead users to treat AI conclusions as more settled than warranted; failures in epistemic access (e.g., inability to inspect or contest outputs) undermine users' capacity to critically evaluate AI contributions; and failures in resistance to epistemic injustice (e.g., marginalizing domain experts' knowledge) silence legitimate epistemic agents. These failures produce harms — such as eroded professional judgment, wrongful legal convictions, misdiagnoses, and discriminatory hiring — that accuracy and fairness metrics alone cannot remediate.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that responsible GenAI deployment must be reoriented around epistemically warranted reliance rather than output correctness alone. This entails embedding epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice into system design and evaluation. The paper outlines implications for design practices and evaluation protocols, advocating that these three conditions serve as constitutive norms for epistemic trustworthiness in AI systems operating within high-stakes professional reasoning environments.

title: Automatic Translation of Unstructured Requirements into Linear Temporal Logic through Large Language Models
comment: Copyright 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. summary: Automatically translating unstructured natural language requirements into formal specifications remains a challenge in requirements engineering and formal methods, particularly for safety- and mission-critical systems whose verification depends on mathematically precise specifications. This paper evaluates whether contemporary off-the-shelf Large Language Models (LLMs) can help bridge this gap by generating Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas directly from unstructured requirements. The study examines six modern LLMs using a few-shot prompting strategy on a heterogeneous benchmark of 15 structurally varied requirements. Five independent generations were collected for each requirement-model pair, yielding 450 candidate LTL formulas in total. Performance was assessed through manual semantic evaluation, pass@k for k in {1, 3, 5}, and a self-consistency measure capturing syntactic reproducibility across stochastic trials. The results indicate that current general-purpose LLMs can achieve practically significant performance on the unstructured NL-to-LTL task without task-specific fine-tuning. The study also considers understandability for non-experts by pairing generated formulas with model-produced natural language explanations and discussing the complementary use of timeline-based LTL visualization. The findings suggest that modern LLMs are becoming viable front-end assistants for semi-automated formalization workflows.

AI.tldr: Evaluates six off-the-shelf LLMs on translating unstructured natural language requirements into Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas using few-shot prompting. Across 15 requirements and 450 candidate formulas, results show current LLMs achieve practically significant performance without task-specific fine-tuning, suggesting viability as front-end assistants for semi-automated formalization workflows.
AI.motivation: Translating unstructured natural language requirements into formal specifications (specifically LTL) is critical for verifying safety- and mission-critical systems, yet remains a persistent challenge in requirements engineering. The authors investigate whether contemporary LLMs can bridge this gap without requiring task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.method: Six modern LLMs were evaluated using a few-shot prompting strategy on a heterogeneous benchmark of 15 structurally varied requirements. Five independent stochastic generations were collected per requirement-model pair, producing 450 candidate LTL formulas. Performance was assessed via manual semantic evaluation, pass@k (k ∈ {1,3,5}), and a self-consistency metric measuring syntactic reproducibility across trials. Understandability was also examined through model-generated natural language explanations and timeline-based LTL visualization.
AI.result: Current general-purpose LLMs achieve practically significant performance on the unstructured NL-to-LTL task without fine-tuning. The self-consistency measure revealed varying degrees of syntactic reproducibility across models, and the combination of generated explanations with visualizations showed promise for non-expert comprehensibility.
AI.conclusion: Modern LLMs are becoming viable front-end assistants for semi-automated formalization workflows, capable of generating semantically correct LTL formulas from unstructured natural language requirements. Their integration with explanation generation and visualization tools can further support adoption by non-experts in requirements engineering contexts.

title: ABC: Numerical Data Collection under Local Differential Privacy without Prior Knowledge
summary:
Local Differential Privacy (LDP) provides strong privacy guarantees for collecting numerical data. A fundamental challenge, however, is that existing LDP mechanisms require a predefined data domain, which is often unknown in practice. This lack of prior knowledge creates a critical dilemma for the data collector: if the chosen domain is too narrow, values outside the range are clipped, leading to information loss. Conversely, if the domain is too wide, excessive noise is added during the privatization process, which degrades the quality of collected data. This highlights the need for methods that can dynamically estimate the data domain.
  In this work, we propose an adaptive LDP framework that addresses this problem. In our method, each user sends two pieces of information: their perturbed numerical data, and a privatized signal indicating if their original value was clipped by the current domain. By aggregating these signals, our proposed method, Adaptive Bounding of Clipping regions (ABC) method, iteratively adjusts the domain to fit the underlying data distribution without prior knowledge. Our theoretical analysis shows that the estimated data domain converges to an appropriate range.
  In the empirical evaluation, the results demonstrate that our framework significantly improves the quality of numerical data collection across various datasets and underlying LDP mechanisms. We also show that the estimated range successfully converges in practice and our approach is robust to its hyperparameters through comprehensive ablation studies.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Adaptive Bounding of Clipping regions (ABC), an LDP framework that dynamically estimates data domain without prior knowledge by having users report both perturbed values and clipping signals, enabling iterative domain adjustment. It converges to an appropriate range and significantly improves data collection quality across datasets and LDP mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Existing LDP mechanisms for numerical data require a predefined data domain, which is often unknown in practice. A too-narrow domain clips out-of-range values (information loss), while a too-wide domain adds excessive noise (utility degradation). This creates a critical need for methods that can dynamically estimate the domain without prior knowledge.
AI.method: The authors propose an adaptive LDP framework where each user transmits two pieces of information: (1) perturbed numerical data via a standard LDP mechanism, and (2) a privatized binary signal indicating whether their original value was clipped by the current domain. The data collector aggregates these clipping signals and uses the Adaptive Bounding of Clipping regions (ABC) method to iteratively adjust the domain bounds to fit the underlying data distribution, without requiring any prior knowledge.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows the framework significantly improves numerical data collection quality across various datasets and underlying LDP mechanisms. The estimated range converges in practice. Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrate robustness to hyperparameter choices.
AI.conclusion: The ABC method effectively resolves the domain-prior dilemma in LDP numerical data collection by enabling dynamic, data-driven domain estimation. It is practical, theoretically grounded, and robust, offering a significant improvement over fixed-domain approaches.

title: Constraint-First Reasoning: A Training-Free Protocol for Exploiting Answer-Space Constraints in Mathematical Problem Solving
summary: Large language models can derive a plausible mathematical object yet still violate explicit requirements--for example, by omitting a modular reduction, returning a non-integer, or using the wrong encoded answer form. We introduce Constraint-First Reasoning (CFR), a training-free two-stage prompting protocol: Stage 1 extracts and summarizes constraints entailed by the problem, and Stage 2 solves while checking intermediate and final results against that summary. Routed-CFR activates the two-stage protocol only when a text-only regex router detects restrictive cues; otherwise it uses direct chain-of-thought (CoT). Across AIME, CMIMC, BRUMO, and AIMO_AMC, the method improves direct CoT on multiple backbones. We further report convention-controlled routing experiments, matched prompting baselines, problem-level paired tests, decoding robustness, constraint-quality audits, total-token accounting, and an OlympiadBench evaluation. These analyses position CFR as a targeted test-time intervention whose benefit depends on recoverable constraints and reliable Stage 1 extraction, rather than as a general-purpose replacement for mathematical reasoning.

AI.tldr: Introduces Constraint-First Reasoning (CFR), a training-free two-stage prompting protocol that extracts problem constraints before solving, with a regex router that activates it only for constraint-heavy problems. Improves CoT across multiple math benchmarks but is positioned as a targeted intervention rather than a general reasoning replacement.
AI.motivation: LLMs can generate plausible mathematical derivations while violating explicit requirements (e.g., missing modular reductions, wrong output formats, non-integer answers). Existing CoT approaches lack explicit mechanisms to enforce these constraints throughout reasoning.
AI.method: CFR is a two-stage prompting protocol: Stage 1 extracts and summarizes all constraints entailed by the problem; Stage 2 solves while checking intermediate and final results against that constraint summary. Routed-CFR adds a text-only regex router that detects restrictive cues to selectively activate the two-stage protocol, defaulting to direct CoT otherwise.
AI.result: CFR improves direct CoT across AIME, CMIMC, BRUMO, and AIMO_AMC on multiple backbones. Supporting experiments include convention-controlled routing, matched prompting baselines, problem-level paired tests, decoding robustness, constraint-quality audits, total-token accounting, and an OlympiadBench evaluation.
AI.conclusion: CFR is a targeted test-time intervention whose benefit depends on the presence of recoverable constraints and reliable Stage 1 extraction. It is not a general-purpose replacement for mathematical reasoning but a useful augmentation when explicit constraints are available and extractable.

title: EvoHarness-RL: Learning Self-Evolving Runtime Harness for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents increasingly rely on external execution support to maintain state, track progress, invoke tools, verify outcomes, and reuse experience across interactions. However, effective harness use raises two coupled challenges: state formation from noisy interaction traces and runtime control over external-state access. Existing agents usually handle both through prompts, heuristics, or domain-specific conventions, leaving the external workspace and its usage policy manually engineered. To address this, we study the problem of harness policy learning, where agents learn harness policies offline and deploy them to construct and update external harness state online during runtime task execution. We introduce EvoHarness-RL, which exposes Belief, Progress, and Experience (BPE) as policy-facing harness state. Supervised harness fine-tuning teaches the base agent the harness action space and how to construct useful external state, while cost-aware GRPO explores coordination policies to selectively read, update, and consolidate that state during long-horizon interaction. Instantiated on ALFWorld with a Qwen3-8B LLM, EvoHarness-RL reaches 96.9% success and reveals two key dynamics: harness annealing, where training internalizes recurring harness-use patterns into the model policy and shifts the agent from frequent harness calls toward selective external-state access, and harness evolution, where progress updates and experience consolidation refine the harness into a compact, task-adaptive state substrate. These results suggest that long-horizon agents benefit from trainable policies for constructing and coordinating with external harness workspaces, beyond simply adding stronger tools or larger memories.

AI.tldr: EvoHarness-RL trains LLM agents to learn policies for constructing and selectively accessing external harness state (Belief, Progress, Experience) during long-horizon tasks, achieving 96.9% success on ALFWorld while revealing emergent dynamics of harness annealing and harness evolution.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents need external execution support (state tracking, tool invocation, outcome verification, experience reuse), but current methods rely on manually engineered prompts, heuristics, or domain-specific conventions. The core challenge is twofold: (1) forming structured state from noisy interaction traces, and (2) learning runtime control policies over when and how to access external state — both remain unautomated.
AI.method: EvoHarness-RL introduces a two-stage training pipeline. First, supervised harness fine-tuning teaches a base LLM (Qwen3-8B) the harness action space and how to construct external state structured as Belief, Progress, and Experience (BPE). Second, cost-aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) explores coordination policies that learn to selectively read, update, and consolidate harness state during runtime. The approach operates offline for policy learning and online for deployment.
AI.result: The method achieves 96.9% success rate on ALFWorld. Analysis reveals two key emergent dynamics: (1) harness annealing — the model internalizes recurring harness-use patterns, progressively reducing frequent harness calls toward selective external-state access; and (2) harness evolution — progress updates and experience consolidation refine the harness into a compact, task-adaptive state substrate over time.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon agents benefit significantly from trainable policies for constructing and coordinating with external harness workspaces. The results suggest that learning when and how to use external state is more impactful than simply adding stronger tools or larger memory, pointing toward a paradigm of learned harness coordination rather than manual engineering.

title: Agentic self-driving microscopy benchmarks support qualification but do not necessarily generalize to unseen tasks
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly being developed to control a wide range of scientific characterization tools including microscopes and synchrotron beamlines. Research into agentic control of physical infrastructure is nascent and there are few well-established paradigms for how to engineer an agentic system. There are many choices to make when designing a microscopy agent, including the choice of LLM, the number of agents to use, agent responsibilities and delegation rules, retrieval-augmented generation parameters, and more. When designing and optimizing an agentic microscope controller, researchers not only want to ensure that the agent can correctly perform known tasks but also that the agent can generalize to new tasks that it has not encountered before. In this study, we develop a benchmark and trace-logging framework that reveals a) how different choices of agent architecture impact performance at microscopy tasks and b) the limitations of benchmarks for predicting if a particular agent will perform well on unseen microscopy tasks. The framework was used to evaluate one-, two-, and three-agent graph topologies, five LLMs, RAG and context parameters, and operational constraints across 53 microscopy benchmark tests. In total, 105 agent configurations, 1,949 individual test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals were recorded. Direct comparisons showed clear differences in latency, token use, cost, and failure mode between configurations. However, surrogate models trained on agent architecture and test results did not reliably predict an agent's performance on new, unseen tasks. These results show that these benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison, but the current heterogeneous test suite does not support a task-independent global configuration model.

AI.tldr: This study develops a benchmark and trace-logging framework to evaluate how different LLM agent architectures (1-, 2-, and 3-agent topologies, five LLMs, RAG settings) perform on microscopy control tasks. Across 105 configurations and 1,949 test runs, clear performance differences emerged, but surrogate models failed to predict generalization to unseen tasks — showing benchmarks are useful for regression testing and comparison but insufficient for building a task-independent global optimizer.
AI.motivation: Agentic control of scientific instruments (microscopes, synchrotrons) is nascent with no established engineering paradigms. Researchers face many design choices (LLM selection, agent count, delegation rules, RAG parameters) and need to know not only whether an agent performs known tasks correctly, but also whether it generalizes to unseen tasks. There is a lack of systematic frameworks for evaluating these trade-offs.
AI.method: The authors built a benchmark and trace-logging framework encompassing 53 microscopy tests. They systematically varied agent graph topologies (1, 2, or 3 agents), five LLMs, RAG and context parameters, and operational constraints, yielding 105 distinct configurations. In total, 1,949 individual test runs and 49,109 RAG retrievals were recorded. Surrogate models were trained on agent architecture features and test results to attempt prediction of generalization to new, unseen tasks.
AI.result: Direct comparisons revealed clear differences across configurations in latency, token usage, cost, and failure modes. However, surrogate models trained on the benchmark results could not reliably predict agent performance on new, unseen microscopy tasks, indicating a fundamental gap between benchmark-based optimization and generalization.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark framework is valuable for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison of microscopy agents. However, the current heterogeneous test suite does not support building a task-independent global configuration model that predicts generalization. This highlights a key limitation in using fixed benchmarks to optimize agentic systems for open-ended scientific instrument control.

title: Unified Agent: Managing Interactions across Devices
summary: As capabilities rapidly increase, AI agents can move from running inside one app to acting across a user's devices over time. Yet existing agent systems still fall short in this scenario. This is because observations are scattered across devices and moments, but mainstream systems are not designed around this fact: a single agent that treats devices as tools lacks effective state management for all devices across time, and multi-agent systems coordinate across agents but do not maintain the compact carried state a cross-device, cross-time request needs. We argue that the agent should maintain an effectively designed state that organizes engagement evidence, stated facts, and the standing request in a compact, action-ready form for deciding its action given the current observation. To compare state designs, we construct a benchmark of user-agent interaction across devices and time. We instantiate this principle in Unified Agent, a stateful agent that carries interaction evidence across devices and moments and uses it with the current observation to act. In the default setting, it significantly outperforms our adaptations of four published designs. Across changes in multimodal large language model (MLLM) family, capability, and reasoning effort, it remains ahead of all compared systems, demonstrating that the state-design advantage is robust across MLLM settings. Our code and data will be publicly available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI agents operating across devices and time need a compact, action-ready state that integrates past observations, facts, and the user's request. The authors propose Unified Agent, a stateful agent design that carries interaction evidence across devices/moments, and show it outperforms four published alternatives across various MLLM settings on a new cross-device, cross-time benchmark.
AI.motivation: As AI agents become more capable, a natural next step is moving from single-app operation to acting across a user's multiple devices over extended time. However, existing systems fall short: single-agent designs treating devices as tools lack effective cross-device, cross-time state management, while multi-agent systems coordinate agents but fail to maintain the compact carried state needed for cross-device, cross-time requests. The core gap is that observations are scattered across devices and moments, yet no system is explicitly designed around this reality.
AI.method: The authors propose a design principle: an agent should maintain an effectively designed state that organizes engagement evidence, stated facts, and the standing request in a compact, action-ready form to decide actions given the current observation. They instantiate this in Unified Agent, a stateful agent that carries interaction evidence across devices and moments. To compare state designs, they construct a benchmark of user-agent interactions spanning multiple devices and time points. They compare Unified Agent against adaptations of four published agent designs, evaluating across different MLLM families, capability levels, and reasoning effort settings.
AI.result: Unified Agent significantly outperforms all four adapted published designs in the default setting. The performance advantage holds robustly across changes in MLLM family, model capability, and reasoning effort, demonstrating that the state-design benefit is not tied to a specific model configuration.
AI.conclusion: Effective state design — organizing engagement evidence, stated facts, and the standing request in a compact, action-ready form — is critical for cross-device, cross-time agent operation. Unified Agent embodies this principle and shows consistent superiority over existing designs, suggesting a promising direction for building practical multi-device AI agents. Code and data will be open-sourced.

title: On the Figures of Merit for Quantum Software Security: Toward a Benchmarking Rubric
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at the 6th International Workshop on Quantum Software Engineering and Technology (Q-SET 2026), co-located with IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing & Engineering (QCE26)
summary: Quantum software is increasingly provided through multi-tenant and cloud-based Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) stacks. A growing concern about the diverse attack vectors across the pipeline has been demonstrated in recent research. Yet the community has converged on three mature pillars: Scale (Qubit Count), Quality (Quantum Volume), and Speed (Circuit Layer Operations per Second (CLOPS)) for the merit performance figures. Moreover, it has also begun to define software-quality metrics. However, the security of quantum software remains largely unmeasured. A few quantitative security indicators, such as Total Variation Distance (TVD) and Degree of Functional Corruption (DFC), exist. Although they were introduced ad hoc for individual circuit obfuscation techniques, they are incompatible. We assert that the security of quantum software deserves the same attention as the performance: an explicit set of Security Figures of Merit (S-FoMs).
