The research of this paper is threefold: (i) characterizes a three-layer measurement gap, (ii) proposes a structured S-FoM set organized by ISO/IEC 25010 security sub-characteristics, QaaS pipeline mapping, and measurement maturity, and (iii) defines a benchmarking rubric that normalizes and aggregates S-FoMs into a combined Quantum Software Security Posture (QSSP) score. Additionally, an illustrative reanalysis of published obfuscation techniques has been presented. Our aim is a first step toward security-aware benchmarking of the Quantum Software Stack (QSS).

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a critical gap in quantum software metrics—performance is well-measured (qubit count, quantum volume, CLOPS) but security is not. It proposes Security Figures of Merit (S-FoMs) organized by ISO/IEC 25010, QaaS pipeline stages, and measurement maturity, culminating in a unified Quantum Software Security Posture (QSSP) score.
AI.motivation: Quantum computing is increasingly delivered via cloud-based QaaS stacks with diverse attack vectors. While the community has standardized on performance metrics (Scale, Quality, Speed) and begun defining software-quality metrics, security remains largely unquantified. Existing security indicators like TVD and DFC are ad hoc, technique-specific, and mutually incompatible, creating a measurement gap that demands a structured, unified approach.
AI.method: The research (i) characterizes a three-layer measurement gap across the quantum software stack, (ii) proposes a structured set of Security Figures of Merit (S-FoMs) organized along three axes: ISO/IEC 25010 security sub-characteristics (confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, etc.), QaaS pipeline mapping (compilation, execution, etc.), and measurement maturity levels, and (iii) defines a benchmarking rubric that normalizes and aggregates individual S-FoMs into a composite Quantum Software Security Posture (QSSP) score. The framework is validated through an illustrative reanalysis of published obfuscation techniques.
AI.result: The three-layer measurement gap was characterized, a structured S-FoM taxonomy was developed, and a QSSP scoring rubric was defined. The illustrative reanalysis of existing obfuscation techniques demonstrated the framework's applicability and highlighted how previously incomparable security claims can be normalized and compared under the proposed system.
AI.conclusion: This work represents a first step toward security-aware benchmarking of the Quantum Software Stack. By establishing S-FoMs and a unified QSSP score, the authors aim to elevate security to the same level of rigorous measurement as performance in the quantum computing ecosystem, enabling meaningful comparison and improvement tracking of quantum software security posture.

title: Evidence Lock Before Commitment: A Frozen Interface Degrades LLM-as-Judge Evaluation
summary: LLM judges are often asked to extract criteria and evidence before choosing between candidate answers. This workflow assumes that the intermediate record preserves the information needed for a later verdict. For reasoning-capable models, visible field order does not reveal internal decision order, so we test an observable alternative: persist the evidence in one call and make it the exclusive input to the next. Across 24,000 judgments over HelpSteer3, FeedbackQA, and CoVal, we compare standard pairwise judging, structured one-call judging, two-call evidence locking, and three-call pointwise locking with Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5. Evidence locking reduces agreement with released human preferences by 4 to 6 percentage points and increases answer-order inconsistency by 8 to 10 points relative to structured one-call judging. Pointwise locking is also harmful, while structured evidence elicitation remains close to standard judging. The result holds for both judges and all three datasets. Persisted evidence can support auditability, but it should not replace the source answers at decision time.

AI.tldr: LLM judges perform worse when extracted evidence is persisted across calls and used as the sole input for final decisions, compared to standard one-call structured judging. Evidence locking reduces human-preference agreement by 4-6 pp and increases order inconsistency by 8-10 pp.
AI.motivation: LLM judging workflows often separate evidence extraction from verdict delivery under the assumption that intermediate records preserve sufficient information. For reasoning-capable models, the visible field order may not reflect internal decision order, motivating an empirical test of whether evidence persistence (locking) helps or harms judgment quality.
AI.method: The authors conduct 24,000 pairwise judgments across three datasets (HelpSteer3, FeedbackQA, CoVal) using Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5. They compare four conditions: standard pairwise judging, structured one-call judging (evidence + verdict in one go), two-call evidence locking (extract evidence in call 1, verdict using only that evidence in call 2), and three-call pointwise locking (each answer evaluated independently before comparison).
AI.result: Evidence locking reduces agreement with released human preferences by 4-6 percentage points and increases answer-order inconsistency by 8-10 points relative to structured one-call judging. Pointwise locking is similarly harmful. Structured evidence elicitation in a single call performs comparably to standard pairwise judging. Results hold across both judges and all three datasets.
AI.conclusion: Persisting extracted evidence can support auditability, but it should not replace the source answers at decision time. The best practice is structured one-call judging where evidence and verdict are produced together.

title: Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotopes for Identifiable and Refinable Predictive Uncertainty
summary: Probabilistic prediction heads in neural networks typically output either a Gaussian mixture or a single conformal region. Neither separates the distinct sources of uncertainty often present in real prediction tasks: a discrete choice among modes, bounded systematic drift within the chosen mode, and irreducible stochastic noise. We introduce the Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ), an output head that represents these three sources as binary, bounded, and stochastic generators of a zonotope, and admits a closed-form likelihood by convolution. Sharing the bounded generator across prediction steps couples future predictions algebraically, so observing one step refines the predictive distribution at every remaining step in a single forward pass. We establish that the three generators are identifiable from the likelihood up to permutation, and that an HProbZ density is representationally distinct from any finite Gaussian mixture. The same shared structure provides analytic per-mode risk and distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets at inference time. Empirical analysis on representative prediction benchmarks supports the effectiveness of the design relative to same-encoder mixture baselines, while offering structural properties that mixture or convex-conformal predictors do not jointly provide.

AI.tldr: HProbZ is a novel probabilistic output head that decomposes predictive uncertainty into three interpretable sources—discrete mode choice, bounded systematic drift, and stochastic noise—using a zonotope representation with closed-form likelihood and algebraic coupling across time steps.
AI.motivation: Existing probabilistic prediction heads (Gaussian mixtures or conformal regions) conflate distinct sources of uncertainty: discrete selection among modes, bounded drift within a mode, and irreducible noise. A representation that explicitly separates these three sources would improve interpretability, enable analytical per-mode risk assessment, and allow distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets.
AI.method: Introduces the Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ), which represents the three uncertainty sources as binary, bounded, and stochastic generators of a zonotope. The bounded generator is shared across prediction steps, coupling future predictions algebraically so that observing one step refines all remaining predictive distributions in a single forward pass. The representation admits a closed-form likelihood via convolution. Identifiability up to permutation is proven, and the density is shown to be distinct from any finite Gaussian mixture.
AI.result: The three generators are identifiable from the likelihood up to permutation. HProbZ densities are representationally distinct from any finite Gaussian mixture. Empirical evaluation on representative prediction benchmarks shows the approach is effective compared to same-encoder mixture baselines.
AI.conclusion: HProbZ provides structural properties—explicit uncertainty decomposition, per-mode analytic risk, and multi-modal conformal sets—that neither mixture models nor convex-conformal predictors jointly offer, while maintaining competitive predictive performance.

title: CASCADE: An Agentic Regulatory Network Framework for Patient-Data-Validated Downstream Perturbation Prediction
summary:
CASCADE is an agentic framework that predicts downstream transcriptional effects of gene perturbation from precomputed
  ARACNe regulatory networks, exposed via MCP. Prior work validates such tools by checking whether predicted genes are
  known cancer genes (membership); we instead test whether the predicted direction of change matches reality, using
  focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown against real TCGA patient
  tumor data.
  For MYC, CASCADE's predicted knockdown targets show strong concordance with real amplified-vs-non-amplified tumor
  expression across three cancer types (BRCA: 90.0%, COAD: 72.0%, STAD: 85.7%; all p<0.0013), well above permutation
  baselines, surviving a PAM50 subtype control and replicating in an independent cohort (METABRIC, 87.2%). Compared
  against curated MSigDB gene-set baselines via Fisher's exact test, CASCADE's accuracy is not shown to exceed existing
  public knowledge of MYC- or E2F-driven biology, though its gene-specific direction-calling clearly outperforms a naive
  uniform guess.
  Extending to fifteen additional genes, validation proves gene-specific rather than universal: proliferation-machinery
  regulators mostly replicate, while lineage-identity transcription factors and one cyclin-D paralog (CCND2)
  consistently fail, a pattern we discuss as a hedged, post-hoc hypothesis.
  We separately benchmark whether an LLM-based agent correctly grounds natural-language requests into CASCADE's real MCP
  tool calls. Across 35 queries, a documented local model reaches 71.4% exact match (85.7% for a larger model); schema
  and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side correction, but both models confidently default to the
  wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries, a failure a targeted fix could not resolve because its trigger condition
  never occurs.

AI.tldr: CASCADE is an agentic framework that predicts transcriptional effects of gene perturbations using ARACNe regulatory networks. Validated against TCGA tumor data using copy-number amplification as a knockdown proxy, it shows strong direction-calling accuracy for MYC across multiple cancer types. Extension to 15 additional genes reveals gene-specific performance: proliferation regulators replicate well, while lineage-identity TFs and CCND2 fail. An LLM grounding benchmark achieves up to 85.7% exact match on MCP tool-call translation, with specific failure modes identified.
AI.motivation: Existing validation approaches for gene perturbation prediction tools merely check whether predicted genes belong to known cancer gene sets (membership testing), which is a weak and indirect form of validation. The authors argue for a more rigorous approach: testing whether the predicted direction of transcriptional change matches reality. They also seek to benchmark whether an LLM-based agent can correctly translate natural-language requests into actual tool calls against a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.
AI.method: CASCADE uses precomputed ARACNe regulatory networks and exposes them through MCP (Model Context Protocol). Validation uses focal-gene copy-number amplification in TCGA patient tumor data as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown. For MYC, predicted knockdown targets are compared against real expression differences between amplified and non-amplified tumors across BRCA, COAD, and STAD cancer types, with PAM50 subtype control and independent replication in METABRIC. Comparison against MSigDB gene-set baselines uses Fisher's exact test. Extension covers 15 additional genes. LLM grounding is benchmarked across 35 natural-language queries against actual MCP tool calls, measuring exact-match accuracy.
AI.result: For MYC, CASCADE achieves strong concordance: BRCA 90.0%, COAD 72.0%, STAD 85.7% (all p<0.0013), replicating in METABRIC (87.2%). Direction-calling significantly outperforms uniform guessing but does not exceed curated MSigDB baselines in Fisher's exact test. Across 15 additional genes, proliferation-machinery regulators mostly replicate; lineage-identity transcription factors and CCND2 consistently fail. LLM grounding: a documented local model achieves 71.4% exact match, a larger model reaches 85.7%. Schema and gene-alias failures resolve with scale or server-side correction. Both models default to wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries; this failure could not be fixed because the trigger condition for the fix never fires.
AI.conclusion: Directional validation using copy-number amplification as a knockdown proxy is a viable and more rigorous alternative to membership-based validation. CASCADE's performance is gene-specific rather than universal, with proliferation regulators validated but lineage-identity TFs and CCND2 failing, suggesting a hedged, post-hoc hypothesis about which gene classes are predictable. LLM grounding to MCP tool calls is feasible but exhibits systematic failure modes on ambiguous queries that resist trivial fixes.

title: An End-to-End Threat Model for the Quantum-as-a-Service Pipeline
comment: 2 pages, 1 Table. Accepted as a poster paper at the IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing & Engineering (QCE26)
summary: Cloud-based accessing of Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) platforms such as IBM Quantum, IonQ Cloud, and Amazon Braket is becoming popular day by day. Hybrid quantum-classical algorithms (VQE, QAOA, QML) transfer data via a long layered pipeline of orchestration, compilation, and execution. Recent works have demonstrated various critical attacks at individual stages: Calibration tampering, SWAP attacks, QubitHammer, and so on. However, these attacks remain separated because of their own terminology, and existing STRIDE-based threat modeling in the context of quantum lacks a structured view towards the QaaS stack itself. We address this concern by decomposing the workflow into six-stage model with STRIDE threat modeling. Our matrix demonstrated attack vectors in quantum-specific, inherited classical, and plausible tiers for each of the stages. We further investigate the underexplored sections (repudiation and elevation-of-privilege) and distinguish three different cross-stage attack chains with higher impacts.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a six-stage decomposition of the QaaS workflow with STRIDE threat modeling, revealing attack vectors across quantum-specific, inherited-classical, and plausible tiers, while identifying underexplored repudiation/elevation-of-privilege threats and three high-impact cross-stage attack chains.
AI.motivation: Existing attacks on QaaS platforms (calibration tampering, SWAP attacks, QubitHammer) remain siloed by disparate terminology, and prior STRIDE-based quantum threat models lack a structured, stage-by-stage view of the entire QaaS stack. This fragmentation hinders systematic security analysis.
AI.method: The authors decompose the QaaS workflow into a six-stage model (orchestration, compilation, execution, etc.) and apply STRIDE threat modeling at each stage. They construct a matrix mapping attack vectors into three categories — quantum-specific, inherited classical, and plausible — and analyze cross-stage attack chains, with particular attention to repudiation and elevation-of-privilege threats.
AI.result: The six-stage STRIDE matrix reveals attack vectors spanning all stages, categorized into quantum-specific, inherited-classical, and plausible tiers. The work highlights repudiation and elevation-of-privilege as underexplored threat categories and identifies three distinct cross-stage attack chains with amplified impact compared to single-stage attacks.
AI.conclusion: A structured, stage-aware STRIDE decomposition of the QaaS workflow exposes previously overlooked threat surfaces and cross-stage attack chains, underscoring the need for holistic, end-to-end security analysis in hybrid quantum-classical cloud platforms.

title: The interface of intonation and lexical tone: Boundary phenomena in Mandarin varieties
comment: to be published in book 'Shaping Phonological and Morphological Representations: Diachrony, Acquisition, and Processing'
summary: This chapter explores the intricate interplay between intonation and tone in Mandarin Chinese varieties, focusing on f0, the primary acoustic cue for both intonation and tone. The main empirical base is intonation boundary phenomena, where intonation and tone intersect and influence each other in conveying a range of sentence-level linguistic functions -- such as question vs. statement -- and a rich array of speakers' attitudinal information. Theoretical models and emerging techniques are also discussed to account for the observed interactions of tonal aspects and boundary phenomena to convey multiple levels of communicative meanings.

AI.tldr: This chapter examines how intonation and tone interact in Mandarin Chinese varieties, with a focus on f0 as the shared acoustic cue. It emphasizes intonation boundary phenomena, where tone and intonation intersect to encode sentence-level functions (e.g., question vs. statement) and speaker attitudes, while also reviewing theoretical models and emerging techniques for analyzing these multilayered communicative meanings.
AI.motivation: Mandarin Chinese poses a unique challenge for prosody research because both lexical tone and sentence-level intonation rely on the same acoustic parameter — fundamental frequency (f0). Understanding how these two systems coexist, interact, and jointly encode linguistic and paralinguistic meanings at intonational boundaries is essential for advancing phonological theory and for applications in speech technology.
AI.method: The chapter takes a survey-based approach, synthesizing empirical findings on intonation boundary phenomena across Mandarin Chinese varieties. It focuses on acoustic analysis of f0 patterns at prosodic boundaries, examining how tone-intonation interactions manifest in sentence-type contrasts (e.g., interrogative vs. declarative) and in the expression of attitudinal information. The chapter also reviews theoretical frameworks and emerging analytical techniques used to model these interactions.
AI.result: Key findings indicate that intonation and tone systematically interact at prosodic boundaries, with boundary tones modifying or combining with lexical tones to signal sentence type and speaker attitude. The chapter documents how Mandarin varieties exploit f0 adjustments at phrase and utterance edges to convey a rich array of communicative functions beyond lexical meaning, and it highlights the capacity of contemporary models to capture these multi-level interactions.
AI.conclusion: The interaction between intonation and tone at prosodic boundaries is central to understanding how Mandarin Chinese encodes multiple layers of meaning simultaneously through f0. Theoretical models that integrate boundary phenomena with tonal specification are crucial for capturing this complexity, and continued development of analytical techniques promises to further illuminate the interface between lexical and post-lexical prosody.

title: Matrix Zonotopic Attention: A Context-Adaptive Value Projection for Set Transformers
summary: Multi-head attention combines an input-dependent softmax routing with an input-independent linear value projection, so the per-sample operator mapping aggregated values to outputs is the same for every input set. We study the consequences of this asymmetry for permutation-invariant set targets. We introduce the Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) of a target operator, a complexity measure counting the input-dependent directions an exact representation requires, and present a depth-separation analysis showing that context-rigid attention needs depth proportional to the target's TDOF, whereas a single layer with a context-adaptive value family can represent the same target. Building on this analysis, we propose Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn), which replaces the fixed value projection with a context-adaptive matrix-zonotope family: a centre matrix plus a sum of generator matrices weighted by input-dependent gates. The construction reduces to standard multi-head attention at initialisation, preserves permutation equivariance, and admits a data-driven reachability interpretation. Experiments on a range of set-prediction tasks are consistent with the TDOF prediction that the architectural advantage is selective: it appears on targets that depend on the input set in a high-rank, sparsely combinatorial way, and is small on aggregate-statistic targets where parameter-matched standard attention is already competitive.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the asymmetry in multi-head attention where softmax routing is input-dependent but value projections are input-independent. It introduces Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) to quantify input-dependent complexity, proves context-rigid attention requires depth proportional to TDOF, and proposes Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn) with context-adaptive value families that achieves the same expressivity in a single layer, showing selective gains on high-rank combinatorial set tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard multi-head attention has an architectural asymmetry: the softmax-based routing is context-dependent (varies per input set), but the value projection matrix is fixed and input-independent. This means the linear operator mapping aggregated values to outputs is identical for every input. The authors investigate whether this rigidity limits expressivity for permutation-invariant set functions, and whether making value projections also context-adaptive can yield representational gains.
AI.method: The authors first define Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF), a complexity measure counting how many distinct input-dependent linear directions are needed to exactly represent a target set operator. They then provide a depth-separation theorem: multi-head attention with fixed value projections (context-rigid) requires depth at least proportional to the target's TDOF, while a single layer with context-adaptive values suffices. Based on this, they propose Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn), where the value projection is replaced by a matrix-zonotope family — a centre matrix plus a sum of generator matrices gated by input-dependent scalars. At initialization, MZAttn reduces to standard multi-head attention, and it preserves permutation equivariance.
AI.result: The TDOF-based depth-separation result formally characterizes when context-adaptive values help. Experiments on set-prediction tasks confirm the predicted selectivity: MZAttn outperforms parameter-matched standard attention on targets requiring high-rank, sparse combinatorial dependence on the input set, while offering little to no advantage on aggregate-statistic targets where standard attention already suffices.
AI.conclusion: The input-independent value projection in standard multi-head attention is a genuine representational bottleneck for permutation-invariant set functions with high TDOF. Context-adaptive value families, as realized by MZAttn, overcome this with a single layer, and the benefits materialize selectively on tasks that match the TDOF characterization. The zonotope parameterization offers a principled, initialization-compatible way to introduce this adaptivity.

title: Counterfactual Analysis via Large Language Models
summary: Counterfactual analysis aims to predict potential outcomes under hypothetical scenarios, offering valuable insights for decision-making. This paper investigates the application of large language models (LLMs), specifically the GPT-3.5 model, for counterfactual analysis. We focus on the online lending context, where the counterfactual return on investment (ROI) is crucial for evaluating different interest rate schemes. We begin by assessing the predictive performance of GPT and comparing it with advanced machine learning algorithms. The results show that prompt engineering can significantly enhance GPT's predictions, with the R-squared increasing from 1.97% to 2.84%, closely approaching the 3.48% achieved by gradient-boosted regression. Subsequently, we utilize GPT to generate counterfactual ROIs under a set of alternative interest rates. GPT exhibits logical coherence and causal reasoning in its responses. The findings underscore the potential of LLMs as effective tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending, suggesting broader applications for LLMs in various predictive and decision-making contexts.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using GPT-3.5 for counterfactual ROI prediction in online lending. Prompt engineering improves GPT's R-squared from 1.97% to 2.84%, approaching gradient-boosted regression's 3.48%. GPT also demonstrates logical coherence and causal reasoning when generating counterfactual ROIs under alternative interest rate scenarios.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether large language models, particularly GPT-3.5, can serve as effective tools for counterfactual analysis — specifically, predicting ROI under hypothetical interest rate scenarios in online lending, a domain where such counterfactual reasoning is critical for decision-making.
AI.method: The authors use GPT-3.5 with prompt engineering to predict ROI in online lending. They benchmark GPT's predictive performance against advanced machine learning algorithms (including gradient-boosted regression). They then prompt GPT to generate counterfactual ROIs under alternative interest rate schemes and evaluate the logical coherence and causal reasoning in its responses.
AI.result: Prompt engineering lifts GPT's R-squared from 1.97% to 2.84%, closely approaching the 3.48% achieved by gradient-boosted regression. GPT exhibits logical coherence and causal reasoning when generating counterfactual predictions across varying interest rates.
AI.conclusion: LLMs, specifically GPT-3.5, show promise as tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending. The authors suggest broader applicability of LLMs in predictive and decision-making contexts beyond this domain.

title: FormBharo: Designing and Evaluating a Voice Agent for Conversational Form Filling in Rural India
summary: In India, almost every social benefit starts with a form, yet the people who need these benefits most are often unable to read or write. Reaching them requires a spoken conversation. Today that work falls to frontline health workers who enroll beneficiaries one at a time, a poor use of stretched capacity. We built FormBharo ("fill the form" in Hindi), a voice agent that fills a structured form over a phone call under tight latency and cost budgets by pairing Large Language Models (LLMs) with deterministic, rule-based validation and flow control. It is being piloted with ARMMAN, an NGO running large-scale maternal and child mobile-health programs in India, to enroll low-income, Hindi-speaking mothers in antenatal and postnatal care. To our knowledge, it is the first voice agent piloted to fill an enrollment form for this population. We openly release FormVoiceAgentBench, a benchmark pairing human-recorded Hindi audio with 3,760 multi-turn conversation tests across 960 simulated calls, to evaluate our agent's components (transcription, extraction, reply generation) and end-to-end form completion under real acoustic variations. Form completion drops by up to ~41 points when LLMs receive error-prone real-speech transcripts instead of reference ones. The rule-based controls recover many turn-level extraction errors, helping smaller, cheaper models match or surpass frontier models on form completion. Component performance does not predict end-to-end performance: GPT-5.5 leads turn-level extraction accuracy on reference transcripts (99.8%) but ranks lower on form completion. Since errors both propagate and cancel across the pipeline, the optimal model choice of models emerges only through end-to-end evaluation. Finally, no single model is best across accuracy, cost, and latency at once, so we use a Pareto-based weighted-sum scalarization to select a deployable configuration balancing the three.

AI.tldr: FormBharo is a voice agent using LLMs with rule-based validation to fill structured forms via phone calls for low-literacy populations. Piloted with an NGO in India for maternal health enrollment, it is the first such agent for this demographic. The paper introduces FormVoiceAgentBench, showing that real-speech transcription errors severely degrade form completion, rule-based controls help smaller models match frontier models, and end-to-end evaluation is essential since component-level metrics don't predict overall performance. A Pareto-based method selects optimal deployable configurations balancing accuracy, cost, and latency.
AI.motivation: Millions of low-income, low-literacy individuals in India cannot access social benefits because enrollment requires filling written forms. Frontline health workers conduct one-on-one spoken enrollments, which is inefficient and stretches limited human capacity. There is a need for an automated voice-based enrollment system that can conduct structured form-filling conversations in Hindi over phone calls under strict latency and cost constraints.
AI.method: FormBharo pairs LLMs (for transcription, information extraction, and reply generation) with deterministic, rule-based validation and flow-control logic. The system is evaluated using FormVoiceAgentBench, a benchmark of 960 simulated calls with human-recorded Hindi audio and 3,760 multi-turn conversation tests. Both component-level metrics (transcription, extraction, reply generation) and end-to-end form completion are measured. Model selection uses Pareto-based weighted-sum scalarization across accuracy, cost, and latency dimensions.
AI.result: (1) Form completion drops by up to ~41 points when using error-prone real-speech transcripts versus reference transcripts. (2) Rule-based controls recover many turn-level extraction errors, enabling smaller, cheaper models to match or surpass frontier models. (3) Component performance does not predict end-to-end performance — e.g., GPT-5.5 leads extraction accuracy on reference transcripts (99.8%) but ranks lower on overall form completion. (4) No single model optimizes accuracy, cost, and latency simultaneously, necessitating Pareto-based selection for deployment.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end evaluation is critical for voice-based form-filling agents, as errors propagate and cancel across the pipeline in ways component-level analysis cannot capture. Rule-based guardrails effectively compensate for LLM weaknesses under noisy real-speech conditions, allowing cost-efficient smaller models to be viable. Practical deployment requires multi-objective optimization across accuracy, cost, and latency rather than single-metric model selection.

title: RustGo: Fairly Directed Greybox Fuzzing for Enforcing Rust Memory Safety
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS 2026). 23 pages
summary: Rust is a popular systems programming language that provides strong memory safety and introduces low-performance overhead. While Rust guarantees memory safety through strict security policies, such as ownership, memory bugs can still occur in unsafe-related Rust codes where these policies are not fully enforced. Although such unsafe Rust code accounts for only a small portion of the entire code (e.g., 10%), existing approaches fuzz the entire code-including safe Rust, whose memory safety is already enforced by the Rust compiler-resulting in inefficient use of fuzzing resources. In this paper, we propose RustGo, the new Rust-directed greybox fuzzer that effectively and fairly focuses on code regions potentially containing memory bugs. For this, RustGo automatically identifies potential memory bug targets and accurately prunes the paths irrelevant to each target by leveraging Rust-specific static analysis. For each identified target, RustGo includes a new fuzzing approach that maintains an independent state and applies dynamic pruning to maximize balanced and focused fuzzing. We evaluate RustGo on various real-world Rust applications. On average, RustGo prunes 78.49% of irrelevant paths, reaches targets x 2.09 to x 5.08 faster than existing fuzzers, and identifies 13 unknown bugs (six assigned RUSTSEC IDs and one assigned CVE ID).

AI.tldr: RustGo is a directed greybox fuzzer for Rust that focuses on unsafe code regions likely to contain memory bugs. It uses Rust-specific static analysis to identify targets and prune irrelevant paths, achieving 78.49% path reduction, 2–5× faster target reachability, and discovering 13 new bugs including RUSTSEC and CVE assignments.
AI.motivation: Existing Rust fuzzers waste resources by fuzzing the entire codebase, even though memory safety is already guaranteed for safe Rust (~90% of code). Memory bugs only arise in unsafe Rust where compiler safety policies are not fully enforced. Efficient fuzzing should focus exclusively on these vulnerable regions.
AI.method: RustGo first performs Rust-specific static analysis to automatically identify potential memory-bug targets within unsafe code regions. It then accurately prunes execution paths irrelevant to each target. For each identified target, RustGo maintains an independent fuzzing state and employs dynamic pruning to ensure balanced, focused allocation of fuzzing resources across all targets.
AI.result: On real-world Rust applications, RustGo pruned 78.49% of irrelevant paths on average, reached targets 2.09× to 5.08× faster than existing fuzzers, and discovered 13 previously unknown bugs — six received RUSTSEC IDs and one received a CVE ID.
AI.conclusion: Targeting fuzzing efforts specifically at unsafe Rust code regions, guided by static analysis and dynamic pruning, significantly outperforms whole-program fuzzing approaches in both speed and bug-finding effectiveness for Rust programs.

title: Mood Matters: How Syntactic Sensitivity Undermines Safety Alignment
summary: Large language models typically undergo post-training to align them with safety policies but there exist many sophisticated jailbreaks that sidestep established safeguards. For instance, prior work by Andriushchenko et al. (2025) has found that changing the grammatical tense from present to past can be enough to elicit harmful responses. In this work, we uncover a more general failure of non-imperative syntactic forms. We demonstrate that this syntactic vulnerability exists in 16 models up to 70B parameters, using behavioral evaluation. To investigate the root cause, we apply causal mediation analysis, finding that refusal is partially conditioned on upstream syntactic features. By steering these purely syntactic features we are able to trigger and suppress refusal. Finally, we trace this ill-conditioning to linguistically biased post-training data of open-source models and show that increasing syntactic diversity can mitigate the issue. Our findings suggest that current alignment approaches introduce confounders that prevent a pure semantic grounding of the refusal decision.

AI.tldr: Non-imperative syntactic forms (e.g., past tense, passive voice, conditionals) can bypass safety alignment in LLMs. The authors demonstrate this across 16 models, use causal mediation analysis to show refusal is conditioned on syntactic features, and trace the root cause to linguistically biased post-training data.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that changing grammatical tense can jailbreak LLMs. This paper investigates whether a broader class of syntactic transformations — specifically non-imperative forms — systematically undermines refusal, revealing a fundamental confound between syntax and safety in current alignment methods.
AI.method: The authors conduct behavioral evaluations on 16 models (up to 70B parameters) using syntactically varied harmful prompts. They apply causal mediation analysis to isolate whether upstream syntactic representations causally influence refusal decisions. They also steer syntactic features to trigger/suppress refusal and analyze post-training data composition to trace the linguistic bias.
AI.result: Non-imperative syntactic forms reliably bypass safety guardrails across all tested models. Causal mediation confirms that refusal is partially driven by syntactic features rather than pure semantic understanding. Steering these features can toggle refusal on/off. The bias originates from syntactically homogeneous post-training data, and increasing syntactic diversity mitigates the vulnerability.
AI.conclusion: Current alignment approaches inadvertently introduce syntactic confounders into the refusal mechanism, preventing semantically grounded safety decisions. Increasing syntactic diversity in post-training data offers a partial remedy, but the deeper issue is that models learn spurious syntax-safety correlations rather than robust semantic understanding of harmful content.

title: KV-Skill: Forging Expertise in the Model's Native Language
comment: 17 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables. Zhaowei Han and Xiang Zhang contributed equally to this work. Code: https://github.com/shawnzhg/KV-Skill
summary: Task knowledge is commonly stored either as text in the prompt or as an update to model weights. Text is modular but must be interpreted on every use, while weight adaptation makes the resulting capability difficult to load, remove, or share independently. We introduce KV-Skill, a design space of external factorized operators that a frozen language model reads through a lightweight interface. KV-Skill supports two complementary paths. Registration converts an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and trains a shared per-backbone interface. Reward learning develops a compact latent operator directly from task outcomes, with or without an authored skill. Neither path adds positions to the prompt. Across ten benchmarks and four backbones from three model families, converting text to a KV-Skill consistently makes the same procedural knowledge more effective. On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, registration reaches 77.2 accuracy, compared with 23.4 for the source text skill, 52.0 for SkillOpt, and 64.5 for SoftSkill. Under matched reward training and parameter budgets, KV-Skill gives the best result in seven of eight matched settings against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA. A post-hoc rank analysis further shows that text-derived operators retain nearly all of their benefit with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while matched random directions fail. Finally, one shared interface retains three independently loadable KV-Skills without measurable forgetting. These results show that task knowledge can be acquired from text or experience, compressed into an external operator, and deployed separately from the backbone. Code is available at: https://github.com/shawnzhg/KV-Skill

AI.tldr: KV-Skill introduces a design space of external factorized operators that a frozen LLM reads through a lightweight KV interface, supporting both text-to-operator registration and reward-driven latent operator learning, achieving superior performance over text-in-prompt, soft prompting, and LoRA baselines while enabling modular, independently loadable skills.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for storing task knowledge face a trade-off: text in prompts is modular but incurs repeated interpretation overhead, while weight adaptation (fine-tuning, LoRA) produces capabilities that are difficult to load, remove, or share independently. There is a need for a paradigm that combines the modularity of text with the efficiency of compiled operators.
AI.method: KV-Skill proposes two complementary paths: (1) Registration — converts an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and trains a shared per-backbone lightweight interface; (2) Reward learning — develops a compact latent operator directly from task outcomes, optionally guided by authored skills. Neither path consumes additional prompt positions. The operators are injected as factorized KV cache modifications that the frozen backbone reads through a lightweight interface, with post-hoc rank analysis validating that benefits concentrate in task-aligned directions.
AI.result: On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, registration achieves 77.2% accuracy vs. 23.4% (source text), 52.0% (SkillOpt), and 64.5% (SoftSkill). Under matched reward training and parameter budgets, KV-Skill wins in 7/8 settings against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA. A single shared interface retains three independently loadable KV-Skills without measurable forgetting. Post-hoc analysis shows text-derived operators retain nearly all benefit with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while random directions fail.
AI.conclusion: Task knowledge can be acquired from text or experience, compressed into an external factorized operator, and deployed separately from the frozen backbone. KV-Skill bridges the gap between prompt-based modularity and weight-adaptation efficiency, enabling skills to be independently loaded, removed, and shared without interference.

title: Decolonizing Linguistic Policies in Automated Speech Recognition: A Framework for Cross-Culturally Competent Speech AI
comment: 10 Pages, 2 Figures, 2 Tables, Interspeech 2026 - Sydney, Australia
summary: This paper focuses on automatic speech recognition (ASR) and ASR-mediated voice interfaces that shape access to public services, healthcare, and education. We argue that persistent failures for low-resource, Indigenous, and non-standard language varieties are not only technical errors, but also implicit linguistic policies that reproduce colonial language hierarchies. Drawing on linguistic capital, raciolinguistic ideology, language policy research, and decolonial computing, we show how data, metrics, and model priors determine whose voices become machine-legible. We introduce the Three Harms (3M) taxonomy---Misrecognition, Misalignment, and Mistrust---and a seven-layer situatedness model for linguistic diversity in ASR and ASR-mediated voice interfaces. We then propose a participatory framework and minimum audit protocol for culturally competent ASR, positioning affected communities as co-designers, evaluators, and governance partners.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques ASR systems as sites of implicit colonial language policy, introduces a Three Harms taxonomy (Misrecognition, Misalignment, Mistrust) and a seven-layer situatedness model, and proposes a participatory framework for culturally competent ASR co-designed with affected communities.
AI.motivation: Persistent ASR failures for low-resource, Indigenous, and non-standard language varieties are not merely technical errors but constitute implicit linguistic policies that reproduce colonial language hierarchies. These failures systematically exclude marginalized communities from public services, healthcare, and education accessed through voice interfaces.
AI.method: The paper draws on four theoretical frameworks—linguistic capital (Bourdieu), raciolinguistic ideology, language policy research, and decolonial computing—to analyze how data curation, evaluation metrics, and model priors determine machine-legibility. From this synthesis, the authors construct the Three Harms (3M) taxonomy and a seven-layer situatedness model for characterizing linguistic diversity in ASR systems. They then propose a participatory framework with a minimum audit protocol.
AI.result: The analysis yields two conceptual contributions: (1) the Three Harms taxonomy—Misrecognition (failure to recognize speech), Misalignment (mismatch between system behavior and user needs), and Mistrust (erosion of user confidence in technology and institutions)—and (2) a seven-layer situatedness model mapping how linguistic diversity interacts with each layer of the ASR pipeline. The proposed participatory framework positions affected communities as co-designers, evaluators, and governance partners.
AI.conclusion: Culturally competent ASR requires shifting from purely technical fixes to participatory governance. Affected communities must be empowered as co-designers and evaluators, supported by a minimum audit protocol that operationalizes accountability. This reframes ASR equity as a matter of language policy, not solely engineering.

authors: Shayell Aharon Salomon Amir Shaked Matan Noga
title: The Vulnerability With No CVE: Managing Persistent Gaps Between Mandate and Authority in AI Coding Agents
summary:
Existing guidance identifies excessive agency, excessive permission, weak task-bound authorization, and inadequate agent controls as important risks. Control frameworks also describe capabilities for constraining, authorizing, observing, validating, and responding to agent activity. Yet security programs still need a way to manage persistent deployed instances that span components and outlive any one event.
  We propose the agentic posture vulnerability (APV) as a task-conditioned vulnerability-management abstraction: a durable record for a composed agent-control exposure. One posture may produce different runtime manifestations across tasks; APV links those manifestations to the invariant posture and remains open until authority is narrowed, a missing control is added, risk is accepted, or closure is verified. APV is not proposed as a new root-cause class of risk; it operationalizes existing excessive-agency, authorization, and control-composition weaknesses.
  We distinguish APVs from CVE-addressable product defects, OWASP Excessive Agency, Agent Baseline control outcomes, and the runtime authorization-execution gap. We then provide a field vignette, a thresholded definition, six recurring APV patterns, a vulnerability lifecycle, a minimum record, a control-and-closure matrix, tooling implications, and a testable research agenda.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Agentic Posture Vulnerability (APV), a durable, task-conditioned vulnerability management abstraction for persistent AI agent deployments. APVs link runtime manifestations across different tasks to an invariant underlying posture, operationalizing known risks (excessive agency, weak authorization, missing controls) into a lifecycle-managed record that remains open until closure is verified.
AI.motivation: Existing risk frameworks identify agentic risks (excessive agency, inadequate controls) and define desired control capabilities, but security programs lack a method to manage persistent, cross-component agent deployments that span multiple events. The gap is a vulnerability management construct that bridges static control definitions and dynamic, task-varying runtime exposures.
AI.method: The authors define APV conceptually as a task-conditioned abstraction, distinguishing it from CVEs, OWASP Excessive Agency, and runtime authorization gaps. They provide: a thresholded definition, six recurring APV patterns, a vulnerability lifecycle, a minimum record schema, a control-and-closure matrix, tooling implications, and a research agenda. A field vignette illustrates the construct in practice.
AI.result: The paper delivers a taxonomy and operational framework: six APV patterns, a lifecycle from discovery through closure, a minimum record structure for tracking APVs, and a control-and-closure matrix mapping controls to closure states. It also surfaces tooling implications and a testable research agenda for empirical validation.
AI.conclusion: APV is not a new root-cause risk class but an operational abstraction that makes existing agentic weaknesses manageable in persistent, multi-component deployments. It provides security programs a durable, verifiable unit of record for agent-control exposures, enabling structured tracking from identification through verified closure.

title: Example-Guided Prompting for Document-Level Text Simplification
summary: Document-level text simplification requires large language models (LLMs) to rewrite complex documents while preserving meaning, readability, and discourse coherence. Although prompt-based LLMs have shown promising performance, they often produce inconsistent simplifications because textual instructions alone provide limited guidance for complex document-level transformations. We investigate whether retrieved document-simplification examples can improve document-level generation by augmenting prompts with examples selected from a parallel simplification corpus. This example-guided prompting approach enables LLMs to exploit relevant simplification patterns without task-specific fine-tuning. Experiments on the OneStopEnglish corpus using multiple state-of-the-art LLMs show that incorporating retrieved examples consistently improves simplification quality over prompt-only generation and achieves competitive or superior performance compared with representative supervised (T5) and planning-based (PlanSimp) document simplification systems. Furthermore, we find that the benefits of example-guided prompting vary across LLMs, suggesting that effective use of retrieved examples depends on a model's ability to integrate contextual information during generation.

AI.tldr: This paper explores augmenting LLM prompts with retrieved document-simplification examples from a parallel corpus, showing consistent quality improvements over prompt-only methods and competitive performance against supervised and planning-based simplification systems.
AI.motivation: Prompt-based LLMs produce inconsistent document-level simplifications because textual instructions alone provide insufficient guidance for complex document-level transformations involving meaning preservation, readability, and discourse coherence.
AI.method: Example-guided prompting: retrieved document-simplification examples from a parallel corpus are appended to prompts, enabling LLMs to exploit relevant simplification patterns without task-specific fine-tuning. Experiments conducted on the OneStopEnglish corpus using multiple state-of-the-art LLMs.
AI.result: Incorporating retrieved examples consistently improves simplification quality over prompt-only generation and achieves competitive or superior performance compared to supervised (T5) and planning-based (PlanSimp) systems. Benefits vary across LLMs, suggesting dependence on each model's ability to integrate contextual information.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-augmented, example-guided prompting is an effective strategy for document-level text simplification, but its efficacy is model-dependent — stronger contextual integration capabilities yield greater benefits from retrieved examples.

title: C$^3$PO: Evaluating Cross-Modal Composition and Counterfactual Performance in Omnimodal Models
summary: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can process diverse sensory inputs, yet their reasoning remains heavily biased toward a dominant modality, resulting in brittle cross-modal reasoning. We introduce C$^3$PO, a benchmark of 3,404 samples spanning video, audio, image, and text, evaluating two abilities: information composition (fusing dispersed evidence) and counterfactual conflict (resolving deliberate contradictions). C$^3$PO's paired IC/CC structure and four-tier design enable targeted diagnosis of when and why cross-modal reasoning fails. Built through a fully automatic pipeline using 25 logically grounded templates, C$^3$PO reveals that while humans achieve 88.64% accuracy, the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches only 73.17%, with open-source models collapsing under conflict. Through attention probes, we find 86-95% of failures stem from modality dominance: models commit to one modality while ignoring contradictory evidence, concentrating 87-95% of attention on text. Mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness-sustained exploration succeeds, premature collapse fails. The 56-point accuracy gap between equally complex templates reveals that performance depends on modalities' structural roles in conflict resolution, not combinations. These findings show multimodal perception does not guarantee robust reasoning; architectures must enable sustained cross-modal attention to avoid premature

AI.tldr: C³PO is a benchmark of 3,404 multimodal samples diagnosing cross-modal reasoning failures in MLLMs. It reveals that even the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro, 73.17%) lags far behind humans (88.64%), with 86–95% of failures caused by modality dominance — models over-attend to text (87–95% attention) and ignore contradictory evidence. Mid-layer attention entropy predicts success; the 56-point accuracy gap between equally complex templates shows performance hinges on modalities' structural roles in conflict, not their combinations.
AI.motivation: Current MLLMs process diverse sensory inputs but exhibit reasoning heavily biased toward a dominant modality, resulting in brittle cross-modal reasoning. There is a need for systematic diagnosis of when and why cross-modal reasoning fails, particularly in tasks requiring information composition across dispersed evidence and resolution of deliberate cross-modal contradictions.
AI.method: The authors introduce C³PO, a benchmark of 3,404 samples spanning video, audio, image, and text modalities. It employs a paired Information Composition (IC) / Counterfactual Conflict (CC) structure with a four-tier design enabling targeted failure diagnosis. The benchmark is built through a fully automatic pipeline using 25 logically grounded templates. Analysis is conducted via attention probes measuring attention distribution across modalities, with mid-layer attention entropy used to predict correctness.
AI.result: Humans achieve 88.64% accuracy; the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches 73.17%, with open-source models collapsing under conflict. 86–95% of failures stem from modality dominance: models concentrate 87–95% of attention on text while ignoring contradictory evidence. Mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness — sustained exploration succeeds, premature collapse fails. A 56-point accuracy gap exists between equally complex templates, showing performance depends on modalities' structural roles in conflict resolution, not on which modalities are combined.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal perception does not guarantee robust cross-modal reasoning. Architectures must enable sustained cross-modal attention to prevent premature commitment to a dominant modality. The findings call for designing models that can maintain balanced attention across modalities during conflict resolution.

title: Tool Demo: Topology analysis with GPML for detection of cyberattacks in Water Distribution Networks
summary: Water distribution networks depends on industrial control systems to integrate the physical process with communication network, making them vulnerable to cyberattacks that alter the traffic pattern and network behavior. Traditional detection approaches that rely on raw traffic or protocol information often oversee structural changes that are induced by such attacks. In this work, we presents a topology-driven approach for detection of cyberattacks in water distribution networks based on Graph Processing for Machine Learning (GPML) framework. The raw traffic is transformed into dynamic graphs, from which community and spectral metrics are extracted and analyzed for any structural and communication modifications with time. The proposed methodology is evaluated on three industrial water distribution datasets such as HITL, SWaT, and CrossTest. Spectral and community graph metrics improve the model performance in detection of cyber and pyhiscal attacks across the three datasets.

AI.tldr: A topology-driven cyberattack detection method for water distribution networks transforms raw network traffic into dynamic graphs, extracts community and spectral metrics, and uses them to identify structural changes induced by attacks. Evaluated on HITL, SWaT, and CrossTest datasets, the approach improves detection of both cyber and physical attacks.
AI.motivation: Water distribution networks rely on industrial control systems (ICS) that integrate physical processes with communication networks. This integration exposes them to cyberattacks that alter traffic patterns and network behavior. Traditional detection methods using raw traffic or protocol information overlook structural changes caused by such attacks, creating a need for topology-aware detection approaches.
AI.method: The authors propose a topology-driven detection framework based on Graph Processing for Machine Learning (GPML). Raw network traffic is transformed into dynamic graphs. Community metrics and spectral metrics are extracted from these graphs and analyzed over time to detect structural and communication modifications indicative of cyberattacks.
AI.result: The methodology was evaluated on three industrial water distribution datasets: HITL, SWaT, and CrossTest. Spectral and community graph metrics improved model performance in detecting both cyber and physical attacks across all three datasets.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based topological features, specifically community and spectral metrics derived from dynamic traffic graphs, provide effective signals for detecting cyberattacks in water distribution ICS networks, outperforming traditional traffic-based approaches.

title: DBLAST: Dependent Block Drafting for Stochastic Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language models' inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple future tokens and a target model to verify them. While recent block and diffusion-style drafters can predict several positions in a single pass, their training and sampling procedures are typically optimized for greedy decoding or assume that positions in the draft block are conditionally independent. This assumption becomes brittle in non-greedy speculative decoding, where the target distribution is deliberately stochastic and multiple continuations become plausible. We study this mismatch for block diffusion drafters and show that the accepted draft length degrades as the entropy of the target sampling distribution increases. We propose a dependent block drafter based on a low-rank latent mixture over token positions, complemented by an acceptance-oriented training objective that directly targets the expected verified length. Experiments with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, MT-Bench, HumanEval, and creative-writing benchmarks show that our approach, namely DBLast, consistently improves accepted length over independent block sampling, especially in higher-entropy decoding regimes.

AI.tldr: Block diffusion drafters assume conditional independence among draft tokens, which fails under non-greedy (stochastic) decoding. The authors propose DBLast, a dependent block drafter using a low-rank latent mixture over positions with an acceptance-oriented training objective, achieving longer accepted draft lengths, especially in high-entropy regimes.
AI.motivation: Existing block and diffusion-style speculative decoding drafters assume conditional independence among positions in a draft block, an assumption that holds for greedy decoding but breaks down under non-greedy sampling where the target distribution is stochastic. This mismatch causes accepted draft length to degrade as target entropy increases, limiting the acceleration benefits of speculative decoding in diverse, creative, or high-temperature generation tasks.
AI.method: The authors introduce DBLast, a dependent block drafter with two key components: (1) a low-rank latent mixture model over token positions that captures inter-position dependencies within the draft block, relaxing the conditional independence assumption; and (2) an acceptance-oriented training objective that directly maximizes the expected verified (accepted) length rather than optimizing for greedy token accuracy. Experiments use Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B models evaluated on GSM8K, MT-Bench, HumanEval, and creative-writing benchmarks.
AI.result: DBLast consistently improves accepted draft length over independent block sampling baselines. The gains are particularly pronounced in higher-entropy decoding regimes (e.g., creative writing, higher-temperature sampling), where the conditional independence assumption of prior methods is most brittle.
AI.conclusion: Capturing inter-position dependencies and directly optimizing for acceptance length are critical for effective non-greedy speculative decoding. DBLast demonstrates that a low-rank latent mixture approach with an acceptance-oriented objective substantially improves block drafter performance under stochastic sampling, broadening the practical applicability of speculative decoding.

title: LC-GRPO: Bridging Train-Inference Gap for Flow-Based GRPO with Langevin Correction
summary: Flow-based generative models are typically sampled by solving a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), whereas online reinforcement learning requires stochastic rollouts for policy exploration and optimization. Existing GRPO methods for flow models therefore replace the inference-time ODE with a stochastic differential equation (SDE) during training. Although the ODE and SDE share the same marginal distributions in continuous time, their finite-step discretizations can differ substantially. In particular, SDE rollouts often become blurry as the exploration noise increases, creating a mismatch between the samples used for reinforcement learning and those generated by the test-time ODE sampler. We introduce LC-GRPO, a flow-based GRPO framework with Langevin correction. Each rollout transition first takes an inference-aligned ODE Euler step and then applies a stochastic Langevin correction targeting the marginal distribution at the resulting timestep. The required score is recovered directly from the flow velocity, requiring no additional score model, while the resulting transition remains an isotropic Gaussian with a tractable likelihood for policy optimization. We theoretically show that, under suitable conditions, one Langevin correction step reduces the Wasserstein error of an imperfect ODE Euler step. At a matched randomness level, we further show that the proposed transition can be more accurate than the standard Euler--Maruyama discretization of the reverse SDE. Experiments on SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, and HunyuanVideo demonstrate that LC-GRPO consistently improves reward optimization across text-to-image and text-to-video tasks, preserves generation quality, and substantially narrows the gap between stochastic training rollouts and deterministic test-time ODE inference.

AI.tldr: LC-GRPO introduces Langevin correction into flow-based GRPO training to align stochastic reinforcement learning rollouts with deterministic test-time ODE sampling. By injecting a score-based Langevin step derived from the flow velocity, it reduces the mismatch between training and inference, improving reward optimization while preserving generation quality.
AI.motivation: In flow-based generative models, inference uses a deterministic ODE, but GRPO requires stochastic rollouts, typically implemented via an SDE. Finite-step discretizations of the ODE and SDE differ, causing SDE samples to become blurry under exploration noise and creating a mismatch between training and test-time distributions. This degrades reward optimization and generation quality.
AI.method: The proposed LC-GRPO framework structures each rollout transition as an ODE Euler step (aligned with inference) followed by a Langevin correction step that targets the marginal distribution at the current timestep. The Langevin step's score function is recovered directly from the flow velocity, requiring no additional score model. The resulting transition kernel is an isotropic Gaussian with tractable likelihood, enabling standard policy optimization. The authors also provide theoretical analysis showing one Langevin step reduces Wasserstein error of the ODE Euler step, and that LC-GRPO can be more accurate than the Euler–Maruyama SDE discretization at matched randomness.
AI.result: Experiments on SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, and HunyuanVideo show LC-GRPO consistently improves reward optimization across text-to-image and text-to-video tasks, preserves generation quality, and substantially narrows the gap between stochastic training rollouts and deterministic test-time ODE inference.
AI.conclusion: LC-GRPO offers a principled way to perform GRPO on flow-based models by correcting the distributional mismatch between SDE training rollouts and ODE inference. The Langevin correction, computed cheaply from the flow velocity, improves both alignment and reward without additional model components.

title: MMAligner: Safeguarding Multimodal Large Language Models through Representation Calibration
comment: To Appear in the Proceedings of The ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS), 2026
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often refuse unsafe text prompts yet generate harmful responses to semantically equivalent multimodal inputs. Existing defenses either rely on external guardrails, which add inference overhead without repairing intrinsic flaws, or safety fine-tuning, which treats alignment as black-box optimization and may sacrifice utility or require large multimodal datasets. To identify the cause of this safety disparity, we analyze MLLM representations geometrically. We find that safety mechanisms learned from text persist across modalities: a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary remain effective, and representations inside this boundary consistently trigger refusals. However, unsafe multimodal inputs undergo a representation shift that places most of them outside the boundary, allowing them to bypass the model's intrinsic safety mechanism. This indicates that multimodal safety degradation stems from representation misalignment rather than the absence of safety capability. Based on this finding, we propose MMAligner, a safeguarding method that calibrates unsafe multimodal representations into the pre-existing refusal region. MMAligner applies a hard lower bound to ensure refusal, a soft upper bound to avoid excessive modification, and a preservation objective for benign inputs. Experiments across multiple open-source MLLMs show that MMAligner raises the average refusal rate on unsafe multimodal inputs to 99% with less than 2% utility degradation and minimal training data, substantially improving the safety-utility trade-off over existing baselines. (*Due to the notification from arXiv, "The Abstract field cannot be longer than 1,920 characters", the Abstract that appeared is shortened.)

AI.tldr: MLLMs have a text-derived safety mechanism that persists across modalities, but unsafe multimodal inputs bypass it due to representation shift. MMAligner fixes this by calibrating representations back into the refusal region, achieving 99% refusal rate with under 2% utility loss.
AI.motivation: MLLMs exhibit a safety disparity: they refuse unsafe text prompts but respond harmfully to equivalent multimodal inputs. Existing defenses (external guardrails, safety fine-tuning) are inefficient, sacrifice utility, or treat alignment as black-box optimization without addressing the root cause. The authors aim to identify why this disparity exists geometrically.
AI.method: The authors geometrically analyze MLLM representations to understand the safety disparity. They discover a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary that persists across modalities, and find that unsafe multimodal inputs undergo a representation shift pushing them outside this boundary. Based on this, they propose MMAligner, which calibrates unsafe multimodal representations into the refusal region using three components: (1) a hard lower bound to enforce refusal, (2) a soft upper bound to prevent excessive modification, and (3) a preservation objective to maintain benign input performance.
AI.result: MMAligner achieves an average refusal rate of 99% on unsafe multimodal inputs with less than 2% utility degradation across multiple open-source MLLMs, using minimal training data. It substantially outperforms existing baselines on the safety-utility trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal safety degradation in MLLMs is caused by representation misalignment, not absence of safety capability. Directly calibrating representations into the learned refusal region (MMAligner) provides a more effective and efficient solution than existing defense methods.

title: Different Perturbations, Different Mechanisms: Understanding Continued Pre-training for Zero-Shot Dialect Robustness
summary: Dialectal variation remains a major challenge for multilingual language models. Perturbation-based continued pre-training (CPT) has emerged as a promising approach to improving robustness, yet existing work largely evaluates individual perturbation strategies in isolation and provides limited insight into why they work. We present a systematic study of perturbation-based CPT for multilingual dialect robustness in LLMs, comparing six training conditions across nine German, Italian, and Arabic dialect tasks. Perturbation-based CPT, especially character-noised CPT, consistently improves zero-shot dialect robustness while largely preserving standard variety performance. More importantly, we show that methods with similar downstream performance induce distinct mechanisms of robustness, exhibiting different patterns of language model adaptation, representational alignment, and prediction repair. Our results provide a more complete understanding of how synthetic surface variation improves robustness and offer practical guidance for selecting CPT strategies in multilingual and dialectal settings.

AI.tldr: A systematic study comparing six perturbation-based continued pre-training strategies across three language families reveals that character-level noise CPT consistently improves zero-shot dialect robustness while preserving standard variety performance. Critically, methods with similar downstream accuracy induce distinct internal mechanisms of robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing work on perturbation-based CPT for dialect robustness evaluates strategies in isolation without explaining why they work. There is a lack of systematic cross-lingual comparison and mechanistic understanding of how different perturbations induce robustness in multilingual LLMs.
AI.method: The authors compare six CPT training conditions (including character-level, word-level, and subword-level perturbations) across nine dialect tasks spanning German, Italian, and Arabic. They evaluate not only downstream accuracy but also internal mechanisms: language model adaptation (perplexity shifts), representational alignment (embedding similarity), and prediction repair (how model predictions change under perturbation).
AI.result: Character-noised CPT consistently yields the best zero-shot dialect robustness across all language families while largely preserving standard variety performance. Methods with similar downstream performance exhibit fundamentally different internal mechanisms — distinct patterns of perplexity adaptation, representational alignment, and prediction repair — indicating that accuracy alone obscures how robustness is achieved.
AI.conclusion: Perturbation-based CPT is effective for multilingual dialectal robustness, but selecting optimal strategies requires looking beyond aggregate accuracy. The mechanistic analysis provides practical guidance for CPT strategy selection and a more complete understanding of how synthetic surface variation improves model robustness.

title: GAUGE: Granularity-Adaptive Counterfactual Gating of Evidence for Incomplete Multimodal Classification
summary: Multimodal classification typically assumes all modalities are available, yet real-world inputs are often incomplete. Imputation and dynamic fusion can mitigate such incompleteness, but existing methods operate at a coarse modality level and thus cannot retain reliable components while suppressing misleading ones within the same recovered modality, compromising prediction reliability. To address this issue, we propose GAUGE, a lightweight counterfactual gating framework for incomplete multimodal classification. GAUGE first imputes missing modalities with a frozen imputer and encodes observed and recovered inputs uniformly as fine-grained evidence units. Rather than intervening on each unit explicitly, GAUGE scores the counterfactual effect of replacing every unit with a reference representation through prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores, all obtained in a single forward-backward pass. These scores are mapped to continuous gates, which are converted into additive attention-logit biases for unit-wise evidence modulation without altering the backbone architecture. Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate that GAUGE outperforms strong baselines across diverse incomplete-input settings. Furthermore, a Taylor remainder theoretical analysis characterizes the error of the first-order approximation relative to the exact counterfactual effect, establishing GAUGE as a principled and scalable framework for fine-grained evidence control under modality incompleteness.

AI.tldr: GAUGE is a lightweight counterfactual gating framework that modulates fine-grained evidence units via Taylor-based scoring to handle incomplete multimodal classification, outperforming baselines across six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for incomplete multimodal classification operate at coarse modality level, failing to retain reliable components while suppressing misleading ones within the same recovered modality. This compromises prediction reliability under input incompleteness.
AI.method: GAUGE first imputes missing modalities with a frozen imputer and encodes all inputs as fine-grained evidence units. It then scores the counterfactual effect of replacing each unit with a reference representation using prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores in a single forward-backward pass. Scores are mapped to continuous gates and converted into additive attention-logit biases for unit-wise modulation, without altering the backbone architecture.
AI.result: Experiments across six benchmarks show GAUGE outperforms strong baselines under diverse incomplete-input settings. A Taylor remainder analysis characterizes first-order approximation error relative to the exact counterfactual effect.
AI.conclusion: GAUGE provides a principled, scalable framework for fine-grained evidence control under modality incompleteness, establishing theoretical grounding via Taylor expansion while maintaining architectural simplicity.

title: Evaluating and Improving Pedagogical Fit in LLM-Based AI Tutors with the Pedagogical Suitability Index
comment: This paper has already been accepted and presented at the IEEE 27th International Conference on Information Reuse and Integration for Data Science (IRI 2026) from July 31 to August 2, 2026, in Seattle, WA, USA
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as AI tutors, but a correct answer is not always a pedagogically appropriate one. In classroom learning, effective help depends not only on correctness, but also on whether a response matches the learner's current foundation, the course sequence, and the timing of concept introduction. Existing evaluations focus mainly on answer quality, leaving this instructional fit under-measured. We present the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI), a composite metric of six theory-informed sub-scores that evaluates how well LLM-generated tutoring responses align with learner readiness and curricular progression, and we further use PSI as a structured feedback signal for response improvement. We evaluate four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, and Qwen3) across 240 scenario-based evaluations using paired standard and defective prompts, then apply a PSI-guided regeneration protocol to 62 weak-performing cases. Baseline differences across the four tested models were modest overall (PSI range: 0.557 to 0.638), and open-weight and closed models did not exhibit a clear separation in pedagogical fit. Under the tested prompt perturbations, overall PSI remained largely stable (Delta = -0.002), though sub-score trade-offs emerged. More importantly, PSI-guided feedback substantially improved weak-performing cases: 51 of 62 cases improved (82.3%). Focused manual evaluation of the 62 PSI-selected weak cases provides initial evidence that the identified weaknesses are instructionally meaningful and that many PSI-guided regenerations correspond to human-judged improvement. These results suggest that learner- and curriculum-aware alignment may matter more for effective tutoring than model category alone, and that such alignment is both measurable and improvable.

AI.tldr: PSI, a six-sub-score composite metric, evaluates how well LLM tutoring responses align with learner readiness and curricular progression. Across 240 scenario-based tests of four LLMs, baseline PSI differences were modest (0.557–0.638). PSI-guided feedback improved 82.3% of weak-performing cases, demonstrating that pedagogical alignment is measurable and improvable.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as AI tutors, but answer correctness alone does not guarantee pedagogical appropriateness. Effective tutoring requires alignment with the learner's current knowledge, course sequencing, and timing of concept introduction. Existing evaluations overemphasize answer quality while neglecting this instructional fit.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI), a composite metric comprising six theory-informed sub-scores measuring alignment with learner readiness and curricular progression. They evaluate four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, Qwen3) across 240 scenario-based evaluations using paired standard and defective prompts. A PSI-guided regeneration protocol is then applied to 62 weak-performing cases to assess improvability.
AI.result: Baseline PSI across models ranged from 0.557 to 0.638 with no clear separation between open-weight and closed models. Prompt perturbations caused minimal overall PSI change (Δ = -0.002), though sub-score trade-offs emerged. PSI-guided feedback improved 51 of 62 weak cases (82.3%). Manual evaluation confirmed that PSI-identified weaknesses are instructionally meaningful and that regenerations correspond to human-judged improvement.
AI.conclusion: Learner- and curriculum-aware alignment matters more for effective tutoring than model category alone. Pedagogical suitability is both measurable via PSI and improvable through structured feedback, suggesting a path toward more instructionally appropriate AI tutoring systems.
