title: A Note on the Influence of a Zero Length Nonce on GCM and GMAC
summary: In this note, we show a simple attack that can recover the hash key of GCM and GMAC by using a zero length nonce. After recovering the hash key, the adversary can forge an arbitrary ciphertext or message as she wants. We note that the ISO/IEC version of GCM and GMAC allows the nonce to be a zero length string, while the NIST version of GCM and GMAC explicitly requires the nonce to be at least one bit. Hence, our attack works for the ISO/IEC version and cannot work for the NIST version.

AI.tldr: A simple attack on the ISO/IEC version of GCM/GMAC exploits zero-length nonces to recover the hash key, enabling unrestricted ciphertext/message forgery. The NIST version is immune due to its minimum nonce length requirement.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate a practical vulnerability in the ISO/IEC standardized version of GCM and GMAC that arises from a subtle but critical difference in nonce-length specification compared to the NIST version.
AI.method: The attack leverages the GCM/GMAC authentication mechanism by supplying a zero-length nonce. Under ISO/IEC rules, this is permitted and causes the computed initial counter block and the subsequent GHASH polynomial evaluation to expose the hash key H directly or indirectly, allowing algebraic recovery of H from the authentication tag.
AI.result: The hash key H can be fully recovered. Once H is known, the adversary can forge valid authentication tags for arbitrary ciphertexts (GCM) or arbitrary messages (GMAC), completely breaking the authenticity guarantees of the scheme.
AI.conclusion: The attack succeeds against the ISO/IEC version but not the NIST version, highlighting how a seemingly minor specification discrepancy—allowing zero-length nonces—can completely undermine AEAD security. This underscores the importance of mandating a minimum nonce length.

title: Where Models Converge and Humans Diverge: A Coverage Framework for Distributional Pluralism in Open-Ended Generation
summary: When a large language model (LLM) writes Harry Potter fanfiction, it reliably produces fundamental elements of the Hogwarts universe, such as recognizable places and characters. Human-written Harry Potter fanfictions, however, typically include these fundamentals and much more, incorporating stylistically irregular content and relationship-diverse plotlines. This gap between LLM and human writing has been noted across a variety of domains. LLMs tend to produce "average" writing, while human writing contains more diverse content that covers a broader distribution. Existing work has shown the existence of this distributional "gap", but no work has proposed a systematic way to measure it. Our paper proposes a human-grounded framework that uses the empirical distribution of human writing on a topic to measure the distributional breadth of LLM-generated content on that same topic. We propose two metrics, LLM Coverage (LLM-Cov) and In-Boundary Rate (IBR), that separate the plausibility of LLM content from its distributional breadth. Across ideation and narrative tasks, we find that current LLMs produce plausible but narrow content that concentrates near the center of the human response space. Our framework can enable researchers to better assess the distributional breadth of LLM-authored content, which we term its "cultural reach".

AI.tldr: LLMs produce plausible but narrow "average" content compared to human writing. This paper proposes a systematic framework with two metrics—LLM Coverage (LLM-Cov) and In-Boundary Rate (IBR)—to quantify the distributional breadth (or "cultural reach") of LLM-generated text against the empirical distribution of human writing.
AI.motivation: While prior work has qualitatively observed that LLMs produce "average" writing that lacks the stylistic irregularity and diversity of human-authored content, no systematic method exists to measure this distributional gap. The paper aims to fill this methodological void by providing a rigorous, human-grounded framework for quantifying distributional breadth.
AI.method: The authors construct a human-grounded framework using the empirical distribution of human writing on a given topic as a reference. They introduce two metrics: (1) LLM Coverage (LLM-Cov), which measures how much of the human response distribution is covered by LLM outputs, and (2) In-Boundary Rate (IBR), which measures the proportion of LLM-generated content falling within the human distribution's support. These decouple plausibility from breadth. The framework is evaluated across both ideation and narrative generation tasks.
AI.result: Current LLMs reliably produce plausible content but with narrow distributional breadth, clustering near the center of the human response space. They fail to capture the full diversity—stylistic irregularity, varied plotlines, and relationship diversity—present in human writing.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a systematic way to assess the "cultural reach" of LLM-authored content, enabling researchers to move beyond anecdotal observations and quantitatively evaluate how well models capture the full diversity of human creative expression.

title: Reasoning Errors Have a Region and a Direction in the Residual-Stream Trajectory of LLMs
summary: As language models are increasingly used for tasks that require verifiable reasoning, reliably distinguishing sound reasoning from flawed reasoning has become an important practical problem. Recent trajectory-based methods seek this signal in layerwise residual-stream displacements, which capture how representations change while attenuating some stable, token-specific information. However, displacement omits the state from which an update originates, whereas restoring the full state risks reintroducing shortcut-prone information. We identify this trade-off and propose a three-stream detector that combines motion with two restricted views of location. A coarse region reader based on vector quantization and a fine direction reader over normalized multi-layer states. This design restores enough state context to interpret the motion without returning to full-state probing. On reasoning benchmarks unseen during training, our method improves selection accuracy by up to 12% over the displacement-only state of the art and 21% over single-layer probing baselines. Although trained only on reasoning benchmarks, it also reads factual completion and fact verification, ahead of every detector we compare against, which places the signal on correctness rather than on a kind of reasoning. Ablations further show that motion, region, and direction provide complementary signals. These results suggest that reasoning validity is better read from state-conditioned motion than from either static states or decontextualized trajectories alone.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a three-stream detector that combines residual-stream displacements (motion) with two restricted views of layer-wise states (region via VQ and direction via normalized states) to distinguish sound from flawed reasoning. It achieves up to 12% improvement over displacement-only methods and generalizes across reasoning formats.
AI.motivation: Distinguishing sound from flawed reasoning in language model outputs is critical. Trajectory-based methods use layerwise residual-stream displacements to capture reasoning dynamics while filtering token-specific noise, but they discard the originating state context. Restoring full states risks reintroducing shortcut-prone information. The authors identify this fundamental trade-off between decontextualized trajectories and shortcut-vulnerable full states.
AI.method: A three-stream detector architecture: (1) a motion stream capturing residual-stream displacements across layers; (2) a coarse region reader using vector quantization to provide discretized location information; and (3) a fine direction reader operating over normalized multi-layer states. These three streams are combined to restore sufficient state context for interpreting motion without reverting to full-state probing. The detector is trained on reasoning benchmarks and evaluated on held-out reasoning, factual completion, and fact verification tasks.
AI.result: The method improves selection accuracy by up to 12% over displacement-only state-of-the-art and 21% over single-layer probing baselines on unseen reasoning benchmarks. It also outperforms all compared detectors on factual completion and fact verification, despite being trained only on reasoning data, suggesting the signal captures general correctness rather than reasoning-type-specific patterns. Ablations confirm that motion, region, and direction provide complementary signals.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning validity is better read from state-conditioned motion than from static states or decontextualized trajectories alone. The three-stream design effectively balances the trade-off between trajectory decontextualization and shortcut vulnerability, and the learned correctness signal transfers across task types.

title: Negotiating Risk Boundaries in AI for Policing Through Mixed-Stakeholder Deliberation
summary: AI tools are being increasingly adopted in policing in the UK and worldwide. Racial bias is a known and well-documented risk, yet representatives of affected communities are rarely included in decisions about AI adoption. We present results from a mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop bringing together 30 community representatives, police officers, and academics to assess the risks of 13 AI use cases in policing, with an explicit focus on racial bias. We found that participants were broadly open to AI adoption, rejecting only three use cases outright, most notably recidivism risk assessment, where objections targeted the premise rather than the implementation. Our analysis reveals that foregrounding racial equity did not narrow the deliberation. Instead, discussions gravitated toward a fundamental set of questions: does this tool actually work, will it deliver genuine benefit, and will that benefit extend to everyone? This integrated reasoning, reminiscent of the curb-cut effect in inclusive design, highlights the benefit of incorporating the racial bias lens into the risk-benefit analysis of AI use cases from the outset.

AI.tldr: A mixed-stakeholder workshop with 30 participants (community representatives, police, academics) assessed 13 AI policing use cases through a racial bias lens. Participants were broadly receptive, rejecting only three—most notably recidivism risk assessment. Foregrounding racial equity did not narrow deliberation; instead, it catalyzed integrated reasoning around efficacy, genuine benefit, and universal accessibility, analogous to the curb-cut effect in inclusive design.
AI.motivation: AI tools are increasingly deployed in UK policing, yet racial bias is a documented risk and affected communities are rarely included in adoption decisions. The study seeks to address this gap by centering community voices and racial equity in the evaluation of AI use cases.
AI.method: Researchers conducted a mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop with 30 participants comprising community representatives, police officers, and academics. Participants collectively assessed the risks of 13 distinct AI use cases in policing, with an explicit framing around racial bias.
AI.result: Participants were broadly open to AI adoption, rejecting only three use cases outright. Recidivism risk assessment was the most prominently rejected, with objections aimed at the fundamental premise rather than implementation. Rather than narrowing the deliberation, the racial equity lens broadened discussion toward core questions: does the tool work, does it deliver genuine benefit, and is that benefit universally distributed?
AI.conclusion: Foregrounding racial equity in AI risk-benefit analysis produces integrated, universally relevant deliberation rather than narrow, identity-specific concerns. This mirrors the curb-cut effect—designing for marginalized groups yields broad societal benefit—and supports embedding the racial bias lens from the outset of AI adoption decisions in policing.

title: dfence: Fine-Grained Speculation Barriers for Efficient and Effective Hardware-Software Protection in the Spectre Era (Extended Version)
summary: Speculative execution attacks such as Spectre-PHT and Spectre-STL remain a critical security concern in modern processors. While software-based mitigations like Speculative Load Hardening (SLH) offer effective protection against Spectre-PHT, they are limited in scope and require software-managed speculative masks, which can be error-prone and costly. Defenses against Spectre-STL, such as the Speculative Store Bypass Disable bit (SSBD), incur additional performance overhead and lack fine-grained control. In this work, we introduce dfence, a new CPU instruction that generalizes SLH to mitigate both Spectre-PHT and Spectre-STL with minimal hardware support. dfence enables developers to annotate sensitive registers, with the hardware ensuring that these values do not leak transiently. We implement dfence in the Proteus CPU and evaluate its security and performance, demonstrating less than 1% average performance overhead for our benchmarks. In addition, to support easy and secure adoption, we design a type system that statically verifies the correct placement of dfence instructions in code.

AI.tldr: dfence is a new CPU instruction that generalizes Speculative Load Hardening to mitigate both Spectre-PHT and Spectre-STL attacks. It allows developers to annotate sensitive registers, with hardware preventing transient leakage, achieving <1% overhead. A companion type system statically verifies correct dfence placement.
AI.motivation: Existing mitigations for speculative execution attacks are insufficient: SLH only addresses Spectre-PHT and requires error-prone software-managed speculative masks, while SSBD for Spectre-STL incurs significant performance overhead and lacks fine-grained control. A unified, low-overhead hardware-software solution is needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce dfence, a novel CPU instruction implemented in the Proteus CPU. It generalizes SLH by letting developers annotate sensitive registers; the hardware then enforces that annotated values cannot leak transiently. A type system is also designed to statically verify correct dfence instruction placement for safe adoption.
AI.result: Evaluation on the Proteus CPU shows dfence achieves less than 1% average performance overhead across benchmarks, while providing protection against both Spectre-PHT and Spectre-STL.
AI.conclusion: dfence offers a minimal-hardware, low-overhead, unified defense against Spectre-PHT and Spectre-STL, with the added safety of a type system for static verification, making it a practical and secure mitigation approach.

title: SkillZip: Contract-Preserving Graph Compression for Scalable Agent Skill Libraries
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly act as agents whose procedural knowledge is stored in reusable skill packages and loaded at inference time. As skill libraries grow, a central challenge is to expose the smallest sufficient executable context under a limited context budget. Existing systems struggle to reuse routines below the whole-skill level, preserve procedural contracts during compression, keep compressed routines executable and expandable, and update the compressed library as skills evolve. These challenges reveal a unit mismatch: skills are retrieved as packages, compressed as text, and converted into execution graphs only after retrieval, whereas reliable reuse requires a contract-bearing procedural unit. We propose SkillZip, an execution-aware procedural abstraction framework that performs contract-preserving compression over section-level graphs. SkillZip rewrites recurring contract-valid motifs into reversible ported macros while preserving boundary signatures, dependency closure, verifier reachability, and source-level expansion. At inference time, it hydrates a compact, dependency-closed context and expands macros only when required. ReZip further integrates new skills and revises risky macros using execution evidence. Comprehensive experiments1 on technical and embodied agent benchmarks show SkillZip consistently outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 12.2 points, while achieving a 3.46x compression ratio with 99.2% dependency preservation and 98.7% verifier reachability. Scaling analyses further confirm robust retrieval across skill libraries ranging from 200 to 100K skills.

AI.tldr: SkillZip is an execution-aware procedural abstraction framework that compresses skill libraries for LLM agents by rewriting recurring execution motifs into reversible macros while preserving contracts, dependencies, and executability, achieving 3.46x compression with minimal fidelity loss.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skill libraries, existing systems face a fundamental unit mismatch: skills are retrieved as whole packages and compressed as unstructured text, but reliable reuse demands contract-bearing procedural units. Current methods cannot reuse sub-skill routines, preserve procedural contracts during compression, maintain executability/expandability, or incrementally update compressed libraries.
AI.method: SkillZip operates on section-level execution graphs rather than flat text. It identifies recurring contract-valid motifs, rewrites them into ported macros with preserved boundary signatures, and ensures dependency closure and verifier reachability. At inference, a compact dependency-closed context is hydrated and macros are expanded lazily. ReZip provides incremental updates by integrating new skills and revising risky macros using execution evidence.
AI.result: SkillZip outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 12.2 points on technical and embodied agent benchmarks, achieves a 3.46x compression ratio with 99.2% dependency preservation and 98.7% verifier reachability, and demonstrates robust retrieval scaling across skill libraries from 200 to 100K skills.
AI.conclusion: Execution-aware procedural abstraction at the sub-skill level resolves the unit mismatch problem in skill retrieval and compression, enabling efficient, contract-preserving, and scalable skill reuse for LLM agents.

title: Potential Matching Optimal Transport: Continuous Normalizing Flows for Exact $p$-Wasserstein Dynamics
summary: We introduce Potential Matching Optimal Transport (PMOT), a potential-flow framework for general $p$-cost optimal transport with $c_p(x,y)=\|x-y\|^p$. PMOT parameterizes the CNF velocity field with a scalar potential in the generalized Benamou--Brenier form for the chosen exponent $p$. It trains the potential gradient with a self-induced matching loss along straight bridges determined by the model's own endpoints, while allowing flexible terminal distribution matching. Our main result establishes zero-loss exactness: under the stated regularity, exact terminal matching, and uniqueness assumptions, any zero-loss solution satisfies the generalized Benamou--Brenier optimality system and recovers the corresponding $p$-optimal transport map and dynamics. On synthetic benchmarks, PMOT learns $p$-specific maps that agree with the corresponding $p$-matched OT references. It also remains competitive as a likelihood-based density model on high-dimensional tabular data, and an MMD-based color transformation experiment demonstrates flexible sample-based terminal matching.

AI.tldr: PMOT introduces a potential-flow framework for p-cost optimal transport, parameterizing CNF velocity fields via a scalar potential in the generalized Benamou-Brenier form. It achieves zero-loss exactness: under regularity and uniqueness assumptions, any zero-loss solution recovers the p-optimal transport map. The method is validated on synthetic benchmarks, high-dimensional tabular density modeling, and color transformation tasks.
AI.motivation: Extend optimal transport beyond the classical squared-Euclidean (p=2) case to general p-costs, enabling learning of p-specific transport maps and dynamics within a continuous normalizing flow framework while maintaining theoretical exactness guarantees.
AI.method: PMOT parameterizes the CNF velocity field with a scalar potential in generalized Benamou-Brenier form for exponent p. The potential gradient is trained with a self-induced matching loss along straight bridges determined by the model's own endpoints, permitting flexible terminal distribution matching (likelihood-based or MMD-based).
AI.result: Under regularity, exact terminal matching, and uniqueness assumptions, zero-loss solutions provably satisfy the generalized Benamou-Brenier optimality system and recover the p-optimal transport map. Experiments show PMOT learns p-specific maps matching OT references on synthetic benchmarks, remains competitive as a density model on high-dimensional tabular data, and enables flexible sample-based terminal matching in color transformation.
AI.conclusion: PMOT provides a theoretically grounded, flexible framework for p-cost optimal transport with continuous normalizing flows, achieving both exactness guarantees and strong empirical performance across diverse tasks including density estimation and distribution matching.

title: SCP-NL2TL: Selective Conformal Prediction with Semantic Verification for Natural Language to Temporal Logic Specifications
summary: Translating natural language instructions into machine-interpretable formal specifications enables robots and autonomous systems to plan, reason, and formally verify their behavior. However, existing translation models typically generate a specification for every input, even when the result is unreliable or fails to capture the user's intent, creating risks in safety-critical applications. Inspired by selective conformal prediction, we propose a selective translation framework that not only generates formal specifications but also determines when they can be trusted. Reliability is scored by two complementary black-box signals, the fidelity of the specification back-translated into natural language and the dispersion of repeated translations under exact semantic equivalence, which fail on different errors and jointly separate incorrect translations more sharply than either alone. Conformal risk control calibrates this score into a decision that accepts a specification or abstains, with a distribution-free bound on the rate at which incorrect specifications are accepted for execution, and a conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings screens out-of-distribution inputs before any translation is attempted. The proposed framework is general across formal specification languages, with experiments on Signal Temporal Logic (STL), Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), and geometric Spatio-Temporal Logic (SpaTiaL) demonstrating improved translation reliability, robustness under the evaluated cross-tier shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize when generated specifications may not be reliable.

AI.tldr: A selective translation framework that uses dual black-box reliability signals (back-translation fidelity and semantic dispersion) calibrated via conformal risk control to decide when to trust or abstain from NL-to-formal-specification translations, with distribution-free error guarantees.
AI.motivation: Existing NL-to-formal-specification translators always produce output regardless of reliability, posing safety risks. There is no mechanism to determine when a generated formal specification can be trusted for execution in safety-critical applications.
AI.method: Two complementary black-box scoring signals: (1) fidelity of back-translating the formal specification into natural language, and (2) dispersion of repeated translations under exact semantic equivalence. These are calibrated via conformal risk control into an accept/abstain decision with a distribution-free bound on incorrect-acceptance rate. A conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings screens OOD inputs before translation.
AI.result: Experiments on STL, LTL, and geometric SpaTiaL demonstrate improved translation reliability, robustness under evaluated cross-tier shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention.
AI.conclusion: The framework establishes a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize when generated specifications may not be reliable.

title: Hardware Keystores for AI Agent Signing Workflows: A Zero-Trust MCP Enforcement Architecture
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures. Accompanying code and artifacts available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Hardware-Keystores-for-AI-Agent-Signing-Workflows-Artifact-357C
summary: AI agents performing cryptographic operations (signing Git commits, authenticating API calls, issuing certificates) currently store private keys in software-accessible locations: plaintext files, environment variables, or container memory. Any process with sufficient read privileges can extract the raw key material. A recent production incident demonstrated the practical severity: private keys were exfiltrated from a widely deployed framework via email injection in under five minutes. We aim to enforce both key confidentiality and content-aware authorisation for key use. To that end, we replace software-resident keys with hardware-confined keys accessible through a vendor-neutral PKCS#11 interface. A hardware keystore (HSM, TPM, smart card) executes cryptographic operations on-device; the host receives only the result via opaque handles. Hardware confinement is the primary contribution; it is enabled by a surrounding five-layer Zero-Trust enforcement stack comprising session identity (SAGA), scope bounds (Smax), semantic validation (RAV), taint tracking, and the hardware execution boundary. We evaluate against 12 injection scenarios derived from AgentDojo's ImportantInstructionsAttack template (Debenedetti et al., arXiv:2406.13352). We run four LLM models; three follow injections in baseline mode (gpt-oss-120b, Qwen2.5-72B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, n=192 combined). Baseline Attack Success Rate (ASR): 19.3% [14.3%, 25.4%]; protected ASR: 0% (Wilson 95% CI upper bound 2.0%). Zero false positives across four benign task scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes replacing software-stored private keys for AI agents with hardware-confined keys accessed via PKCS#11, enforced by a five-layer Zero-Trust stack. Evaluated against 12 AgentDojo injection scenarios across four LLMs, the protected system achieved 0% Attack Success Rate versus 19.3% baseline, with zero false positives.
AI.motivation: AI agents currently store cryptographic private keys in software-accessible locations (plaintext files, environment variables, memory), making them vulnerable to exfiltration by any process with read privileges. A recent production incident demonstrated keys being exfiltrated via email injection within five minutes, motivating the need for both key confidentiality and content-aware authorization for key use.
AI.method: The authors replace software-resident keys with hardware-confined keys accessible through a vendor-neutral PKCS#11 interface (HSM, TPM, smart card). Cryptographic operations execute on-device; the host receives only results via opaque handles. This is enforced by a five-layer Zero-Trust stack: (1) session identity (SAGA), (2) scope bounds (Smax), (3) semantic validation (RAV), (4) taint tracking, and (5) the hardware execution boundary. Evaluation uses 12 injection scenarios from AgentDojo's ImportantInstructionsAttack template across four LLM models (gpt-oss-120b, Qwen2.5-72B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, n=192).
AI.result: Baseline Attack Success Rate: 19.3% (95% CI: 14.3%–25.4%). Protected ASR: 0% (Wilson 95% CI upper bound: 2.0%). Zero false positives across four benign task scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Hardware confinement via PKCS#11 combined with a multi-layer Zero-Trust enforcement stack effectively eliminates prompt-injection-based key exfiltration attacks against AI agents, achieving a 0% ASR without introducing false positives on legitimate tasks.

title: FOCUS: Decoupling Expert Personas in LLMs to Enhance Domain Expert Capabilities
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can exhibit diverse personas, and activating expert personas has been shown to improve domain expertise and task accuracy. However, existing persona control methods often suffer from cross-domain coupling, which may lead to overly aggressive behavior in high-caution domains such as healthcare, or excessive conservatism in risk-sensitive domains such as financial trading. To address this issue, we propose FOCUS (\textbf{\underline{F}}ine-tuning with \textbf{\underline{O}}rthogonal \textbf{\underline{C}}ontrol for \textbf{\underline{U}}ncoupled persona\textbf{\underline{S}}). FOCUS first automatically extracts expert persona vectors from LLMs, then applies orthogonal decomposition to decouple domain-specific expert personas, and finally introduces an expert gating module to adaptively control persona activation according to task contexts. With a two-stage training strategy and a gated selection regularizer, the model learns to activate appropriate personas for both single-domain and cross-domain tasks. Experiments on financial, legal, medical, and cross-domain benchmarks show that FOCUS improves task accuracy and outperforms existing persona control methods. Our code is available at \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/openpersona-48F4}{this url}.

AI.tldr: FOCUS is a fine-tuning method that decouples domain-specific expert personas in LLMs using orthogonal decomposition and a gated selection mechanism, enabling adaptive persona activation for both single-domain and cross-domain tasks without unwanted cross-domain behavioral interference.
AI.motivation: Existing persona control methods suffer from cross-domain coupling — activating an expert persona in one domain (e.g., finance) can inadvertently cause overly aggressive behavior in high-caution domains (e.g., healthcare) or excessive conservatism in risk-sensitive domains. A decoupled approach is needed for safe, domain-appropriate persona activation.
AI.method: FOCUS operates in three stages: (1) automatic extraction of expert persona vectors from LLMs, (2) orthogonal decomposition to decouple domain-specific personas so they become independent, and (3) an expert gating module that adaptively selects which persona to activate based on task context. A two-stage training strategy and a gated selection regularizer ensure proper persona activation for single-domain and cross-domain tasks.
AI.result: Experiments on financial, legal, medical, and cross-domain benchmarks demonstrate that FOCUS improves task accuracy and outperforms existing persona control methods.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonal decoupling of domain-specific expert personas combined with adaptive gating effectively resolves cross-domain coupling issues in LLM persona control, enabling safer and more accurate deployment across diverse professional domains.

title: When Does Consensus Mean Correctness? Measuring the Agreement-Accuracy Coupling with Semantics-Preserving Re-Rendering
summary: A model's agreement across perturbed inputs is used both as a label-free reliability signal and as a self-training target, on the premise that agreement tracks correctness. That coupling is rarely measured directly: natural-image perturbations preserve meaning only by assumption, and no exact answer key localizes errors. Scientific figures remove both obstacles, a figure is drawn from data by a program, so redrawing it yields images that are semantically equivalent by construction and share a programmatically exact answer. We build RENDEQ, a generator of such render-equivalence sets, and measure the coupling on three open-weight VLMs, checking every finding across three independent instantiations. Re-rendering beats resampling on both accuracy and reliability. Agreement beats an evidence-carrying baseline, mean token log-probability, on two of three models and ties on the third, reversing an intermediate, buggy replication traced to a rendering-pipeline failure. The dispersion behind this is concentrated in one style factor, the plotting library, more than double the next-largest factor and an order of magnitude above the noise floor. Fine-tuning on the model's own cross-render consensus inverts: accuracy falls in every one of five replication runs, the opposite sign to published results on natural images. Agreement certifies correctness only above a threshold set by how diffuse a model's errors are, and an objective that rewards agreement destroys exactly that diffuseness.

AI.tldr: RENDEQ introduces render-equivalent scientific figures to rigorously measure whether model agreement across perturbed inputs tracks correctness. Key findings: re-rendering outperforms resampling; agreement beats token log-probability baselines on 2/3 VLMs; plotting library dominates dispersion; fine-tuning on cross-render consensus backfires, reducing accuracy — reversing prior natural-image results.
AI.motivation: Prior work uses input perturbations to gauge model reliability or as self-training targets, assuming that agreement across perturbations correlates with correctness. However, this coupling is rarely directly measured because natural-image perturbations only preserve meaning by assumption, and no exact answer key exists to localize errors. Scientific figures eliminate both confounds: they are procedurally generated from data by a program, so re-rendering produces semantically equivalent images with a programmatically exact ground truth.
AI.method: The authors build RENDEQ, a generator that produces sets of render-equivalent scientific figures — figures redrawn from the same underlying data/program, guaranteeing semantic equivalence by construction. They measure the agreement–correctness coupling on three open-weight vision-language models (VLMs), with every finding replicated across three independent instantiations. They compare re-rendering against resampling, benchmark agreement against mean token log-probability, decompose dispersion across style factors (plotting library, etc.), and fine-tune models on their own cross-render consensus to test self-training effects.
AI.result: Re-rendering outperforms resampling on both accuracy and reliability metrics. Agreement surpasses the evidence-carrying baseline (mean token log-probability) on two of three models and ties on the third — an earlier buggy replication showing the opposite was traced to a rendering-pipeline failure. Dispersion analysis reveals plotting library as the dominant style factor, contributing more than double the next-largest factor and an order of magnitude above the noise floor. Fine-tuning on cross-render consensus inverts: accuracy drops in all five replication runs, the opposite of published natural-image results. Agreement only certifies correctness above a threshold determined by error diffuseness; optimizing for agreement destroys that diffuseness.
AI.conclusion: Agreement is not an unconditional proxy for correctness. It works only when model errors are sufficiently diffuse, and self-training objectives that reward agreement eliminate the very diffuseness that makes agreement informative. This explains why fine-tuning on consensus failed across all runs and challenges the premise underlying agreement-based reliability and self-training methods. Render-equivalent scientific figures provide a principled testbed for measuring such couplings exactly.

title: Stochasticity Is Not the Hard Part: Reduction and Complexity in Instructional Sequencing over Prerequisite DAGs
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Equal contribution among Y. Chen, J. Jiang, and T. Shi (alphabetical order)
summary: When a student must learn concepts connected by prerequisite dependencies, when does the order of instruction matter, and what does it cost to find the best one? We study instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path problem in which attempting a concept succeeds with a state-dependent probability and failure leaves the learner state unchanged. We first prove that this stochasticity can be eliminated exactly: the problem collapses to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals, preserving optimal values and actions. The collapse removes stochastic complexity but not combinatorial complexity: optimal sequencing remains NP-hard -- via reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments -- even with no prerequisite edges, unit costs, uniform binary nonnegative transfer, and success probabilities at least $1/2$. Hardness is not uniform: when realizable transfer preferences remain jointly acyclic with the prerequisites, any topological order of the residual joint graph is optimal, and fixed prerequisite width yields polynomial-time exact dynamic programming. A computable diagnostic, $mΔ$, bounds the value of sequencing before optimization. On 70,893 interactions from an introductory CS course, the diagnostic certifies a doubly easy regime -- little value to optimize and little space to search -- while constructed transfer instances realize the challenging regime, where myopic sequencing suffers large regret yet exact A* with a consistent heuristic expands only linearly many states on that family.

AI.tldr: Instructional sequencing with prerequisite dependencies is a stochastic shortest-path problem that collapses deterministically onto a lattice of order ideals. Optimal sequencing is NP-hard even under strong constraints, but polynomial-time solvable when transfer preferences are jointly acyclic with prerequisites or prerequisite width is fixed. A diagnostic metric, mΔ, bounds optimization value, and empirical validation on CS course data reveals an "easy" regime, while constructed hard instances are efficiently solved via A* search.
AI.motivation: Understanding when instructional order matters for learning concepts with prerequisites, and characterizing the computational cost of finding optimal sequences. Prior work lacks a rigorous treatment of how stochastic learning outcomes interact with prerequisite constraints and transfer relationships between concepts.
AI.method: The authors model instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path problem, then prove a deterministic collapse to a shortest-path problem on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals. They establish NP-hardness via reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments, identify tractable special cases (joint acyclicity, bounded prerequisite width), introduce the mΔ diagnostic to bound optimization value, and evaluate on real CS course interaction data alongside constructed hard instances solved with A* search.
AI.result: (1) Stochasticity is eliminable: the problem collapses to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the order ideal lattice. (2) NP-hardness holds even with no prerequisites, unit costs, uniform binary transfer, and success probability ≥ 1/2. (3) Polynomial-time cases: jointly acyclic transfer/prerequisites and fixed prerequisite width. (4) On 70,893 CS course interactions, mΔ certifies minimal optimization value and search space. (5) On constructed hard instances, myopic sequencing incurs large regret, but exact A* with a consistent heuristic expands only linearly many states.
AI.conclusion: Instructional sequencing exhibits a sharp dichotomy: it can be computationally trivial or NP-hard depending on structural properties of prerequisites and transfer. The mΔ diagnostic effectively identifies easy real-world instances, while A* search can handle hard instances efficiently with a well-designed heuristic, bridging theory and practical optimization.

title: Reversible Unlearnable Examples: Towards the Copyright Protection in Deep Learning Era
summary: Significant advancements in deep learning have been made possible by the utilization of large datasets, underscoring the critical importance of copyright protection. Adding meticulously designed perturbations to examples, making them unlearnable has become a crucial approach for safeguarding data copyright. Existing methods for creating unlearnable examples overlook the risk of data leakage, which can threaten data ownership. Thus, copyright protection in deep learning faces two main threats: illegal model training and malicious data leakage. We investigate that these two threats cannot be solved by straightforwardly combining existing availability attacks and watermarking techniques as their negative interaction effects. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a novel copyright protection mechanism for the aforementioned security concerns. Considering that the prevention of unauthorized model training requires powerful generalizability of unlearnable perturbations, we generate perturbations to induce the model to learn uncorrelated features of input images. It works by minimizing the mutual information of the input and output of the model. On the other hand, to eliminate the side impact of unlearnable perturbations on the watermark extraction, we design a dual extraction strategy by using two distinct watermark extractors. Extensive experiments on the image datasets {ImageNet, CIFAR10, and Pets} show that our proposed method could provide comprehensive copyright protection to images. The code is available at {https://github.com/Yeah21/ReversibleUnlearnableExamples}.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel copyright protection mechanism that simultaneously prevents unauthorized model training (via unlearnable examples) and prevents data leakage (via watermarking), addressing the negative interaction between these two techniques through mutual information minimization and a dual watermark extraction strategy.
AI.motivation: Existing unlearnable example methods only address unauthorized model training but overlook data leakage risks. Simply combining availability attacks with watermarking fails due to negative interaction effects — unlearnable perturbations interfere with watermark extraction. A unified solution is needed to address both threats simultaneously.
AI.method: The method has two components: (1) Generating unlearnable perturbations by minimizing mutual information between model input and output, forcing the model to learn uncorrelated features, which provides strong generalizability against unauthorized training. (2) A dual extraction strategy employing two distinct watermark extractors to decouple watermark extraction from the unlearnable perturbations, eliminating their negative interaction.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and Pets datasets demonstrate that the proposed method provides comprehensive copyright protection, effectively preventing both unauthorized model training and malicious data leakage.
AI.conclusion: The proposed mechanism successfully addresses the dual threats of illegal model training and data leakage in a unified framework, overcoming the limitations of naive combinations of existing techniques.

title: Human-Like Anaphor Resolution in Large Language Models
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Presented at CogSci 2026 and the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Society for Text & Discourse. Code: https://github.com/wristy/anaphor
summary: Anaphors are expressions that refer to other expressions, called antecedents. The process of connecting the two is called resolution. Cognitive science has identified multiple factors that affect the speed and success of anaphor resolution, including discourse structure, situation-model properties, and semantic factors. Here, we investigate whether these factors also affect anaphor resolution in five Large Language Models (LLMs) with open weights: GPT-2-XL, Llama-3.1-8B, Pythia-12B, Mistral-7B, and Mistral-24B. To model processing difficulty, we adopt the standard linking hypothesis that relates human reading times to model surprisal at the anaphor. As a second behavioral measure, we compare model accuracy to human accuracy on comprehension questions probing the antecedents of anaphors. The results show selective cognitive alignment: some LLMs exhibit human-like sensitivity to discourse prominence and distance-based factors in anaphor resolution, while showing weaker or absent sensitivity to semantic interference effects. These findings delimit the conditions under which LLMs approximate human anaphor resolution.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether cognitive factors known to affect human anaphor resolution (discourse structure, situation-model properties, semantic factors) similarly influence five open-weight LLMs, using surprisal-based reading time modeling and comprehension accuracy as behavioral measures. Results show selective cognitive alignment: LLMs partially mirror human sensitivity to discourse prominence and distance effects but show weaker sensitivity to semantic interference.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the cognitive factors known to influence human anaphor resolution—discourse structure, situation-model properties, and semantic factors—also govern anaphor resolution in Large Language Models, thereby assessing the degree of cognitive alignment between LLMs and human language processing.
AI.method: Five open-weight LLMs (GPT-2-XL, Llama-3.1-8B, Pythia-12B, Mistral-7B, Mistral-24B) were tested. Processing difficulty was operationalized via surprisal at the anaphor (linking hypothesis relating reading times to model surprisal). A second behavioral measure compared model accuracy against human accuracy on comprehension questions probing antecedent identification.
AI.result: Selective cognitive alignment was observed: LLMs displayed human-like sensitivity to discourse prominence and distance-based factors, but showed weaker or absent sensitivity to semantic interference effects.
AI.conclusion: LLMs approximate human anaphor resolution only under specific conditions, primarily those involving structural and distance-based cues rather than semantic competition, thus delimiting the scope of their cognitive plausibility.

title: Consistency Has a Computable Blind Spot: A Commutation Theory of Label-Free Reliability for Vision-Language Figure Reading
summary: Label-free reliability for vision-language models rests on invariance: perturb the input and a faithful reader's answer should not change. This has a known blind spot, a systematic misreading survives the perturbation and gets certified wrong, which we show is computable, not just real: an error is invisible to an edit exactly when the two commute, so the errors a suite cannot reach form its joint centralizer, a set that shrinks as edits are added and can be written down rather than guessed at. We act on the complementary relation, equivariance: edit a figure's data and the correct answer must change by a computable amount. Two matched edits are provably complete for affine reading errors; no suite of swap edits is complete for label permutations, and cyclic relabeling closes most of that gap. We instantiate the theory as the Equivariance-Consistency Score, a label-free, training-free detector, and release REND-EQUIV, pairing matched invariance and equivariance sets over identical data. The predicted ordering holds across three models and a hand-labeled population immune to the one circularity in how it is selected; a second invariance-family method confirms the blind spot belongs to the relation, not to any implementation; and cyclic relabeling delivers its predicted gain on a matched real sample. The same characterization explains a reported inversion of this ordering in the classifier metamorphic-testing literature: detectability is a joint property of the relation and the fault class, never of the relation alone.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that invariance-based reliability testing for vision-language models has a computable blind spot: errors that commute with perturbations are undetectable. The authors characterize this via centralizers and propose equivariance as a complementary principle, leading to the Equivariance-Consistency Score—a label-free, training-free detector validated across multiple models.
AI.motivation: Existing label-free reliability methods for vision-language models rely on invariance under input perturbation, but these methods have a systematic blind spot—certain misreadings survive all perturbations and get erroneously certified as correct. The authors aim to characterize this blind spot formally and develop a complementary detection strategy based on equivariance.
AI.method: The authors formalize the blind spot using group theory: an error is invisible to an edit exactly when the error and edit commute, meaning undetectable errors form the joint centralizer of the edit suite. They introduce equivariance as the complementary relation—editing the input data should change the answer by a computable amount. They prove two matched edits are complete for affine reading errors, show no swap-edit suite is complete for label permutations, and demonstrate cyclic relabeling closes most of that gap. The Equivariance-Consistency Score is instantiated as a label-free, training-free detector, and they release REND-EQUIV, a benchmark pairing matched invariance and equivariance sets.
AI.result: The predicted ordering of error detectability holds across three models and a hand-labeled population. A second invariance-family method confirms the blind spot is inherent to the relation, not any implementation. Cyclic relabeling delivers its predicted gain on matched real samples. The characterization also explains a reported inversion of detectability ordering in the classifier metamorphic-testing literature, showing detectability is a joint property of the relation and fault class.
AI.conclusion: Invariance-based reliability testing has a fundamental, computable blind spot—errors commuting with edits—that cannot be overcome by adding more invariance tests of the same family. Equivariance provides a principled complementary signal, and the Equivariance-Consistency Score offers a practical, label-free detection method. Detectability is always a joint property of the test relation and the fault class, never of the relation alone.

title: Recursive Synthesis for Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks
summary: High-quality long-horizon training data for terminal agents is expensive to produce, often costing hundreds to thousands of dollars per task, because each task must keep the instruction, environment, reference solution, and verifier mutually consistent. Human authoring does not scale, and direct generation with large language models (LLMs) often breaks these dependencies. We present Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks (RST), a recursive verified synthesis framework for constructing long-horizon terminal-agent tasks at scale. Starting from verified seed tasks, RST extends the reference solution, realigns the verifier and instruction to the new workflow, validates the result in a fresh sandbox, and reuses accepted tasks as seeds for subsequent rounds. Across fifteen recursive rounds, RST produces 37,484 synthesized terminal-agent tasks at roughly \$0.05 per task. Task difficulty increases substantially over rounds: the median reference solution grows from 67 to 374 lines, the median number of executed commands grows from 40 to 244, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 drops from 90\% at $R_1$ to 2.5\% at $R_{15}$. To demonstrate training utility, we collect rejection-sampled Qwen3.5 trajectories on the synthesized tasks and use them for supervised fine-tuning. Fine-tuning on these trajectories improves Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B by up to 10 points on Terminal-Bench~2, Terminal-Bench Hard, and Long-Horizon Terminal Bench, while agentic PPO lifts Qwen3.5-27B to 49.44\%, 32.00\%, and 22.07\% on the three benchmarks, corresponding to relative gains of 20.0\%, 41.2\%, and 21.9\% over the base model. Moreover, after 15 rounds, the recursion shows no ceiling: synthesis yield and validation rates remain stable as difficulty keeps climbing, indicating that the process can continue well beyond the scale reported here.

AI.tldr: RST recursively synthesizes long-horizon terminal-agent tasks at $0.05/task by extending seed tasks, realigning verifiers/instructions, and validating in sandboxes. Over 15 rounds, 37,484 tasks are generated with steeply increasing difficulty. Fine-tuning and PPO on these tasks yield up to 10-point and 20%+ relative gains on terminal benchmarks, with no observed ceiling.
AI.motivation: High-quality long-horizon training data for terminal agents is prohibitively expensive to produce manually (hundreds to thousands of dollars per task) because it requires maintaining consistency across instructions, environments, reference solutions, and verifiers. Human authoring does not scale, and direct LLM generation often breaks these inter-dependencies, creating a need for a scalable, verified synthesis framework.
AI.method: RST (Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks) is a recursive verified synthesis framework. Starting from verified seed tasks, it iteratively: (1) extends the reference solution, (2) realigns the verifier and instruction to the new workflow, (3) validates the result in a fresh sandbox, and (4) reuses accepted tasks as seeds for subsequent rounds. This process runs for 15 rounds, yielding 37,484 tasks. The synthesized tasks are used to collect rejection-sampled Qwen3.5 trajectories for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and agentic PPO training.
AI.result: RST produces 37,484 tasks at ~$0.05 per task. Difficulty scales substantially: median reference solution grows from 67 to 374 lines, median executed commands from 40 to 244, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 drops from 90% (Round 1) to 2.5% (Round 15). SFT on synthesized trajectories improves Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B by up to 10 points on Terminal-Bench 2, Terminal-Bench Hard, and Long-Horizon Terminal Bench. Agentic PPO lifts Qwen3.5-27B to 49.44%, 32.00%, and 22.07% (relative gains of 20.0%, 41.2%, and 21.9% over base). The recursion shows no ceiling: synthesis yield and validation rates remain stable as difficulty climbs.
AI.conclusion: RST demonstrates that recursive verified synthesis is a scalable, cost-effective method for generating high-quality, increasingly difficult terminal-agent training data. The sustained yield and validation rates after 15 rounds, with no ceiling, suggest the framework can scale well beyond the reported results, enabling continuous improvement of terminal agents through both SFT and RL.

title: Game Hopping in Lean
comment: The accompanying HOPSCOTCH artifact, is available under the MIT License at https://github.com/ravst/Hopscotch
summary: We present HOPSCOTCH, a Lean 4 framework for mechanizing computationally sound, game-based cryptographic proofs. Security definitions are expressed as indistinguishability between stateful probabilistic oracles, and proofs follow the standard game-hopping paradigm. HOPSCOTCH uses a shallow embedding: oracles and reductions are ordinary Lean definitions, enabling direct integration with the full Lean ecosystem, including general mathematical theories from Mathlib, such as finite-group theory. A game-hopping proof in HOPSCOTCH is represented as an explicit formal object whose constructors correspond to the standard steps of a game-hopping argument, making proofs easier to construct, automate, and inspect. We prove a general computational soundness theorem that interprets these proof objects by constructing reductions against the assumptions they use and deriving a concrete bound on the advantage of any distinguisher. Observational equivalence between oracles is established using a state-abstraction methodology: a simple yet powerful approach that supports transformations such as adding or forgetting state and replacing eager sampling with lazy sampling. We illustrate the framework with formalized proofs of the IND-CCA security of encrypt-then-MAC, the security of ElGamal encryption from DDH, the implication from one-time secrecy to public-key IND-CPA security, and the GGM pseudorandom-function construction. To the best of our knowledge, the last is the first mechanized proof of GGM for non-constant depth.

AI.tldr: HOPSCOTCH is a Lean 4 framework for mechanizing game-based cryptographic proofs using a shallow embedding. It represents game-hopping proofs as explicit formal objects, supports state abstraction for observational equivalence, and includes a general computational soundness theorem. The framework is demonstrated on IND-CCA, ElGamal, public-key IND-CPA, and GGM proofs.
AI.motivation: Mechanizing game-based cryptographic proofs is challenging due to the need to manage stateful probabilistic oracles, reductions, and game transformations. Existing approaches either use deep embeddings that limit integration with general-purpose math libraries or lack a structured, inspectable representation of proof steps. The authors aim to provide a framework that combines shallow embedding (for full ecosystem integration), explicit proof objects (for constructability and automation), and formal computational soundness.
AI.method: HOPSCOTCH uses a shallow embedding in Lean 4, where oracles and reductions are ordinary Lean definitions, enabling direct use of Mathlib. Security is defined via indistinguishability of stateful probabilistic oracles. Game-hopping proofs are represented as explicit inductive objects whose constructors map to standard proof steps (e.g., failure events, lazy sampling). A general computational soundness theorem interprets these objects to construct reductions and derive concrete advantage bounds. Observational equivalence is handled through a state-abstraction methodology supporting state addition/forgetting and eager-to-lazy sampling transformations.
AI.result: The framework is validated with formalized proofs of: (1) IND-CCA security of encrypt-then-MAC, (2) ElGamal encryption security from DDH, (3) the implication from one-time secrecy to public-key IND-CPA security, and (4) the GGM pseudorandom-function construction—reportedly the first mechanized proof of GGM for non-constant depth.
AI.conclusion: HOPSCOTCH demonstrates that shallow embedding with explicit proof objects is a viable and effective methodology for mechanizing game-based cryptographic proofs in a general-purpose proof assistant, enabling both formal rigor and practical integration with existing mathematical libraries.

title: Relay, Don't Route: Adaptive Population Handoff for Cost-Efficient LLM-Driven Evolution
summary:
Large language model (LLM)-driven evolution has shown promise for program search and algorithm discovery, but relying on strong models throughout long evolutionary runs is costly. A natural alternative is to combine cheap and strong models under a fixed inference budget. However, existing approaches typically allocate models at the level of individual queries or mutation steps, overlooking that evolutionary search is \textit{stateful}: each generated candidate changes the population from which subsequent mutations are produced.
  We empirically analyze LLM-driven evolutionary trajectories and find that search progress is strongly front-loaded, early trajectory performance is informative but noisy, and cheap models recover much of the early progress achieved by strong models at lower cost. Motivated by these findings, we propose \textbf{\model}, a training-free framework that shifts budget allocation from individual calls to evolving populations through adaptive \textit{population handoff}. A cheap model explores multiple trajectories in short blocks allocated by a bandit scheduler. Relay Gain, defined as the marginal improvement of a compact, quality-diverse candidate bank constructed for handoff, serves as the scheduler reward and determines when to hand off. The curated candidates initialize a shared strong model population for refinement. Across four benchmarks and three budgets, \model achieves the highest mean score in 11 of 12 settings, outperforming competitive baselines. Our results suggest that in stateful search, budget allocation should be organized around the population, not the individual call.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Relay, a training-free framework for LLM-driven evolutionary search that shifts budget allocation from per-call to population-level scheduling. A cheap model explores multiple trajectories via bandit allocation, and a "Relay Gain" metric determines when to hand off a curated candidate bank to a strong model for refinement. Relay wins 11/12 benchmark-budget settings.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven evolutionary search is costly when strong models are used throughout. Existing approaches allocate cheap vs. strong models at the individual query/mutation level, ignoring that evolution is stateful—each candidate changes the population for subsequent mutations. The authors aim to exploit this statefulness for smarter budget allocation.
AI.method: Relay is a training-free, population-handoff framework. A cheap LLM explores multiple evolutionary trajectories in short blocks, allocated by a bandit scheduler. A compact, quality-diverse candidate bank is constructed for handoff. "Relay Gain"—the marginal improvement from this bank—serves as the bandit reward and triggers handoff timing. Curated candidates then seed a strong-model population for refinement.
AI.result: Empirically, LLM-driven evolution is front-loaded: early trajectory performance is noisy but informative, and cheap models recover much of the early progress of strong models. Relay achieves the highest mean score in 11 of 12 settings across 4 benchmarks and 3 budgets, outperforming competitive baselines.
AI.conclusion: In stateful evolutionary search, budget allocation should be organized around the population rather than individual calls. Population-level handoff between cheap and strong models, guided by Relay Gain, yields superior cost-effectiveness.

title: SEAM: Global consistency beyond local accuracy in scientific machine learning
summary: Scientific machine learning commonly validates models at the level of a subdomain, a benchmark split, or an explanation for one prediction. Yet such local checks cannot establish whether the resulting explanations can be assembled into one globally admissible explanation. We introduce Scientific Explanation-Admissibility Machines (SEAM), a generator-agnostic framework that makes this local-to-global consistency question computable across regions, sensors, regimes, and model components. The finite explanation-sheaf instantiation SEAM-$Ω$ represents each region by a structured explanation with state, closure, and observation channels together with optional contract metadata; compares neighboring explanations on their overlaps; and converts disagreement into a channel-resolved obstruction. This obstruction locates inconsistency and tests competing declared accounts by restricting each repair to the revisions that one account permits. Exact feasibility refutes or retains an account; when exact repair is unavailable, residual-aware regularized records provide a separately labeled empirical attribution. The framework also separates inconsistency from non-identifiability and monitors learned generators under distribution shift. We establish theorems for minimum-cost intervention and conservation-contract detectability, together with companion results for identifiability and closure recoverability. Across nineteen experiments involving synthetic partial differential equation systems and out-of-distribution Fourier neural operator (FNO) monitoring, SEAM detects incompatible explanations even when local predictions are accurate, and attributes failures to specific channels and overlaps. SEAM adds a global explanation-consistency audit to existing solvers and learning models, testing whether their local explanations form a coherent scientific account.

AI.tldr: SEAM introduces a framework for checking whether local scientific ML explanations (across regions, sensors, regimes) can be assembled into a globally consistent account, using explanation sheaves to detect and attribute inconsistencies.
AI.motivation: Current scientific ML validation is predominantly local (subdomain checks, benchmark splits, single-prediction explanations), which cannot guarantee that individual explanations cohere into one globally admissible scientific account. There is no existing computable framework for assessing local-to-global explanation consistency across distributed model components.
AI.method: SEAM is a generator-agnostic framework using a finite explanation sheaf (SEAM-Ω) where each region has a structured explanation with state, closure, and observation channels plus optional contract metadata. Neighboring explanations are compared on overlaps, with disagreement converted into channel-resolved obstructions. The framework provides exact feasibility testing to refute/retain accounts, residual-aware regularized records for empirical attribution when exact repair is unavailable, and separates inconsistency from non-identifiability. Theorems are established for minimum-cost intervention, conservation-contract detectability, identifiability, and closure recoverability.
AI.result: Across 19 experiments on synthetic PDE systems and out-of-distribution Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) monitoring, SEAM detected incompatible explanations even when local predictions were accurate, and attributed failures to specific channels and overlaps.
AI.conclusion: SEAM provides a global explanation-consistency audit layer that can be added to existing solvers and learning models, testing whether local explanations form a coherent scientific account rather than merely accurate isolated predictions.

title: Innovation-Residual Auditing of Autonomous Analysis Agents: Localization, Detection Limits, Error Control, and Identifiability
summary: Autonomous agents now carry out entire data analyses, selecting cohorts, joining tables, and fitting models with little step-by-step supervision. When such an analysis turns out to be wrong, someone must determine which operation caused it. A recent approach does this without any labelled mistakes, learning instead from analyses known to be sound and flagging operations that depart from what that model predicts; how reliable such audits are has not been studied. This paper supplies that analysis. The choice of score determines whether an error can be localized at all. If each operation is scored by how surprising it is given the operation immediately preceding it, then operations that merely inherit an earlier error are indistinguishable from correct ones, so one mistake produces one flag; scores computed against a longer reconstruction of the intended analysis instead spread a single mistake across many operations. We quantify how far they spread, and how to choose the comparison length when an error accumulates gradually rather than at once. We then give procedures that control the proportion of falsely flagged operations within a single audited analysis, requiring only that sound analyses be exchangeable rather than that the fitted model be correct, and we quantify how much the guarantees weaken when the model is imperfect or when the analysis was selected for review in a way that depends on its content. Finally we establish a limit on what any such audit can report: errors below a certain magnitude cannot be attributed at all, being indistinguishable from ordinary variation among sound analyses. This limit falls so slowly as more sound analyses are collected that at the representation sizes now in use a hundredfold increase reduces it by under two percent, so the dimension of the representation rather than the volume of training data is the binding constraint.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first rigorous analysis of reliability guarantees for automated audits of autonomous data analysis agents. It examines how score design affects error localization, establishes procedures for controlling false flag rates under exchangeability assumptions, quantifies degradation when models are imperfect or analyses are selectively reviewed, and proves a fundamental lower bound on the magnitude of detectable errors determined primarily by representation dimension rather than training data volume.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents increasingly perform end-to-end data analyses without step-by-step supervision. When errors occur, auditing which operation caused the failure is critical. A recent approach flags suspicious operations by learning from sound analyses rather than labelled mistakes, but the reliability of such audits has never been formally studied. The authors aim to fill this gap.
AI.method: The paper theoretically analyzes score function design for error localization, comparing local (preceding-operation) scoring versus reconstruction-based scoring, and quantifies error spread. It develops procedures for false-flag-rate control under exchangeability of sound analyses. It derives degradation bounds when the predictive model is imperfect or when analyses are selected for review based on content. Finally, it establishes an information-theoretic lower bound on minimum detectable error magnitude as a function of representation dimension and training set size.
AI.result: Local scoring makes inherited errors indistinguishable from correct operations (one mistake → one flag), while reconstruction-based scoring spreads one mistake across many operations. False-flag-rate control is achievable assuming only exchangeable sound analyses, not model correctness. The lower bound on detectable error magnitude decays extremely slowly with additional training data — a hundredfold increase reduces it by under 2% — making representation dimension the binding constraint.
AI.conclusion: Reliable automated auditing of autonomous analysis agents is possible with formal guarantees, but score function design fundamentally shapes error localization patterns. The principal practical bottleneck is the dimensionality of the representation used, not the volume of sound-analysis data collected. This has direct implications for system design in autonomous data science platforms.

title: A Sound Translation from Tamarin to ProVerif: Enabling Comparative Analysis
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Full version of the corresponding ACM CCS '26 paper
summary:
Tamarin and ProVerif are two prominent tools for the formal verification of security protocols. They share the same high-level goal but differ significantly in their underlying formalisms and verification techniques, making a systematic comparison challenging: Tamarin uses multiset rewrite rules with sound and complete verification, whereas ProVerif employs an extension of the applied-pi calculus that provides fast but potentially incomplete results.
  We present a sound translation from Tamarin to ProVerif that enables a rigorous comparison of the two tools. It introduces novel techniques for formula rewriting, encoding multiset rewrite semantics, and handling simultaneous events, supporting an extensive subset of Tamarin's features, including multiset rewrite rules, lemmas, and restrictions, while precisely characterizing the cases where faithful translation is not possible. We provide formal proofs: within the faithful fragment, soundness ensures that any property verified in ProVerif also holds in the original Tamarin model, and completeness ensures that exists-trace properties not involving attacker knowledge are preserved. Best-effort encodings, in particular XOR, are reported separately and are outside these guarantees.
  Finally, we evaluate our translation on 121 Tamarin models. The translation covers 562 of 566 lemma tasks. Among non-XOR tasks with definitive results from both tools, 246 of 247 agree, with the remaining verdict explicitly flagged as using an incomplete model. Among the 362 tasks for which Tamarin returns a Boolean result and ProVerif completes with a logical result, ProVerif is faster in 334 cases (92.3%), with median per-task runtime and peak-memory ratios of 6.74x and 6.24x, respectively.

AI.tldr: A sound translation from Tamarin to ProVerif is presented, enabling rigorous comparison. The translation covers an extensive subset of Tamarin's features with formal soundness and completeness guarantees within a "faithful fragment." Evaluation on 121 models shows 562/566 lemma tasks covered, 246/247 non-XOR tasks agree, and ProVerif is faster in 92.3% of comparable tasks (median 6.74x speedup).
AI.motivation: Tamarin and ProVerif are two leading security protocol verifiers with fundamentally different formalisms—Tamarin uses multiset rewrite rules with sound-and-complete verification, while ProVerif uses applied-pi calculus with fast but potentially incomplete results. No systematic, rigorous comparison exists due to their divergent underlying models. The authors aim to bridge this gap by providing a translation that enables direct, principled comparison.
AI.method: The authors develop a sound translation from Tamarin to ProVerif featuring: (1) novel formula rewriting techniques, (2) encoding of multiset rewrite rule semantics into ProVerif's process calculus, (3) handling of simultaneous events, and (4) precise characterization of a "faithful fragment" where translation is guaranteed correct. Formal proofs establish soundness (any property verified in ProVerif holds in Tamarin) and completeness (exists-trace properties not involving attacker knowledge are preserved) within this fragment. Best-effort encodings (e.g., XOR) are handled separately with explicit caveats.
AI.result: The translation was evaluated on 121 Tamarin models encompassing 566 lemma tasks, covering 562 of them. Among non-XOR tasks with definitive results from both tools, 246 out of 247 agree; the single disagreement is explicitly flagged as an incomplete model. For 362 tasks where Tamarin yields a Boolean result and ProVerif finishes with a logical result, ProVerif is faster in 334 cases (92.3%), with median per-task runtime ratio of 6.74x and peak-memory ratio of 6.24x in favor of ProVerif.
AI.conclusion: The translation provides a principled foundation for comparing Tamarin and ProVerif, demonstrating near-perfect agreement on the faithful fragment while quantifying ProVerif's substantial performance advantage. The formal guarantees and explicit delineation of unfaithful cases (e.g., XOR) make the translation a reliable bridge between the two tools, enabling users to leverage ProVerif's speed while understanding when results must be interpreted with caution.

title: Answer First, Reason Later: Commitment Order in Diffusion LLMs
summary: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) can commit tokens in any order -- a freedom marketed as their core advantage over autoregressive decoding. We show that on reasoning tasks this freedom is instead the axis of failure. Logging every commitment during decoding of LLaDA-8B on GSM8K, we find that unconstrained (pure) decoding commits the final answer at 15-24% of the trajectory while half the reasoning region is still masked, and collapses to answer-only outputs on up to 90% of problems as the canvas grows. The cause is not the model's termination beliefs -- EOS "pressure" is nearly identical across decoders -- but reachability: whether the sampler may act on those beliefs at distant positions. A 2x2 prompt-decoder design shows that chain-of-thought helps only under ordered commitment (interaction +34.8 percentage points, 95% CI [26.8, 42.8]; without reasoning text the decoders are indistinguishable), an interaction we decompose into a collapse channel and an order channel and replicate on Dream-7B and MATH-500. A single-knob intervention -- frontier-gated commitment -- causally recovers the full gap (0.528 to 0.852) while preserving up to 4x parallel decoding, along a measured frontier whose optimal window flips from w=1 at full refinement to unconstrained at 8 tokens/step. Our results reframe existing window-style samplers, previously motivated by efficiency, as the minimal fix for a reasoning pathology they were never designed to address.

AI.tldr: Masked diffusion language models fail on reasoning tasks because their unconstrained commitment order causes premature answer selection; frontier-gated commitment fixes this pathology, recovering full accuracy while preserving parallel decoding speed.
AI.motivation: Masked diffusion LMs are marketed as superior to autoregressive models due to their ability to commit tokens in any order. However, the authors hypothesize that this freedom is actually detrimental for reasoning tasks, where structured, ordered generation may be critical.
AI.method: The authors analyze LLaDA-8B on GSM8K by logging every token commitment during decoding. They employ a 2×2 prompt-decoder design (with/without chain-of-thought × ordered/unconstrained commitment) to isolate effects. They introduce frontier-gated commitment, a single-knob intervention that restricts which positions can be committed based on a moving frontier, and measure performance across varying window sizes. Replication is performed on Dream-7B and MATH-500.
AI.result: Unconstrained decoding commits the final answer at only 15-24% of the trajectory, with up to 90% of problems collapsing to answer-only outputs. Chain-of-thought prompting helps only under ordered commitment (+34.8 pp interaction). Frontier-gated commitment causally recovers the full accuracy gap (0.528 → 0.852) while preserving up to 4× parallel decoding. The optimal frontier window flips from w=1 at full refinement to unconstrained at 8 tokens/step.
AI.conclusion: The freedom of unordered commitment in masked diffusion LMs is a fundamental pathology for reasoning. Existing window-style samplers, previously motivated by efficiency concerns, serve as the minimal fix. Frontier-gated commitment reframes these samplers as necessary for reasoning fidelity, not merely speed.

title: Spectral Aliasing Pretext: A novel task for Self-Supervised fault diagnosis in rotating machinery
summary: Deep learning is a new way for machinery fault diagnosis but requires extensive labeled data, a scarce resource in industrial settings. We propose Spectral Aliasing Pretext (SAP), a self-supervised learning method that pretrains models on unlabeled vibration data by exploiting spectral aliasing. We deliberately undersample signals to create folded spectrum, then train a Transformer to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum. This pretext task forces the model to learn frequency-domain invariants characteristic of mechanical faults, without potentially destructive augmentations. Experiments on the CWRU dataset show that SAP learns stable and highly discriminative representations. In a linear probing setting, SAP quickly achieves very high classification performance with only a small fraction of labeled data and low variance. In contrast, full fine-tuning, including fully supervised training, does not lead to more stable or better results. Overall, these findings suggest that SAP combined with linear probing can be more effective and reliable than fully supervised training for fault diagnosis with limited labeled data.

AI.tldr: SAP is a self-supervised pretraining method for machinery fault diagnosis that uses deliberate undersampling and spectral aliasing as a pretext task, enabling a Transformer to learn discriminative frequency-domain representations from unlabeled vibration data, achieving strong linear-probe performance with minimal labeled samples.
