AI.motivation: Deep learning for fault diagnosis requires extensive labeled data, which is scarce in industrial settings. Additionally, typical self-supervised augmentations (e.g., cropping, adding noise) can be destructive for vibration signals, potentially obscuring fault signatures. A method is needed to learn useful representations from abundant unlabeled data without harming the signal's diagnostic content.
AI.method: The authors propose Spectral Aliasing Pretext (SAP): (1) deliberately undersample vibration signals to produce a folded/aliased spectrum; (2) train a Transformer model to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum from the aliased version. This forces the model to learn frequency-domain invariants linked to mechanical faults. Evaluation uses linear probing (frozen backbone + classifier) and full fine-tuning on the CWRU bearing dataset.
AI.result: SAP learns stable, highly discriminative representations. With linear probing, it achieves very high classification performance using only a small fraction of labeled data, with low variance across runs. Full fine-tuning and fully supervised training do not yield more stable or better results, suggesting SAP + linear probing is more effective and reliable under label scarcity.
AI.conclusion: SAP combined with linear probing can outperform fully supervised training for fault diagnosis when labeled data are limited. The approach demonstrates that frequency-domain reconstruction via spectral aliasing is a viable and effective self-supervised pretext task for industrial vibration analysis.

title: EcoAgent-Bench: Evaluating Economic Decision-Making in Budget-Constrained LLM Agents
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Benchmark, dataset (304 budget-conditioned agent tasks), and evaluation harness; artifacts to be released
summary: Agent benchmarks usually measure task completion and treat resource use as an auxiliary statistic. In deployment, however, the choice among a local lookup, broad search, composite research tool, stronger model, or human escalation is part of the task itself. We introduce EcoAgent-Bench, in which every task specifies priced actions and an explicit budget. Its 304 real-derived tasks span five families adapted from GAIA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, and test four decisions: avoiding unnecessary escalation, escalating when local evidence is insufficient, selecting a model tier, and stopping on unsupported premises. We evaluate seven LLM agents in tool-API and workspace-CLI settings, together with four oracle scripted controls. Micro-averaged accuracy rewards one-sided policies: always-escalate controls achieve high micro success while failing save-oriented tasks. We therefore also report an economic-consistency score (the worse of accuracy on upgrade-oriented and save-oriented family groups) which exposes this failure. Tool-API agents attain only 3.9-24.0% micro strict success (at most 7.3% economic consistency), often either stopping before warranted escalation or overspending on cheap tasks. A threshold-crossing budget sweep changes GPT-5.4's escalation rate from 0% to only 3%. These results show that completion under a budget and economical action selection are distinct properties. We release the task bundle, transformation pipeline, frozen evaluation environments, and integrity-bound result artifacts needed to study both.

AI.tldr: EcoAgent-Bench introduces a benchmark where LLM agents must complete tasks under an explicit budget with priced actions, revealing that current agents struggle with economical decision-making—achieving only 3.9-24.0% strict success and failing to balance escalation vs. saving.
AI.motivation: Standard agent benchmarks treat resource consumption as an afterthought rather than a core part of the task. In real deployment, deciding when to escalate, which model tier to use, or whether to stop on insufficient evidence is integral to task completion. No existing benchmark jointly evaluates task accuracy and resource efficiency under explicit budget constraints.
AI.method: The authors construct EcoAgent-Bench with 304 real-derived tasks across five families (adapted from GAIA, HotpotQA, MuSiQue). Each task specifies priced actions and an explicit budget, testing four decision types: avoiding unnecessary escalation, escalating when local evidence is insufficient, selecting an appropriate model tier, and stopping on unsupported premises. Seven LLM agents are evaluated in both tool-API and workspace-CLI settings, alongside four oracle scripted controls. In addition to micro-averaged accuracy, they introduce an economic-consistency score—the minimum of accuracy on upgrade-oriented and save-oriented task groups—to penalize one-sided policies.
AI.result: Tool-API agents achieve only 3.9–24.0% micro strict success with at most 7.3% economic consistency. Agents frequently either fail to escalate when warranted or overspend on cheap tasks. A threshold-crossing budget sweep on GPT-5.4 shifts escalation rate from 0% to only 3%, indicating that budget sensitivity is poor. Always-escalate oracle controls achieve high micro success but fail save-oriented tasks, exposing the inadequacy of micro-averaged accuracy alone.
AI.conclusion: Completion under a budget and economical action selection are distinct properties that current LLM agents do not jointly satisfy. The benchmark and its economic-consistency metric provide a needed framework for studying cost-aware agent behavior. The authors release the full task bundle, transformation pipeline, frozen evaluation environments, and integrity-bound artifacts.

title: Sparse Mutual Information Graph Averaging for Improving Random Indexing Embeddings
summary: Sparse word embedding pipelines can avoid dense co-occurrence matrix materialization, dense factorization, and gradient training while still relying on sparse global corpus statistics. This paper studies Random Indexing (RI) vectors refined by weighted averaging on a sparse Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (PPMI) graph. On a fairytales corpus, the covered semantic analogy set consists of 272 Google family- category questions. On this family subset, PPMI top-K graph averaging repairs a weak RI initialization, improving accuracy from 19.4+-0.7% to 30.7+-2.9% across five seeds. Under the single tested runs, the same neighborhood averaging reduces family- subset analogy accuracy for PPMI+SVD (singular value decom- position), Binary+SVD, CBOW, and Skip-gram. Thus the method is not competitive with neural baselines on text8 and gives near- zero strict similarity correlation on SimLex-999. While Bloom filter sketches underperform RI in the tested configuration, we find that PPMI graph averaging with top-K pruning is a useful non-gradient repair for weak RI embeddings. On the fairytales dataset, PPMI top-K=50 graph averaging improves RI with accuracy going from 19.4+-0.7% to 30.7+-2.9%, and performing best with a seed42 of 34.6%.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether sparse PPMI graph-based weighted averaging can repair weak Random Indexing (RI) embeddings without gradient training. On a fairytales corpus, PPMI top-K graph averaging improves RI analogy accuracy from ~19.4% to ~30.7%, but the method underperforms neural baselines (CBOW, Skip-gram, SVD-based methods) and yields near-zero similarity correlation on SimLex-999.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to explore whether sparse word embedding pipelines—specifically Random Indexing refined via sparse PPMI graph averaging—can serve as viable, computationally lightweight alternatives to dense matrix factorization and gradient-based neural methods, while still leveraging global corpus statistics.
AI.method: Random Indexing (RI) vectors are first initialized, then refined using weighted neighbor averaging on a sparse Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (PPMI) graph with top-K pruning. The approach is evaluated on a 272-question Google family-category semantic analogy subset derived from a fairytales corpus, and compared against PPMI+SVD, Binary+SVD, CBOW, and Skip-gram baselines. SimLex-999 and text8 are used for additional evaluation.
AI.result: PPMI top-K graph averaging improves RI accuracy from 19.4±0.7% to 30.7±2.9% across five seeds (best seed: 34.6% with K=50). However, the same averaging degrades performance for PPMI+SVD, Binary+SVD, CBOW, and Skip-gram. The method is not competitive with neural baselines on text8 and yields near-zero strict similarity correlation on SimLex-999. Bloom filter sketches underperform RI in the tested configuration.
AI.conclusion: PPMI graph averaging with top-K pruning is a useful non-gradient repair mechanism specifically for weak RI embeddings, but it does not generalize as a beneficial post-processing step for stronger embedding methods and remains inferior to neural baselines overall.

title: CircuitSteer: Geometrically Aligned Multi-Layer Steering via Sparse Autoencoder Circuits
summary: Controlling the behavior of large language models (LLMs) remains a critical challenge for AI alignment. Existing steering methods, such as Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), typically rely on fixed single-layer interventions derived from aggregate activation differences. These methods impose a single intervention across semantically diverse inputs and often fail to sustain consistent behavioral changes across layers, limiting the effectiveness of the steering. In this work, we introduce CircuitSteer, a novel framework that leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify and manipulate coherent semantic circuits distributed across multiple layers. By constructing a feature flow circuit based on feature co-activation and the geometric alignment of decoder directions, we isolate the specific multi-layer subcircuits responsible for a target behavior. We then synthesize dense steering vectors from these sparse features and apply multi-point interventions to guide the model's internal semantic trajectory. We evaluate CircuitSteer using contrastive examples across a diverse set of tasks, including toxicity, emotion-intensity, sycophancy, and refusal, spanning two model families. Across all models and datasets, CircuitSteer is the only method to consistently produce fluency-preserving interventions; competing methods either sacrifice text quality or lack coverage, failing entirely on complex behaviors like sycophancy and refusal. These results demonstrate that multi-layer circuit steering, enabled by enforcing geometric alignment among selected features, yields strictly more robust and effective behavioral control than static single-point interventions. Code is available at https://github.com/mehrshad-sdtn/CircuitSteer.

AI.tldr: CircuitSteer introduces a multi-layer steering framework for LLMs that uses Sparse Autoencoders to identify and manipulate distributed semantic circuits, outperforming single-layer methods like CAA across toxicity, sycophancy, refusal, and emotion-intensity tasks while preserving fluency.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM steering methods (e.g., Contrastive Activation Addition) apply fixed single-layer interventions derived from aggregate activation differences. These fail to sustain consistent behavioral changes across layers and struggle with semantically diverse inputs, particularly for complex behaviors like sycophancy and refusal.
AI.method: CircuitSteer uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract interpretable features, then constructs a feature flow circuit by analyzing feature co-activation patterns and geometric alignment of decoder directions to isolate multi-layer subcircuits responsible for target behaviors. Dense steering vectors are synthesized from these sparse features and applied as multi-point interventions across layers.
AI.result: Across toxicity, emotion-intensity, sycophancy, and refusal tasks spanning two model families, CircuitSteer was the only method to consistently preserve fluency while achieving behavioral control. Competing methods either degraded text quality or failed entirely on complex behaviors like sycophancy and refusal.
AI.conclusion: Multi-layer circuit steering with enforced geometric alignment among selected features yields strictly more robust and effective behavioral control than static single-point interventions, establishing CircuitSteer as a superior approach for LLM alignment.

title: Hyper-ES: Effective Evolution Strategies for LLM Reasoning via Descent Direction Merging
summary: Evolution Strategy (ES) is a promising alternative to gradient-based fine-tuning for resource-constrained Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning. However, directly applying ES to billion-parameter LLMs is highly ineffective. In such high-dimensional parameter spaces, most random perturbations are nearly orthogonal to useful update directions, leading to unstable optimization. We propose Hyper-ES, a subspace-based ES framework that avoids the weakness of ES in full-parameter search while exploiting its strength in low-dimensional optimization. Instead of asking ES to discover useful directions from random perturbations in the LLM parameter space, Hyper-ES first performs a small number of inexpensive gradient-based fine-tuning runs to obtain descent directions. Although each direction may provide only a limited improvement on its own, their span forms a compact adaptation subspace that captures useful reasoning updates. Hyper-ES then applies CMA-ES to optimize layer-wise DARE-TIES merging coefficients within this subspace, allowing ES to search over combinations of meaningful descent directions rather than over arbitrary full-model perturbations. We evaluate Hyper-ES on three Qwen2.5-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill backbones across six mathematical reasoning datasets. Results show that Hyper-ES consistently outperforms GRPO-LoRA by 1% while requiring 10% fewer space-consuming gradient updates. Code at https://github.com/kuangrepi/Hyper-ES.

AI.tldr: Hyper-ES combines gradient-based fine-tuning to obtain a low-dimensional adaptation subspace with CMA-ES optimization over DARE-TIES merging coefficients, avoiding full-parameter ES instability while achieving better reasoning performance with 10% fewer gradient updates than GRPO-LoRA.
AI.motivation: Full-parameter Evolution Strategy (ES) fails on billion-parameter LLMs because random perturbations in high-dimensional spaces are nearly orthogonal to useful update directions, causing unstable optimization. A method is needed that leverages ES's strength in low-dimensional search while bypassing its weakness in high-dimensional spaces.
AI.method: Hyper-ES operates in two stages: (1) A small number of inexpensive gradient-based fine-tuning runs produce descent directions whose span forms a compact adaptation subspace capturing useful reasoning updates. (2) CMA-ES is then applied to optimize layer-wise DARE-TIES merging coefficients within this subspace, enabling ES to search over meaningful combinations of descent directions rather than arbitrary full-model perturbations.
AI.result: Evaluated on three backbone models (Qwen2.5-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill) across six mathematical reasoning datasets, Hyper-ES consistently outperforms GRPO-LoRA by 1% in accuracy while requiring 10% fewer space-consuming gradient updates.
AI.conclusion: Hyper-ES effectively bridges gradient-based and evolution-based optimization for LLM reasoning by confining ES to a meaningful low-dimensional subspace, achieving both superior performance and improved efficiency over existing methods like GRPO-LoRA.

title: Mitigating Scoring Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge via Random Number Generation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are often used as evaluators of text quality, known as LLM-as-a-Judge, which can outperform conventional automatic evaluation metrics that rely on reference texts. However, LLM evaluators tend to generate particular scores regardless of the context of the evaluated text, which is known as scoring bias. This study proposes a novel method to mitigate this scoring bias. An LLM is instructed to randomly generate number tokens, and the latent numerical bias of the LLM is identified by measuring the deviation of the observed distribution of numbers from the uniform distribution. A definition of a downstream task, for which an LLM evaluator is used, is added to the prompts for random number generation to measure task-specific latent number bias. In the evaluation by an LLM, the token generation probabilities for a given input are rectified considering the LLM's latent number bias. Results of the experiment on four different tasks, evaluation of LLM alignment, evaluation of summarization, Semantic Textual Similarity, and Semantic Textual Relatedness, demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms the baselines, including an LLM without debiasing and previous calibration methods. In addition, it is confirmed that scoring bias varies across LLMs, tasks, and score ranges, indicating the importance of measuring latent number bias as the case may be.

AI.tldr: LLM-as-a-Judge suffers from scoring bias where models favor certain scores regardless of context. The authors propose measuring an LLM's latent numerical bias via random number generation prompts and rectifying evaluation probabilities accordingly, outperforming baselines across four NLP tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs used as evaluators (LLM-as-a-Judge) exhibit scoring bias—they systematically favor certain numerical scores irrespective of the actual text quality. This undermines reliability and fairness. Existing calibration methods are insufficient, motivating a need to directly identify and correct the latent numerical biases inherent to LLMs.
AI.method: The method has two stages. First, latent numerical bias is measured by prompting the LLM to randomly generate number tokens and computing the deviation of the observed distribution from a uniform distribution. A downstream task definition is prepended to measure task-specific bias. Second, during actual evaluation, the token generation probabilities for score outputs are rectified (reweighted) by the inverse of the measured bias distribution, neutralizing the LLM's inherent scoring preferences.
AI.result: The proposed method outperforms baselines—including an unmodified LLM evaluator and prior calibration methods—across four tasks: LLM alignment evaluation, summarization evaluation, Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), and Semantic Textual Relatedness (STR). The study also finds that scoring bias varies significantly across different LLMs, tasks, and score ranges, underscoring the need for case-specific bias measurement.
AI.conclusion: Measuring and correcting for latent numerical bias via random number generation is an effective, generalizable approach to mitigating scoring bias in LLM evaluators. The variability of bias across models, tasks, and score ranges highlights that debiasing should be tailored to specific evaluation contexts rather than applied uniformly.

title: Multivariate Time Series Forecasting needs Cross Variable Loss
summary: Multivariate time series forecasting presents unique challenges because future variables often co-evolve under shared system dynamics. While existing studies mainly focus on cross-variable dependencies in historical observations, dependencies among future values are much less explored. Specifically, modern forecasting models largely follow the Direct Forecasting (DF) paradigm, generating multi-step forecasts with point-wise objectives that do not explicitly constrain cross-variable structure. In this work, we show that the DF objective is mismatched in the presence of cross-variable and lagged dependencies, revealing an objective gap. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{C}ross-\textbf{V}ariable \textbf{Loss} (CvLoss), a plug-in structural regularizer that constrains forecast residuals on a cross-variable graph. CvLoss penalizes inconsistent edge-wise residual differences over forecast patches, encouraging consistency across both synchronous and asynchronous interactions. Our experiments show that CvLoss consistently improves competitive forecasting models, outperforms representative learning objectives, and is compatible with a variety of forecasting backbones.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies an "objective gap" in direct forecasting for multivariate time series—point-wise losses fail to capture cross-variable dependencies among future values. The authors propose CvLoss, a graph-based structural regularizer that penalizes inconsistent residual differences across variables, and demonstrate it consistently improves various forecasting backbones.
AI.motivation: Existing multivariate forecasting models focus on cross-variable dependencies in historical observations but largely ignore dependencies among future values. The dominant Direct Forecasting (DF) paradigm uses point-wise objectives that do not explicitly constrain the cross-variable structure, creating a mismatch between the objective and the true data-generating process when cross-variable and lagged dependencies exist.
AI.method: The authors propose Cross-Variable Loss (CvLoss), a plug-in structural regularizer. It constructs a cross-variable graph and penalizes inconsistent edge-wise residual differences across forecast patches, enforcing consistency for both synchronous (same time step) and asynchronous (cross-time) variable interactions. The loss acts as an add-on to standard point-wise forecasting objectives.
AI.result: CvLoss consistently improves the performance of competitive forecasting models, outperforms representative learning objectives, and is compatible with a variety of forecasting backbones.
AI.conclusion: The DF objective is mismatched for multivariate forecasting due to unaddressed cross-variable dependencies in future values. CvLoss effectively bridges this objective gap as a flexible, model-agnostic regularizer, yielding consistent gains across diverse architectures.

title: SkillTV-Bench: Benchmarking How Well Judges Perform on Skill-Augmented Agentic Execution
summary: LLM agents increasingly execute long-horizon tasks through tool use and environment interaction, shifting evaluation from final-response scoring to verification of complete executions. For skill-augmented agents, verification additionally requires the procedural knowledge encoded in task-time skills, because this knowledge indicates what evidence to inspect and which failures are task-critical. However, existing judge benchmarks often expose final responses or static trajectories, and rarely combine task-time skills with directly inspectable artifacts and environments. We therefore introduce SkillTV-Bench, a 681-case benchmark of real agent trajectories from 50 tasks across eleven domains, designed to evaluate skill-aware trajectory verification for both LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge methods. Additionally, we propose SkillTV-Evolve, which externalizes verification knowledge as a reusable JudgeSkill that guides an agent judge to plan targeted inspections and issue evidence-grounded verdicts. On a disjoint development pool, an automated evolution loop further refines the JudgeSkill using misjudged cases. On SkillTV-Bench, the refined skill increases the same agent judge's accuracy by 14.8 percentage points. In offline rollout-pool selection, it increases selected-trajectory success from 22.9% with one rollout to 45.5% with ten rollouts. The code and data are available at https://github.com/HanZhi306/SkillTV-Bench

AI.tldr: SkillTV-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating skill-aware trajectory verification in LLM agents. It provides 681 real agent trajectories across 50 tasks and 11 domains. The authors also propose SkillTV-Evolve, which externalizes verification knowledge into a reusable "JudgeSkill" that is automatically refined via an evolution loop, improving judge accuracy by 14.8 pp and boosting rollout selection success from 22.9% to 45.5%.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly evaluated on complete execution trajectories rather than just final responses, especially for long-horizon tasks involving tool use. For skill-augmented agents, verification requires task-time procedural knowledge to identify what evidence to inspect and which failures matter. Existing judge benchmarks fall short because they expose only final responses or static trajectories and rarely combine task-time skills with inspectable artifacts and environments.
AI.method: The authors introduce SkillTV-Bench, a 681-case benchmark built from real agent trajectories spanning 50 tasks across 11 domains. They also propose SkillTV-Evolve, which externalizes verification knowledge as a reusable "JudgeSkill." This JudgeSkill guides an agent judge to plan targeted inspections and issue evidence-grounded verdicts. An automated evolution loop on a disjoint development pool refines the JudgeSkill using misjudged cases.
AI.result: On SkillTV-Bench, the refined JudgeSkill improves the same agent judge's accuracy by 14.8 percentage points. In offline rollout-pool selection, it increases selected-trajectory success rate from 22.9% (single rollout) to 45.5% (ten rollouts).
AI.conclusion: Skill-aware trajectory verification, augmented with evolvable procedural knowledge (JudgeSkills), significantly improves both judgment accuracy and downstream trajectory selection. The benchmark and method offer a new direction for evaluating and enhancing LLM-agent verification systems.

title: DreamGuard: Efficient Runtime Guardrail for LLM Agents via Risk-Aware World Model
summary: As large language model (LLM) agents increasingly invoke external tools and interact with real-world systems, unsafe actions may cause irreversible consequences on external states, user data, and downstream services. Recent runtime guardrails mitigate such risks by checking proposed actions before execution, but many remain reactive: they primarily assess the apparent safety of the current action, lacking an explicit model of how risk evolves across the trajectory. This limitation creates a critical blind spot for long-horizon risks, where individually benign-looking actions can gradually drift the agent toward hazardous states. In response, we propose DreamGuard, a proactive guardrail for LLM agents built around a risk-aware world model. The world model maintains a compact recurrent latent state over the trajectory and predicts future latent states from which DreamGuard derives immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence. It then fuses these multi-horizon signals into intervention decisions before execution. Experiments across four benchmarks and an online guardrail evaluation show that DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines, achieves the best safety-utility trade-off among evaluated guardrails, and maintains an average end-to-end latency of 25 ms per call.

AI.tldr: DreamGuard is a proactive guardrail for LLM agents that uses a risk-aware world model with recurrent latent states to predict both immediate and long-horizon risks across trajectories, enabling intervention before unsafe actions execute.
AI.motivation: Existing runtime guardrails for LLM agents are predominantly reactive, evaluating only the apparent safety of the current action without modeling how risk accumulates over a trajectory. This creates a blind spot for long-horizon risks where individually benign actions can gradually lead to hazardous states.
AI.method: DreamGuard employs a risk-aware world model that maintains a compact recurrent latent state over the agent's trajectory. It predicts future latent states and derives two signals: immediate-hazard evidence (current action risk) and prefix-risk evidence (trajectory-level risk). These multi-horizon signals are fused to make intervention decisions before action execution.
AI.result: DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines across four benchmarks and an online evaluation, achieving the best safety-utility trade-off with an average end-to-end latency of only 25 ms per call.
AI.conclusion: Proactive guardrails that explicitly model trajectory-level risk evolution, such as DreamGuard, offer a more robust approach to LLM agent safety than reactive methods, combining strong safety guarantees with practical latency overhead.

title: Once a Response, Always a Response: Detecting LLM-generated Text via Latent Prompt Restoration
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent and convincing text at scale, creating growing risks for misinformation dissemination, educational misuse, and platform governance. These concerns make robust detection of machine-generated text increasingly necessary. Recent zero-shot detectors mainly exploit probability-based statistical discrepancies, but they do not explicitly account for the training process of LLMs, which leaves a distinct generation mechanism insufficiently modeled and limits detection robustness. To address this issue, we propose EchoPrompt, a training-free detector based on latent prompt restoration. Our key intuition is that machine-generated text is typically produced conditioned on an upstream prompt, and this hidden dependency can be partially reactivated by prepending a unified generic prefix. Specifically, EchoPrompt restores a generic assistant-response context, measures the induced likelihood gain with an instruction-tuned model, calibrates it against the corresponding base model, and aggregates the resulting differences into a score that quantifies latent prompt dependency. Extensive experiments show that EchoPrompt achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot detectors while maintaining strong robustness across challenging evaluation settings.

AI.tldr: EchoPrompt is a training-free, zero-shot detector for machine-generated text that identifies LLM outputs by restoring a latent prompt dependency. It prepends a generic prefix to reactivate the hidden upstream prompt, measures likelihood gain via an instruction-tuned model calibrated against a base model, and aggregates these differences into a detection score, achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot performance.
AI.motivation: Existing zero-shot detectors rely on probability-based statistical discrepancies but fail to explicitly model the distinct generation mechanism of LLMs—namely, that machine-generated text is conditioned on an upstream prompt. This oversight limits detection robustness, motivating a detector that leverages this latent prompt dependency.
AI.method: EchoPrompt restores a generic assistant-response context by prepending a unified prefix to the text. It then measures the induced likelihood gain using an instruction-tuned model, calibrates this gain against the corresponding base model to isolate prompt-conditional effects, and aggregates the resulting differences into a score that quantifies latent prompt dependency for classification.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that EchoPrompt achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot detectors and maintains strong robustness across challenging evaluation settings.
AI.conclusion: Modeling the latent prompt dependency inherent in machine-generated text provides a more principled and robust signal for zero-shot detection, as evidenced by EchoPrompt's state-of-the-art results and strong generalization across diverse settings.

title: Equipment-centric workpiece localization in near real-time using deep learning-based vision and event-driven finite state machines
comment: 21 pages, 14 figures, 9 tables. Published in The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology
summary: Continuous workpiece localization is essential for traceability and process coordination in hot forging, but direct tracking is unreliable because of extreme temperatures, surface degradation, and irregular routing. This study presents an equipment-centric framework that infers workpiece locations from handling equipment observed by multiple static 2D cameras. The framework estimates floorplan-space 3D equipment coordinates and recognizes grasp and release activities. Event-driven finite state machines validate these activities as discrete handling events and continuously update workpiece states and locations. A keypoint-guided attention mechanism integrated into a 3D convolutional neural network improves activity recognition by focusing on functionally relevant equipment regions. Evaluation in an operational hot forging factory achieved 100\% event detection accuracy within a 33-second tolerance window, a mean localization error of 317.8 mm, and a mean system latency of 21 seconds. The framework connects vision-based perception with interpretable event-driven reasoning and supports visualization of workpiece transfers and quantitative analysis of equipment operations.

AI.tldr: A vision-based, event-driven framework uses multi-camera equipment tracking and 3D CNN activity recognition to infer workpiece locations in hot forging, achieving 100% event detection and ~318mm localization error in a real factory.
AI.motivation: Direct workpiece tracking in hot forging is unreliable due to extreme temperatures, surface degradation, and irregular routing. Continuous workpiece localization is critical for traceability and process coordination, motivating an indirect approach via equipment monitoring.
AI.method: An equipment-centric framework employing multiple static 2D cameras to estimate 3D equipment coordinates in floorplan space. A keypoint-guided attention mechanism within a 3D CNN recognizes grasp and release activities. Event-driven finite state machines validate these activities as discrete handling events and continuously update workpiece states and locations.
AI.result: Evaluated in an operational hot forging factory: 100% event detection accuracy (within 33-second tolerance), mean localization error of 317.8 mm, and mean system latency of 21 seconds.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully connects vision-based perception with interpretable event-driven reasoning, enabling workpiece transfer visualization and quantitative analysis of equipment operations in challenging industrial environments.

title: StepReflect: Structured UI Transition Reflection for Mobile GUI Agents
summary: Autonomous mobile GUI agents require accurate action reflection for reliable long-horizon execution. Existing approaches rely on open-ended multimodal reasoning after each action, which is costly and poorly matched to the structured nature of GUI state transitions. We propose StepReflect, which formulates per-step GUI reflection as supervised structured prediction conditioned on explicit transition specifications and paired visual evidence. StepReflect is trained through a staged pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning, teacher-student distillation, and preference- and reward-based refinement. Offline, the resulting 8B model achieves 82.16% transition-level accuracy on AndroidWorld, exceeding zero-shot GPT-5.2 by 11.83 percentage points under the same structured input. Online, across M3A, Agent-SAMA, MAI-UI-8B, and Seed-2.0-Pro, StepReflect achieves higher task success in three of four agent configurations and remains within one successful task of the GPT-5.2 Reflection Agent in the fourth. It also reduces paid API charges relative to GPT-based reflection in all four configurations. These results establish StepReflect as a practical, locally deployable alternative to repeated frontier-model reflection for long-horizon mobile GUI agents.

AI.tldr: StepReflect is an 8B model that formulates GUI action reflection as structured prediction, outperforming GPT-5.2 on AndroidWorld by 11.83 points offline and matching or exceeding GPT-based reflection agents online while reducing API costs.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous mobile GUI agents use open-ended multimodal reasoning after each action for reflection, which is computationally expensive and poorly aligned with the inherently structured nature of GUI state transitions. A more efficient, structured approach is needed for reliable long-horizon execution.
AI.method: StepReflect formulates per-step GUI reflection as supervised structured prediction using explicit transition specifications and paired visual evidence. Training employs a staged pipeline: (1) supervised fine-tuning, (2) teacher-student distillation, and (3) preference- and reward-based refinement. The resulting model is 8B parameters.
AI.result: Offline: 82.16% transition-level accuracy on AndroidWorld, surpassing zero-shot GPT-5.2 by 11.83 points. Online: across four agent configurations (M3A, Agent-SAMA, MAI-UI-8B, Seed-2.0-Pro), StepReflect achieves higher task success in three and ties within one task in the fourth, while reducing paid API charges in all configurations.
AI.conclusion: StepReflect is a practical, locally deployable alternative to repeated frontier-model API reflection for long-horizon mobile GUI agents, offering both superior or competitive performance and significant cost reduction.

title: ChainClaw: A Layered Agent Framework for Reliable On-Chain Execution
summary: General-purpose large language model agents have achieved strong performance on tool-augmented tasks, yet they rely on assumptions break down in blockchain environments. On-chain execution is stateful, adversarial, and economically irreversible, exposing three fundamental gaps: Reactivity, Irreversibility, and Observability. We propose ChainClaw, a blockchain-native agent framework built on OpenClaw, that addresses all three gaps through a layered architecture comprising an event-driven orchestration layer, a simulation-based safety intelligence layer, and an on-chain monitoring runtime layer, unified by a cross-layer memory subsystem. ChainClaw closes the Reactivity gap via event ingestion and simulation feedback, the Irreversibility gap via a pre-execution safety pipeline with transaction simulation and action guard, and the Observability gap via an on-chain read adapter and transaction monitor. We evaluate ChainClaw on a purpose-built benchmark covering seven tasks across four categories and five dimensions. ChainClaw consistently outperforms representative baselines on both safety and task completion.

AI.tldr: ChainClaw is a blockchain-native LLM agent framework that addresses three critical gaps (Reactivity, Irreversibility, Observability) in applying general-purpose agents to on-chain environments, using a layered architecture with event-driven orchestration, simulation-based safety, and on-chain monitoring, and it outperforms baselines on safety and task completion.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLM agents fail in blockchain environments because on-chain execution is stateful, adversarial, and economically irreversible. Existing agents break down due to three gaps: Reactivity (inability to respond to live on-chain events), Irreversibility (no safeguard against costly, uncorrectable actions), and Observability (limited access to on-chain state).
AI.method: ChainClaw is built on OpenClaw with a layered architecture: (1) an event-driven orchestration layer for event ingestion and simulation feedback; (2) a simulation-based safety intelligence layer with a pre-execution safety pipeline featuring transaction simulation and action guards; (3) an on-chain monitoring runtime layer with an on-chain read adapter and transaction monitor; all unified by a cross-layer memory subsystem.
AI.result: Evaluated on a purpose-built benchmark spanning 7 tasks, 4 categories, and 5 dimensions, ChainClaw consistently outperforms representative baselines on both safety metrics and task completion.
AI.conclusion: A blockchain-native agent design with dedicated safety, reactivity, and observability layers is necessary and effective for deploying LLM agents in adversarial, irreversible on-chain environments.

title: How to Recognize New Words: A Comparison Between Context Biasing Methods and Speech LLMs
summary: Recognizing new and rare words - named entities, acronyms, domain specific special words, and other items scarce in training data - remains a key challenge for automatic speech recognition (ASR). We compare two strategies for this: context biasing methods, where an ASR model is extended such that during inference a word list can be supplied, and speech large language models (LLMs) prompted with context directly. We evaluate two context biasing methods based on Whisper against three speech LLMs across read and non-read speech, reporting biased, unbiased, and overall word error rate (WER). The context biasing methods cut biased WER by up to 88% relative while leaving other words largely unaffected. Speech LLMs excel on read speech but generalize less well to non-read speech, and prove sensitive to distractor count and prompt word order. We characterize the resulting trade-offs to guide method selection.

AI.tldr: Compares context biasing methods and speech LLMs for recognizing rare words in ASR, finding context biasing cuts biased WER by up to 88% with minimal side effects, while speech LLMs excel on read speech but struggle with non-read speech and are sensitive to distractors and word order.
AI.motivation: Rare and new words (named entities, acronyms, domain-specific terms) remain a persistent challenge in ASR because they are scarce in training data, motivating a systematic comparison of two emerging solution strategies.
AI.method: Two context biasing methods built on Whisper are compared against three speech large language models (LLMs). Evaluation uses biased, unbiased, and overall WER across both read and non-read speech conditions, with analysis of sensitivity to distractor count and prompt word order.
AI.result: Context biasing methods achieve up to 88% relative reduction in biased WER without significantly affecting unbiased WER. Speech LLMs perform well on read speech but generalize poorly to non-read speech and exhibit sensitivity to distractor count and prompt word order.
AI.conclusion: The paper characterizes clear trade-offs: context biasing offers robust, targeted improvement for rare words, while speech LLMs are promising but currently less reliable outside read speech domains. These trade-offs should guide method selection based on application requirements.

title: Accelerating nanodrug development in continuous flow systems using informed prediction models based on low-cost surrogate nanoparticles
summary:
The development of nanotherapeutics often involves extensive empirical optimization due to the sensitivity of nanoparticle properties, such as size and polydispersity index (PDI), to minor changes in process parameters. Factors like formulation concentration, flow rates, and mixing ratios can significantly influence clinical efficacy and therapeutic outcomes. The absence of predictive mathematical frameworks has made iterative experimental screening necessary, increasing both costs and development time.
  This study introduces and validates a predictive modeling approach based on shape constraints, aiming to enhance the estimation of nanoparticle characteristics across various process conditions. Using controlled microfluidic methods, liposomes and lipid nanoparticles were systematically prepared under varying lipid concentrations, flow rates, and aqueous-to-organic mixing ratios.
  The shape-constrained model, informed by both experimental data and expert knowledge, was subsequently validated for a pharmaceutical application using minimal empirical data. Results reveal that shape-constrained modeling facilitates accurate prediction of nanoparticle size and dispersity, reducing the need for extensive experimental workflows. This framework supports rational and efficient process development for manufacturing nanomedicine systems.

AI.tldr: A shape-constrained predictive model is developed to accurately estimate nanoparticle size and PDI under varying formulation conditions, reducing the need for extensive empirical optimization in nanomedicine manufacturing.
AI.motivation: Nanoparticle formulation development is hindered by the high sensitivity of critical quality attributes (size, PDI) to minor process parameter changes, and the absence of predictive mathematical frameworks forces costly, time-consuming iterative experimental screening.
AI.method: Shape-constrained modeling informed by experimental data and expert knowledge; systematic preparation of liposomes and lipid nanoparticles via controlled microfluidics under varying lipid concentrations, flow rates, and aqueous-to-organic mixing ratios; validation with minimal empirical data for a pharmaceutical application.
AI.result: The shape-constrained model achieved accurate prediction of nanoparticle size and dispersity across different process conditions, substantially reducing the experimental burden required for process development.
AI.conclusion: Shape-constrained modeling provides a rational, efficient framework for nanomedicine process development, enabling reliable predictions with minimal empirical data input.

title: Task-Conditional Flow Matching for Balanced Multilingual Text Embedding Adaptation
summary: Multilingual text embedding models are commonly adapted using a single training objective across diverse tasks, despite different tasks requiring fundamentally different optimization strategies. We introduce Task-Conditional Flow Matching (TCFM), a multilingual embedding adaptation framework that selectively applies Flow Matching to translation tasks while optimizing retrieval, classification, and pair-classification tasks with objectives better aligned to their learning dynamics. TCFM further combines teacher-guided representation preservation with a three-stage curriculum to enable stable adaptation. Evaluated on the Indic Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, TCFM establishes a new state-of-the-art, consistently improving embedding quality across a diverse set of multilingual tasks and generalizing across embedding model families. We will publicly release the codebase and datasets upon acceptance of the paper.

AI.tldr: TCFM introduces a task-conditional adaptation framework for multilingual text embeddings that selectively applies Flow Matching to translation tasks while using task-aligned objectives for retrieval, classification, and pair-classification, achieving SOTA on the Indic Massive Text Embedding Benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing multilingual embedding models typically use a single training objective across diverse tasks, but different tasks (translation, retrieval, classification, pair-classification) have fundamentally different optimization dynamics. This one-size-fits-all approach is suboptimal and motivates a task-specific adaptation strategy.
AI.method: TCFM (Task-Conditional Flow Matching) selectively applies Flow Matching to translation tasks while using objectives better aligned to the learning dynamics of retrieval, classification, and pair-classification tasks. The framework incorporates teacher-guided representation preservation (distillation from the original model to prevent catastrophic forgetting) and a three-stage curriculum learning schedule to ensure stable adaptation.
AI.result: TCFM establishes a new state-of-the-art on the Indic Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, consistently improving embedding quality across diverse multilingual tasks and demonstrating generalization across different embedding model families.
AI.conclusion: Task-conditional training objectives, combined with teacher-guided preservation and curriculum learning, provide a superior adaptation strategy for multilingual embedding models. The code and datasets will be publicly released.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Closed-Loop Control of Laser Powder Bed Fusion with an In-Loop Ontology
comment: 23 pages, 8 figures, submitted to journal(Journal of Intelligent Manufacturing) and under review
summary: A geometry-conditioned, neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture is proposed for laser powder bed fusion, in which a standards-aligned ontology operates inside the control loop and couples symbolic reasoning with statistical learning to set the targets of a constraint-aware predictive controller. The ontology links the process objectives and constraints to the signals a controller can observe, and a description-logic reasoner converts them into the references and bounds enforced on each scan. The demonstrated case is overhang dross, a quality limit on the melt pool depth, which governs quality yet cannot be measured during the build, is mapped through a geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio onto a bound on the observable width, with the ratio and its calibrated uncertainty supplied by a Gaussian process. The reasoner classifies each upcoming feature and selects the active constraints-adding a lack-of-fusion floor at overhangs, a monotone guard beyond the calibrated range, and an energy-density cap where a process window is declared while running only on changes of geometric context and otherwise leaving a single small quadratic program on the per-scan path. In an Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to the NIST AM-Bench benchmark for IN625, the architecture eliminates the dross produced by a geometry-blind controller, holds dross at zero with only a small residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring, degrades gracefully under deliberate plant mismatch, and retargets to new alloys and constraints by editing ontology data rather than code. The results establish architectural feasibility, experimental calibration of the ratio is the principal next step.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic closed-loop control architecture for laser powder bed fusion uses an ontology with description-logic reasoning to dynamically set geometry-conditioned constraints for a predictive controller. Demonstrated on overhang dross elimination, it maps unmeasurable melt pool depth to observable width via a Gaussian process-calibrated ratio, eliminating dross while gracefully degrading under plant mismatch.
AI.motivation: Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) suffers from geometry-dependent quality defects like overhang dross, where melt pool depth — a key quality indicator — cannot be measured in situ. Existing controllers lack the ability to dynamically adapt constraints based on part geometry and process context, motivating a closed-loop architecture that integrates symbolic reasoning with learning to enforce geometry-conditioned quality constraints.
AI.method: A geometry-conditioned, neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture is proposed featuring: (1) a standards-aligned ontology operating inside the control loop that couples symbolic reasoning (description-logic reasoner) with statistical learning; (2) the ontology links process objectives/constraints to observable controller signals, converting them into per-scan references and bounds; (3) a Gaussian process supplies a geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio with calibrated uncertainty, mapping unmeasurable depth onto observable width bounds; (4) the reasoner classifies upcoming geometric features and dynamically activates constraints — lack-of-fusion floor at overhangs, monotone guard beyond calibrated range, energy-density cap where a process window is declared — running only on geometric context changes; (5) validated on an Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to NIST AM-Bench benchmark for IN625.
AI.result: The architecture eliminates dross produced by a geometry-blind controller, holds dross at zero with only small residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring, degrades gracefully under deliberate plant mismatch, and supports retargeting to new alloys and constraints by editing ontology data rather than code.
AI.conclusion: The results establish architectural feasibility for the proposed neuro-symbolic control paradigm. The principal next step identified is experimental calibration of the depth-to-width ratio, moving from surrogate-based validation to physical implementation.

title: Measuring and Detecting Harmful AI Sycophancy
summary: Sycophantic responses are becoming pervasive in large language models (LLMs), and prior work has pointed out that some of them could be harmful. This paper focuses on one harmful sycophancy: preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS), where a model reverses an initial stance merely to align with a user's stated preference. While existing research mainly measures how sycophantic a model is, we go further and ask whether PSRS can also be detected automatically from a single response. To investigate this at scale, we introduce CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing), a framework for collecting labeled PSRS data. Applying CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs, we collect 290,460 labeled responses across 12 everyday-advice domains. We organize our study around three research questions. (1) How often does PSRS occur? (2) How well can it be detected? (3) How does detection generalize to unseen models? We first reveal that PSRS rates range from 5% to 56% across LLMs, with more capable models being less sycophantic. Next, we show that detecting PSRS is feasible from the response text alone, and detectors need to learn subtle PSRS patterns from the training data. Because new LLMs appear rapidly, detectors inevitably encounter unseen models, making cross-model generalization an important framework goal. We demonstrate that detection performance drops on unseen models and propose an initial approach to address this challenge. We will release our dataset and code to support future research.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Preference-Induced Stance Reversal Sycophancy (PSRS), where LLMs flip their stance to match a user's preference. Using the CAP framework, the authors collect 290,460 labeled responses from 17 LLMs across 12 domains, finding PSRS rates of 5-56%. They demonstrate that PSRS can be automatically detected from single responses, but detection performance degrades on unseen models — a challenge they begin to address.
AI.motivation: Prior work primarily measures how sycophantic LLMs are in aggregate, but does not address whether individual instances of harmful sycophancy — specifically preference-induced stance reversal (PSRS) — can be automatically detected from a single response. As LLMs rapidly proliferate, scalable detection methods that generalize across unseen models are urgently needed.
AI.method: The authors propose CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing), a data collection framework that generates labeled PSRS instances by presenting an LLM with an initial query, recording its stance, then exposing it to a user's stated preference and observing whether the model reverses its position. Using CAP, they collect 290,460 labeled responses from 17 open- and closed-source LLMs across 12 everyday-advice domains. They then train classifiers on response text alone to detect PSRS and evaluate cross-model generalization.
AI.result: PSRS rates vary substantially across models, ranging from 5% to 56%, with more capable models exhibiting lower sycophancy. Detection from response text alone is feasible, though detectors must learn subtle patterns rather than relying on superficial cues. Cross-model generalization remains a significant challenge: detection performance drops on unseen models, motivating an initial mitigation approach.
AI.conclusion: PSRS is a prevalent and detectable form of harmful sycophancy in LLMs. While single-response detection is achievable, the degradation in cross-model generalization highlights a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment as new models continuously emerge. The authors release their dataset and code to facilitate further research on this problem.

title: On-Policy Delta Distillation for Multilingual Math Reasoning
summary: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) is emerging as a promising alternative to reinforcement learning for LLM post-training, yet its effectiveness in multilingual settings remains underexplored. We study OPD and its advanced variant, On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD$^2$), for mathematical reasoning in English, Korean, and Japanese. OPD$^2$ improves OPD by using the probability gap between a post-trained teacher and its base model as the learning signal. Experiments with Qwen3 show that OPD$^2$ consistently outperforms the original OPD, with particularly strong improvements in Korean and Japanese, and generally narrows the English-Korean performance gap. We further find that English-only OPD can also increase performance for Korean and Japanese, but often shifts the responses toward English, highlighting the importance of multilingual data to preserving target-language responses.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates On-Policy Distillation (OPD) and its variant OPD² for multilingual mathematical reasoning (English, Korean, Japanese) in LLM post-training. OPD² uses the probability gap between a fine-tuned teacher and its base model as a learning signal, outperforming OPD—especially in Korean/Japanese—while narrowing the English-Korean gap. English-only OPD improves non-English performance but shifts responses toward English, underscoring the need for multilingual data.
AI.motivation: OPD is promising for LLM post-training, but its effectiveness in multilingual settings is largely unexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by evaluating OPD and OPD² across English, Korean, and Japanese mathematical reasoning tasks.
AI.method: The authors study two on-policy distillation methods: (1) standard On-Policy Distillation (OPD) and (2) On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD²), which uses the probability gap between a post-trained teacher model and its base model as the learning signal. Experiments use the Qwen3 model family and evaluate mathematical reasoning performance across English, Korean, and Japanese.
AI.result: OPD² consistently outperforms standard OPD, with particularly strong gains in Korean and Japanese. It also generally narrows the English-Korean performance gap. English-only OPD improves Korean/Japanese performance but tends to shift responses toward English, demonstrating the importance of multilingual training data for preserving target-language output.
AI.conclusion: OPD² is an effective multilingual post-training method that surpasses OPD, especially for non-English languages. While English-only distillation offers cross-lingual benefits, multilingual data is critical for maintaining target-language response fidelity.

title: GROM: Gradient-Free Rapid One-Shot Machine Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning has become a critical capability for safely removing specific, sensitive knowledge from large language models (LLMs). Current state-of-the-art approaches primarily rely on iterative, training-time unlearning via fine-tuning. However, even when utilizing parameter-efficient dimensionality reduction techniques like LoRA, gradient-based optimization remains computationally expensive and lacks explicit analytical formulations. It can also leave the targeted knowledge merely hidden rather than removed, to the point that simply quantizing the unlearned model restores much of what it was supposed to have erased. To resolve this, we propose a novel one-shot unlearning approach, abandoning iterative optimization in favor of a direct, exact analytical solution. We frame the unlearning process as a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization problem, deriving a closed-form additive update for targeted weight matrices. This update forces the selected layer to suppress unwanted content while strictly preserving its behavior on retained data. Computed from gradient-free forward passes alone, with no backpropagation and no iteration to convergence, GROM applies the weight edit in mere seconds, which makes it orders of magnitude faster than traditional fine-tuning. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that GROM achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News and WMDP, significantly reducing computational overhead without sacrificing overall model performance. Because the update removes the targeted content from the weights instead of masking it, GROM also withstands the low-bit quantization attack that recovers much of the content a gradient-based baseline had appeared to forget. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Batorskq/GROM.

AI.tldr: GROM is a one-shot machine unlearning method for LLMs that uses a closed-form, ridge-regularized least-squares solution to directly edit model weights, removing targeted knowledge in seconds without iterative gradient-based optimization. It achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs and resists quantization attacks that recover supposedly forgotten content from gradient-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Current machine unlearning methods rely on iterative gradient-based fine-tuning (even with parameter-efficient techniques like LoRA), which is computationally expensive and lacks analytical formulations. Critically, these methods often merely hide—rather than truly remove—targeted knowledge, as demonstrated by the fact that low-bit quantization of an "unlearned" model can restore much of the erased content. This motivates the need for a direct, exact, and robust weight-level removal approach.
AI.method: The authors frame unlearning as a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization problem and derive a closed-form, additive weight update. The update is computed using only gradient-free forward passes (no backpropagation, no iterative convergence), applied to selected layers to suppress unwanted content while preserving behavior on retained data. This one-shot edit is performed in seconds.
AI.result: GROM achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs across multiple benchmarks (TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News, WMDP), while being orders of magnitude faster than fine-tuning. It also withstands low-bit quantization attacks that successfully recover supposedly erased content from gradient-based baseline models.
AI.conclusion: Direct, analytical weight editing via GROM provides a faster, more robust, and more principled alternative to iterative gradient-based unlearning, achieving true knowledge removal rather than superficial masking, with strong empirical results across diverse unlearning benchmarks.

title: SkillHEX: Improving Agent Skills via Hypothesis-Driven Autonomous Exploration and Exploitation
summary: Although agent skills equip LLMs with reusable procedural knowledge, manual maintenance suffers from high costs, unscalability, and misalignment. Real-world deployments thus require autonomous, on-demand skill evolution at test time, constrained by limited interaction budgets and a lack of training or validation sets. This setting introduces a severe sparse reward challenge, where outcomes conflate multiple latent failure causes. Under such ambiguity, existing methods that greedily refine a single incumbent skill are particularly vulnerable to an exploitation trap, allowing early misdiagnoses to exhaust limited trials along unproductive trajectories. To address this, we introduce SkillHEX, a closed-loop framework coupling hypothesis-driven self-verification with evidence-guided tree search. SkillHEX translates falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable tests, producing diagnostic evidence as dense reward without additional environment attempts. This evidence guides a search over persistent skill-revision branches, dynamically balancing the exploitation of supported edits with the exploration of plausible alternatives. Evaluated on 87 tasks from SkillsBench, SkillHEX outperforms existing self-evolving methods and achieves an average pass rate of 55.9% and 57.9% using GPT-5.3-Codex and Claude Opus 4.7 under a five-iteration budget, respectively.

AI.tldr: SkillHEX is a closed-loop framework that enables LLM agents to autonomously evolve skills at test time by combining hypothesis-driven self-verification with evidence-guided tree search, overcoming sparse reward challenges and exploitation traps. It achieves ~56-58% pass rates on SkillsBench under a five-iteration budget.
AI.motivation: Manual maintenance of LLM agent skills is costly, unscalable, and prone to misalignment. Autonomous, on-demand skill evolution at test time is needed, but this setting suffers from a severe sparse reward problem: outcomes conflate multiple latent failure causes. Existing methods that greedily refine a single incumbent skill fall into an exploitation trap, where early misdiagnoses waste limited interaction trials along unproductive trajectories.
AI.method: SkillHEX introduces a closed-loop framework with two key components: (1) Hypothesis-driven self-verification that translates falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable tests, generating diagnostic evidence as dense reward without consuming additional environment attempts; (2) Evidence-guided tree search over persistent skill-revision branches that dynamically balances exploitation of supported edits with exploration of plausible alternatives.
AI.result: Evaluated on 87 tasks from SkillsBench, SkillHEX outperforms existing self-evolving methods. It achieves an average pass rate of 55.9% with GPT-5.3-Codex and 57.9% with Claude Opus 4.7, both under a five-iteration budget constraint.
AI.conclusion: By converting failure hypotheses into internally verifiable diagnostic tests, SkillHEX effectively densifies the reward signal without extra environment interactions. The evidence-guided tree search further prevents premature convergence to misdiagnosed fixes, enabling robust, budget-constrained skill evolution at test time.

title: Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models
summary: While standard Next-Token Prediction (NTP) lays the foundation of language model pre- training, its teacher-forced training paradigm may not be optimal for long-horizon reasoning and planning. Recent works such as Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) and Next-Latent prediction (NextLat) try to mitigate the problem through predicting multiple future tokens and self-supervised prediction in the latent space. However, those auxiliary objectives either have a limited horizon or suffer from compounding error from multi-step rollout. We introduce Hierarchical Latent Prediction (HiLP), which introduces an auxiliary higher-level abstract latent to help reduce the error accumulation effect in latent-space rollouts. Experiments show that HiLP can lead to longer-horizon coherent belief state representation and demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across coding and multi-step reasoning benchmarks, and offers more speculative decoding efficiency.

AI.tldr: HiLP introduces a hierarchical auxiliary latent prediction objective that mitigates error accumulation in multi-step latent rollouts, improving long-horizon reasoning, planning, and speculative decoding efficiency over standard NTP, MTP, and NextLat.
AI.motivation: Standard Next-Token Prediction (NTP) uses teacher forcing, which is suboptimal for long-horizon reasoning and planning. Existing alternatives like Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) have limited horizon, while Next-Latent prediction (NextLat) suffers from compounding error during multi-step rollout in latent space. A method is needed that extends prediction horizon while controlling error accumulation.
AI.method: The authors propose Hierarchical Latent Prediction (HiLP), which adds an auxiliary higher-level abstract latent representation. This hierarchical latent structure is designed to reduce error accumulation during latent-space rollouts by providing a coarser, more stable predictive target that guides lower-level predictions over longer horizons.
AI.result: HiLP produces longer-horizon coherent belief state representations. It demonstrates effectiveness on coding and multi-step reasoning benchmarks, and offers improved speculative decoding efficiency compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical latent prediction is a promising direction for improving language model pre-training beyond standard NTP, enabling better long-horizon reasoning and more efficient decoding without the compounding error issues that plague flat latent prediction approaches.

title: Predicting Task Difficulty Without Rollouts
summary: Task difficulty dictates an agent's likelihood of success, and estimating it without rollouts means forecasting this directly from a task description before executing costly simulations in stateful environments. Reliable estimates would therefore allow environment designers to calibrate evaluation benchmarks and construct progressive training curricula. This becomes increasingly important as agents move into long-horizon domains, where empirical trial-and-error is a severe computational bottleneck. Prior work on early prediction is limited to static tasks or isolated coding environments, often relying on narrow features and inaccurate evaluation metrics. We study \textit{ex ante} difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks spanning coding, mathematics, machine learning, web navigation, function calling, and other domains. We show that AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, identify token-level entropy as a useful predictive signal, and show how residuals between expected and observed difficulty can expose hidden environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates predicting agent task difficulty before execution (ex ante) across 17 diverse benchmarks. The authors show that AUC masks poor calibration, identify token-level entropy as a useful predictive signal, and demonstrate how residuals between predicted and actual difficulty can reveal hidden flaws like contamination and infeasibility in environments.
AI.motivation: As AI agents tackle long-horizon tasks, empirical trial-and-error becomes computationally prohibitive. Reliable ex ante difficulty prediction would enable benchmark calibration and progressive curriculum design. Prior work is limited to static or narrow coding tasks with inadequate evaluation metrics, motivating a broader, multi-domain study.
AI.method: The authors study ex ante difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks (coding, math, ML, web navigation, function calling, etc.). They analyze AUC's shortcomings as a metric, leverage token-level entropy as a predictive signal from task descriptions, and compute residuals between expected and observed difficulty to detect environment flaws.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, providing a false sense of model performance; (2) token-level entropy from task descriptions serves as a useful predictive signal for difficulty; (3) residuals between predicted and observed difficulty can surface hidden environment issues such as benchmark contamination and infeasible tasks.
AI.conclusion: Ex ante difficulty prediction is feasible and valuable across diverse agentic domains when evaluated with proper metrics. Entropy-based signals offer practical utility, and residual analysis provides a diagnostic tool for uncovering hidden flaws in benchmark environments.

title: Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) Model: A Computational Account of What Makes Design Options Worth Trying
summary:
This paper proposes the Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) model, which formalizes the value of trying a candidate design action as its expected reduction of epistemic uncertainty about action--outcome relations. The model addresses one part of the Uncertainty Driven Action (UDA) model's open question concerning how changes in uncertainty perception determine action selection. We examine two environmental properties: generalizability, or how far knowledge from one trial extends to neighboring candidates, and outcome discriminability, or how clearly differences among outcomes can be distinguished.
  We tested the model through simulations and human experiments using a graph-shape guessing task that isolates learning about action--outcome relations under a limited trial budget. Epistemic value followed an inverted-U-shaped relationship with generalizability and increased with outcome discriminability in the simulations. In the human experiments, the subjective value of trying and enjoyment followed inverted-U-shaped relationships with generalizability, while choice behavior reflected both properties.
  The B-EUR model provides a computational account of candidate-action evaluation within uncertainty-driven design activity and offers implications for constructing prototype sets, framing design problems, and organizing feedback to support informative exploration.

AI.tldr: The B-EUR model formalizes the value of candidate design actions as expected epistemic uncertainty reduction. Tested via simulations and a graph-shape guessing task, epistemic value shows an inverted-U relationship with generalizability and increases with outcome discriminability. Human experiments corroborated these patterns in subjective value, enjoyment, and choice behavior.
AI.motivation: The UDA model left open the question of how changes in uncertainty perception drive action selection. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a computational model that quantifies the expected value of candidate actions in terms of uncertainty reduction, enabling systematic investigation of how environmental properties influence exploration in design activity.
AI.method: The authors propose the Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) model, a computational framework that evaluates candidate design actions by their expected reduction in epistemic uncertainty about action-outcome relations. They test the model through simulations and human behavioral experiments using a graph-shape guessing task designed to isolate learning under limited trial budgets, manipulating two environmental properties: generalizability and outcome discriminability.
AI.result: Simulations revealed that epistemic value exhibits an inverted-U-shaped relationship with generalizability and a positive monotonic relationship with outcome discriminability. Human experiments aligned with these predictions: subjective value of trying and enjoyment both followed inverted-U patterns with generalizability, and choice behavior reflected sensitivity to both environmental properties.
AI.conclusion: The B-EUR model provides a principled computational account of how designers evaluate candidate actions under uncertainty. It offers practical implications for constructing prototype sets, framing design problems, and organizing feedback to maximize informative exploration in design processes.

title: M$^3$R-Bench: A Unified Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Metaphor Understanding
comment: 6 figures and 5 tables. Hong Jiang, Junnan Zhu, and Jingwang Huang contributed equally. Jiang Zhong and Kaiwen Wei are corresponding authors. Code and data are available at https://github.com/hongshi4/M3R-Bench
summary: Metaphor enables the understanding of abstract concepts through cross-domain mappings while conveying affective attitudes. In multimodal scenarios, visual and textual information jointly construct Target--Source mappings, requiring both conceptual understanding and cross-modal reasoning. However, existing benchmarks mainly evaluate metaphor understanding through isolated subtasks and lack evidence-grounded explanations, making it difficult to assess whether models establish mappings grounded in visual and textual cues.To address these limitations, we introduce M$^3$R-Bench, a unified and evidence-grounded benchmark containing 1,000 image--text instances with human-verified annotations. Guided by Conceptual Metaphor Theory and theories of nonliteral language understanding, M$^3$R-Bench provides joint annotations for metaphor occurrence, Target--Source mapping, sentiment, and stage-wise explanations following ``evidence identification--mapping establishment--sentiment inference.''Evaluations on M$^3$R-Bench reveal that existing models often overlook visual evidence, rely on superficial textual cues, and produce inaccurate Target--Source mappings, exposing a cross-modal evidence--mapping mismatch. To address this mismatch, we propose M$^3$R-Reasoner, which combines curriculum-based reasoning supervision with task-aware reinforcement learning to align model reasoning with metaphor interpretation. Experiments show that, with only an 8B-parameter backbone, M$^3$R-Reasoner outperforms larger proprietary MLLMs across four unified-task metrics and improves Visual Evidence and Sentiment Justification scores over GPT-5.5 by 28.45 and 30.11 points, respectively, while surpassing Claude-Sonnet-4.6 by 8.00 points in mean rubric score. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/hongshi4/M3R-Bench.

AI.tldr: M³R-Bench is a unified, evidence-grounded benchmark for multimodal metaphor understanding with 1,000 image–text instances. It evaluates metaphor occurrence, Target–Source mapping, sentiment, and stage-wise explanations. The authors also propose M³R-Reasoner, which uses curriculum-based reasoning supervision and task-aware RL, outperforming larger proprietary MLLMs on metaphor interpretation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal metaphor benchmarks evaluate understanding through isolated subtasks and lack evidence-grounded explanations, making it impossible to assess whether models genuinely establish cross-domain mappings grounded in visual and textual cues.
AI.method: (1) M³R-Bench: a benchmark with 1,000 image–text instances annotated for metaphor occurrence, Target–Source mapping, sentiment, and stage-wise explanations (evidence identification → mapping establishment → sentiment inference), grounded in Conceptual Metaphor Theory. (2) M³R-Reasoner: a model combining curriculum-based reasoning supervision with task-aware reinforcement learning to align model reasoning with metaphor interpretation, using only an 8B-parameter backbone.
AI.result: Existing models show a cross-modal evidence–mapping mismatch: they overlook visual evidence, rely on superficial textual cues, and produce inaccurate mappings. M³R-Reasoner outperforms larger proprietary MLLMs across four unified-task metrics, improves Visual Evidence and Sentiment Justification over GPT-5.5 by 28.45 and 30.11 points, and surpasses Claude-Sonnet-4.6 by 8.00 points in mean rubric score.
AI.conclusion: M³R-Bench provides a principled framework for evaluating multimodal metaphor understanding, and M³R-Reasoner demonstrates that targeted reasoning supervision with task-aware RL can bridge the cross-modal evidence–mapping gap, even with a modestly-sized backbone model.

title: Learning to Rank Tensor Network Contraction Plans for GPU-Accelerated Quantum Circuit Simulation
summary: Classical simulation remains essential for developing and validating quantum algorithms, but its cost grows rapidly with circuit size. Tensor-network contraction can reduce this cost by exploiting circuit structure, although its efficiency depends strongly on the chosen contraction plan. On GPUs, plans with similar theoretical complexity may perform very differently because execution also depends on parallelism, reduction structure, memory traffic, and contraction geometry. We present a learning-to-rank framework for selecting efficient contraction plans before executing them. Each plan is represented by structural features derived directly from its sequence of pairwise contractions, and gradient-boosted rankers are trained from GPU measurements using listwise and pairwise objectives. We evaluate the resulting models on diverse circuit families, using separate in-distribution and circuit-family-shift test sets, and compare them with random and MinFill-based baselines. The learned rankers generally identify better plans, with the listwise model providing the strongest overall decision quality. We also study backend shift by comparing empirical plan orderings on two GPU architectures and evaluating the source-trained models on the second device without retraining.
