The rankings remain substantially, though not perfectly, stable across GPUs, and the models retain useful decision quality. These results support Learning to Rank as a practical way to reduce contraction-plan search, while showing that performance remains partly backend dependent.

AI.tldr: A learning-to-rank framework using gradient-boosted models and structural features from pairwise contraction sequences is proposed to select efficient tensor-network contraction plans for quantum circuit simulation on GPUs, outperforming random and MinFill baselines, with demonstrated cross-GPU ranking stability.
AI.motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits via tensor-network contraction is computationally expensive. Contraction plans with similar theoretical complexity can exhibit drastically different GPU performance due to parallelism, reduction structure, memory traffic, and contraction geometry. Existing heuristics (e.g., MinFill) do not directly model actual execution cost, motivating a data-driven approach to plan selection.
AI.method: Each contraction plan is represented by structural features extracted from its sequence of pairwise contractions. Gradient-boosted rankers (LambdaMART-style) are trained using listwise and pairwise learning-to-rank objectives on GPU-measured execution times. Evaluation uses diverse circuit families with both in-distribution and circuit-family-shift test sets, plus a backend-shift study where models trained on one GPU architecture are tested on another without retraining.
AI.result: Learned rankers consistently outperform random and MinFill baselines. The listwise model yields the strongest overall decision quality. Cross-GPU evaluation shows rankings remain substantially stable across architectures, and source-trained models retain useful decision quality on the second device, though performance is partly backend-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Learning to Rank is a practical and effective method for reducing contraction-plan search cost in GPU-based tensor-network simulation. While plan rankings are largely transferable across GPU architectures, some backend dependence persists, suggesting retraining or adaptation may be beneficial for optimal cross-device deployment.

title: Refining Over Resampling: Test-Time Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning
summary: Test-time scaling improves LLM reasoning by using additional inference compute, but wider sampling alone can suffer from diminishing returns: new rollouts often repeat existing answer patterns instead of adding useful reasoning diversity. Verifier-based selection offers an alternative, but its performance depends on the calibration of an external reward model. We propose a verifier-free breadth--depth refinement framework that uses test-time compute to both explore and improve candidate solutions. The method samples multiple independent reasoning rollouts, refines each rollout through iterative self-critique and self-correction, and aggregates the refined answers by majority voting. Breadth preserves diverse initial attempts, while depth repairs local reasoning errors before aggregation. Across AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500, our method consistently improves over greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based best-of-$N$, beam search, and lookahead decoding across multiple open-weight models. For instance, with Qwen2.5-1.5B, accuracy increases from the strongest verifier-based baseline to $58.0\%$ on MATH500, and from $25.0\%$ to $32.5\%$ on AMC. These results show that test-time compute can be more effective when used to refine sampled trajectories rather than only to sample more candidates or rely on verifier-guided selection.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a verifier-free breadth-depth refinement framework that first samples diverse reasoning rollouts (breadth), then iteratively self-corrects each rollout (depth), and finally aggregates via majority voting. This outperforms greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based best-of-N, beam search, and lookahead decoding across multiple benchmarks and open-weight models.
AI.motivation: Test-time scaling via wider sampling suffers from diminishing returns because new rollouts tend to repeat existing answer patterns rather than introducing reasoning diversity. Verifier-based selection depends critically on the calibration quality of an external reward model. The authors seek a method that uses test-time compute more effectively — by refining sampled trajectories rather than merely sampling more or relying on verifier-guided selection.
AI.method: A verifier-free breadth-depth refinement framework: (1) Breadth: sample multiple independent reasoning rollouts to preserve diverse initial attempts; (2) Depth: refine each rollout through iterative self-critique and self-correction to repair local reasoning errors; (3) Aggregation: combine the refined answers via majority voting. No external verifier or reward model is required.
AI.result: The method consistently improves over greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based best-of-N, beam search, and lookahead decoding across AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500. With Qwen2.5-1.5B, accuracy rises from the strongest verifier-based baseline to 58.0% on MATH500 and from 25.0% to 32.5% on AMC.
AI.conclusion: Test-time compute is more effective when allocated to refining sampled trajectories (via iterative self-correction) rather than exclusively to sampling more candidates or relying on verifier-guided selection. The breadth-depth framework demonstrates a practical, verifier-free path to improved LLM reasoning.

title: Decomposed Entailment for Factuality Checking and Hallucination Detection
summary: The reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) is often compromised by factual inconsistencies, including hallucinations---cases where generated content is not supported by the underlying source. We present HallDetect, a lightweight, reference-free, and black-box framework for hallucination detection that we evaluate not only on summarization but across a broader range of source-grounded generation settings. HallDetect builds on decomposition-based factuality evaluation: generated content is decomposed into atomic claims, each verified by a compact encoder-based entailment model through a contrastive formulation over a multi-scale library of source chunks, and aggregated with an asymmetric score in which a single confidently contradicted claim flags the response. Under a controlled protocol in which all methods share the same 4-bit quantized backbones and consumer-grade hardware budget, HallDetect outperforms comparably resourced generative and embedding-based baselines on three of four benchmarks while remaining stable across backbone families, and yields a claim-to-span audit trail that localizes each error.

AI.tldr: HallDetect is a lightweight, reference-free, black-box hallucination detection framework that decomposes generated text into atomic claims, verifies each against multi-scale source chunks using a contrastive encoder-based entailment model, and flags responses via an asymmetric aggregation score where a single confidently contradicted claim triggers a positive detection.
AI.motivation: Hallucinations — factually inconsistent content unsupported by source material — compromise LLM reliability. Existing detection methods are often computationally expensive, require white-box access, or are narrowly evaluated only on summarization. There is a need for a lightweight, reference-free, black-box method that generalizes across diverse source-grounded generation tasks.
AI.method: HallDetect uses a three-stage pipeline: (1) decomposition of generated text into atomic claims, (2) verification of each claim against a multi-scale library of source chunks using a compact encoder-based entailment model with a contrastive formulation, and (3) asymmetric score aggregation where a single high-confidence contradiction classifies the entire response as hallucinated. The system operates under a controlled 4-bit quantized, consumer-grade hardware budget.
AI.result: Under a controlled protocol with 4-bit quantized backbones and consumer hardware, HallDetect outperforms comparably resourced generative and embedding-based baselines on three of four benchmarks, remains stable across different backbone families, and provides a claim-to-span audit trail for error localization.
AI.conclusion: HallDetect demonstrates that a decomposition-based, contrastive entailment approach with asymmetric scoring is an effective, resource-efficient, and interpretable solution for hallucination detection across diverse source-grounded generation tasks, offering both strong performance and practical deployability.

title: Evidential Rule Learning for Interpretable Classification with Abstention
summary: Interpretable classification often requires more than accurate predictions for real-life deployment: models should be transparent about the evidence behind their decisions and abstain when they cannot decide reliably. We introduce Fast Evidential Rule Learning (FERL), a method that learns interpretable, accurate fuzzy rule models whose outputs are evidential. Unlike post-hoc calibration, FERL's belief, plausibility, and abstention capabilities arise directly from the fuzzy memberships in a single deterministic pass, with no auxiliary head, held-out set, or repeated inference. Our theoretical analysis further shows that FERL is Lipschitz stable, which means that its evidential outputs vary smoothly with the input. Against state-of-the-art rule learners, FERL is statistically significantly more accurate across a 30 tabular-dataset benchmark ($+2.6\%$ average accuracy over the second best). Its native set predictions attain the best utility-discounted accuracy among credal classifiers ($u_{65}/u_{80}=0.80/0.83$ vs.\ $0.79/0.80$ for the naive credal classifier), at higher set coverage ($0.92$ vs.\ $\le0.82$). FERL also matches dedicated out-of-distribution detectors on tabular near-OOD detection ($77.7$ vs.\ $77.4$ AUROC for the strongest baseline). Under detector-class-disjoint concept-bottleneck evaluation, its it is within $2.3$ AUROC points of the strongest dedicated detector on both CUB and AwA2, while attaining the best AwA2 AUPR-Out ($68.3$) and novel-class rejection ($57.2$), while being able to name which attributes are anomalous.

AI.tldr: FERL learns interpretable fuzzy rule models with built-in evidential outputs (belief, plausibility, abstention) in a single deterministic pass, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy, reliable set predictions, and competitive out-of-distribution detection.
AI.motivation: Interpretable classifiers for real-world deployment need to not only predict accurately but also provide transparent evidence for decisions and reliably abstain when uncertain. Existing methods often rely on post-hoc calibration, auxiliary components, or multiple inference passes, which undermines both efficiency and interpretability.
AI.method: FERL is a fuzzy rule learning method that directly produces evidential outputs (belief, plausibility, abstention) from fuzzy memberships in a single deterministic forward pass, without needing an auxiliary head, held-out calibration set, or repeated inference. It is theoretically proven to be Lipschitz stable, ensuring smooth variation of evidential outputs with input changes.
AI.result: FERL outperforms state-of-the-art rule learners by +2.6% average accuracy on 30 tabular datasets. It achieves best utility-discounted accuracy among credal classifiers (u65/u80 = 0.80/0.83), higher set coverage (0.92 vs. ≤0.82), matches dedicated OOD detectors on tabular near-OOD (77.7 AUROC), and is within 2.3 AUROC points of the strongest detector on CUB and AwA2 benchmarks while achieving best AUPR-Out (68.3) and novel-class rejection (57.2) on AwA2.
AI.conclusion: FERL demonstrates that native evidential reasoning can be integrated directly into interpretable fuzzy rule models without sacrificing accuracy or requiring post-hoc components, offering a unified, stable, and transparent solution for reliable classification with abstention and anomaly detection.

title: A Unified Framework for Trajectory Prediction with Explicit Planning and Reaction Decomposition
summary: Trajectory prediction has shifted toward structured formulations with explicit social modeling. However, existing methods inadequately distinguish the functional roles of social influence in trajectory planning. Observing that agents typically form motion plans by anticipating others' future behaviors before making local reactive adjustments, we identify social interactions as playing staged roles, namely planning precedes reaction. We propose INTraJ, a unified framework that decomposes social influence into two stages: a planning stage constructs reference trajectories using future social information, and a reaction stage recovers local adjustments from the residual between full-context prediction and the reference. INTraJ supports both multi-target and single-target paradigms. Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks, including Argoverse 2, Argoverse 2-ped, ETH/UCY, and SDD, demonstrate consistent improvements, particularly in FDE and long-horizon consistency, with state-of-the-art performance achieved in several settings. INTraJ reframes trajectory prediction as a planning-driven two-stage process, validating that staged social modeling is critical for stable predictions. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/11isnotavailable/INTraJ.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes INTraJ, a two-stage trajectory prediction framework that decomposes social influence into a planning stage (anticipating future behaviors to construct reference trajectories) and a reaction stage (recovering local adjustments from residuals), achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing trajectory prediction methods fail to distinguish the functional roles of social influence. The authors observe that agents form motion plans by first anticipating others' future behaviors (planning) and then making local reactive adjustments (reaction). Prior methods conflate these two distinct stages, leading to suboptimal social modeling.
AI.method: INTraJ is a unified framework that explicitly decomposes social interaction into two stages: (1) a planning stage that uses future social information to construct reference trajectories, and (2) a reaction stage that recovers local adjustments from the residual between full-context prediction and the reference. The framework supports both multi-target and single-target prediction paradigms.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks — Argoverse 2, Argoverse 2-ped, ETH/UCY, and SDD — demonstrate consistent improvements, particularly in Final Displacement Error (FDE) and long-horizon consistency. State-of-the-art performance is achieved in several settings.
AI.conclusion: INTraJ reframes trajectory prediction as a planning-driven two-stage process, validating that explicitly staging social modeling into planning and reaction phases is critical for achieving stable and accurate predictions. The code is publicly released.

title: MoCA: Implicit Social Context Analysis
summary: Human social communication, such as affection and intent, is often conveyed in highly implicit ways, where underlying meanings are expressed through indirect, socially and culturally grounded signals rather than explicit statements. Such implicit social contexts are pervasive in real-world interactions, yet there remains a lack of a formal and systematic framework for studying them. In this paper, we introduce Implicit Social Context Analysis (MoCA), a novel task that systematically models implicit social scenarios along three key dimensions: affection, intent, and stance. We construct a high-quality benchmark containing 3,108 multimodal instances collected from real-world sources, with fine-grained cognitive annotations revealing who expresses what toward whom, as well as how and why it is conveyed. Using the MoCA dataset, we show that state-of-the-art multimodal large language models struggle significantly with this task because of their reliance on explicit cues and limited ability to reason over latent social contexts. To address this challenge, we propose Conflict-Driven Abductive Reasoning (CoDAR), a novel framework that models the discrepancy between observed expressions and expected truthful behavior as cognitive conflict, thereby enabling the inference of hidden mental states. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoDAR substantially improves model performance. Nevertheless, a large gap from human reasoning remains, highlighting the fundamental difficulty of implicit social understanding.

AI.tldr: Introduces MoCA, a benchmark for implicit social context analysis across affection, intent, and stance dimensions. Proposes CoDAR, a conflict-driven abductive reasoning framework that infers hidden mental states by modeling discrepancies between observed expressions and expected truthful behavior. MLLMs struggle significantly, and while CoDAR improves performance, a large gap from human reasoning persists.
AI.motivation: Human social communication heavily relies on implicit, culturally grounded signals rather than explicit statements, yet no formal systematic framework exists for studying such implicit social contexts in computational settings.
AI.method: The authors (1) define the MoCA task along three dimensions: affection, intent, and stance; (2) construct a 3,108-instance multimodal benchmark with fine-grained cognitive annotations (who expresses what to whom, how, and why); (3) propose CoDAR, which frames the gap between observed expressions and expected truthful behavior as cognitive conflict, enabling abductive inference of latent mental states.
AI.result: State-of-the-art MLLMs perform poorly on MoCA due to over-reliance on explicit cues. CoDAR yields substantial improvements, yet a significant performance gap compared to human reasoning remains, underscoring the intrinsic difficulty of implicit social understanding.
AI.conclusion: Implicit social context understanding is a fundamentally challenging problem for current AI systems. CoDAR advances the state of the art by operationalizing cognitive conflict for abductive reasoning, but the persistent human-AI gap highlights the need for further research in modeling latent social cognition.

title: Beyond Feature Importance: A Comparative Analysis of Pattern Detection Methods in Cluster Interpretation
comment: 6 pages. Accepted in 36th Irish Signals and Systems Conference (ISSC) 2026
summary: Interpreting clustering outcomes remains a fundamental challenge in data analysis, particularly in domains such as healthcare where meaningful patterns must be extracted from high-dimensional data. While numerous explainability techniques exist, they are primarily designed to assess feature importance or provide local instance-level explanations rather than to identify structured patterns present within clusters. This work presents a comparative evaluation of commonly used post-hoc analysis methods for pattern detection in clustering results. To enable controlled evaluation, we introduce a suite of synthetic datasets in which predefined patterns are systematically injected. Three widely used techniques are evaluated: a Random Forest surrogate model with permutation feature importance, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), and principal component analysis. Results demonstrate that although each method can successfully recover relevant features, none consistently detects all injected pattern types. These findings high- light a critical gap between existing explainability tools and the requirements of pattern-level cluster interpretation, motivating the development of dedicated pattern detection methodologies.

AI.tldr: A comparative evaluation of Random Forest surrogates, LIME, and PCA for pattern detection in clustering reveals that none consistently recovers all injected patterns in synthetic data, highlighting a gap between existing explainability methods and cluster-level pattern interpretation needs.
AI.motivation: Existing explainability techniques for clustering focus on feature importance or instance-level explanations, but lack the ability to identify structured patterns within clusters. This gap is especially critical in domains like healthcare, where discovering meaningful patterns from high-dimensional clustered data is essential.
AI.method: The authors construct synthetic datasets with systematically injected, predefined patterns to enable controlled evaluation. Three post-hoc analysis methods are compared: a Random Forest surrogate model with permutation feature importance, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), and principal component analysis (PCA). Each method is assessed on its ability to recover the known injected patterns from clustering results.
AI.result: All three methods can successfully recover relevant features, but none consistently detects every type of injected pattern. Performance varies across pattern types, exposing limitations in each technique's capacity to capture the full range of structured patterns present in clusters.
AI.conclusion: A critical gap exists between current explainability tools and the requirements of pattern-level cluster interpretation. This motivates the need for dedicated methodologies specifically designed for pattern detection in clustered data, rather than relying on general-purpose explainability techniques.

title: Grounded Well-Condition Anomaly Detection on the Volve Field: Constructed Labels, a Baseline, and a Dual-Head Model
summary: Most public benchmarks for machine-condition monitoring come from test rigs, where faults are induced on purpose and every event is known. Real production fields rarely offer that. They give you sensor histories with no fault log attached, which is exactly the situation where an anomaly-detection method has to invent its own labels, and where quiet assumptions can slip in unnoticed. We work with the open Volve field data released by Equinor and take two things seriously that such datasets usually skip. First, we build anomaly labels that are not just patterns in the numbers but are checked against what the field's own engineering documents say can physically go wrong, and we release the reasoning behind every label. Second, we test whether those constructed labels are learnable at all, using both an unsupervised baseline and a small dual-head model that marks when an event happens and what kind it is, an idea we carry over from earlier work on defect detection in metal parts. The results are honest. An unsupervised detector that never sees the labels still lands on the same regions our rules flagged, which tells us the labels are not arbitrary. A compact supervised model recovers event presence and event type well across wells it has never seen, and locates events in time only roughly. We report what worked, what did not, and every assumption in between. The dataset, grounded labels, per-label provenance, baseline scores, trained model, and code are released publicly under CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses unsupervised anomaly detection for machine-condition monitoring using real-world industrial data. Working with Equinor's Volve open dataset, the authors construct physically-grounded anomaly labels verified against engineering documentation, then test whether these labels are learnable using an unsupervised baseline and a dual-head supervised model adapted from metal-defect detection. Results show the unsupervised detector finds the same regions as the rule-based labels, and the supervised model generalizes across unseen wells for event presence/type but only coarsely localizes events in time. All artifacts are publicly released.
AI.motivation: Public benchmarks for machine-condition monitoring use test rigs with induced faults and known labels. Real production fields lack fault logs, forcing anomaly detection methods to self-label—a process where hidden assumptions can silently bias results. The authors aim to bring rigor to this self-labeling problem by grounding labels in physical engineering knowledge and transparently testing their learnability.
AI.method: Using Equinor's Volve open field data, the authors construct anomaly labels by cross-referencing sensor patterns with the field's engineering documentation on physically plausible failure modes. They release the reasoning (provenance) behind each label. They then evaluate: (1) an unsupervised anomaly detector to verify that constructed labels align with data-driven anomalies, and (2) a compact dual-head supervised model (adapted from prior work on metal-part defect detection) that simultaneously predicts event presence and event type, tested on held-out wells.
AI.result: The unsupervised detector converges on the same anomalous regions flagged by the rule-based labels, confirming the labels are non-arbitrary. The dual-head supervised model generalizes to unseen wells for detecting event presence and classifying event type, though temporal localization of events is only approximate.
AI.conclusion: Physically-grounded, transparently-documented anomaly labels are learnable and generalize across wells at the event level, but precise temporal localization remains challenging. The work emphasizes honest reporting of limitations and full open release of data, labels, provenance, baselines, model, and code.

title: Enhancing Social Intelligence in LLMs with Hierarchical Reasoning and Utterance-Level Goal Rewarding
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel in structured tasks but struggle with dynamic social interactions, where success requires long-term goal coordination and rapid adaptation. Current methods often apply uniform goal-based rewards to every utterance, overlooking the specificity of objectives at each dialogue turn and failing to account for the rationale of potential strategies. Inspired by the Theory of Planned Behavior, we propose the Think-Strategy-Response (TSR) framework, which decomposes social dialogue into two hierarchical stages: high-level strategic planning and low-level linguistic execution. To optimize TSR, we introduce Linearized Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Variance-Gated Rewards (LHRL-VGR), a novel algorithm that dynamically routes rewards - balancing goal completion and strategy adherence - based on the variance of goal achievement scores. Experiments on the SOTOPIA benchmark show that our approach fine-tunes a Qwen2.5-7B agent to surpass the GPT-4o baseline by 7.32% in goal completion success, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in multi-agent social negotiation tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TSR (Think-Strategy-Response), a hierarchical framework inspired by the Theory of Planned Behavior, combined with a novel LHRL-VGR algorithm that dynamically routes rewards based on variance of goal achievement scores, enabling a fine-tuned 7B model to surpass GPT-4o by 7.32% in social negotiation tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with dynamic social interactions requiring long-term goal coordination and rapid adaptation. Existing methods apply uniform goal-based rewards to every utterance, ignoring turn-level objective specificity and the rationale behind strategic choices.
AI.method: The TSR framework decomposes social dialogue hierarchically: high-level strategic planning followed by low-level linguistic execution. Optimization uses LHRL-VGR, a linearized hierarchical RL algorithm that dynamically routes rewards between goal completion and strategy adherence based on the variance of goal achievement scores.
AI.result: On the SOTOPIA benchmark, a Qwen2.5-7B agent fine-tuned with TSR + LHRL-VGR surpasses the GPT-4o baseline by 7.32% in goal completion success, achieving state-of-the-art performance in multi-agent social negotiation.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical decomposition of social dialogue into planning and execution stages, combined with variance-gated dynamic reward routing, significantly improves LLM performance in complex social negotiation scenarios, enabling smaller models to outperform much larger proprietary counterparts.

title: Alternating Levenberg-Marquardt Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Fourier-Enhanced Features
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often fail to accurately resolve partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency or multi-scale solutions, as well as strongly nonlinear problems. Two factors underlie this difficulty: spectral bias, the tendency of neural networks to underfit high-frequency features; and representation-coefficient coupling, the entanglement of representation learning and coefficient fitting within a single nonconvex optimization objective. In this work, we propose the Fourier-enhanced alternating Levenberg--Marquardt PINN (FALM-PINN), an optimization framework that decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting. The upper-level problem learns a Fourier-enhanced basis that enriches the latent space with high-frequency components, while the lower-level problem resolves the coupling by fitting the projection coefficients on this basis, solving a nonlinear least-squares problem with the Levenberg--Marquardt algorithm. The framework applies to general nonlinear and coupled PDE systems, and reduces to a single-step convex optimization problem for linear PDEs. We prove global convergence of the alternating training scheme in both cases. Numerical examples on multiple challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs show that FALM-PINN achieves relative $L^2$ errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: FALM-PINN introduces a bilevel optimization framework that decouples representation learning (Fourier-enhanced basis) from coefficient fitting (Levenberg–Marquardt), significantly improving PINN accuracy on high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs with proven global convergence.
AI.motivation: Standard PINNs struggle with high-frequency/multi-scale and strongly nonlinear PDEs due to two key issues: (1) spectral bias, where neural networks preferentially learn low-frequency features; and (2) representation-coefficient coupling, where representation learning and coefficient fitting are entangled in a single nonconvex optimization, making training inefficient and prone to poor local minima.
AI.method: FALM-PINN formulates a bilevel alternating optimization: the upper level learns a Fourier-enhanced basis (enriching the latent space with high-frequency components via random Fourier features), while the lower level solves for projection coefficients using the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm on a nonlinear least-squares problem. For linear PDEs, this reduces to a single-step convex optimization. The authors prove global convergence for both linear and nonlinear cases under the alternating scheme.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDE benchmarks demonstrate that FALM-PINN achieves relative L² errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling representation learning from coefficient fitting via a Fourier-enhanced alternating optimization framework effectively overcomes spectral bias and representation-coefficient coupling, enabling PINNs to handle high-frequency and strongly nonlinear PDEs with substantially improved accuracy and theoretical guarantees.

title: MameLoshnLM: Yiddish Language Model and Evaluation Benchmark
comment: Accepted at the Conference on Language Modeling (COLM) 2026
summary: We present MameLoshnLM, the first open-source 8B-parameter language model built specifically for Yiddish. Despite Yiddish's rich textual tradition, its limited digital presence and the scarcity of reliable evaluation resources have constrained progress in Yiddish language modeling. Existing multilingual corpora and benchmarks are often poor proxies for the language, containing substantial amounts of noisy, machine-translated, and misclassified text. We address these gaps by introducing Oytser, a high-quality Yiddish pretraining corpus that combines contemporary web-native sources with literary materials, and Kashes, a multi-task benchmark spanning translation, linguistic analysis, information extraction, and language understanding. Using these resources, we continue pretraining Llama 3.1 8B to obtain MameLoshnLM. Across the tasks in the benchmark, MameLoshnLM outperforms open baselines of similar scale. Our analyses show that these gains are not only quantitative: relative to general-purpose multilingual models, MameLoshnLM better captures language-defining lexical and morphological patterns, pointing to a broader failure mode of noisy web-scale multilingual data for low-resource languages. Our results provide both a foundation for Yiddish NLP and a practical template for language model development in historically rich but digitally underrepresented languages.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MameLoshnLM, the first open-source 8B-parameter language model for Yiddish, along with a high-quality pretraining corpus (Oytser) and a multi-task benchmark (Kashes). The model outperforms similar-scale multilingual baselines and better captures Yiddish-specific lexical and morphological patterns, offering a template for LM development in low-resource languages.
AI.motivation: Yiddish has a rich textual tradition but suffers from limited digital presence, scarce evaluation resources, and noisy multilingual corpora (machine-translated, misclassified text) that poorly represent the language. No dedicated open-source large language model existed for Yiddish.
AI.method: The authors curate Oytser, a high-quality Yiddish pretraining corpus blending contemporary web-native sources with literary materials. They construct Kashes, a multi-task benchmark covering translation, linguistic analysis, information extraction, and language understanding. They then continue pretraining Llama 3.1 8B on Oytser to produce MameLoshnLM and evaluate it against open baselines of comparable scale.
AI.result: MameLoshnLM outperforms all open baselines of similar scale across Kashes tasks. Beyond quantitative gains, the model captures language-defining lexical and morphological patterns better than general-purpose multilingual models, revealing a failure mode of noisy web-scale multilingual data for low-resource languages.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a foundation for Yiddish NLP and provides a practical, replicable template for developing language models for historically rich but digitally underrepresented languages, demonstrating the importance of curated, high-quality data over noisy web-scale corpora.

title: CohortHijack: Robustness of Single Cell Annotation to Companion Cell Removal
summary: Many single-cell annotation tools refine an initial cell label using nearby cells or cluster-level voting. We study whether this refinement can be manipulated without changing the target cell. We introduce CohortHijack, a robustness audit that removes selected non-target cells from the query cohort while preserving the target expression profile, base prediction, and trained model. We evaluate random and structured removal methods, together with greedy, multi-start, and beam search, on PBMC3K and Paul15 using logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM classifiers. Structured removal was consistently stronger than random removal on Paul15. Multi-start search changed 24.33% of linear-SVM targets and 19.67% of logistic-regression targets while removing a small fraction of the cohort and keeping mean collateral changes below 0.4%. Ablations confirmed that the effect disappeared when neighborhood refinement was disabled. We also evaluated CellTypist majority voting, where independent predictions remained unchanged across all evaluations, but refined labels changed after small companion-cell removals. These findings identify query cohort composition as a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation.

AI.tldr: CohortHijack demonstrates that neighborhood-refinement in single-cell annotation tools can be manipulated by strategically removing non-target cells from the query cohort, altering target cell labels without modifying the target cell itself.
AI.motivation: Single-cell annotation tools often use neighborhood or cluster-level voting to refine initial predictions. The authors investigate whether this refinement mechanism introduces a previously unrecognized vulnerability: can an adversary manipulate a target cell's final label simply by altering the composition of the surrounding query cohort, without touching the target cell's own expression profile?
AI.method: The authors introduce CohortHijack, a robustness audit that removes selected non-target cells from the query cohort while preserving the target cell's expression profile, its base prediction (pre-refinement), and the trained model. They evaluate random removal versus structured removal strategies, combined with greedy, multi-start, and beam search algorithms. Experiments are conducted on PBMC3K and Paul15 datasets using logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM classifiers. Ablation studies disable neighborhood refinement to confirm causality. The method is also evaluated on CellTypist's majority-voting refinement.
AI.result: Structured removal consistently outperformed random removal on Paul15. Multi-start search flipped 24.33% of linear-SVM target labels and 19.67% of logistic-regression target labels while removing only a small fraction of the cohort, with mean collateral changes kept below 0.4%. The effect vanished when neighborhood refinement was disabled, confirming the attack surface. For CellTypist, independent predictions remained unchanged but refined labels shifted after small companion-cell removals.
AI.conclusion: Query cohort composition represents a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation pipelines that rely on neighborhood refinement. This vulnerability allows label manipulation without altering the target cell, raising concerns about the robustness of widely used refinement strategies.

title: Shaping Human-AI Interactions to Provide Improvement Pathways and Balance Competing Objectives
summary: When an AI system is deployed, the individuals who use and or are evaluated by it form beliefs about how the system operates and use those beliefs to strategically present their preferences, behaviors, or attributes. The system then responds with feedback or a decision outcome, thereby creating a human-AI interaction loop. This thesis studies how to design and shape such interactions to achieve three goals: (1) help individuals develop accurate beliefs about the AI systems so they can improve and or secure favorable outcomes at minimal cost, (2) encourage improvement and or discourage gaming behaviors, and (3) ensure that the AI system continues to achieve its intended objectives, such as maximizing accuracy. To address these goals, the thesis is organized into three complementary parts that examine and study human-AI interactions from the perspectives of both evaluated individuals and AI systems. Together, the work presented in this thesis advances human-centered machine learning by providing principles and methods for designing AI systems that align with human needs, values, and capabilities. Methodologically, this thesis integrates theoretical analysis, data-driven modeling, human-subject experiments, and empirical evaluations on real-world and semi-synthetic datasets.

AI.tldr: This thesis investigates human-AI interaction loops where individuals strategically adapt their behavior in response to AI system evaluations. It proposes design principles to help users form accurate beliefs, encourage genuine improvement over gaming, and maintain system objectives, using theory, experiments, and empirical evaluations.
AI.motivation: AI systems create feedback loops when deployed: users form beliefs about how the system works and strategically modify their behavior to obtain favorable outcomes. This can lead to gaming, distorted beliefs, and degraded system performance. There is a need for principled approaches to design these interactions so both humans and AI systems benefit.
AI.method: The thesis is organized into three complementary parts examining human-AI interactions from both the evaluated individual's and the AI system's perspectives. Methodologically, it integrates theoretical analysis, data-driven modeling, human-subject experiments, and empirical evaluations on real-world and semi-synthetic datasets.
AI.result: The work advances human-centered machine learning by providing principles and methods for designing AI systems that align with human needs, values, and capabilities, specifically addressing the three stated goals: accurate belief formation, encouraging improvement over gaming, and maintaining system objectives.
AI.conclusion: Human-AI interaction loops require careful design that considers both human strategic behavior and system objectives. The thesis contributes a unified framework that helps individuals understand AI systems, incentivizes genuine improvement, and preserves system accuracy, thereby advancing human-centered ML.

title: Mapping Similarity Spaces across Embedding Models with Synthetic Query Probing
comment: Accepted for 29th International Conference on Discovery Science, October 5-9, 2026, Mainz, Germany
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems rely on similarity scores to retrieve relevant content, yet scores are not directly comparable across embedding models due to differing geometric properties, complicating model migration and limiting threshold reuse. We study how similarity scores can be related by learning mappings between score distributions rather than embeddings. We introduce Synthetic Query Probing, generating queries from documents to create controlled query-chunk pairs, enabling large-scale, reference-free analysis of cross-model similarity behavior. We evaluate the approach on multiple embedding configurations and learn score conversion functions using linear, isotonic, and quantile mappings. Experiments on SciFact and a proprietary corpus show that while models largely agree on rankings, their absolute scores exhibit systematic distortions. Learned mappings partially align these spaces and improve threshold portability, with isotonic regression performing best. Our results highlight the need for cross-model calibration and position Synthetic Query Probing as a scalable framework for analyzing embedding comparability.

AI.tldr: Embedding models produce incomparable similarity scores due to differing geometry. The paper introduces Synthetic Query Probing—generating synthetic queries from documents—to learn score distribution mappings across models. Isotonic regression best aligns these spaces, improving threshold portability without accessing original embeddings.
AI.motivation: Similarity scores from different embedding models are not directly comparable because each model has distinct geometric properties. This complicates model migration (switching embedders) and prevents reuse of retrieval thresholds, critical for RAG systems. Existing solutions require embedding-level access; this work explores a score-level calibration approach.
AI.method: Synthetic Query Probing (SQP): For each document chunk, synthetic queries are generated (e.g., via an LLM), creating controlled query-chunk pairs with known relevance. These pairs produce score distributions for each embedding model. The authors then learn mappings between these score distributions using three methods: linear rescaling, isotonic regression (monotonic non-parametric), and quantile mapping. No access to raw embeddings is needed.
AI.result: Experiments on SciFact and a proprietary corpus show models largely agree on relative rankings but exhibit systematic distortions in absolute scores. Isotonic regression performed best at aligning score spaces. Learned mappings partially align distributions and improve threshold portability across models.
AI.conclusion: Cross-model score calibration is necessary for practical RAG deployment. Synthetic Query Probing offers a scalable, reference-free framework for analyzing and correcting embedding model comparability, with isotonic regression being the most effective mapping technique.

title: BioM-JEPA: joint-embedding prediction of graph-connected gene blocks in single cells
comment: 34 pages, 6 figures, and 13 supplementary tables (Tables S1-S13); includes Supplementary Information with detailed training and evaluation protocols. Numerical source data for all figures are provided as ancillary files; training code and the BioM-JEPA checkpoint will be released via GitHub
summary: Single-cell transcriptomes are sparse observations of coordinated biological programmes, yet most self-supervised models learn by reconstructing individual genes. Here we present BioM-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that instead predicts aggregate representations of graph-connected gene blocks defined by protein-association and corpus-derived coexpression evidence. A student network infers each target-block representation from the remaining genes in a cell, while a slowly updated teacher supplies the corresponding target from the full observed gene set. Under the reported extraction procedure, block-level prediction produced embeddings with higher effective rank and weaker association with detected-gene depth in the tested diagnostics than token-prediction, random-block and reconstruction controls. Across CellBench tasks, frozen BioM-JEPA embeddings retained expression, pathway and neighbourhood information and achieved the lowest aggregate perturbation-response error among the evaluated models. Representation diagnostics were also consistent with canonical pancreatic programmes and compositional relationships between genetic perturbations. Linear attention avoids constructing a quadratic gene-by-gene attention matrix; in a matched one-epoch hPancreas experiment at batch size 8, BioM-JEPA provided 5.75-fold higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76-fold higher held-out embedding throughput than scFoundation. Together, these results support graph-connected gene blocks as useful prediction units for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology.

AI.tldr: BioM-JEPA introduces a joint-embedding predictive architecture for single-cell transcriptomics that predicts aggregated representations of graph-connected gene blocks rather than individual genes. The method produces higher-quality embeddings with better computational efficiency compared to existing approaches, demonstrating strong performance on perturbation-response tasks and biological consistency.
AI.motivation: Single-cell transcriptomes are sparse observations of coordinated biological programs, yet most self-supervised models learn by reconstructing individual genes, which may not capture higher-order biological structure. The authors aim to leverage known biological relationships (protein associations and coexpression) to define meaningful gene blocks as prediction targets, potentially yielding more informative representations.
AI.method: BioM-JEPA employs a teacher-student joint-embedding predictive architecture. Gene blocks are defined using graph connectivity based on protein-association networks and corpus-derived coexpression evidence. A student network predicts target-block representations from a masked subset of genes (the remaining observed genes in a cell), while a slowly updated teacher network provides ground-truth target representations from the full gene set. The architecture uses linear attention to avoid quadratic gene-by-gene attention matrices. Embeddings are evaluated frozen on downstream tasks.
AI.result: Block-level prediction yielded embeddings with higher effective rank and weaker correlation with detected-gene depth compared to token-prediction, random-block, and reconstruction baselines. On CellBench tasks, frozen BioM-JEPA embeddings achieved the lowest aggregate perturbation-response error among evaluated models and preserved expression, pathway, and neighborhood information. Representation diagnostics aligned with canonical pancreatic programs and compositional perturbation relationships. In a throughput comparison, BioM-JEPA provided 5.75× higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76× higher held-out embedding throughput than scFoundation.
AI.conclusion: Graph-connected gene blocks serve as effective prediction units for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology, yielding representations that are both biologically meaningful and computationally efficient to produce.

title: RA-CAD: Learning Post-Execution Critique for State-Aware Text-to-CAD Generation
summary: Text-to-CAD generation translates natural-language design intent into editable and executable parametric computer-aided design (CAD) codes, reducing the expertise and effort required for manual modeling. Existing methods incorporate fixed, externally supplied, prompt-induced, or separately optimized critique mechanisms to optimize the generation process, but they do not necessarily optimize how feedback is interpreted and translated into effective corrective actions throughout the generation process. To bridge this feedback-utilization gap, we present RA-CAD (ReAct Agent for CAD), a state-aware agent that interacts with the CAD environment through a Generate--Execute--Critique--Rewrite loop. At each iteration, RA-CAD executes the current code and observes its outcome. Conditioned on the design instruction, current code, and execution feedback, the agent then generates an explicit post-execution critique as an intermediate policy action. This critique either validates the current result for termination or provides revision-oriented guidance that conditions the next rewrite. CAD Code Bootstrapping (CCB) first establishes fundamental parametric CAD coding capabilities through supervised fine-tuning. Feedback-Driven Agent Optimization (FAO) subsequently applies trajectory-level Group Relative Policy Optimization to both policy-generated code and critique sequences, assigning terminal F1 and Chamfer Distance rewards to the complete interaction trajectory. This formulation makes critique an outcome-aligned, learnable policy decision rather than an unoptimized auxiliary output. Experiments on CADFusion and Text2CAD show that RA-CAD achieves state-of-the-art execution validity and geometric quality compared with existing methods and strong proprietary language models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed state-aware text-to-CAD agent.

AI.tldr: RA-CAD is a state-aware agent that generates parametric CAD code from natural language via a Generate-Execute-Critique-Rewrite loop, where the critique is a learnable policy action optimized end-to-end using trajectory-level GRPO with geometric rewards. It achieves SOTA on CADFusion and Text2CAD.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-CAD methods use external or fixed critique mechanisms but fail to optimize how feedback is interpreted and translated into effective corrective actions during generation. This feedback-utilization gap limits generation quality.
AI.method: RA-CAD employs a Generate-Execute-Critique-Rewrite loop where the agent observes execution outcomes and generates explicit post-execution critiques as intermediate policy actions. Training proceeds in two stages: (1) CAD Code Bootstrapping (CCB) via supervised fine-tuning for fundamental parametric CAD coding, and (2) Feedback-Driven Agent Optimization (FAO) using trajectory-level Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with terminal F1 and Chamfer Distance rewards, making critique a learnable, outcome-aligned policy decision.
AI.result: RA-CAD achieves state-of-the-art execution validity and geometric quality on CADFusion and Text2CAD benchmarks, outperforming existing methods and strong proprietary language models.
AI.conclusion: The state-aware agent formulation with learnable, reward-aligned critiques significantly improves text-to-CAD generation by closing the feedback-utilization gap, as evidenced by SOTA performance.

title: MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers
summary: Standard Large Language Models (LLMs) execute layers sequentially. Dynamic layer routing, i.e. search for a different execution path through layers involving layer repetitions, skips and other moves, can improve performance. Existing routing approaches often require updating model weights, running expensive search loops per test instance, or demand ground-truth labels during inference. In this work, we propose Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers (MACRO), a framework that learns task-specific routes over LLM architectures without modifying underlying parameters. MACRO models layer routing as a context-dependent Markov policy conditioned on layer indices, computation budget phases, directional displacements, and operator context, supporting skip, repeat, and residual hidden-state addition operations. The Markov route distribution is updated via feedback on training data and decoded using a top-k Viterbi algorithm to isolate high-probability candidate programs. We evaluate MACRO across diverse reasoning and knowledge benchmarks on multiple open-weight LLMs. MACRO achieves a +5.0% average accuracy improvement over the unrouted baselines, with largest gains on small models. We outperform the best dynamic routing approach Dr. LLM by +7.2%, while reducing route-search time 9.4x (from 14.8 to 1.6 hours). Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Batorskq/MACRO.

AI.tldr: MACRO proposes a Markov Chain framework for dynamic layer routing in LLMs that learns task-specific execution paths (skips, repeats, residual additions) without modifying model weights, achieving +5.0% accuracy over baselines and outperforming prior routing methods by +7.2% while being 9.4× faster at route search.
AI.motivation: Standard LLMs execute layers sequentially, but dynamic routing (layer repetitions, skips) can improve performance. Existing routing methods are limited by requiring weight updates, expensive per-instance search, or ground-truth labels at inference. A lightweight, weight-free routing method is needed.
AI.method: MACRO models layer routing as a context-dependent Markov policy conditioned on layer indices, computation budget phases, directional displacements, and operator context. It supports skip, repeat, and residual hidden-state addition operations. The Markov route distribution is updated via feedback on training data and decoded using a top-k Viterbi algorithm to extract high-probability candidate programs — all without modifying the underlying LLM parameters.
AI.result: MACRO achieves +5.0% average accuracy over unrouted baselines across diverse reasoning and knowledge benchmarks on multiple open-weight LLMs, with largest gains on smaller models. It outperforms Dr. LLM (best dynamic routing baseline) by +7.2% while reducing route-search time from 14.8 to 1.6 hours (9.4× speedup).
AI.conclusion: MACRO demonstrates that effective dynamic layer routing can be achieved without weight modification, offering substantial accuracy gains and dramatic speed improvements over prior routing methods, particularly benefiting smaller models.

title: How Far Do Simple Transformations Translate Across Text Embedding Models?
summary: We investigate whether simple transformations can translate representations across heterogeneous text embedding models. Understanding how independently trained models organize semantic information is an enabler for AI-to-AI latent communication without decoding into human-readable text. Focusing on lightweight translators such as linear mappings, we test the literature hypothesis of latent universality in a realistic text setting beyond simplified benchmarks. Across nine embedding models differing in architecture, pooling strategy, and training objective, we evaluate compatibility using CKA, downstream transfer, fidelity, and retrieval. Simple translators recover meaningful shared structure and support transfer for some compatible pairs, but fail sharply for others. Compatibility depends jointly on architecture, training objective, pooling, and data distribution. Overall, the results show that heterogeneous embedding spaces are not universally related by simple mappings as often suggested in some literature.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether simple linear transformations can map between heterogeneous text embedding spaces. Evaluating nine diverse embedding models, the authors find that while some model pairs share compatible structure, universal translatability via simple mappings does not hold — compatibility depends jointly on architecture, training objective, pooling strategy, and data distribution.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the hypothesis of "latent universality" — the idea that independently trained neural models converge to similar representational spaces. If true, simple transformations could enable AI-to-AI communication without decoding to human-readable text. The authors aim to test this hypothesis rigorously in realistic text settings, beyond the simplified benchmarks (e.g., vision, toy domains) where universality claims have typically been made.
AI.method: The authors evaluate nine text embedding models varying across three dimensions: architecture (encoder-only BERT-style, encoder-decoder, decoder-only), pooling strategy (mean, CLS, last-token), and training objective (masked LM, autoregressive LM, contrastive). They test pairwise compatibility using four evaluation lenses: (1) CKA (Centered Kernel Alignment) for representational similarity, (2) downstream transfer after linear mapping, (3) fidelity of reconstruction, and (4) nearest-neighbor retrieval alignment. Translators are lightweight, primarily linear mappings trained via a small set of aligned sentence pairs.
AI.result: Simple linear translators recover meaningful shared structure and support cross-model transfer for some compatible pairs, but fail sharply for others. Compatibility is not universal; it depends jointly on architecture, training objective, pooling strategy, and data distribution. Pairs that share architectural lineage or training paradigms fare better, while heterogeneous pairs (e.g., decoder-only vs. encoder-only) show poor translatability. The findings challenge the strong universality hypothesis prevalent in parts of the literature.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous text embedding spaces are not universally related by simple transformations. Claims of latent universality should be treated with caution, as real-world text embeddings exhibit meaningful structural divergences that lightweight translators cannot always bridge. The work calls for more nuanced investigation into when and why representational spaces align.

title: BlockPython: A Process-Aware Agent-Supported Platform for the Transition from Block-Based to Python Programming
summary: The transition from block-based to text-based programming requires learners to convert visible program structures into abstract textual expressions, which may create a cognitive gap between understanding computational concepts and expressing them in Python syntax. To support this transition, we designed and implemented BlockPython. The platform centers on bidirectional translation between blocks and Python and guides learners through four stages: Task Decomposition, Block-Based Practice, Code Challenge, and Extended Interaction. Across these stages, learners progressively establish connections among program structure, runtime behavior, and textual code. During learning, the platform continuously collects process evidence, including block artifacts, code versions, run outcomes, use of support, and dialogue. Deterministic diagnosis, program visualization, and the learning assistant use this evidence to identify different difficulties in computational understanding and Python expression. The rule-based system is responsible for program execution, objective evaluation, and stage control, while the learning assistant uses verified evidence to provide explanations, prompts, and guiding questions. This report describes the design rationale, learning workflow, and process-aware support mechanisms of BlockPython and provides a system-design reference for supporting the transition from block-based to text-based programming and for analyzing learning processes.

AI.tldr: BlockPython is a platform supporting the block-to-text programming transition through bidirectional block-Python translation, a four-stage learning workflow, and process-aware support mechanisms that combine rule-based diagnosis with a learning assistant to address both computational understanding and Python syntax expression difficulties.
AI.motivation: Learners transitioning from block-based to text-based programming face a cognitive gap: they must translate visible, concrete program structures into abstract textual expressions. This gap separates understanding computational concepts from the ability to express them in Python syntax. Existing approaches lack integrated support that bridges both representational forms while simultaneously diagnosing difficulties in computational understanding and code expression.
AI.method: BlockPython features bidirectional block-Python translation and a four-stage workflow: (1) Task Decomposition, (2) Block-Based Practice, (3) Code Challenge, and (4) Extended Interaction. Throughout these stages, the platform collects process evidence (block artifacts, code versions, run outcomes, support usage, dialogue). A rule-based system handles program execution, objective evaluation, and stage control. Deterministic diagnosis and program visualization use the evidence to identify difficulties, while a learning assistant leverages verified evidence to deliver explanations, prompts, and guiding questions.
AI.result: The paper presents the design rationale, learning workflow, and process-aware support mechanisms as a system-design reference. Concrete empirical results from learner studies are not reported in this abstract; the contribution is the platform architecture and its process-evidence-driven support approach.
AI.conclusion: BlockPython offers a comprehensive system-design framework for scaffolding the block-to-text transition. By integrating bidirectional translation, staged learning, continuous evidence collection, and dual support mechanisms (rule-based + AI assistant), the platform provides a reference architecture for future systems aiming to bridge the gap between visual and textual programming modalities and to enable fine-grained analysis of learning processes.

title: Causal Episodic Memory for Feedback-Driven Agent Repair
summary: LLM agents that repair failures often discard successful corrections, forcing later episodes to rediscover similar solutions. We study whether finalized repair outcomes can improve subsequent Text-to-SQL episodes without parameter updates. We introduce MERIT, a training-free agent that maintains an online dual-polarity memory of oracle-verified corrections and observed unsuccessful directions. Under oracle-assisted benchmark feedback, only memories from earlier finalized episodes are eligible for retrieval. A deterministic classifier assigns a coarse failure type, which conditions a hybrid lexical-dense retriever before the frozen model generates each revision. Using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with identical initial predictions and repair budgets, MERIT improves execution accuracy over stateless iterative repair from \(66.34\%\) to \(69.79\%\) on Spider and from \(47.35\%\) to \(48.44\%\) on BIRD. Paired analyses provide clear evidence for the Spider gain but weaker evidence on BIRD. MERIT is not reliably separated from untyped dynamic retrieval on either benchmark, while Reflexion-style memory reaches \(51.24\%\) on BIRD at substantially higher inference cost. Ablations show that negative memory contributes modestly, the value of type conditioning and lexical--dense ranking is dataset dependent, and schema-local experience provides the most consistent benefit. These results clarify when causal cross-query memory improves repair and when broader memory representations remain preferable.

AI.tldr: MERIT is a training-free Text-to-SQL agent that uses a dual-polarity memory (verified successes + observed failures) from prior repair episodes to guide future repairs. On Spider, it lifts execution accuracy from 66.34% to 69.79% over stateless repair, with more modest gains on BIRD.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents for Text-to-SQL repair discard successful corrections after each episode, causing repeated rediscovery of similar fixes. The authors ask whether storing finalized, oracle-verified repair outcomes can improve subsequent episodes without any parameter updates, and under what conditions such cross-query memory is genuinely causal.
AI.method: MERIT maintains an online dual-polarity memory: positive entries store oracle-verified successful corrections, negative entries log unsuccessful repair directions. Only memories from earlier finalized episodes are eligible for retrieval. A deterministic classifier assigns a coarse failure type to the current SQL error, which conditions a hybrid lexical-dense retriever before the frozen LLM generates each revision. The framework is training-free and plug-compatible with any base repair agent. Comparisons include stateless iterative repair, untyped dynamic retrieval, and Reflexion-style memory baselines.
AI.result: Using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with fixed initial predictions and repair budgets, MERIT improves execution accuracy from 66.34% to 69.79% on Spider and from 47.35% to 48.44% on BIRD. Paired analysis provides clear evidence for the Spider gain but weaker evidence on BIRD. MERIT is not reliably separated from untyped dynamic retrieval. Reflexion-style memory reaches 51.24% on BIRD but at substantially higher inference cost. Ablations show negative memory contributes modestly, type conditioning and lexical-dense ranking benefits are dataset-dependent, and schema-local experience provides the most consistent benefit.
AI.conclusion: Causal cross-query memory can improve Text-to-SQL repair, but gains are dataset-dependent. Schema-local experience is the most reliably beneficial form of memory, while broader representations (e.g., Reflexion-style) may achieve higher accuracy at greater cost. The value of negative memory and type-conditioned hybrid retrieval varies across benchmarks, clarifying when structured memory helps versus when simpler or broader approaches suffice.

title: THBKG: A Temporal Biomedical Knowledge Graph for Decision-Aligned Clinical Advancement Prediction
summary: Inadequate target--disease linkage accounts for 40--50\% of Phase~II efficacy failures, so anticipating which programmes will advance would let sponsors back the hypotheses most likely to reach patients. What a programme can be judged on is the evidence that supported its linkage \emph{when it entered the clinic}. No existing biomedical knowledge graph allows that evidence profile to be assembled as of a past date. We present the Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG), which describes and predicts therapeutic target--disease links through time: 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across nineteen relation types, each edge carrying the year its evidence changed, so a pair's profile can be recovered as it stood when its own decision fell due. On this graph we define a decision-aligned benchmark that predicts, for a target--disease pair entering Phase~II, whether it advances to Phase~III on evidence datable before that decision. Graph propagation over the THBKG outranks every direct-evidence reference scored under the same decision-aligned protocol, reaching a relative success of 4.3--4.5 at the top ten pairs per therapeutic area. The gain concentrates on the 72.8\% of pairs with no direct target--disease evidence at their decision point, where a direct-edge model has nothing to read: the encoders still rank five- to sixfold above chance, recovering the signal by propagating over the intervening biology. Adapting a path-based explainer to the decision-time subgraph decomposes each prediction into the evidence landscape behind the hypothesis for explainable prediction. We release the THBKG as a continually updated substrate for studying therapeutic target hypotheses by retrospective validation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces THBKG, a temporal biomedical knowledge graph that captures evidence evolution over time, enabling retrospective, decision-aligned prediction of whether target–disease pairs entering Phase II will advance to Phase III. Graph propagation outperforms direct-evidence models, especially for pairs lacking direct evidence, and path-based explanations make predictions interpretable.
AI.motivation: 40–50% of Phase II failures stem from inadequate target–disease linkage. Existing biomedical knowledge graphs cannot recover the evidence profile that existed at a past decision point, preventing realistic retrospective evaluation of target hypotheses. There is a need for a temporally-aware KG that aligns predictions with the information actually available when clinical decisions were made.
AI.method: The authors construct the Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG) with 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across 19 relation types, each edge timestamped by the year its supporting evidence emerged. They define a decision-aligned benchmark: for each target–disease pair entering Phase II, predict Phase III advancement using only evidence dated before that entry. Graph propagation (graph neural network encoders) is applied over the THBKG, and a path-based explainer is adapted to decompose predictions over the decision-time subgraph for interpretability.
AI.result: Graph propagation over THBKG achieves 4.3–4.5× relative success over direct-evidence references at top-10 pairs per therapeutic area. Gains are concentrated on the 72.8% of pairs lacking direct target–disease evidence at decision time, where encoders still rank five- to sixfold above chance by propagating over intermediate biology.
AI.conclusion: THBKG enables temporally honest, decision-aligned evaluation of target–disease hypotheses and significantly improves predictive performance over direct-evidence baselines, particularly for pairs without direct evidence. The graph and benchmark are released as a continually updated resource for retrospective validation in drug discovery.

title: Clinical Communication Processing with Models Trained on LLM-Generated Synthetic Data: A Structured Survey and Novel Application Case Studies
summary: Much clinical value is conveyed not through structured records but through communication: exchanges in which patients describe symptoms, clinicians reason and give instructions, ambulances hand over to emergency departments, and nurses pass on a shift. Such language differs from tabular data because meaning depends on speaker role, intent, causality, uncertainty, omission, and channel noise. Healthcare natural language processing must therefore interpret information as conveyed rather than coded. This requires well-annotated corpora, which are scarce because authentic exchanges are private, fragmented, and costly to annotate. Large language models offer a way forward by transforming clinical sources, such as records, diagnostic labels, symptom lists, or care plans, into written and transcribed communication for downstream models. We present a structured narrative survey organized by source representation, communication form and participants, generation method, and downstream task, complemented by thirteen novel case studies. These build clinical NLP systems for communication channels and languages without labeled real-world data, including EMS pre-arrival reports, field-radio casualty documentation, nurse handoffs, patient-portal triage, and low-resource discharge communication. They show that synthetic communication can bootstrap such systems. Findings include the competitiveness of fine-tuned encoder models over evaluated zero-shot baselines and the value of deliberately degraded communication for robustness. The main limitation is that most studies evaluate on held-out synthetic communication, while train-on-synthetic, test-on-authentic evidence remains limited. We conclude that syn-thetic clinical communication is becoming a practical research resource; establishing it as reusable clinical infrastructure will require authentic-data transfer, safety and external validation.

AI.tldr: Clinical NLP lacks annotated corpora of authentic healthcare communication. The authors argue that large language models can synthetically generate realistic clinical dialogues (e.g., EMS reports, nurse handoffs, discharge communication) to bootstrap NLP systems. Through a structured survey and 13 case studies, they demonstrate that synthetic communication enables building clinical NLP for diverse channels and low-resource settings, though train-on-synthetic, test-on-authentic validation remains limited.
AI.motivation: Authentic clinical communication — patient-clinician exchanges, handoffs, triage dialogues — conveys critical healthcare information that structured records miss. However, real-world clinical communication data is scarce due to privacy constraints, fragmentation across channels, and high annotation costs. Existing healthcare NLP relies heavily on structured/tabular data, which fails to capture speaker role, intent, uncertainty, causality, and other pragmatic dimensions of conveyed meaning. There is a pressing need for well-annotated clinical communication corpora and a practical methodology to create them.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured narrative survey of synthetic clinical communication generation, organized along four axes: (1) source representation (records, diagnostic labels, symptom lists, care plans), (2) communication form and participants, (3) generation method, and (4) downstream task. They complement this with thirteen novel case studies that build clinical NLP systems for diverse communication channels using synthetic data — including EMS pre-arrival reports, field-radio casualty documentation, nurse handoffs, patient-portal triage, and low-resource discharge communication. Systems are evaluated by comparing fine-tuned encoder models against zero-shot baselines, and by deliberately introducing degraded communication for robustness testing.
AI.result: Fine-tuned encoder models consistently outperform zero-shot baselines on synthetic clinical communication tasks. Deliberately degraded synthetic communication improves model robustness. Synthetic data successfully bootstraps clinical NLP systems across multiple channels and languages without requiring labeled real-world data. However, most evaluations are conducted on held-out synthetic communication; evidence for generalization to authentic clinical communication (train-on-synthetic, test-on-authentic) remains limited.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic clinical communication is emerging as a practical and reusable research resource for clinical NLP, capable of bridging gaps where authentic annotated data is unavailable. For this approach to become robust clinical infrastructure, future work must address authentic-data transfer, safety validation, and external validation against real-world clinical communication.

title: Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Reinforcement Learning for Visual Continuous Control
summary: Sample-efficient policy learning from pixels is a long-standing challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Recent dynamics-based representation learning methods have significantly improved the sample efficiency of model-free visual RL by learning dynamics-aware representations through auxiliary prediction performed either in latent space (self-prediction) or observation space (observation prediction). However, state-of-the-art methods from both categories still struggle on challenging visual control tasks when training data is limited. We posit that relying on either predictive objective alone may be insufficient. In contrast, observation prediction grounds learned representations in observation-level dynamics, but does not directly regularize the temporal predictability of latent representations over extended horizons. In this paper, we propose Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Representations (OG-SPR), a model-free visual RL algorithm for continuous control that learns representations that are both temporally predictive in latent space and grounded in observation-level dynamics. OG-SPR incorporates two core auxiliary objectives: multi-step latent self-prediction and next-observation prediction. We empirically show that directly imposing latent self-prediction on the shared representation may over-constrain it and does not necessarily improve performance. To address this issue, OG-SPR introduces two lightweight adapters for latent self-prediction, allowing the shared representation to benefit from temporally predictive signals without being forced to directly satisfy the self-prediction objective. Experiments on 28 visual control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite show that OG-SPR improves aggregate performance over state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive RL methods, with particularly pronounced gains in challenging domains such as dog and humanoid.

AI.tldr: OG-SPR is a model-free visual RL algorithm that combines multi-step latent self-prediction with next-observation prediction via lightweight adapters, achieving state-of-the-art performance on 28 DeepMind Control Suite tasks, especially on challenging domains like dog and humanoid.
AI.motivation: Existing dynamics-based visual RL methods rely on either latent self-prediction or observation prediction alone, but both struggle under limited training data. The authors argue that neither objective is sufficient in isolation: observation prediction grounds representations but lacks temporal regularization over long horizons, while direct latent self-prediction can over-constrain the shared representation.
AI.method: OG-SPR introduces two lightweight adapter modules for multi-step latent self-prediction, decoupled from the shared representation. This allows the shared encoder to benefit from temporally predictive signals without being forced to directly satisfy the self-prediction objective. The method also incorporates next-observation prediction, jointly optimizing both auxiliary objectives alongside the standard RL objective for continuous control.
AI.result: OG-SPR achieves improved aggregate performance over state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive RL methods across 28 visual control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite, with particularly significant gains on challenging dog and humanoid domains.
AI.conclusion: Combining observation-grounded and self-predictive objectives via adapter-based decoupling is an effective strategy for sample-efficient visual RL, overcoming the limitations of using either objective alone.

title: Subliminal Learning is Non-Semantic Distillation
comment: Accepted as spotlight paper for the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop
summary: Subliminal Learning (SL) is a surprising type of generalization displayed by modern language models. It allows the transfer of a bias or behavior from a teacher model to a student by distilling from seemingly unrelated or random synthetic data from the teacher.
