We place nine frontier models in the role of a chief executive officer and evaluate their decision-making ability. Multimodal inputs consistently improve evidence-centric reasoning, with the largest and most reliable gains appearing in risk forecasting and board-facing justification. However, we uncover a multimodal integration paradox: adding visual business information degrades constrained resource allocation for all nine models, even as visual grounding itself improves. Ablation experiments reveal that this failure emerges from signal crowding, although each visual channel helps individually, their combination disrupts constraint satisfaction during decoding. These findings demonstrate that visual perception and constrained action are separable bottlenecks in multimodal agents, and that indiscriminate visual augmentation can harm high-stakes decision making, motivating selective grounding strategies for future executive AI systems.

AI.tldr: C-SUITEBENCH is a multimodal benchmark testing LLMs as CEOs across 50 scenarios. While visual inputs improve evidence reasoning and risk forecasting, they paradoxically degrade resource allocation due to signal crowding—revealing that visual perception and constrained action are separable bottlenecks in executive AI agents.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLMs as decision-making agents are text-only, leaving unclear whether models can perceive and integrate visual business evidence. The authors aim to test whether multimodal inputs improve or impair high-stakes executive decisions.
AI.method: The authors introduce C-SUITEBENCH, a controlled multimodal benchmark with five decision tasks across 50 scenarios, each with paired text-only and multimodal conditions. Nine frontier models are evaluated in the role of CEO. Ablation experiments isolate the effects of individual visual channels on constrained decision-making.
AI.result: Multimodal inputs consistently improve evidence-centric reasoning, especially in risk forecasting and board-facing justification. However, a "multimodal integration paradox" emerges: visual information degrades constrained resource allocation across all nine models. Ablations reveal this stems from signal crowding—individual visual channels help, but their combination disrupts constraint satisfaction during decoding.
AI.conclusion: Visual perception and constrained action are separable bottlenecks in multimodal agents. Indiscriminate visual augmentation can harm high-stakes decisions, motivating the need for selective grounding strategies in future executive AI systems.

title: RP-OPSD: Reasoning-Pivot-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation for Multilingual Reasoning Transfer
summary: Multilingual reasoning transfer is crucial for extending reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) beyond high-resource languages. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) and its variants have emerged as a promising paradigm, providing dense token-level supervision on student-generated rollouts, yet their objectives do not explicitly prioritize reasoning signals most critical to cross-lingual transfer. We characterize that target-language reasoning comprises the generation of both surface text and reasoning pivots, which are decisions that advance or redirect the reasoning process and shape subsequent inference. This motivates concentrating privileged distillation around such pivots. We therefore propose RP-OPSD, Reasoning-Pivot-guided On-Policy Self-Distillation, using the distributional shift between matched teacher views with and without an English reference solution as an operational proxy to guide privileged distillation and reference anchoring. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks covering 17 languages and multiple difficulty levels show that our method outperforms strong multilingual reasoning baselines and OPSD variants. Further analysis reveals that RP-OPSD concentrates privileged distillation on reasoning-control and problem-condistioned state-update tokens, while downweighting it for tokens that mainly support surface realization. Our code is available at https://github.com/NJUNLP/RP-OPSD.

AI.tldr: RP-OPSD proposes a reasoning-pivot-guided on-policy self-distillation method for multilingual LLM reasoning transfer, using distributional shifts between teacher views with/without English references to identify and privilege critical reasoning tokens, outperforming baselines across 17 languages on math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Multilingual reasoning transfer for LLMs lacks methods that explicitly prioritize reasoning-signal tokens critical for cross-lingual transfer. Existing OPSD variants provide dense token-level supervision but treat all tokens uniformly, failing to focus on "reasoning pivots" — decisions that advance or redirect reasoning and shape subsequent inference. The key insight is that target-language reasoning involves both surface text generation and reasoning-pivot generation, motivating concentrated distillation around these pivots.
AI.method: RP-OPSD (Reasoning-Pivot-guided On-Policy Self-Distillation) uses the distributional shift between two matched teacher views — one with and one without an English reference solution — as an operational proxy to identify reasoning pivots. Tokens exhibiting large distributional divergence between these views are treated as reasoning pivots and receive privileged distillation weight, while surface-realization tokens are downweighted. This guides the student model to focus on reasoning-control and problem-conditioned state-update tokens during cross-lingual transfer.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks across 17 languages and multiple difficulty levels demonstrate that RP-OPSD outperforms strong multilingual reasoning baselines and standard OPSD variants. Further analysis confirms that RP-OPSD successfully concentrates privileged distillation on reasoning-control and problem-conditioned state-update tokens while downweighting surface-realization tokens.
AI.conclusion: RP-OPSD provides an effective, principled approach to multilingual reasoning transfer by identifying and privileging reasoning pivots through teacher distributional shift analysis, without requiring explicit annotation of reasoning steps. The method advances cross-lingual reasoning capabilities of LLMs beyond the OPSD paradigm.

title: LLM Inference Under Bursty Workload Distribution: Modifying the WAIT Algorithm
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Claude are widely used for information retrieval and problem-solving. Recent work has focused on improving scheduling algorithms to boost throughput while maintaining low latency. However, these approaches often assume Poisson request arrivals with constant rates - an assumption that fails to reflect the inherently bursty and dynamic nature of real-world traffic. We propose a lightweight extension to the state-of-the-art WAIT algorithm [1], which adapts to time-varying arrival rates without prior traffic knowledge. The proposed algorithm performs online estimation of request intensity based on observed interarrival times. Using Markov Modulated Poisson Process (MMPP)-based synthetic workloads with diverse request types, we conduct a simulation-based evaluation demonstrating that the proposed method achieves higher throughput than Sarathi-Serve [2], ORCA [3], and vLLM [4] in the evaluated low arrival-rate shift scenarios while maintaining comparable latency.

AI.tldr: A lightweight extension to the WAIT scheduling algorithm is proposed that adapts to time-varying, bursty request arrivals by estimating request intensity online from interarrival times, outperforming Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, and vLLM in throughput under low arrival-rate shift scenarios while maintaining comparable latency.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM serving schedulers (Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, vLLM, WAIT) assume Poisson request arrivals with constant rates. This assumption fails to capture the bursty, dynamic nature of real-world traffic, motivating the need for a scheduler that adapts to time-varying arrival rates without requiring prior traffic knowledge.
AI.method: The authors propose a lightweight extension to the WAIT algorithm that performs online estimation of request intensity based on observed interarrival times. Evaluation uses Markov Modulated Poisson Process (MMPP)-based synthetic workloads with diverse request types in a simulation-based setting, comparing against Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, and vLLM.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves higher throughput than Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, and vLLM in low arrival-rate shift scenarios while maintaining comparable latency.
AI.conclusion: Adapting scheduling to time-varying arrival rates via online intensity estimation yields throughput gains over existing schedulers without sacrificing latency, demonstrating the value of moving beyond constant-rate Poisson assumptions in LLM serving systems.

title: Improving Interoperability among Defence and National Security Ontologies: Analysis and Evaluation Tasks
comment: Paper accepted at the Resource Track, the 25th International Semantic Web Conference (ISWC 2026), 25 - 29 October 2026, Bari, Italy
summary: The use of ontologies and knowledge graphs is becoming increasingly widespread in the defence and national security domain. Numerous ontologies have been developed through initiatives led by academia, industry, and government. Achieving interoperability across diverse defence and national security ontologies remains a major challenge due to the domain's breadth and specialisation. In this work, we analyse and document over 60 publicly available ontologies and introduce a new track for the Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative (OAEI). This track comprises eight matching tasks, consensus alignments and manually-curated (silver-standard) mappings. The consensus alignments are derived by aggregating the outputs of several state-of-the-art ontology alignment systems. The silver-standard is obtained from the manual validation of the consensus alignment together with a subset of the unique mappings (i.e., mappings suggested by only one system).

AI.tldr: The paper surveys over 60 publicly available defence and national security ontologies, addressing interoperability challenges, and introduces a new OAEI track with eight matching tasks, consensus alignments, and manually-curated silver-standard mappings.
AI.motivation: The defence and national security domain has produced numerous ontologies through academia, industry, and government initiatives, but interoperability among them remains a major challenge due to the domain's breadth and specialization. There is a need for systematic evaluation methods to assess and improve ontology alignment in this domain.
AI.method: The authors analyze and document over 60 publicly available defence and national security ontologies. They introduce a new track within the Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative (OAEI) consisting of eight matching tasks. Consensus alignments are generated by aggregating outputs from multiple state-of-the-art ontology alignment systems. A silver-standard is then produced through manual validation of the consensus alignment combined with a subset of unique mappings (those suggested by only one system).
AI.result: The paper delivers a comprehensive survey of 60+ defence/national security ontologies, a new OAEI benchmark track with eight matching tasks, consensus reference alignments derived from multiple alignment systems, and manually-curated silver-standard mappings that serve as evaluation references.
AI.conclusion: The new OAEI track provides a structured benchmark for evaluating ontology alignment systems within the defence and national security domain, offering both consensus and silver-standard alignments to facilitate more robust interoperability assessment and to drive progress in this specialized area of ontology matching.

title: The Bitter Lesson of Tool Calling
summary: Tool use transforms LLMs into agents that act beyond their training data, and for code-capable models, programmatic tool calling extends this further by replacing rigid JSON calls with scripts that chain and parallelize naturally. However, a systematic evaluation of tools as code on an established benchmark across current and prior model generations under real-world task conditions has not been conducted. In this work, we empirically compare programmatic tool calling (PTC) to native JSON tool calling across 14 language models on BFCL v4. In the programmatic tool calling paradigm, tools are exposed as typed Python stubs that the model invokes through code, with execution and results handled in a single agent turn. Programmatic tool calling matches or exceeds native JSON tool calling in 11 of 14 models on BFCL v4, with the GPT-5.6 family achieving a 10.6% improvement over the JSON tool calling baseline. Further, it matches or outperforms baseline in 13 of 14 models under parallel fan-out, and holds stable under context rot conditions where baseline degrades 2.3% on average. Our results demonstrate that programmatic tool calling is a viable and robust alternative to JSON tool calling, with performance tracking model capability across release generations.

AI.tldr: Programmatic tool calling (PTC), where models invoke typed Python stubs via code, matches or outperforms native JSON tool calling in 11 of 14 LLMs on BFCL v4, with up to 10.6% improvement. PTC also proves more robust under parallel fan-out and context rot conditions.
AI.motivation: No systematic evaluation of programmatic tool calling against native JSON tool calling on an established benchmark across multiple model generations under realistic task conditions had been conducted, leaving a gap in understanding whether code-based tool invocation is a viable alternative.
AI.method: The authors empirically compared programmatic tool calling (tools exposed as typed Python stubs, invoked through code, with execution and results in a single agent turn) against native JSON tool calling across 14 language models using the BFCL v4 benchmark. They also tested performance under parallel fan-out and context rot conditions.
AI.result: PTC matched or exceeded JSON tool calling in 11 of 14 models, with the GPT-5.6 family achieving a 10.6% improvement. Under parallel fan-out, PTC matched or outperformed baseline in 13 of 14 models. Under context rot, baseline degraded 2.3% on average while PTC remained stable.
AI.conclusion: Programmatic tool calling is a viable and robust alternative to JSON tool calling, with performance that tracks model capability across release generations.

title: SkillTFM: Gated Skill Evolution for Training-Free Adaptation of Tabular Foundation Models
summary:
Tabular data are ubiquitous in real-world applications and are crucial for data-driven prediction and decision-making across science, industry, finance, healthcare, and public services. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose tabular learning, offering reusable predictors across diverse datasets and substantially reducing the need for task-specific training, tuning, and model development. However, their practical deployment remains constrained by distribution shifts, heterogeneous feature semantics, and task-specific patterns that are difficult to capture without costly fine-tuning or additional labeled data.
  To this end, we propose SkillTFM, a training-free system that shifts TFM adaptation from parameter updates to the gated evolution of agentic skills. The core of SkillTFM is a verifiable and extensible skill bank that couples boundary evidence identification with gated skill evolution: the former characterizes task structure and base-model failure patterns, whereas the latter retrieves and extends reusable skills subject to explicit validation. Across simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128--0.142, raises nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898. Furthermore, experiments across TFM backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of SkillTFM.

AI.tldr: SkillTFM is a training-free system that adapts tabular foundation models to new tasks by gated evolution of agentic skills stored in a verifiable skill bank, rather than parameter updates. It couples boundary evidence identification with gated skill retrieval and extension, achieving significant AUC gains on synthetic and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) offer reusable prediction across datasets but suffer from distribution shifts, heterogeneous feature semantics, and task-specific patterns that typically require costly fine-tuning or additional labeled data to address.
AI.method: SkillTFM introduces a training-free adaptation mechanism via a verifiable and extensible skill bank. It has two core components: (1) boundary evidence identification, which characterizes task structure and base-model failure patterns; and (2) gated skill evolution, which retrieves and extends reusable skills subject to explicit validation, enabling adaptation without parameter updates.
AI.result: In simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128–0.142, and raises nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898. Experiments across multiple TFM backbones demonstrate both effectiveness and generality.
AI.conclusion: SkillTFM provides a viable training-free alternative to fine-tuning for adapting TFMs, using an extensible, verifiable skill bank. Its strong empirical gains suggest agentic skill evolution is a promising direction for deployment under distribution shifts and heterogeneous data.

title: Personalized Deep Research Query Refinement with Graph-Scaffolded Evidence Grounding
summary: User requests serve as research specifications for deep research agents, shaping what evidence to seek and how to synthesize it. In personalized deep research, these specifications must additionally reflect user goals, constraints, preferences, and evaluation criteria. User context can be incorporated either within the deep research pipeline or into the research specification provided as its input. We focus on the latter, refining the user request into a personalized research specification before passing it to an unchanged deep research agent. This requires resolving three coupled decisions: which framing factors are relevant, whether the available user context sufficiently supports them, and whether to retrieve user memory, ask the user, or stop and refine the query. For training, G-STEER organizes framing factors as elicitation targets in an Intent Elicitation Graph that captures their dependencies. It learns a clarification policy from graph-scaffolded trajectories spanning diverse factor dependencies and evidence conditions. The policy produces a refined query while balancing target coverage against the costs of evidence acquisition. Experiments show that G-STEER achieves the strongest overall weighted target coverage and the highest downstream report personalization across both evaluated DRAs, while asking roughly one third as many user questions as a strong clarification baseline.

AI.tldr: G-STEER refines user requests into personalized research specifications for deep research agents by learning a clarification policy that balances target coverage against evidence acquisition costs, using an Intent Elicitation Graph to model factor dependencies.
AI.motivation: Personalized deep research requires incorporating user goals, constraints, preferences, and evaluation criteria. Rather than modifying the deep research agent itself, the authors focus on refining the input research specification to reflect personalization, which requires navigating a complex decision space: selecting relevant framing factors, assessing whether existing user context suffices, and deciding whether to retrieve memory, ask the user, or stop and refine.
AI.method: G-STEER models framing factors as elicitation targets in an Intent Elicitation Graph that captures their dependencies. It learns a clarification policy from graph-scaffolded trajectories spanning diverse factor dependencies and evidence conditions. The policy produces a refined query while optimizing the trade-off between target coverage and evidence acquisition costs (memory retrieval vs. user questions).
AI.result: G-STEER achieves the strongest overall weighted target coverage and the highest downstream report personalization across two evaluated deep research agents (DRAs), while asking approximately one third as many user questions as a strong clarification baseline.
AI.conclusion: Personalizing deep research by refining the input specification — rather than altering the agent — is effective. G-STEER's graph-based clarification policy successfully balances personalization quality with interaction cost, substantially reducing user burden while improving downstream report personalization.

title: Learning When to Trust via Selective Context Preference Optimization
comment: Project Page at https://worldbench.github.io/scope GitHub Repo at https://github.com/worldbench/SCOPE HF Dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/worldbench/MIST-Bench
summary: Language models increasingly condition their answers on external signals, and a single misleading one can turn a correct answer wrong. The obvious remedy, training models to resist such signals, hides a failure mode: a model that ignores all context looks robust yet is useless when the context is worth trusting. We recast the problem as selective trust and introduce MIST, a human-annotated benchmark that renders each reasoning item under four matched conditions (clean, misleading, correct-context, and irrelevant-context), together with SC2W, a paired metric counting how often a misleading signal flips a clean-correct answer to wrong. Across a comprehensive benchmark study, we observe that such a susceptibility is universal. We then propose SCOPE, which mines clean-correct/misleading-wrong failures and optimizes a standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) objective over matched preference pairs balanced equally across all four conditions, rather than over misleading items alone. Our approach substantially reduces SC2W on popular open-sourced models while preserving accuracy when the added context is clean, correct, or irrelevant. With this work, we argue that models should be judged on selective trust, not on resistance alone.

AI.tldr: MIST benchmark with SC2W metric reveals language models are universally susceptible to misleading context. The proposed SCOPE method uses balanced DPO over matched preference pairs across four context conditions, reducing susceptibility while preserving trust in valid context.
AI.motivation: Current approaches train models to resist misleading signals, but this creates a failure mode where models ignore all context—including trustworthy context. The authors reframe the problem as "selective trust": models should resist misleading signals while still utilizing correct context.
AI.method: Two contributions: (1) MIST, a human-annotated benchmark with reasoning items under four matched conditions (clean, misleading, correct-context, irrelevant-context) and SC2W, a paired metric measuring how often misleading context flips correct answers; (2) SCOPE, a training method that mines clean-correct/misleading-wrong failure pairs and applies DPO over preference pairs balanced equally across all four conditions.
AI.result: Susceptibility to misleading signals is universal across tested models. SCOPE substantially reduces SC2W on popular open-source models while preserving accuracy when context is clean, correct, or irrelevant.
AI.conclusion: Models should be evaluated on selective trust—the ability to accept trustworthy context while rejecting misleading signals—rather than on resistance alone.

title: Threshold-Based Early Stopping of Accumulations in Neural Networks with Binary Activation
summary: Binary neural networks are very attractive for constrained deployment, enabling small footprint and low-power inference. For binary activations, the dot products become sign-controlled additions or subtractions, but the number of operations is unchanged. Indeed, every neuron or output channel still accumulates all of its input, even though only the sign will be retained, which is often wasteful. As the accumulation progresses, the running partial sum frequently drifts so far from zero that its final sign becomes highly predictable long before the last term is reached; every contribution evaluated after that point changes the value of the sum but not the final output activation. This paper turns this observation into a post-training early-stopping mechanism. We characterize the behavior of the running accumulations on the training dataset and use this information to predict the final sign as soon as possible. No model parameter is retrained. We count the number of operations under an idealized ordering of weights. On VGG11 applied to the CIFAR-10 dataset, the method removes $86.6\%$ of the accumulation terms of the deepest convolution for a $0.37$-point accuracy drop, and $25\%$ of the full-network arithmetic when used on the three deepest convolutions simultaneously, for a $1.36$-point drop.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a post-training early-stopping mechanism for binary neural networks that skips redundant accumulation operations once the final sign of a partial sum becomes predictable, achieving significant computational savings with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: In binary neural networks with binary activations, dot products reduce to sign-controlled additions/subtractions, but the number of operations remains unchanged. During accumulation, the running partial sum often drifts far enough from zero that its final sign becomes predictable well before all terms are processed. Evaluating remaining contributions after this point wastes computation without affecting the output activation.
AI.method: The authors propose a post-training early-stopping mechanism that requires no retraining. They characterize running accumulation behavior on the training dataset to learn when final signs become predictable. Under an idealized weight ordering, accumulations are terminated as soon as the sign is confidently determined, thereby skipping the remaining terms.
AI.result: On VGG11 with CIFAR-10, the method removes 86.6% of accumulation terms in the deepest convolution layer for only a 0.37-point accuracy drop. When applied simultaneously to the three deepest convolutions, it eliminates 25% of full-network arithmetic at a cost of 1.36 accuracy points.
AI.conclusion: Early stopping of accumulation in binary neural networks is an effective post-training optimization that substantially reduces computational cost with minimal accuracy degradation, demonstrating that many operations in BNN inference are redundant and can be safely pruned without retraining.

title: AppDeltaWorld: Transition-Grounded Delta Code World Model for Mobile GUI Agents
summary: Mobile GUI agents can operate apps through pixel perception and touch actions, making them a promising interface for collecting and improving long-horizon mobile interaction policies. However, real trajectories are difficult to obtain for sensitive apps and privacy-critical operations. At the same time, existing simulated environments are costly to scale up, and GUI world models still suffer from unstable generation, limited modality coverage, and inconsistent action-transition logic. To address these limitations, we propose AppDeltaWorld, a transition-grounded delta code world model that predicts the next GUI as a reachable code update rather than as an unconstrained image or text description. AppDeltaWorld retrieves app-specific Level-1 HTML references under an action-transition constraint, generates Level-2 executable HTML conditioned on the current screen, action, predicted next-screen text, and retrieved structure, and inserts generated visual assets into image slots before browser rendering. As a world model, AppDeltaWorld achieves the highest fidelity on CMGUIBench-500 under Code2World evaluation, with clear gains in structural layout and UI element reconstruction over image-only and code-only baselines. As a training environment, AppDeltaWorld supports filtered closed-loop SFT data construction that, when combined with public supervision, enables AppDeltaAgent to achieve state-of-the-art performance on AndroidLens and consistent gains on MobileGym and MobileWorld. Moreover, world-model-based test-time reinforcement learning enables policy adaptation and shows further improvements without additional interaction with real apps.

AI.tldr: AppDeltaWorld proposes a delta code world model for mobile GUI agents that predicts next GUI states as reachable code updates (HTML/CSS) rather than unconstrained images or text. It achieves state-of-the-art world model fidelity and enables effective training data construction and test-time RL-based policy adaptation.
AI.motivation: Real mobile interaction trajectories are hard to collect for privacy-sensitive apps, existing simulators are costly to scale, and current GUI world models suffer from unstable generation, limited modalities, and inconsistent action-transition logic. A more reliable, scalable world model is needed for training and improving mobile GUI agents.
AI.method: AppDeltaWorld is a transition-grounded delta code world model with three stages: (1) retrieve app-specific Level-1 HTML references under action-transition constraints; (2) generate Level-2 executable HTML conditioned on current screen, action, predicted next-screen text, and retrieved structure; (3) insert generated visual assets into image slots before browser rendering. It produces the next GUI as a reachable, executable code update rather than free-form generation. This world model supports filtered closed-loop SFT data construction and world-model-based test-time reinforcement learning.
AI.result: AppDeltaWorld achieves highest fidelity on CMGUIBench-500 under Code2World evaluation, with clear gains in structural layout and UI element reconstruction over image-only and code-only baselines. Using its filtered closed-loop SFT data combined with public supervision, AppDeltaAgent achieves SOTA on AndroidLens and consistent gains on MobileGym and MobileWorld. Test-time RL via the world model yields further policy improvements without additional real-app interaction.
AI.conclusion: A delta code world model constrained by action-transition logic provides a more faithful and scalable alternative to image/text-based world models for mobile GUI agents, enabling both effective training data generation and real-world-free policy adaptation through test-time reinforcement learning.

title: A Study of LLMs' Preferences for Libraries and Programming Languages
comment: 21 pages, 10 tables, 3 figures. Accepted to Findings of ACL 2026
summary: Despite the rapid progress of large language models (LLMs) in code generation, existing evaluations focus on functional correctness or syntactic validity, overlooking how LLMs make critical design choices such as which library or programming language to use. To fill this gap, we perform the first empirical study of LLMs' preferences for libraries and programming languages when generating code, covering eight diverse LLMs. We observe a strong tendency to overuse widely adopted libraries such as NumPy; in up to 45% of cases, this usage is not required and deviates from the ground-truth solutions. The LLMs we study also show a significant preference toward Python as their default language. For high-performance project initialisation tasks where Python is not the optimal language, it remains the dominant choice in 58% of cases, and Rust is not used once. These results highlight how LLMs prioritise familiarity and popularity over suitability and task-specific optimality; underscoring the need for targeted fine-tuning, data diversification, and evaluation benchmarks that explicitly measure language and library selection fidelity.

AI.tldr: An empirical study of eight LLMs reveals systematic biases in library and programming language selection during code generation: LLMs overuse popular libraries like NumPy (up to 45% unnecessarily) and default heavily to Python (58% of high-performance tasks where Python is suboptimal), prioritizing familiarity over task-appropriate choices.
AI.motivation: Existing code generation evaluations focus narrowly on functional correctness and syntactic validity, ignoring how LLMs make critical design decisions — specifically, which libraries and programming languages they select. This gap matters because suboptimal library/language choices can undermine performance, maintainability, and project suitability.
AI.method: The authors conduct an empirical study across eight diverse LLMs, systematically analyzing their library and language preferences during code generation tasks. They compare LLM-generated solutions against ground-truth references to quantify unnecessary library usage and suboptimal language selection, particularly in high-performance project initialization scenarios.
AI.result: LLMs exhibit a strong bias toward overusing widely adopted libraries like NumPy — in up to 45% of cases, this usage is unnecessary and diverges from ground-truth solutions. Python dominates as the default language: for high-performance project initialization tasks where Python is not optimal, it remains the choice in 58% of cases, while Rust is never selected.
AI.conclusion: LLMs prioritize familiarity and popularity over task-specific optimality in library and language selection. This underscores the need for targeted fine-tuning, training data diversification, and new evaluation benchmarks that explicitly measure library and language selection fidelity.

title: SAGA: Score-Weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment for Low-Resource Nordic Language Models
summary: Preference optimisation has proven effective for improving large language models but typically relies on costly human preference annotations. Extending these methods to morphologically rich, low-resource languages remains challenging because such annotations are scarce. We present SAGA (Score-weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment), a parser-guided preference optimisation framework that replaces human labels with dependency-parser supervision. SAGA converts parser judgements into preference pairs for delta-DPO, combines parser quality with lexical diversity in a composite reward, filters low-information pairs using a reward-gap criterion, and monitors reward hacking to maintain reliable supervision. Across Danish, Icelandic, and Norwegian Bokmål using GPT-SW3-1.3B, SAGA consistently improves grammatical quality without requiring human preference labels. Danish parse success increases from 69.0% to 93.8%, Icelandic achieves a +4.5 percentage-point improvement on an independent Stanza evaluation (three-run mean +3.3 percentage points) while native speakers prefer SAGA outputs in 80% of pairwise comparisons, and Norwegian Bokmål improves by +28 percentage points. These results demonstrate that parser-derived supervision is a practical alternative to human preference annotation for grammatical alignment in low-resource languages where high-quality dependency parsers are available.

AI.tldr: SAGA is a parser-guided preference optimisation framework that replaces costly human annotations with dependency-parser supervision to improve grammatical quality in morphologically rich, low-resource languages. It achieves significant parse success gains across Danish, Icelandic, and Norwegian Bokmål without human labels.
AI.motivation: Preference optimisation methods like DPO improve LLMs but require expensive human preference annotations, which are scarce for morphologically rich, low-resource languages. The authors aim to replace human labels with automatically derived parser supervision to enable grammatical alignment in such settings.
AI.method: SAGA (Score-weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment) converts dependency-parser quality judgments into preference pairs for delta-DPO training. It combines parser quality scores with lexical diversity into a composite reward, filters low-information pairs via a reward-gap criterion, and monitors reward hacking to maintain reliable supervision.
AI.result: On GPT-SW3-1.3B: Danish parse success rose from 69.0% to 93.8%; Icelandic improved +4.5 percentage points on Stanza evaluation (three-run mean +3.3 pp) with native speakers preferring SAGA in 80% of pairwise comparisons; Norwegian Bokmål improved by +28 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Parser-derived supervision is a practical, effective alternative to human preference annotation for grammatical alignment in low-resource languages where high-quality dependency parsers exist.

title: ECG-LENS: Lead-Aware Clinical Context Enriched ECG Report Generation and Evaluation
summary: Electrocardiography (ECG) is one of the most widely used non-invasive tools for diagnosing cardiovascular disease, but transforming multi-lead ECG recordings into reliable clinical reports remains challenging. Automating ECG report generation could reduce clinicians' interpretive workload, improve diagnostic efficiency, and expand access to cardiac assessment in underserved communities. Unlike image-based report-generation tasks, ECG interpretation requires the analysis of subtle temporal morphologies, followed by coherent diagnostic reasoning expressed in dense clinical terminology. Existing systems predominantly focus on classification, while current report-generation methods often produce outputs that remain inadequate for practical clinical use. To address these challenges, we propose ECG-LENS, an end-to-end ECG report-generation framework that jointly integrates multi-lead signal modeling, diagnosis-aware representations, and clinically grounded text generation. ECG-LENS combines lead-wise encoders that preserve localized waveform morphology with a global encoder that captures inter-lead dependencies. To guide report generation, we fuse signal representations with clinically enriched textual prompts that condition a GPT-2 decoder. We further introduce an ECG-specific report-preprocessing strategy that helps the model focus on clinically meaningful findings. Finally, because lexical metrics may under- or overestimate report quality, we propose F1-ECGBERT, a BERT-based, ECG-specific metric that measures agreement between diagnostic labels extracted from generated and reference reports. In-domain experiments on PTB-XL and cross-domain evaluation on MIMIC-IV-ECG show that ECG-LENS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with absolute gains of 4.0%, 6.3%, and 11.5% in METEOR, ROUGE-L, and F1-ECGBERT, respectively, over the strongest baselines.

AI.tldr: ECG-LENS is an end-to-end framework for automated ECG report generation that jointly models multi-lead signals, diagnosis-aware representations, and clinical text generation. It introduces lead-wise + global encoders, GPT-2 decoding conditioned on clinically enriched prompts, a specialized preprocessing strategy, and a novel F1-ECGBERT evaluation metric. It achieves SOTA on PTB-XL and MIMIC-IV-ECG.
AI.motivation: Automating ECG report generation can reduce clinicians' interpretive workload and expand cardiac diagnostics access. Existing systems focus on classification rather than report generation, and current generative methods produce clinically inadequate outputs. There is also a lack of reliable ECG-specific evaluation metrics, as lexical metrics like METEOR/ROUGE may misrepresent clinical quality.
AI.method: ECG-LENS uses: (1) lead-wise encoders preserving localized waveform morphology alongside a global encoder capturing inter-lead dependencies; (2) diagnosis-aware representations fused with clinically enriched textual prompts to condition a GPT-2 decoder for report generation; (3) an ECG-specific preprocessing strategy that filters for clinically meaningful findings; and (4) F1-ECGBERT, a BERT-based metric measuring diagnostic label agreement between generated and reference reports by extracting and comparing labels.
AI.result: On PTB-XL (in-domain) and MIMIC-IV-ECG (cross-domain), ECG-LENS outperforms all SOTA baselines with absolute gains of +4.0% METEOR, +6.3% ROUGE-L, and +11.5% F1-ECGBERT over the strongest competing methods.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling localized waveform features, global inter-lead context, and clinically grounded text priors significantly improves ECG report generation. The proposed F1-ECGBERT metric provides a more clinically meaningful evaluation than standard lexical metrics, and the framework generalizes well across datasets.

title: Continual Learning in Transition
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Survey on continual learning in the LLM and agentic-AI era
summary: Classical continual learning (CL) has primarily focused on enabling models to update and retain knowledge through parameter-centric mechanisms, e.g., training strategies, architectural designs, and weight adaptation. However, emerging paradigms are reshaping the scope of CL beyond this traditional model adaptation view. For instance, on-policy learning broadens the space of update mechanisms; test-time training extends CL from the training phase to inference; and external harness components such as memory, skill libraries, and interaction protocols extend the evolutionary boundaries of model capabilities far beyond the static parameter space. Collectively, these developments indicate a transition from parameter-centric learning toward system-level adaptation. To characterize this transition, we examine the evolution of continual learning through three dimensions: When, How, and Where learning occurs. The How dimension encompasses off-policy, on-policy, and beyond-gradient optimization mechanics. The When dimension captures evolution across pre-training, post-training, and inference-time stages. The Where dimension delineates updates occurring within internal parameters versus external structural constraints. Anchored by this tri-axial framework, we systematically survey representative methods, trace the ongoing transition of continual learning, and discuss the key challenges, broader implications, and future directions arising from this paradigm shift.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a tri-axial framework (How, When, Where) to characterize the evolution of continual learning from traditional parameter-centric adaptation toward system-level adaptation, surveying methods across off-policy/on-policy/beyond-gradient optimization, pre-training/post-training/inference stages, and internal vs. external update loci.
AI.motivation: Traditional continual learning research has been narrowly scoped around parameter-centric model adaptation. Emerging paradigms—on-policy learning, test-time training, external memory, skill libraries, and interaction protocols—are expanding CL beyond static parameter spaces, signaling a paradigm shift that lacks a unified conceptual framework to systematically characterize and navigate.
AI.method: The authors introduce a tri-axial taxonomy structured around three dimensions: How (off-policy, on-policy, and beyond-gradient optimization mechanics), When (pre-training, post-training, and inference-time stages), and Where (internal parameter updates vs. external structural components). They systematically survey representative CL methods anchored by this framework, tracing the transition from parameter-centric to system-level adaptation.
AI.result: The survey maps the landscape of modern continual learning along the three axes, identifying that the field is undergoing a fundamental transition from narrow parameter-space adaptation to holistic system-level evolution involving external harnesses, inference-time adaptation, and diverse optimization regimes. Key challenges and future directions arising from this shift are discussed.
AI.conclusion: Continual learning is evolving from a parameter-centric paradigm to a system-level adaptation paradigm. The proposed When-How-Where framework effectively captures this transition and provides a structured lens for understanding existing methods, identifying gaps, and guiding future research toward more flexible, scalable, and robust continual learning systems.

title: GSBF: Gaussian Splatting for Environment-Aware Beamforming
summary: Beamforming plays a key role in multiple-input-multiple-output (MIMO) communication systems. However, conventional beamforming design normally requires accurate instantaneous channel state information (CSI) and iterative optimization, which incur substantial pilot overhead and computational complexity. Recognizing that radio propagation is intrinsically governed by the physical geometry, we develop a 3D Gaussian splatting for environment-aware beamforming (GSBF) pipeline based on multi-modal data, which characterizes the environment through a persistent 3D Gaussian representation. Specifically, GSBF models the environmental scattering response with reciprocity-preserving bidirectional spherical Gaussian (Bi-SG) kernels and performs two-sided electromagnetic rasterization to render an angular propagator map. The rendered map is then aggregated through an over-complete array-manifold dictionary and projected to the constant-modulus beamformers, thereby synthesizing beams directly from the access point (AP) pose and user position without online instantaneous CSI. Simulations demonstrate that GSBF consistently outperforms baselines such as exhaustive beam alignment (EBA) with lower latency.

AI.tldr: GSBF uses 3D Gaussian splatting with bidirectional spherical Gaussian kernels to render angular propagator maps from environmental geometry, enabling direct beam synthesis from AP pose and user position without instantaneous CSI, outperforming exhaustive beam alignment with lower latency.
AI.motivation: Conventional MIMO beamforming requires accurate instantaneous CSI and iterative optimization, causing high pilot overhead and computational complexity. Since radio propagation is fundamentally governed by physical geometry, a persistent environmental representation can eliminate the need for online CSI acquisition.
AI.method: The GSBF pipeline models environmental scattering using reciprocity-preserving bidirectional spherical Gaussian (Bi-SG) kernels within a 3D Gaussian splatting framework. It performs two-sided electromagnetic rasterization to render an angular propagator map, which is then aggregated through an over-complete array-manifold dictionary and projected to constant-modulus beamformers, enabling beam synthesis directly from AP pose and user position.
AI.result: Simulations show GSBF consistently outperforms baselines such as exhaustive beam alignment (EBA) while achieving lower latency.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging persistent 3D environmental representations with 3D Gaussian splatting enables efficient, geometry-aware beamforming that bypasses the need for instantaneous CSI, offering both performance gains and latency reduction.

title: Timestep-Conditioned Transformers for Global Weather Forecasting
summary: Existing machine-learning weather forecasting models rely on predetermined and fixed autoregressive timesteps. The choice of model timestep involves a fundamental trade-off: shorter timesteps (e.g. 1 to 6 hours) finely resolve atmospheric dynamics within the diurnal cycle but increase error accumulation for a given forecast horizon, while longer timesteps (e.g. 24 hours) reduce error accumulation but limit the usability of short-range forecasts where sub-daily predictability is high. In this work, we present GEM-3, a probabilistic global weather model that addresses this trade-off through explicit multi-timestep inference. With a single set of trained weights, the model timestep can be configured at inference time to balance predictability and usability across a broad forecast horizon. Additionally, we find that mixed-timestep training consistently improves rollout stability relative to timestep-specialist models. Under the hood, GEM-3 is a lightweight neighborhood-attention transformer with ~134M parameters on an equirectangular grid with a number of architectural advancements beyond its predecessor GEM-2. The result is a practical forecasting system that couples near-SOTA medium-range probabilistic skill, stable extended-range rollouts, efficient training and inference, and decision-relevant diagnostics.

AI.tldr: GEM-3 is a probabilistic global weather model that uses multi-timestep inference to resolve the trade-off between short autoregressive timesteps (fine diurnal resolution but high error accumulation) and long timesteps (lower error but poor short-range usability), achieving this with a single set of weights and mixed-timestep training for improved rollout stability.
AI.motivation: Existing ML weather models use fixed autoregressive timesteps, forcing a fundamental trade-off: short timesteps (1–6h) resolve diurnal dynamics well but accumulate errors rapidly over long horizons, while long timesteps (24h) reduce error accumulation but sacrifice short-range forecast granularity where sub-daily predictability is high. A single-timestep model cannot optimally serve both use cases.
AI.method: GEM-3 proposes explicit multi-timestep inference: a single set of trained weights supports configurable timesteps at inference time. Mixed-timestep training (vs. timestep-specialist models) is used to improve rollout stability. Architecturally, it is a lightweight neighborhood-attention transformer (~134M parameters) operating on an equirectangular grid, with several advancements over its predecessor GEM-2.
AI.result: The model achieves near state-of-the-art medium-range probabilistic skill with stable extended-range rollouts. Mixed-timestep training consistently improves rollout stability compared to timestep-specialist models. The system also provides efficient training/inference and decision-relevant diagnostics.
AI.conclusion: GEM-3 demonstrates that multi-timestep inference with mixed-timestep training is an effective strategy for building practical, flexible global weather forecasting systems that balance predictability and usability across a wide range of forecast horizons, without requiring separate specialist models.

title: CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities
summary: Student mobility programs such as Erasmus+ enable students to take courses at other universities, broadening their academic and cultural horizons. However, this flexibility also leads to a practical challenge: ensuring that students do not take courses elsewhere that substantially overlap with courses in their home curriculum. In this work, we propose CourseGraph, a methodology that automates the evaluation of external courses based on insights obtained from the process followed by curriculum administrators when assessing courses for inclusion in a degree program. Course- Graph extracts information such as course titles, descriptions, and learning outcomes from the course webpage. Then, this information is represented semantically using a BERT-based language model, after which the pair-wise similarity between courses can be computed. This information is then used by a Random Forest classifier to determine whether a candidate course abroad overlaps with a course already contained in the student's curriculum. We evaluate CourseGraph using (1) the Computer Science program at Eindhoven University of Technology, which contains information about courses with substantial overlap, and (2) six approved international programs from students enrolled in the Computer Science program at Lund University, including the corresponding decisions made by a curriculum administrator. The experimental results indicate that CourseGraph provides an effective approach for identifying overlapping courses and supporting curriculum alignment across universities.

AI.tldr: CourseGraph is a BERT-based methodology with a Random Forest classifier that automates the detection of overlapping courses across universities, helping curriculum administrators evaluate whether external courses duplicate content in a student's home degree program.
AI.motivation: Student mobility programs like Erasmus+ allow cross-university course enrollment, but this creates a practical challenge: ensuring students don't take external courses that substantially overlap with their home curriculum. Currently, this evaluation is done manually by curriculum administrators, which is time-consuming and inconsistent.
AI.method: CourseGraph extracts course titles, descriptions, and learning outcomes from course webpages, then represents this information semantically using a BERT-based language model to compute pairwise course similarity. A Random Forest classifier then uses these similarity features to determine whether a candidate course abroad overlaps with courses in the student's home curriculum.
AI.result: Evaluated on two datasets — the Computer Science program at Eindhoven University of Technology (containing known overlapping courses) and six approved international programs from Lund University with corresponding administrator decisions — CourseGraph demonstrated effective identification of overlapping courses and supported curriculum alignment across institutions.
AI.conclusion: CourseGraph provides an effective, automated approach for identifying course overlap across universities, offering a practical tool to assist curriculum administrators in evaluating external courses within student mobility programs.

title: A Six-Dimensional Taxonomy of Post-Training Adaptation Techniques with Applications in AI Governance
summary: Post-training adaptation has become central to modern machine learning practice and includes techniques such as retraining, fine-tuning, parameter-efficient adaptation, alignment, retrieval augmentation, model editing, unlearning, calibration, and Multimodal Instruction Tuning. However, the literature remains fragmented across technique families, model classes, and deployment contexts, making it difficult to compare methods or describe how a trained model has been modified. This survey synthesizes the post-training adaptation literature and introduces a six-dimensional taxonomy organized by mechanism, goal, data requirement, persistence, structural scope, and model type. The taxonomy distinguishes commonly conflated terms such as fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, and prompting, and shows how adaptation strategies evolve from traditional machine learning through deep learning, foundation models, large language models, and multimodal large language models. It also maps relationships among techniques, including inheritance, supersession, hybridization, and layered deployment stacks. The resulting vocabulary can support technical documentation, model-change tracking, and governance analysis. The survey concludes by identifying open challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, persistent inference-time adaptation, unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance-aware post-training workflows.

AI.tldr: This survey synthesizes the fragmented post-training adaptation literature by introducing a six-dimensional taxonomy (mechanism, goal, data requirement, persistence, structural scope, model type) that disambiguates commonly conflated terms and maps evolutionary relationships among adaptation techniques across traditional ML, deep learning, foundation models, LLMs, and multimodal LLMs.
AI.motivation: The post-training adaptation literature is highly fragmented across technique families (retraining, fine-tuning, PEFT, alignment, RAG, model editing, unlearning, calibration, etc.), model classes, and deployment contexts, making method comparison and clear description of model modifications difficult. A unified taxonomy is needed.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comprehensive literature survey and propose a six-dimensional taxonomy: (1) mechanism — how adaptation operates; (2) goal — the objective; (3) data requirement — what data is needed; (4) persistence — whether changes are permanent or transient; (5) structural scope — which model components are modified; and (6) model type — the class of model being adapted. They also map inter-technique relationships: inheritance, supersession, hybridization, and layered deployment stacks.
AI.result: The taxonomy successfully distinguishes commonly conflated terms (e.g., fine-tuning vs. retrieval augmentation vs. prompting) and traces the evolution of adaptation strategies across paradigms. The resulting vocabulary supports technical documentation, model-change tracking, and governance analysis.
AI.conclusion: Open challenges remain in evaluation standardization, reproducibility, persistent inference-time adaptation, reliable unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance-aware post-training workflows.

title: GAUGE: A Measurement-Grounded Benchmark for Physical Fidelity in Simulation Engines and Video World Models
summary: Physics engines facilitate large-scale training and evaluation for embodied intelligence, while generative video world models are emerging as implicit simulators of future states and interactions. However, existing evaluations of physical fidelity are often conducted in isolation and rely heavily on perceptual similarity or human judgments, providing limited insight into which physical principles or parameters are violated. We introduce GAUGE, a real-world-grounded diagnostic benchmark for jointly evaluating how numerical simulators and generative video world models reproduce or deviate from real-world physics. It comprises 22 controlled task families covering rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformable objects. Grounded in real-world trajectories and paired with calibrated physical metadata, uncertainty annotations, and task-specific observables, these tasks cover fundamental physical processes including collision, friction, momentum transfer, oscillation, self-contact, and deformation across diverse materials and conditions. We benchmark Isaac Sim, Genesis, and Newton on 14 task families using generalized trajectory errors, and evaluate 6 image-to-video models on 5 rigid-body tasks by testing physical-law consistency and the temporal stability of inferred parameters. Our results reveal no uniformly faithful physics engine, with the largest discrepancies arising in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation. We further find that video world models can produce trajectories with the expected equation form while recovering incorrect accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing. GAUGE lays the groundwork for developing more physically faithful simulators and world models for embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: GAUGE is a real-world-grounded benchmark with 22 task families for jointly evaluating physics engines and generative video world models on physical fidelity, revealing that no simulator is uniformly faithful and video models often recover correct equation forms but incorrect physical parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of physical fidelity in simulators and video world models are conducted in isolation, rely on perceptual similarity or human judgments, and fail to identify which specific physical principles or parameters are violated.
AI.method: GAUGE comprises 22 controlled task families spanning rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformable objects, grounded in real-world trajectories with calibrated physical metadata, uncertainty annotations, and task-specific observables. It uses generalized trajectory errors for physics engines and tests physical-law consistency plus temporal stability of inferred parameters for video models.
AI.result: No uniformly faithful physics engine emerged; Isaac Sim, Genesis, and Newton showed largest discrepancies in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation. Six image-to-video models produced trajectories with correct equation forms but recovered incorrect accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing.
AI.conclusion: GAUGE provides a foundation for developing more physically faithful simulators and world models for embodied intelligence by enabling systematic, principle-level diagnosis of physical violations.

title: MetaboLLM: a metabolomics-specialized large language model for biochemical knowledge integration and predictive metabolite graph construction
comment: 60 pages, 3 figures, 16 tables; includes Supplementary Information
summary: Metabolomics knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous resources and remains difficult to translate into predictive representations. We developed MetaboLLM, a metabolomics-specialized large language model adapted through continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and structured retrieval, together with MetaboLLM-GIN, which converts generated biochemical descriptions into metabolite graphs for patient-level prediction using a graph isomorphism network. Across four backbone families, MetaboLLM outperformed corresponding base and medically adapted models on metabolomics knowledge, relational, and description tasks, and transferred to an external public benchmark. MetaboLLM-GIN achieved the highest AUC for stress hyperglycemia prediction after coronary artery bypass grafting (0.8616) and postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification (0.8123), outperforming conventional models, alternative graph constructions, and graphs generated from unadapted or non-retrieval LLM configurations. Model interpretation further produced biologically meaningful findings in both applications. These results show that domain-specialized language models can organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive and interpretable metabolite graph representations.

AI.tldr: MetaboLLM is a metabolomics-specialized LLM that, together with MetaboLLM-GIN (a graph isomorphism network using LLM-generated metabolite graphs), outperforms general and medical models on biochemical tasks and achieves state-of-the-art AUCs for stress hyperglycemia prediction and hormone-regimen classification, with interpretable outputs.
AI.motivation: Metabolomics knowledge is siloed across heterogeneous databases and difficult to convert into predictive, machine-learning-ready representations. Existing models lack the domain specialization needed to bridge unstructured biochemical text with structured metabolite-level predictions.
AI.method: The authors developed MetaboLLM through a multi-stage pipeline: (1) continual pretraining on metabolomics corpora, (2) supervised fine-tuning on domain-specific tasks, and (3) structured retrieval augmentation. Separately, MetaboLLM-GIN uses MetaboLLM to generate biochemical descriptions of metabolites, which are then converted into molecular graphs and processed by a graph isomorphism network (GIN) for patient-level prediction. The framework was evaluated across four LLM backbone families on knowledge, relational, and description benchmarks, and validated on two clinical tasks.
AI.result: MetaboLLM consistently outperformed both base and medically adapted LLMs on metabolomics-specific evaluations and transferred successfully to an external public benchmark. MetaboLLM-GIN achieved the highest AUC for stress hyperglycemia prediction post-CABG (0.8616) and postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification (0.8123), surpassing conventional models, alternative graph constructions, and graphs from unadapted or non-retrieval LLMs. Model interpretation yielded biologically plausible insights in both clinical applications.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specialized LLMs can effectively organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive and interpretable metabolite graph representations, demonstrating a viable paradigm for integrating unstructured metabolomics knowledge with structured machine learning for clinical prediction.

title: VLMs for Videogame Data Annotation
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents have revolutionized how engineers approach complex problems in real-world applications. Their adoption in video games is on the other hand limited by the extreme variability of the synthetic scenarios and their poor compliance with real-world physics. Here we investigate the use of VLMs for annotating video game frame sequences with reward signals, a task with several potential applications including, among others, conditioned training and offline reinforcement learning. We show that VLMs often struggle to answer basic questions on racing video games (although we observed a similar behavior on other game genres) and discuss countermeasures such as VLM output mixing and prompt optimization. We also show how input sequence length, resolution, and question batching affect the annotation quality and its token consumption.

AI.tldr: VLMs struggle to annotate video game frames with reward signals due to synthetic variability and physics non-compliance. The paper evaluates VLM performance on racing games, finding basic question-answering difficulties, and explores countermeasures including output mixing, prompt optimization, and the effects of sequence length, resolution, and batching on annotation quality and token cost.
AI.motivation: While VLMs and AI agents excel in real-world applications, their adoption in video games is hindered by high synthetic scenario variability and poor real-world physics compliance. The authors aim to explore VLMs for annotating game frame sequences with reward signals — useful for conditioned training and offline RL — but find that VLMs struggle even with basic game understanding.
AI.method: The paper empirically evaluates VLMs on racing video game frame sequences, testing their ability to answer basic questions and generate reward annotations. The authors systematically vary input sequence length, frame resolution, and question batching strategies. They also propose and assess countermeasures: VLM output mixing (ensembling multiple VLM responses) and prompt optimization techniques.
AI.result: VLMs frequently fail to answer basic questions on racing video games, with similar behavior observed across other genres. Input sequence length, resolution, and question batching all significantly affect both annotation quality and token consumption. Countermeasures such as output mixing and prompt optimization partially mitigate these limitations.
AI.conclusion: VLMs are currently unreliable for annotating video game frame sequences with reward signals. Careful tuning of input parameters and the use of mitigation strategies like output mixing and prompt engineering can improve performance, but fundamental limitations remain due to the domain gap between synthetic game environments and real-world training data.

title: RxnCLF: Contrastive Transformation-Aware Reaction Foundation Model for Improved Reactivity Prediction
summary: Reaction yield prediction remains challenging because labeled data are scarce and reaction space is both combinatorially large and sparsely populated, limiting the generalization of existing reaction representations. String-, fingerprint-, and graph-based reaction encodings only partially capture chemical transformations, making accurate prediction difficult for reactions with complex substrates. We propose reaction contrastive learning foundation (RxnCLF), a self-supervised contrastive framework for reaction representation learning. RxnCLF is built on a condensed reaction graph (CRG) that unifies reactant and product information into a single graph, enabling the model to learn explicit and enriched transformation structure rather than disconnected graphs. Pretrained on 1.7 million Pistachio reactions, RxnCLF learns a compact and continuous latent space that captures both reaction-center features and broader side chain contexts, making it transformation-aware and chemically interpretable. Fine-tuned on multiple yield prediction benchmarks, including Buchwald-Hartwig, Pd-catalyzed BH coupling, and proprietary HTE C-N coupling and amide formation datasets, RxnCLF consistently outperforms graph and sequence-based baselines, improving R2 and achieving the best performance overall. Our results highlight the promise of CRG-based RxnCLF as a scalable reaction foundation model, with the potential to generalize across broader reaction spaces and support diverse downstream reaction informatics tasks, including regioselectivity prediction, enantioselectivity prediction, and reaction condition optimization.

AI.tldr: RxnCLF introduces a self-supervised contrastive learning framework built on Condensed Reaction Graphs (CRG) that unifies reactants and products into a single graph representation. Pretrained on 1.7M reactions, it learns a chemically interpretable latent space and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple reaction yield prediction benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reaction yield prediction is hindered by scarce labeled data and a combinatorially large, sparsely populated reaction space. Existing string-, fingerprint-, and graph-based encodings only partially capture chemical transformations, especially for reactions with complex substrates, limiting generalization.
AI.method: RxnCLF employs a self-supervised contrastive learning framework built on a Condensed Reaction Graph (CRG) that merges reactant and product information into a single unified graph. This design enables the model to learn explicit transformation structures rather than disconnected representations. The model is pretrained on 1.7 million Pistachio reactions and then fine-tuned for downstream yield prediction tasks.
AI.result: Fine-tuned on multiple benchmarks—Buchwald-Hartwig, Pd-catalyzed BH coupling, and proprietary HTE C-N coupling and amide formation datasets—RxnCLF consistently outperforms both graph-based and sequence-based baselines, achieving superior R² scores and the best overall performance.
AI.conclusion: The CRG-based RxnCLF framework demonstrates strong potential as a scalable reaction foundation model, capable of generalizing across broader reaction spaces and supporting diverse downstream tasks such as regio- and enantioselectivity prediction and reaction condition optimization.

title: Training a Conditioned Video Game Agent on a VLM Annotated Dataset
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a powerful but far from easy-to-use technique for policy learning. In the specific case of video games, access to the game engine is required to get rewards for training (e.g. to collect rewards from the environment). Furthermore, the proper identification and weighting of the rewards generally requires a difficult trial-and-error approach. Lastly, rewards are often sparse and understanding how they eventually affect the learned policy is a non-trivial exercise. To ease these issues we propose annotating a video game dataset with Vision Language Models (VLMs) instructed to extract human defined rewards. We show that offline RL can then be used to train a conditioned agent that responds accordingly to the desired returns and we discuss the difficulties and limitations that emerged in our early experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using Vision Language Models (VLMs) to annotate video game datasets with human-defined reward signals, enabling offline reinforcement learning for training conditioned agents that respond to desired returns, while also discussing early experimental challenges.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement Learning for video games suffers from three key pain points: (1) requiring direct access to the game engine for reward collection, (2) the trial-and-error burden of identifying and weighting rewards, and (3) the difficulty of interpreting how sparse rewards influence the learned policy. The authors seek to bypass these issues by leveraging VLMs for reward extraction from offline datasets.
AI.method: The authors annotate an existing video game dataset using Vision Language Models (VLMs) that are prompted to extract human-defined reward signals from gameplay observations. This annotated dataset is then used to perform offline reinforcement learning, training a return-conditioned agent — i.e., an agent whose behavior can be modulated by specifying a desired return value.
AI.result: The paper reports that offline RL with VLM-annotated rewards can successfully train a conditioned agent that responds to desired returns. However, the authors also present and discuss various difficulties and limitations encountered during these early experiments.
AI.conclusion: VLM-based reward annotation combined with offline RL presents a promising direction for reducing the engineering overhead of traditional RL in video game domains, though significant challenges remain to be addressed in future work.

title: Hypothesis Testing with Conditional Queries: Learnability and the Value of Interaction
summary: Model evaluations may fix all tests before observing any responses or select later tests using earlier responses. We study this choice in a conditional-query model on a finite outcome space $\mathcal{X}$ with $|\mathcal{X}|=N$. We first ask which pairs of distribution classes can be reliably distinguished. We then ask how many additional queries are required to match an adaptive tester when all queried events must be fixed in advance. We show that learnability holds if and only if the two classes have positive separation in their pairwise conditional probabilities. When this separation is zero, the optimal worst-case error is exactly $1/2$ at every finite query budget. For any $T$-query adaptive policy and any $ρ\in (0,1)$, we construct a randomized non-adaptive procedure using $O(N^2(T + \log(1/ρ)))$ pair queries chosen before any response is observed. Its simulated transcript is within $ρ$ in total variation of the adaptive transcript, uniformly over all distributions in the model. We also construct a matching family with constant adaptive query complexity and $Ω_\varepsilon(N^2)$ non-adaptive query complexity. Consequently, the worst-case fixed-error adaptivity gap is $Θ_\varepsilon(N^2)$. Thus interaction can reduce the required number of tests by a quadratic factor, but the apparent exponential branching of an interactive evaluation does not yield an exponential query advantage.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the power of adaptive vs. non-adaptive testing in conditional-query models. The key finding: adaptivity provides at most a quadratic reduction in query complexity (Θ(N²) gap), but no exponential advantage. Learnability between two distribution classes holds iff their pairwise conditional probabilities have positive separation.
AI.motivation: Model evaluations often face a design choice: fix all test queries in advance (non-adaptive) or select later queries based on earlier responses (adaptive). Understanding the fundamental gap between these two paradigms reveals how much benefit interaction truly provides. Prior intuition suggested interaction might yield exponential savings; this paper investigates whether such an exponential branching advantage exists in conditional-query models.
AI.method: The authors work in a conditional-query model over a finite outcome space X of size N. They analyze pairs of distribution classes, establishing precise conditions for reliable distinguishability (positive separation in pairwise conditional probabilities). They construct a randomized non-adaptive procedure using O(N²(T + log(1/ρ))) pair queries that simulates any T-query adaptive policy within ρ total variation distance, uniformly over all distributions. A matching lower bound family with constant adaptive complexity but Ω_ε(N²) non-adaptive complexity establishes tightness.
AI.result: Three main results: (1) Learnability between two distribution classes holds iff their pairwise conditional probabilities have positive separation; otherwise optimal worst-case error is exactly 1/2 at any finite budget. (2) A non-adaptive simulation of any T-query adaptive policy requires O(N²(T + log(1/ρ))) queries. (3) A matching lower bound shows constant adaptive complexity vs. Ω_ε(N²) non-adaptive complexity, yielding a tight Θ_ε(N²) adaptivity gap for fixed-error testing.
AI.conclusion: Interaction reduces the required number of tests by a quadratic factor — significant but far from the exponential savings that the branching structure of interactive evaluations might suggest. The adaptivity gap is exactly Θ_ε(N²), rigorously characterizing the power of adaptivity in conditional-query models.

title: Stability of Ranking-dependent Pair-wise Comparison Patterns in the Analytic Hierarchy Process
summary: The paper addresses several ranking-dependent decision support methods. Ordinal information on compared objects can be used to improve the quality of expert data during estimation and help reduce the number of comparisons that the experts need to perform. In the paper we compare three incomplete ranking-dependent pair-wise comparison patterns which can be used in the Analytic Hierarchy Process - Best-worst method, Best-Second Best (Top 2) method, and the original maximum difference method. The first two comparison patterns (and respective methods) are incomplete, while the third can be a complete one. We determine conditions under which these three methods can be compared in terms of stability to expert errors. We also present the results of a simulation-type experiment, in which the three methods are compared. The research allows us to define the most stable incomplete ranking-dependent pair-wise comparison pattern and reduce the number of comparisons without loss of credibility of expert session results. The research contributes to algorithmic, cognitive, and applied aspects of decision support in uncertain environments.

AI.tldr: The paper compares three pairwise comparison patterns used in AHP — Best-Worst Method, Top 2 (Best-Second Best) Method, and Maximum Difference Method — to identify which incomplete ranking-dependent pattern offers the greatest stability against expert errors while minimizing comparisons.
AI.motivation: To improve expert data quality and reduce the cognitive burden of pairwise comparisons in decision support, the authors aim to determine which incomplete ranking-dependent comparison pattern is most robust to expert errors without sacrificing result credibility.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comparative analysis of three pairwise comparison patterns (Best-Worst, Best-Second Best, Maximum Difference) within the Analytic Hierarchy Process framework, establishing theoretical conditions for comparability in terms of error stability, and validating findings through a simulation experiment.
AI.result: The research identifies the most stable incomplete ranking-dependent pairwise comparison pattern, demonstrating that the number of required comparisons can be reduced without loss of credibility in expert session outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Incomplete ranking-dependent pairwise comparison patterns can maintain decision quality while reducing expert workload; the findings contribute to algorithmic, cognitive, and applied aspects of decision support under uncertainty.

title: The Tamed Subgradient Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm beyond Convexity
summary: We study the problem of sampling from target distributions whose potentials are simultaneously non-smooth, subject to superlinear gradient growth, and non-convex.
