We introduce the Subgradient Tamed Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (SG-TULA), a discretisation of the Langevin diffusion that operates directly on subgradients, without relying on computationally demanding smoothing procedures. To handle the superlinear regime, taming techniques are employed to produce a stable, explicit scheme. We derive non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 distance, with all constants tracked explicitly in terms of dimension and inverse temperature, improving upon the currently known rates for subgradient-based Langevin algorithms. We further provide excess risk estimates for the associated optimisation problem. We verify the assumptions, with explicit constants, for the regularized pretraining potential of a LLM in the GPT-2 lineage and the boosted coordinate-wise variant of SG-TULA pretrains the former competitively against finetuned AdamW and Muon, for which no comparable non-asymptotic guarantees are presently available.

AI.tldr: Introduces SG-TULA, a subgradient-based tamed Langevin algorithm for sampling from non-smooth, non-convex potentials with superlinear gradient growth. Provides non-asymptotic Wasserstein-2 convergence bounds with explicit dimensional and temperature dependence, excess risk guarantees, and validates the approach by pretraining a GPT-2-style LLM competitively against AdamW and Muon.
AI.motivation: Existing Langevin-based sampling methods struggle with potentials that are simultaneously non-smooth (requiring subgradients), non-convex, and exhibit superlinear gradient growth. Standard approaches rely on computationally expensive smoothing or fail to provide non-asymptotic guarantees. The authors aim to fill this gap with an algorithm that operates directly on subgradients while maintaining theoretical tractability and practical efficacy, particularly for large-scale problems like LLM pretraining.
AI.method: The authors propose SG-TULA, a discretization of the Langevin diffusion that combines: (1) direct subgradient evaluation (avoiding smoothing), and (2) taming techniques to control superlinear growth. They derive non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 distance with explicit constants tracking dimension and inverse temperature dependence. Excess risk bounds for the associated optimization problem are also provided. The method is extended to a boosted coordinate-wise variant for practical LLM pretraining.
AI.result: SG-TULA achieves improved non-asymptotic convergence rates in Wasserstein-2 distance compared to existing subgradient-based Langevin algorithms, with all constants explicitly tracked. The assumptions are verified for the regularized pretraining potential of a GPT-2 lineage LLM. Empirically, the boosted coordinate-wise variant pretrains competitively against fine-tuned AdamW and Muon optimizers, for which no comparable non-asymptotic guarantees exist.
AI.conclusion: SG-TULA offers the first algorithm for non-smooth, non-convex sampling under superlinear gradient growth with explicit non-asymptotic guarantees and practical viability at scale. The theoretical improvements over prior subgradient Langevin methods, combined with competitive LLM pretraining results, suggest tamed subgradient schemes are a promising direction for both sampling and optimization in large-scale machine learning.

title: Temporal Bridges for Spatial Resolution: Enhancing Climate Data Super-Resolution with Bidirectional Alignment
summary: High-resolution climate data is crucial for meteorological predictions and for informing decision support across diverse domains. However, the acquisition of such high-resolution climate information is often prohibitively costly, necessitating the development of data-driven meteorological prediction models. These models aim to generate fine-grained climate data from low-resolution inputs, a process termed climate data super-resolution (SR). Nevertheless, recent advancements in deep learning for climate data SR have primarily focused on leveraging single-frame spatial information, largely neglecting the temporal correlations between different time frames that could enhance SR outcomes. Furthermore, climate data are inherently stochastic and noisy, rendering widely used temporal alignment methods, such as optical flow models, ineffective in this context. Consequently, the development of a framework tailored for climate data SR that effectively captures implicit temporal correlations remains an unresolved challenge. To this end, we propose a novel Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional temporal alignment. In essence, our framework establishes a temporal bridge to enhance spatial resolution in climate data SR through bidirectional alignment, leading to improved SR performance. Within this framework, Paired Latent Mapping achieves spatial alignment and noise reduction by unifying latent spaces. Then a Bidirectional Temporal Alignment captures temporal correlations by training forward and backward networks on consecutive latent frames. Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution then optimizes the entire framework for climate data SR. Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets demonstrated the superior performance of our framework.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Temporal-Enhanced framework for climate data super-resolution that uses bidirectional temporal alignment to exploit inter-frame correlations, overcoming limitations of single-frame spatial methods. The framework integrates Paired Latent Mapping for spatial alignment/noise reduction, Bidirectional Temporal Alignment for capturing temporal dependencies, and Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution for end-to-end optimization, demonstrating superior performance on large-scale real-world climate datasets.
AI.motivation: Climate data super-resolution (SR) is essential for cost-effective high-resolution meteorological predictions. Existing deep learning methods predominantly rely on single-frame spatial information and ignore temporal correlations across frames. Additionally, climate data's inherent stochasticity and noise make standard temporal alignment techniques like optical flow ineffective, leaving a gap for a framework that can effectively model implicit temporal dependencies in climate SR.
AI.method: The proposed Temporal-Enhanced framework comprises three key components: (1) Paired Latent Mapping, which unifies latent spaces of low- and high-resolution frames to achieve spatial alignment and noise reduction; (2) Bidirectional Temporal Alignment, which trains forward and backward networks on consecutive latent frames to capture temporal correlations; and (3) Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution, which jointly optimizes the entire framework for climate data SR.
AI.result: Experiments on large-scale real-world climate datasets show that the proposed framework achieves superior super-resolution performance compared to existing methods, validating the effectiveness of bidirectional temporal alignment in enhancing spatial resolution.
AI.conclusion: The Temporal-Enhanced framework successfully addresses the underexploited temporal dimension in climate data SR by establishing a temporal bridge via bidirectional alignment. This approach significantly improves SR quality, demonstrating that modeling implicit temporal correlations is both feasible and beneficial for climate data super-resolution tasks.

title: Surv-IPTB: An Attention-Based Model for Estimating Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit with Survival Data
summary: This work presents a novel attention-based framework for estimating the Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit (IPTB) in survival analysis contexts. The proposed model, called Surv-IPTB, directly quantifies the probability that a specific patient will experience extended survival time under treatment versus control. We reformulate IPTB estimation as a binary classification problem, leveraging pairwise patient comparisons across treatment and control cohorts. The framework incorporates a principled handling of right-censored observations through imprecise probability representations, where uncertain treatment effects are characterized by interval-valued probabilities. An attention mechanism with learnable query-key transformations enables flexible, data-driven aggregation of pairwise comparisons, while simultaneously learning soft class probabilities for censored cases. Through extensive experiments on synthetic datasets with complex nonlinear structures, including spiral, bell-shaped, and circular feature spaces, we demonstrate that our approach maintains robust performance across varying censoring rates and treatment effect strengths. The model consistently outperforms meta-learner baselines (T-learner and S-learner) equipped with random survival forests, Cox proportional hazards, and Beran estimators, particularly in challenging nonlinear scenarios where conventional methods exhibit significant degradation. The results establish the proposed attention-based framework as a scalable and statistically principled solution for personalized treatment benefit assessment in survival settings. The code implementing the model is publicly available.

AI.tldr: Surv-IPTB is an attention-based framework that estimates individual probability of treatment benefit in survival analysis by reformulating the problem as binary classification with pairwise patient comparisons, using imprecise probability to handle censoring and attention mechanisms for flexible aggregation.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for individualized treatment effect estimation in survival contexts struggle with complex nonlinear relationships and right-censored data. There is a need for a principled, scalable framework that directly quantifies the probability of treatment benefit for individual patients rather than relying on conditional average treatment effect estimates.
AI.method: The Surv-IPTB framework reformulates IPTB estimation as binary classification using pairwise comparisons between patients in treatment and control cohorts. Right-censored observations are handled via imprecise probability representations producing interval-valued probabilities. An attention mechanism with learnable query-key transformations enables data-driven aggregation of pairwise comparisons and learns soft class probabilities for censored cases. The approach is evaluated against T-learner and S-learner baselines using random survival forests, Cox models, and Beran estimators on synthetic datasets with nonlinear structures (spiral, bell-shaped, circular).
AI.result: Surv-IPTB consistently outperformed all meta-learner baselines across varying censoring rates and treatment effect strengths, with particularly pronounced advantages in challenging nonlinear scenarios (spiral, bell-shaped, circular feature spaces) where conventional methods showed significant performance degradation.
AI.conclusion: The attention-based framework provides a scalable and statistically principled solution for personalized treatment benefit assessment in survival settings, with strong empirical performance in complex nonlinear environments and robust handling of censored data.

title: AgentOPSD: Recursive Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards constructs trajectory-level advantage estimates, yet it often fails to credit the few pivotal decisions that determine outcomes in long-horizon, multi-turn agentic tasks. Recent work introduces privileged self-distillation for credit assignment, providing denser supervision, but it remains unclear how such local signals should represent sequential credit. We propose AgentOPSD, a critic-free, recursive method for turn-level credit assignment in agentic reinforcement learning. AgentOPSD aggregates token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence and recursively updates a Bayesian belief state in log-odds space. This yields a principled reweighting scheme that converts sparse outcome supervision into turn-level credit signals and identifies pivotal turns through the marginal belief revision between consecutive states. The method is fully compatible with standard policy optimization and requires neither an additional critic nor extra rollouts. We evaluate AgentOPSD on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA using Qwen2.5 models at two scales (3B and 7B). AgentOPSD outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines, achieving 89.1% success on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablation studies attribute the gains to turn-level aggregation and history-dependent recursive belief updates.

AI.tldr: AgentOPSD introduces a critic-free, recursive Bayesian method that converts sparse outcome rewards into turn-level credit signals for agentic RL, outperforming GRPO and self-distillation baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA.
AI.motivation: Standard RL with verifiable rewards uses trajectory-level advantage estimates that fail to identify the few critical decisions in long-horizon, multi-turn agentic tasks. While privileged self-distillation provides denser supervision, it lacks a principled framework for representing sequential credit across turns.
AI.method: AgentOPSD aggregates token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence, then recursively updates a Bayesian belief state in log-odds space. This produces a reweighting scheme that converts sparse outcome signals into turn-level credit, with pivotal turns identified via marginal belief revision between consecutive states. The method is critic-free, requires no extra rollouts, and is compatible with standard policy optimization.
AI.result: AgentOPSD achieves 89.1% success on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B, outperforming GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA using Qwen2.5 models at 3B and 7B scales. Ablations confirm gains stem from turn-level aggregation and history-dependent recursive belief updates.
AI.conclusion: Turn-level credit assignment via recursive Bayesian belief updates in log-odds space effectively addresses the credit attribution problem in agentic RL, yielding significant gains without the overhead of a critic network or additional rollouts.

title: BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians
summary: We accelerate a family of algorithms for neural network quantization whose geometry is informed by any Kronecker-factored approximation of the Hessian. GPTQ-style adaptive rounding typically uses one-sided information derived from input activations. Two-sided Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations can additionally capture correlations across output coordinates, but applying GPTQ directly in the vectorized weight domain is computationally expensive. Building on the two-sided adaptive-rounding formulation used by BoA and YAQA, we introduce BaKron, an efficient solver that combines anti-diagonal parallelism with a recursive divide-and-conquer construction. For an $m\times n$ weight matrix, BaKron uses $O(m+n)$ sequential steps while reducing the total work from $O(m^2n^2)$ to $O(mn(m+n))$. Thus, it matches the cubic scaling of GPTQ while exploiting richer curvature information. Moreover, BaKron is modular with respect to both the base quantizer and the Hessian estimator. We also provide practical benchmarks, consider a range of Hessians that BaKron can be called with, find an efficient technique to compute these Hessians, and evaluate the algorithm experimentally.

AI.tldr: BaKron is an efficient two-sided adaptive rounding algorithm for neural network quantization that uses Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations. It reduces total work from O(m²n²) to O(mn(m+n)) via anti-diagonal parallelism and recursive divide-and-conquer, matching GPTQ's cubic scaling while exploiting richer curvature information from both input and output correlations.
AI.motivation: GPTQ-style quantization uses one-sided Hessian information from input activations only. Two-sided Kronecker-factored approximations (as in BoA and YAQA) capture correlations across output coordinates too, but applying them in the vectorized weight domain is computationally prohibitive. The authors seek an efficient solver that retains the richer two-sided curvature information without the O(m²n²) cost.
AI.method: BaKron reformulates two-sided adaptive rounding using a recursive divide-and-conquer strategy combined with anti-diagonal parallelism. This construction processes the m×n weight matrix in O(m+n) sequential steps, reducing total work to O(mn(m+n)). The solver is modular: it works with any base quantizer and any Kronecker-factored Hessian estimator. The authors also develop an efficient technique to compute these Hessians in practice.
AI.result: BaKron achieves cubic scaling O(mn(m+n)), matching GPTQ's asymptotic complexity while using richer two-sided curvature. Practical benchmarks and experimental evaluations demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness across various Hessian estimators.
AI.conclusion: BaKron makes two-sided Kronecker-factored adaptive rounding computationally practical, enabling quantization algorithms to leverage both input- and output-space curvature at a cost comparable to one-sided methods like GPTQ.

title: OPERA: Operator-residual feedback for reliable autonomous optical experiments with language-model agents
summary: Autonomous agents choose actions using scores that may not reflect experimental success. We developed OPERA, an operator-residual framework for optical experiments. It represents experimental actions as optical operators and evaluates their outcomes using physically interpretable residuals. Operators specify executable changes to measurement, control or reconstruction, while residuals report departures from specified physical conditions. The agent uses both to select, combine or generate operators, and physical performance is evaluated independently against a withheld reference. Across three optical tasks, score-only feedback produced score increases without physical improvement in 23.6--39.0\% of decisions, compared with 0.9--1.9\% for operator-residual feedback. Operator-residual feedback increased the probability of reaching and maintaining task targets and reduced experimental budgets. Protocols selected in digital twins were transferred to three optical instruments, and repeated experiments showed a lower projection budget in structured-light reconstruction. Together, operators and residuals guide autonomous decisions using measurable physical evidence.

AI.tldr: OPERA is an operator-residual framework for autonomous optical experiments that uses physically interpretable residual feedback instead of abstract scores, dramatically reducing decisions that increase scores without genuine physical improvement (from 23.6–39.0% down to 0.9–1.9%) and improving task-target attainment and experimental budget efficiency.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents in experimental settings typically rely on abstract scores to guide decision-making, but these scores can be gamed or fail to reflect actual physical performance. The authors identify that score-only feedback frequently produces "reward hacking" — score increases without corresponding physical improvement — undermining the reliability of autonomous experimentation.
AI.method: The OPERA framework represents experimental actions as optical operators (executable changes to measurement, control, or reconstruction) and evaluates outcomes using physically interpretable residuals (departures from specified physical conditions). The agent uses both operators and residuals to select, combine, or generate new operators. Physical performance is independently evaluated against a withheld reference. Protocols were designed in digital twins and then transferred to three real optical instruments for validation.
AI.result: Across three optical tasks, score-only feedback yielded score increases without physical improvement in 23.6–39.0% of decisions, versus only 0.9–1.9% for operator-residual feedback. Operator-residual feedback also increased the probability of reaching and maintaining task targets and reduced experimental budgets. In structured-light reconstruction, repeated experiments on real instruments demonstrated a lower projection budget when using operator-residual-selected protocols.
AI.conclusion: Operators and residuals together provide a physically grounded alternative to abstract scoring for guiding autonomous experimental decisions, yielding more reliable physical performance, reduced susceptibility to reward hacking, and efficient use of experimental resources across both simulated and real-world optical instruments.

title: On-Policy Self-Distillation without Any Supervision
summary: On-policy (Self-)Distillation (OPD / OPSD) has shown strong potential for post-training large language models (LLMs). However, existing methods still rely heavily on external supervision, including ground-truth signals, environmental feedback, or guidance from larger models, and therefore fall short of genuine "self"-distillation. In this study, we show that on-policy self-distillation can be achieved using only a model's own generations via internal consistency. We propose Unsupervised On-Policy Self-Distillation (U-OPSD). U-OPSD first samples multiple rollouts and constructs a pseudo-solution by majority vote under a self-consistency threshold. It then conditions a teacher distribution on the shortest pseudo-solution and distills it into prefixes of the model's longest incorrect completion, allowing the model to correct itself precisely where it is confidently wrong. Across diverse benchmarks, base models, and training settings, U-OPSD consistently improves over the base models and matches or surpasses supervised methods with ground truth (GT), such as OPSD and GRPO. On AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, MATH500, and AMC23, U-OPSD improves over the base model by 8.5% and 10.7% on Qwen3 non-thinking mode at the 4B and 8B scales, respectively, and outperforms OPSD by an average of 3.2% and 2.3%. In thinking mode, U-OPSD remains on par with OPSD, outperforming it by 0.9% at 4B and matching it at 8B, while surpassing GRPO by 0.7% and 1.1%, respectively.

AI.tldr: U-OPSD is an unsupervised on-policy self-distillation method for LLMs that uses only the model's own generations. It constructs pseudo-solutions via majority vote, then distills a teacher distribution conditioned on the shortest correct solution into prefixes of the longest incorrect completion, enabling self-correction without external supervision. It matches or surpasses supervised methods like OPSD and GRPO across math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy (self-)distillation methods (OPD/OPSD) still depend on external supervision such as ground-truth signals, environmental feedback, or larger teacher models, falling short of genuine self-distillation. The authors aim to achieve true self-distillation using only internal consistency signals from the model's own rollouts.
AI.method: U-OPSD operates in three stages: (1) Sample multiple rollouts per problem and construct a pseudo-solution via majority vote under a self-consistency threshold. (2) Form a teacher distribution conditioned on the shortest correct pseudo-solution. (3) Distill this teacher distribution into prefixes of the model's longest incorrect completion, targeting positions where the model is confidently wrong to enable precise self-correction.
AI.result: On AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, MATH500, and AMC23, U-OPSD improves over base models by 8.5% (4B) and 10.7% (8B) in non-thinking mode on Qwen3. It outperforms supervised OPSD by 3.2% and 2.3% on average. In thinking mode, it surpasses OPSD by 0.9% at 4B, matches at 8B, and beats GRPO by 0.7% and 1.1% respectively.
AI.conclusion: U-OPSD demonstrates that genuine on-policy self-distillation without external supervision is feasible and effective, consistently improving LLM performance and matching or exceeding supervised alternatives across diverse benchmarks and model scales.

title: Hybrid Machine Learning Framework for Herd-Level Cattle Growth Pattern and Weight Gain Forecasting in Grazing-Based Production Systems
summary: Commercial grazing systems yield irregular livestock observations, which challenge cattle growth forecasting. This study developed a hybrid machine learning framework for herd level cattle weight forecasting using automated sensing observations collected between 2022 and 2024 in southeastern Australia. Weekly live weight observations, demographic variables, and lagged environmental predictors were integrated into structured forecasting datasets. Herd level forecasting trajectories were generated through temporal aggregation of animal level predictions. Four hybrid architecture families were evaluated, including residual, stacked, cascade, and ensemble assisted frameworks. ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU models were used as comparative baselines. Independent testing demonstrated strong predictive agreement across multiple forecasting horizons. The cascade GB to RF to NN architecture achieved the best performance, with a test R^2 of 0.889, RMSE of 21.319 kg, and MAE of 15.462 kg. Hybrid architectures maintained greater robustness than recurrent sequential models under sparse observation conditions. Forecasting error increased progressively across extended prediction horizons. Feature importance analysis identified animal age, rainfall, and temperature as dominant predictors influencing herd level growth forecasting. The proposed framework may support feed allocation, grazing management, and livestock marketing decisions under heterogeneous sensing environments.

AI.tldr: A hybrid ML framework using cascade architecture (GB→RF→NN) achieved strong herd-level cattle weight forecasting (R²=0.889, RMSE=21.319 kg) under sparse automated sensing conditions, outperforming recurrent sequential baselines like LSTM and GRU.
AI.motivation: Commercial grazing systems produce irregular, sparse livestock observations that challenge traditional cattle growth forecasting. Reliable weight prediction is needed for feed allocation, grazing management, and marketing decisions.
AI.method: The authors developed a hybrid machine learning framework trained on 2022–2024 automated sensing data from southeastern Australia. Weekly live weights, demographic variables, and lagged environmental predictors were structured into forecasting datasets. Herd-level trajectories were obtained by temporally aggregating animal-level predictions. Four hybrid architecture families (residual, stacked, cascade, ensemble-assisted) were evaluated against ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU baselines.
AI.result: The cascade GB→RF→NN architecture achieved the best performance (test R²=0.889, RMSE=21.319 kg, MAE=15.462 kg). Hybrid architectures showed greater robustness than recurrent sequential models under sparse observations. Forecasting error increased with longer prediction horizons. Feature importance analysis identified animal age, rainfall, and temperature as dominant predictors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid cascade framework effectively handles irregular sensing data for herd-level weight forecasting and can support practical decision-making in feed allocation, grazing management, and livestock marketing under heterogeneous sensing environments.

title: RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction
summary: Recent advances in reward modeling show a paradigm shift from discriminative reward models to generative reward models. However, despite their strong capabilities in response ranking, generative reward models have not realized their potential in reinforcement learning (RL). Our analysis reveals that this limitation arises from a mismatch between the comparative nature of generative reward modeling and the scalar scoring paradigm adopted by existing RL algorithms. To bridge this gap, we propose a Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC) approach, which enables generative reward models to provide more effective RL learning signals by deriving rewards from relative preference rankings. RRC introduces two complementary strategies: self-competitive ranking, which exploits comparisons among sampled responses, and anchor-guided ranking, which enables scalable ranking-based reward construction with a small set of reference responses. Experiments across open-ended chat and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RRC substantially improves RL training with generative reward models, achieving consistent gains over existing reward construction approaches. Our code can be found at https://github.com/wangclnlp/RRC.

AI.tldr: Generative reward models (GRMs) excel at ranking but underperform in RL due to a scalar-vs-comparative mismatch. The authors propose Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC), which derives scalar RL rewards from relative preference rankings via self-competitive and anchor-guided strategies, achieving consistent RL training improvements.
AI.motivation: Generative reward models show strong response ranking capabilities but fail to deliver proportional gains when used for reinforcement learning. The core issue is a fundamental mismatch: GRMs naturally produce comparative judgments (ranking), while standard RL algorithms require scalar reward signals. This gap prevents GRMs from realizing their full potential as RL reward providers.
AI.method: The paper proposes Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC) with two complementary strategies: (1) Self-competitive ranking, which exploits comparisons among multiple sampled responses from the policy to construct relative rankings and derive reward signals; (2) Anchor-guided ranking, which uses a small set of fixed reference responses to enable scalable ranking-based reward construction without requiring a large number of online samples. These rankings are then converted into scalar rewards suitable for RL optimization.
AI.result: Experiments on open-ended chat and reasoning benchmarks show that RRC substantially improves RL training with generative reward models, yielding consistent gains over existing reward construction approaches.
AI.conclusion: RRC effectively bridges the gap between generative reward modeling and RL by converting comparative ranking signals into effective scalar rewards, enabling GRMs to serve as superior RL reward providers. The two complementary ranking strategies offer both effectiveness and scalability.

title: HERALD: Counterfactual Audits and Minimal Repairs for Proof-of-Retrieval Rewards
summary: Search-agent rewards mix answer quality, citation grounding, tool cost, and anti-hacking terms; a high score therefore need not imply that cited evidence was retrieved, and added penalties can cancel. We introduce HERALD, an offline audit that applies exact same-question interventions, separates candidate-visible from oracle information, and enumerates detector contracts before policy optimization. On four Qwen3-8B pools from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, $R_0$ rejects search deletion and fake IDs, but a label-free citation-laundering attack succeeds. A complete $2^3$ ablation identifies targeted strengthening of $L$---citing a corpus passage absent from the retrieved evidence---as the observed inclusion-minimal repair: $R[L]$ has zero empirical ASR with a 0.50% one-sided cluster upper bound. The gap persists across pool rules, a visible BM25 attacker, and four models; broader hardening remains vulnerable when the attack removes an oracle support-ID penalty. Under strict 5M-token matched training evaluated on 256 paired questions per benchmark, $R[L]$ meets the EM non-inferiority gate on HotpotQA and 2Wiki but not MuSiQue. Equal-suite citation precision and support recall improve by 2.02 and 1.46 points, unsupported citations fall by 1.69, and laundering attackability falls on 2Wiki and MuSiQue. Natural $L$ is not reduced, and the detector appears in only 18 of 58,368 training trajectories. HERALD thus separates robust scoring, sparse learning signal, and policy transfer.

AI.tldr: HERALD is an offline audit framework that identifies and repairs vulnerabilities in search-agent reward functions. It reveals that a label-free citation-laundering attack can bypass existing defenses, and pinpoints a specific detector penalty ($L$) as the minimal repair. Training with $R[L]$ eliminates the attack empirically, improves citation quality, and preserves answer accuracy, all while appearing in only a tiny fraction of training trajectories.
AI.motivation: Search-agent reward functions composite multiple terms (answer quality, citation grounding, tool cost, anti-hacking), making high scores ambiguous—they do not guarantee that cited evidence was actually retrieved. The authors aim to systematically audit these reward functions for vulnerabilities, particularly against attacks that manipulate citations without triggering existing penalties.
AI.method: HERALD performs offline audits via exact same-question interventions, separating candidate-visible from oracle information, and enumerating detector contracts before policy optimization. A $2^3$ ablation over reward components identifies which penalties prevent citation-laundering attacks. The key repair, $R[L]$, penalizes citing a corpus passage absent from retrieved evidence. Training uses strict 5M-token matched budgets on 256 paired questions per benchmark (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue) with Qwen3-8B pools.
AI.result: $R_0$ (base reward) rejects search deletion and fake IDs but fails against citation laundering. $R[L]$ achieves zero empirical ASR with a 0.50% one-sided cluster upper bound. Under matched training, $R[L]$ meets the EM non-inferiority gate on HotpotQA and 2Wiki but not MuSiQue. Citation precision improves by 2.02 points, support recall by 1.46, unsupported citations drop by 1.69, and laundering attackability falls on 2Wiki and MuSiQue. Natural $L$ is not reduced; the detector appears in only 18 of 58,368 training trajectories.
AI.conclusion: HERALD demonstrates that offline auditing can separate robust scoring, sparse learning signals, and effective policy transfer. The minimal repair $R[L]$ provides strong defense against citation laundering with negligible impact on natural behavior, though broader hardening remains vulnerable when oracle support-ID penalties are removed.

title: CalibForge: Adversarial Solver Calibration for Scaling Learnable Terminal Tasks
summary: Training terminal agents requires executable and verifiable tasks that are not merely solvable, but appropriately challenging for learning. Executable validation establishes feasibility, yet does not reveal how a task behaves relative to a given solver setting. In this paper, we present CalibForge, an autonomous terminal-task synthesis system that uses verified solver behavior to revise candidate tasks through adversarial solver calibration. Multi-solver calibration targets disagreement within a heterogeneous solver pool, whereas contrastive solver calibration targets a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation; both operationalize a solver-relative learnable zone anchored in demonstrated solvability. Using CalibForge, we construct 5,431 calibrated terminal tasks. Our ablations show that both strategies yield more effective supervision than authoring and validation alone or ordinary single-solver feedback. Models trained on the full collection achieve 32.58% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.0. The largest improvements over the corresponding base model reach 24.71 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.0, 27.68 points on SWE-bench Pro, and 30.04 points on Doc2Repo. Together, these results support solver-relative learnability as a practical target for constructing effective and transferable agent training data.

AI.tldr: CalibForge is an autonomous system that generates terminal tasks for training agents by using adversarial solver calibration—leveraging disagreement among heterogeneous solvers or a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation—to create tasks within a solver-relative learnable zone, producing 5,431 calibrated tasks that significantly improve agent performance on Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Pro, and Doc2Repo.
AI.motivation: Training terminal agents requires tasks that are executable and verifiable but also appropriately challenging for learning. Existing methods that only validate executability do not reveal how a task behaves relative to a given solver, leaving a gap in identifying tasks that fall within a productive "learnable zone" for a target model.
AI.method: The authors propose CalibForge, an autonomous terminal-task synthesis system employing two adversarial solver calibration strategies: (1) multi-solver calibration, which targets disagreement within a heterogeneous solver pool, and (2) contrastive solver calibration, which targets a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation between solvers. Both strategies operationalize a solver-relative learnable zone anchored in demonstrated solvability, using verified solver behavior to revise candidate tasks.
AI.result: CalibForge produced 5,431 calibrated terminal tasks. Both calibration strategies yielded more effective supervision than authoring with validation alone or ordinary single-solver feedback. Models trained on the full collection achieved 32.58% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.0. The largest improvements over the base model reached 24.71 pp on Terminal-Bench 2.0, 27.68 pp on SWE-bench Pro, and 30.04 pp on Doc2Repo.
AI.conclusion: Solver-relative learnability is a practical and effective target for constructing agent training data that is both effective and transferable across benchmarks, as demonstrated by the strong gains across Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Pro, and Doc2Repo.

title: From Economic Agents to Agentic Economies: A Systems Blueprint for Economic World Models
summary: Economic World Models (EWMs) are generative economic models that simulate how economies evolve from within by modeling heterogeneous agents, their beliefs and actions, and the market and institutional mechanisms through which their interactions produce aggregate outcomes. This paper develops an implementation roadmap for building economic world models as generative engines in which heterogeneous agents act, interact, adapt, and co-evolve with markets and institutions, thereby producing economic dynamics from the inside. We organize EWM systems into a six-level capability ladder, from fixed rule-based agent worlds to adaptive and LLM-based agent worlds, self-evolving agents, evolving institutional worlds, and sim-to-real economic twins aligned with real observations. A systematic literature survey across these levels reveals that existing work remains concentrated in lower-level agent and simulation environments, while systems with self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare. By translating the EWM agenda into an implementation blueprint, this paper aims to accelerate the development of the next generation of economic simulation environments that can serve as high-fidelity sandboxes for human decision-makers and as training, planning, evaluation, and safety substrates for AI agents. We release a curated paper list and related resources to support future research.

AI.tldr: Proposes a six-level capability ladder for building Economic World Models (EWMs) — generative simulations with heterogeneous, adaptive agents. A systematic survey reveals current work clusters at lower levels, while self-evolving agents and empirically aligned models remain rare. The paper provides an implementation blueprint to accelerate next-generation economic simulation environments.
AI.motivation: Existing economic simulation work is fragmented across agent types and environments. There is no unified roadmap for building EWMs that progress from simple rule-based agents to fully adaptive, LLM-based, empirically aligned economic twins. The authors aim to organize the field, identify gaps, and accelerate development of high-fidelity sandboxes for both human decision-makers and AI agent training/safety.
AI.method: The authors propose a six-level EWM capability ladder (fixed rule-based agents → adaptive/LLM-based agents → self-evolving agents → evolving institutional worlds → sim-to-real economic twins) and conduct a systematic literature survey mapping existing work onto these levels. They translate the EWM agenda into a concrete implementation blueprint covering agent architectures, market mechanisms, institutional evolution, and empirical alignment strategies.
AI.result: The survey finds that most existing work concentrates on lower-level agent and simulation environments. Systems featuring self-evolving agents, endogenous institutional change, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare, exposing significant research gaps at higher capability levels.
AI.conclusion: The EWM capability ladder and implementation blueprint provide a structured pathway for advancing economic simulation research. Bridging the gap between current lower-level systems and the vision of empirically grounded, self-evolving economic twins will enable high-fidelity sandboxes for policy analysis, AI training, planning, and safety evaluation.

title: An Optimal Agnostic PAC Algorithm

AI.tldr: Constructs a learner achieving statistically optimal risk bounds for agnostic PAC learning, matching known lower bounds, thereby settling the sample complexity question up to universal constants for VC classes.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to resolve the open problem of constructing an agnostic PAC learner that achieves statistically optimal sample complexity—matching the lower bounds of Devroye, Györfi, and Lugosi—for classes of finite VC dimension. Prior work had gaps between upper and lower bounds.
AI.method: The authors construct a learner based on minimizing empirical risk, combined with a careful analysis using uniform convergence and VC theory techniques to achieve tight multiplicative and additive dependencies on the optimal risk L* and the VC dimension d.
AI.result: With probability at least 1−δ over an i.i.d. sample of size n, the learner's risk satisfies L(ĥ) ≤ L* + 7·10⁸(√(L*(d+log(1/δ))/n) + (d+log(1/δ))/n). This matches Devroye et al.'s lower bounds up to universal constants.
AI.conclusion: The paper definitively settles the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning for VC classes, showing that the statistically optimal rate is achieved by an explicit learner, with the derived bound being tight in all regimes of L*, d, and n up to universal constants.

title: Integrating Implicit and Explicit Relational Biases through Graph-Based Multiple Instance Learning: A Case Study in Skin Lesion Diagnosis
comment: Accepted as a short paper for presentation at the 21st International Conference on Computational Intelligence Methods for Bioinformatics and Biostatistics (CIBB 2026)
summary: Relational inductive biases are essential for capturing structural dependencies among data. This study investigates a dual-level relational framework for image classification, bridging the gap between implicit representation learning and explicit structural modelling. We begin by establishing a baseline using an EfficientNetB3 architecture. To move beyond standard convolutional biases, we adopt a patch-based strategy, employing a convolutional masked autoencoder to learn implicit inter-patch relationships through self-supervised reconstruction. We then extend this approach by incorporating explicit relational modelling, organizing the learned embeddings into various graph topologies, including grid-based, random, and k-nearest neighbour structures. Experimental results on the ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019 skin lesion diagnosis benchmarks show that combining implicit inter-patch modelling with explicit graph-based message passing yields the best performance. On the ISIC-2018 test set, the baseline model achieves a balanced accuracy of 76.17%, which improves to 77.12% with implicit patch-based relational modelling. The fully integrated grid-structured Graph Attention Network further increases performance to 79.27%. Similarly, on ISIC-2019, the implicit approach reaches 59.84% balanced accuracy, while the combination of implicit and explicit modelling yields 60.67%.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a dual-level relational framework for skin lesion classification that combines implicit relational learning via a convolutional masked autoencoder (patch-based self-supervised reconstruction) with explicit graph-based message passing. Tested on ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019 benchmarks using an EfficientNetB3 backbone, the combined approach outperforms both the baseline and implicit-only variants, with the grid-structured Graph Attention Network achieving the best results.
AI.motivation: Standard convolutional neural networks rely on local receptive fields and lack explicit mechanisms for modeling long-range structural dependencies among image regions. The authors aim to bridge the gap between implicit representation learning and explicit structural modeling by introducing relational inductive biases that capture inter-patch relationships, which is particularly relevant for medical image analysis where spatial context and structural patterns are diagnostically important.
AI.method: The framework uses EfficientNetB3 as the backbone. First, a patch-based strategy paired with a convolutional masked autoencoder (MAE) learns implicit inter-patch relationships via self-supervised reconstruction. Then, explicit relational modeling is introduced by organizing the learned patch embeddings into graph topologies — specifically grid-based, random, and k-nearest neighbor structures — and applying Graph Attention Networks (GAT) for message passing. The dual-level approach is evaluated on ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019 skin lesion classification datasets using balanced accuracy as the metric.
AI.result: On ISIC-2018: Baseline EfficientNetB3 achieves 76.17% balanced accuracy. Adding implicit patch-based relational modeling improves to 77.12%. The full model with grid-structured GAT reaches 79.27%. On ISIC-2019: Implicit-only achieves 59.84%, while the combined implicit + explicit model yields 60.67% balanced accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Combining implicit inter-patch relational learning (via masked autoencoding) with explicit graph-based message passing (via GAT) consistently improves skin lesion classification performance over both the standard CNN baseline and the implicit-only variant. The grid-structured graph topology proved most effective, demonstrating that injecting structural relational inductive biases benefits medical image diagnosis tasks.

title: When History Lies: Evaluating and Improving Tool Use under Misleading Multi-Turn Histories
summary: Tool-calling agents infer task state from accumulated dialogue and tool traces. In persistent interactions, however, historical traces may remain structurally valid and semantically plausible after they cease to be authoritative for the current request. We show that such history can hijack a policy the model already possesses: on Qwen3-1.7B, pollution flips 32.1% of decisions that are correct under the original trajectory and frequently induces reuse of corrupted entities or interface conventions. We introduce bench, a paired benchmark with synchronized Original, Polluted, and Oracle State views that preserve the system policy, current tools, latest request, and gold next action. Eleven gold-preserving interventions isolate failures in decision state, entity binding, and interface execution across complete calls and non-call decisions. We further propose ours, which transfers an Oracle-conditioned teacher policy to a student observing only polluted history through soft supervision on student-generated prefixes. On Qwen3-1.7B, ours achieves 87.0% Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy, outperforming Gold-SFT (66.3%), Oracle sequence distillation (82.3%), and off-policy token distillation (85.0%). The method scales consistently: an 8B teacher raises the same compact 1.7B student to 91.9%, while an 8B student reaches 93.0%. The resulting policies further transfer to clean histories, unseen functions, independently regenerated evaluation contexts, external tool-use benchmarks, and noisy multi-hop question answering. These results establish history reliability as a distinct tool-use bottleneck and demonstrate reliable-state policy transfer as an effective and scalable solution.

AI.tldr: Historical dialogue/tool traces in persistent agent interactions can become stale yet still appear valid, misleading tool-calling agents into incorrect decisions. The authors introduce a benchmark with paired clean/polluted/oracle states and a teacher-student distillation method that transfers oracle-conditioned knowledge to a student observing only polluted history, achieving significant accuracy gains and establishing history reliability as a key bottleneck in tool use.
AI.motivation: In persistent tool-calling agent interactions, accumulated historical traces can remain structurally valid and semantically plausible even after they are no longer authoritative for the current request. This "history pollution" can hijack a model's otherwise correct policy, causing incorrect tool calls, reuse of corrupted entities, or adoption of outdated interface conventions. No existing benchmark systematically isolates and evaluates this failure mode.
AI.method: (1) A paired benchmark ("bench") with three synchronized views per instance — Original (clean), Polluted, and Oracle State — that preserve system policy, current tools, latest request, and gold next action uniformly. Eleven gold-preserving interventions isolate failures across decision state, entity binding, and interface execution. (2) A method ("ours") that transfers an Oracle-conditioned teacher policy to a student observing only polluted history via soft supervision on student-generated prefixes, using token-level distillation.
AI.result: On Qwen3-1.7B, pollution flips 32.1% of originally correct decisions. The proposed method achieves 87.0% Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy, outperforming Gold-SFT (66.3%), Oracle sequence distillation (82.3%), and off-policy token distillation (85.0%). Scaling: an 8B teacher raises the 1.7B student to 91.9%; an 8B student reaches 93.0%. Policies transfer to clean histories, unseen functions, regenerated contexts, external tool-use benchmarks, and noisy multi-hop QA.
AI.conclusion: History reliability is a distinct and critical bottleneck in tool-use agents. The proposed reliable-state policy transfer method is both effective and scalable, producing policies that generalize well beyond the training distribution and establishing a new paradigm for handling stale historical context in persistent agent interactions.

title: Signal or Spurious Cue? A Randomized Audit of Survey-Country Metadata in LLM Social Inference
summary: Survey-country metadata can improve an LLM's forecast of an individual response when informative, yet the same cue may redirect the forecast when assigned at random. A within-record audit tests whether disclosing a random label's uniform, record-independent origin reduces its country-directed uptake, and whether verified survey country lowers held-out Brier loss. Independent population anchors and recorded human answers measure direction and consequence across five fixed API models, six countries, and seven development-selected targets. In the primary post-review 72-record panel, opaque and disclosed-random labels each produced country-direction shifts of 0.214. Paired attenuation was 0.0003 (95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166]). Verified country reduced Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), while random-label regret included zero. A non-overlapping mixed-coverage consistency panel retained positive disclosed-random movement and verified utility, while attenuation remained uncertain. On the selected targets, verified metadata was useful in both panels, but disclosure did not reliably attenuate random-label uptake. PROV-FORECAST contains 14,400 paired item-level probability distributions from the corrected panel.

AI.tldr: An audit experiment tests whether disclosing that a country label is randomly assigned reduces an LLM's tendency to use it as a forecasting cue. Verified survey country improves forecast accuracy, but disclosure of random assignment does not reliably attenuate the model's reliance on uninformative labels.
AI.motivation: LLMs can improve individual response forecasts using survey-country metadata, but may also be misled by the same cue when it is assigned at random. This paper investigates whether transparency about a label's random, non-informative origin can mitigate such spurious reliance, and whether verified metadata provides genuine predictive utility.
AI.method: A within-record audit design: independent population anchors and recorded human answers are used to measure direction and consequence of model forecasts. Five fixed API models forecast across six countries and seven development-selected targets. The primary panel (72 records, post-review) compares opaque vs. disclosed-random country labels. A non-overlapping mixed-coverage consistency panel replicates findings. Metrics include country-direction shifts, paired attenuation, Brier loss reduction from verified country, and random-label regret.
AI.result: Both opaque and disclosed-random labels produced country-direction shifts of 0.214. Paired attenuation was near zero (0.0003, 95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166]). Verified country reduced Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), while random-label regret included zero. The consistency panel retained positive disclosed-random movement and verified utility, but attenuation remained uncertain. Disclosure did not reliably reduce random-label uptake.
AI.conclusion: Verified survey-country metadata is useful for improving LLM forecast accuracy, but merely disclosing that a label is randomly assigned does not reliably prevent models from incorporating it. This suggests a form of cue-resistant anchoring in LLM forecasting behavior, with implications for responsible metadata handling in survey-based prediction tasks.

title: Evaluating Investment Logic in Large Language Models: A Real-World Benchmark Towards Personalzied Financial Agents
summary:
Investment competence is inherently personalized: the same market evidence can justify different actions for investors with different goals, horizons, portfolios, and risk boundaries. Yet financial LLMs are evaluated either by static question answering or by terminal profit and loss. The former omits agency; the latter cannot reveal whether a profitable action was grounded, profile-consistent, or merely lucky. We ask whether the community is using the wrong ruler for consequential agents.
  We introduce \textsc{InvestLogicBench}, a process-native benchmark containing 201,247 documented decisions from 151 real-world investors. Each episode instantiates a \textbf{P$\rightarrow$E$\rightarrow$R$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$O} trace: investor \textit{Profile}, observable market \textit{Events}, investment \textit{Reasoning}, executable \textit{Decision}, and delayed \textit{Outcome}. The release includes profile construction, point-in-time event binding, structured logic, horizons, outcomes, and post-mortems, and supports comprehension, profile-conditioned generation, and end-to-end replay. Across four leading LLMs, logical plausibility remains near 4/5 while event grounding is only 0.8--2.8/5; return and process quality also disagree. These results expose polished but weakly grounded reasoning that outcome-only evaluation hides. We further argue that P$\rightarrow$E$\rightarrow$R$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$O should be a data-system interface, requiring versioned profiles, temporal provenance, inspectable retrieval, decision ledgers, and replayable outcomes. Finance is our stress test for a broader class of personalized, consequential agents.

AI.tldr: InvestLogicBench introduces a process-native benchmark of 201,247 real investor decisions structured as Profile→Events→Reasoning→Decision→Outcome traces, revealing that LLMs exhibit polished but weakly grounded reasoning that outcome-only evaluation conceals.
AI.motivation: Current financial LLM evaluation relies on static QA or terminal P&L, both of which fail to capture the personalized, profile-consistent nature of investment reasoning. Static QA omits investor agency; P&L cannot distinguish grounded decisions from luck. The community needs evaluation that assesses the full reasoning process.
AI.method: The authors construct InvestLogicBench, comprising 201,247 documented decisions from 151 real investors. Each episode follows a P→E→R→D→O trace: investor Profile, observable market Events, investment Reasoning, executable Decision, and delayed Outcome. The benchmark supports comprehension, profile-conditioned generation, and end-to-end replay, with point-in-time event binding and structured logic documentation.
AI.result: Across four leading LLMs, logical plausibility scores near 4/5, but event grounding scores are only 0.8–2.8/5. Return-based metrics and process-quality metrics disagree, exposing polished yet weakly grounded reasoning that outcome-only evaluation masks.
AI.conclusion: The P→E→R→D→O framework should serve as a data-system interface for consequential agents, requiring versioned profiles, temporal provenance, inspectable retrieval, decision ledgers, and replayable outcomes. Finance serves as a stress test for broader personalized, consequential agent evaluation.

title: ECHO: A Locally-Deployable Agentic Health Assistant with Temporal Memory, Safety Guardrails, and Speech Assessment
summary: This paper presents ECHO (Enhanced Care \& Health Observer), a locally-deployable conversational health assistant for long-term chronic care management. ECHO integrates three complementary software modules developed under shared supervision as a unified system. The core module is an agentic chatbot built on a ReAct loop orchestrated via LangGraph, equipped with 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for persistent cross-session memory; it achieves a 94.9\% tool-execution pass rate across a 59-scenario benchmark with GPT-5 Mini. A two-stage hybrid safety layer intercepts all incoming queries: a rule-based layer handles explicit crisis signals and jailbreak attempts in under 1ms, while a signed graph neural network (GNN) with APPNP-style propagation classifies boundary cases by clinical intent, achieving 88.8\% accuracy and 90.6\% unsafe recall on a 2,537-query annotated Turkish health dataset while outperforming zero-shot LLM baselines including Llama 3.3 70B. A multimodal speech assessment module combining Whisper acoustic encoding and BERT text encoding with cross-attention fusion estimates emotion, depression, and pain, reaching a mean macro F1 of 0.652. The full system is implemented as a web application that can run entirely on consumer hardware, with no patient data transmitted to external services, supporting compliance with GDPR and KVKK.

AI.tldr: ECHO is a locally-deployable conversational health assistant for chronic care that combines an agentic chatbot with persistent memory, a two-stage hybrid safety layer, and a multimodal speech assessment module, achieving strong clinical tool execution and safety performance while maintaining full data privacy compliance.
AI.motivation: Chronic care management requires long-term, context-aware conversational support with robust safety guarantees, yet existing solutions often rely on cloud services that compromise patient data privacy. There is a need for a fully local, privacy-preserving health assistant that integrates clinical reasoning, cross-session memory, safety filtering, and multimodal affect assessment into a unified system deployable on consumer hardware.
AI.method: ECHO integrates three modules: (1) an agentic chatbot using a ReAct loop orchestrated by LangGraph, equipped with 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for cross-session memory, evaluated on a 59-scenario benchmark with GPT-5 Mini; (2) a two-stage hybrid safety layer combining a rule-based stage (<1ms) for crisis/jailbreak signals and a signed graph neural network with APPNP-style propagation for clinical intent classification of boundary cases, benchmarked on 2,537 annotated Turkish health queries; and (3) a multimodal speech assessment module fusing Whisper acoustic encoding and BERT text encoding via cross-attention to estimate emotion, depression, and pain. The system runs entirely on consumer hardware with no external data transmission.
AI.result: The agentic chatbot achieves a 94.9% tool-execution pass rate across 59 scenarios. The safety layer attains 88.8% accuracy and 90.6% unsafe recall, outperforming zero-shot LLM baselines including Llama 3.3 70B. The speech assessment module yields a mean macro F1 of 0.652 for emotion, depression, and pain estimation.
AI.conclusion: ECHO demonstrates that a fully local, privacy-compliant conversational health assistant can deliver competitive performance across clinical tool use, safety filtering, and multimodal affect assessment, supporting GDPR and KVKK compliance without relying on cloud infrastructure.

title: Mind the Gaps: Mixture-of-Minds for Human Simulation
summary: Predicting how a population will answer a new question is a long-standing goal. Statistical methods succeed at the level of the mass but falter at the level of the individual. Large language model simulators inherit this gap. They recover a population's central tendencies while flattening its heterogeneity, and they carry social biases and prompt brittleness that distort individual predictions. This paper introduces Anacreon, an audience simulation model that targets the individual level within a narrow, well-specified domain. Anacreon learns an authorship embedding that separates individuals, clusters a real qualitative corpus around seed people, and trains a dedicated adapter for each cluster, a mixture of minds, on a Gemma~4 12B base. It harvests demographics, psychological traits, and survey responses from public text, and augments each record with a chain-of-emotion. It reduces prompt brittleness by shuffling response options and reduces positive bias by balancing the training distribution. On a large, externally sourced survey, Anacreon reaches a state-of-the-art ordinal alignment of 0.775, the individual-level accuracy measure on which the field has converged, with a small residual bias. The work is a step toward drawing aggregate insight from faithfully simulated individuals.

AI.tldr: Anacreon is an audience simulation model that achieves state-of-the-art individual-level prediction accuracy (ordinal alignment 0.775) by clustering individuals, training per-cluster adapters on a Gemma 12B base, and mitigating biases through chain-of-emotion augmentation, response shuffling, and balanced training distribution.
AI.motivation: Statistical methods and existing LLM simulators capture population-level trends but fail at individual-level prediction — they flatten heterogeneity, carry social biases, and suffer from prompt brittleness. There is a need for faithful individual-level simulation to draw valid aggregate insights.
AI.method: Anacreon uses: (1) an authorship embedding to separate individuals; (2) clustering of a real qualitative corpus around seed people; (3) a mixture-of-minds architecture with a dedicated adapter trained per cluster on Gemma 4 12B; (4) harvesting demographics, psychological traits, and survey responses from public text; (5) chain-of-emotion augmentation; (6) response option shuffling to reduce prompt brittleness; and (7) training distribution balancing to reduce positive bias.
AI.result: On a large, externally sourced survey, Anacreon achieves state-of-the-art ordinal alignment of 0.775 — the field's converged individual-level accuracy measure — with only small residual bias remaining.
AI.conclusion: The work represents a step toward drawing aggregate insight from faithfully simulated individuals, demonstrating that targeting individual-level prediction within a narrow, well-specified domain is feasible through careful clustering, adapter-based fine-tuning, and bias mitigation strategies.

title: Poli-Bias: Understanding and Measuring Large Language Model Biases in International Political Conflicts
summary: Measuring political bias in large language models (LLMs) remains challenging as it can manifest through subtle differences in framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning that are difficult to capture with a single metric. In this work, we introduce Poli-Bias, a counterfactual framework for measuring whether LLMs treat legally equivalent conflict scenarios differently depending on the countries involved. Poli-Bias compares responses to paired prompts in which country identities are systematically swapped across diverse geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks. Rather than reducing bias to a single judgment, our framework decomposes response disparities into five interpretable dimensions, revealing how and where unequal treatment manifests. Across 13 contemporary LLMs spanning diverse model families and sizes, we find that country identities and user affiliations can systematically affect how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended under international law. Our results thus establish Poli-Bias as a fine-grained framework for auditing political even-handedness and sycophancy in LLMs.

AI.tldr: Poli-Bias is a counterfactual framework that measures political bias in LLMs by systematically swapping country identities in legally equivalent conflict scenarios and decomposing response disparities across five interpretable dimensions.
AI.motivation: Existing methods fail to capture the subtle, multi-dimensional nature of political bias in LLMs, which manifests through framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning rather than overt judgments. A single-metric approach is insufficient for auditing political even-handedness.
AI.method: Poli-Bias uses counterfactual paired prompts where country identities are systematically swapped across diverse geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks. Response disparities are decomposed into five interpretable dimensions rather than reduced to a single bias score. The framework was evaluated on 13 contemporary LLMs of varying families and sizes.
AI.result: Across 13 LLMs, country identities and user affiliations systematically affected how equivalent actions were described, evaluated, and defended under international law, revealing significant political uneven-handedness and sycophancy.
AI.conclusion: Poli-Bias provides a fine-grained, multi-dimensional framework for auditing political bias and sycophancy in LLMs, establishing that LLMs do not treat legally equivalent scenarios uniformly when country identities differ.

title: Contextual Information Policy Optimization for Search Agents
summary: Search agents extend large language models beyond static parametric memory by enabling them to acquire and use ex ternal evidence during multi-step reasoning. For knowledge intensive tasks involving complex or evolving information, their reliability depends not only on retrieving relevant ev idence but also on using it to guide subsequent reasoning. However, existing methods primarily reward final-answer cor rectness or intermediate progress, without directly assessing whether post-retrieval actions are grounded in the retrieved evidence. This misalignment encourages prior-driven reason ing: agents form conclusions based on internal knowledge and use retrieval mainly to confirm them, resulting in confirma tion bias and inefficient evidenceuse.Toaddressthisissue, we propose Contextual Information Policy Optimization (CIPO), an evidence-oriented reinforcement learning framework that explicitly aligns policy optimization with external evidence use. CIPO assigns dense, turn-level credit to reasoning ac tions influenced by retrieved information, while combining this evidence-use signal with a global outcome reward to pre serveanswercorrectness.Withthismanner,CIPOdiscourages evidence-detached guesses and promotes reasoning trajecto ries in which retrieved facts can guide or revise subsequent reasoning. Importantly, CIPO requires neither human process annotations nor an additional reward model. Extensive exper iments on seven in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks show that CIPO reduces the prevalence of prior-driven rea soning and achieves excellent performance on most tasks.

AI.tldr: CIPO is an evidence-oriented RL framework that aligns agent policy optimization with actual evidence use via turn-level credit assignment, reducing confirmation bias without needing human process labels or reward models.
AI.motivation: Existing methods reward final-answer correctness or intermediate progress but fail to assess whether reasoning actions are grounded in retrieved evidence. This causes prior-driven reasoning, where agents use retrieval merely to confirm internal beliefs (confirmation bias), leading to inefficient evidence use.
AI.method: CIPO (Contextual Information Policy Optimization) assigns dense, turn-level credit to reasoning actions that are influenced by retrieved information, combining this evidence-use signal with a global outcome reward. It requires no human process annotations or auxiliary reward models.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across seven in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that CIPO reduces prior-driven reasoning and achieves excellent performance on most tasks.
AI.conclusion: CIPO effectively aligns policy optimization with external evidence use, discouraging evidence-detached guessing and promoting reasoning trajectories where retrieved facts guide or revise subsequent steps.

title: FinEvo-Bench: A Longitudinal Benchmark for Self-Evolving Agents in Professional Financial Workflows
summary: Most agent benchmarks evaluate tasks independently and cannot measure whether experience from one task helps with later tasks. Existing self-evolution benchmarks do not jointly cover professional workflows, open-ended deliverables, and multi-aspect evaluation. We introduce FinEvo-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark with 120 real-case-grounded tasks, 20 business scenes across six financial domains. Institution-provided professional procedures define the required operations and constraints. Eligible institution-provided and publicly documented cases supply the task facts. Each scene contains six related but substantively distinct cases that share a professional procedure and a manually reviewed rubric for task quality and financial compliance. We compare four self-evolving agent scaffolds using the same Qwen3.7-Max backbone and three independently shuffled, globally interleaved task streams. Paired non-evolving controls estimate each scaffold's self-evolution gain from retained experience, while an independent Claude Code scoring agent backed by Claude Opus 4.6 evaluates all outputs. Letta achieves the highest evolved score (91.65) and fewest compliance issues (0.09 per task); Codex achieves the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37). Across scaffolds, the evolving condition raises scores by 9.33-19.37 points and reduces compliance issues by 0.12-0.44 per task. Paired score gains at within-scene ranks 4-6 exceed those at ranks 1-3 by 6.10-8.70 points. In Claude Code, skill-only evolution produces higher task quality and fewer compliance issues than memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution. Across all four scaffolds, rubric feedback also yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback. FinEvo-Bench measures both professional performance and self-evolution ability: how effectively an agent turns prior experience into later improvement.

AI.tldr: FinEvo-Bench is a longitudinal benchmark for evaluating self-evolving AI agents on 120 real financial tasks across six domains. It measures both professional performance and how effectively agents convert prior experience into later improvement, finding that evolving agents significantly outperform non-evolving controls, with Letta achieving the highest scores and Codex showing the largest self-evolution gain.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks evaluate tasks independently and fail to measure cross-task learning. Current self-evolution benchmarks do not jointly cover professional workflows, open-ended deliverables, and multi-aspect evaluation. There is a need for a benchmark that captures how agents improve from retained experience across related, realistic professional tasks.
AI.method: FinEvo-Bench comprises 120 real-case-grounded tasks across 20 business scenes spanning six financial domains. Each scene contains six related but distinct cases sharing a professional procedure and a manually reviewed rubric covering task quality and financial compliance. Four self-evolving agent scaffolds (using Qwen3.7-Max) are compared across three independently shuffled, globally interleaved task streams. Paired non-evolving controls estimate self-evolution gains. An independent Claude Code scoring agent (backed by Claude Opus 4.6) evaluates all outputs. The benchmark also ablates skill-only, memory-only, and combined evolution, as well as rubric versus reference-answer feedback.
AI.result: Letta achieved the highest evolved score (91.65) and fewest compliance issues (0.09 per task). Codex showed the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37). Across scaffolds, evolution raised scores by 9.33–19.37 points and reduced compliance issues by 0.12–0.44 per task. Within-scene ranks 4–6 showed paired score gains 6.10–8.70 points higher than ranks 1–3. Skill-only evolution outperformed memory-only and combined approaches in Claude Code. Rubric feedback yielded better outcomes than reference-answer feedback across all scaffolds.
AI.conclusion: FinEvo-Bench effectively measures both professional task performance and self-evolution capability in AI agents. Self-evolution yields substantial and consistent improvements across diverse scaffolds, with later within-scene tasks benefiting more from accumulated experience. Skill-based evolution and rubric-based feedback are particularly effective design choices for agent self-improvement.

title: Schema-Guided Hierarchical Information Extraction and Semantic Evaluation Using Generative AI
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. To be published in Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE 22nd International Conference on e-Science (e-Science), Naples, Italy
summary:
We present a schema-based framework for extracting complex, structured information from unstructured text documents using generative AI, followed by automated semantic evaluation of the extracted information against a gold standard. The schema, serving as an information model encoding domain knowledge, provides a unified, systematic, and consistent framework for extraction of hierarchical, nested information, with attributes of variable cardinality, and subsequent evaluation of the results. Information extraction from a document is performed in a single call to the model, in zero-shot mode.
  In the evaluation step, we introduce a path-based semantic matching algorithm to align the nested, variable-cardinality attributes in the extracted results with those in the gold standard. We use generative AI for semantic comparison of the extracted and gold standard values of an attribute, and introduce a rubric to classify the result of the comparison, according to domain-specific considerations, as an exact, semantic, useful, or non-match.
  We were able to extract 12 out of 14 attributes with an F1 score of $>$90\% from documents published by the health technology assessment organisation NICE, using the generative AI model Claude Opus 3. The time needed to extract the attributes from a document was $\sim$30 times lower than the time taken by a human domain expert. We further demonstrate generalisability of this framework across different generative AI models and transferability across different HTA organisations and languages.

AI.tldr: A schema-based framework using generative AI extracts complex, nested, variable-cardinality structured information from unstructured text in a single zero-shot call, followed by a path-based semantic matching algorithm for automated evaluation against a gold standard. Achieved >90% F1 on 12/14 attributes from NICE documents using Claude Opus 3, with ~30× speedup over human experts, and demonstrated generalisability across models, organisations, and languages.
AI.motivation: Extracting complex, hierarchical, nested information with variable-cardinality attributes from unstructured text remains challenging. Manual extraction by domain experts is time-consuming and costly. Existing approaches lack a unified framework for both extraction and rigorous, automated semantic evaluation that accounts for domain-specific nuances in matching.
AI.method: A schema serves as a domain information model encoding the structure of desired outputs (hierarchical, nested, variable-cardinality attributes). Information extraction is performed via a single zero-shot call to a generative AI model (Claude Opus 3). Evaluation uses a path-based semantic matching algorithm to align nested extracted attributes with the gold standard, followed by generative AI-driven semantic comparison of attribute values. Results are classified via a rubric into four match categories: exact match, semantic match, useful match, or non-match.
AI.result: 12 out of 14 attributes extracted with F1 >90% from NICE HTA documents. Extraction time was ~30× faster than a human domain expert. The framework generalised across different generative AI models and transferred across different HTA organisations and languages.
AI.conclusion: The schema-based generative AI framework provides an efficient, accurate, and generalisable solution for complex structured information extraction from unstructured documents, with a robust semantic evaluation methodology that captures domain-specific matching nuances.

title: PaDoc: Layout-Grounded Parallel Decoding for Document Parsing
summary: End-to-end document parsers provide a unified interface, but serialize page layouts and regional contents into one autoregressive sequence. This formulation forces independent regions onto a decoding path whose length grows with the total content, whereas crop-based two-stage parsers expose region-level parallelism at the cost of repeated visual prefills and fragmented page context. To retain full-page context while removing dependencies, we propose PaDoc, a layout-grounded parser that treats the predicted layout as a branching structure over a shared page representation. Under a region-sufficiency assumption, we derive a prefix-conditioned factorization in which the layout stream and regional content branches advance concurrently, reducing the decoding depth to the longest layout-content path. We realize this factorization within a single MLLM: packed variable-length ancestor attention preserves the visibility under standard next-token training, while masked parallel decoding creates branches that the evaluated vLLM backend serves as concurrent requests with cache-resident shared-prefix reuse. On OmniDocBench Full, PaDoc attains an Overall layout F1 of 91.1 and, among end-to-end parsers, a top-tier Overall score of 94.24 together with the best Text Edit (0.038) and Formula CDM (95.59).
