On a 384-page subset and one A800 GPU, it is the fastest end-to-end parser at five concurrency levels, improving valid-page throughput by 67.4-118% and reducing P95 latency by 39.2-54.9% relative to a same-backbone Sequential SFT baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/Longin-Yu/Padoc

AI.tldr: PaDoc is a layout-grounded document parser that factorizes page decoding into a shared layout stream and concurrent regional content branches within a single MLLM, enabling faster end-to-end parsing through reduced decoding depth and parallel inference with shared-prefix reuse.
AI.motivation: Existing end-to-end document parsers serialize layout and content into one long autoregressive sequence, creating unnecessary sequential dependencies and long decoding paths. Crop-based two-stage parsers offer region-level parallelism but suffer from repeated visual computation and fragmented page context. The goal is to retain full-page context while eliminating inter-region decoding dependencies.
AI.method: PaDoc treats the predicted layout as a branching structure over a shared page representation. Under a region-sufficiency assumption, it derives a prefix-conditioned factorization where the layout stream and regional content branches advance concurrently, reducing decoding depth to the longest layout-content path. This is implemented in a single MLLM using packed variable-length ancestor attention (preserving visibility under next-token training) and masked parallel decoding, with the vLLM backend serving branches as concurrent requests with cache-resident shared-prefix reuse.
AI.result: On OmniDocBench Full, PaDoc achieves 91.1 Overall Layout F1 and a 94.24 Overall score among end-to-end parsers, with best Text Edit (0.038) and Formula CDM (95.59). On a 384-page subset with one A800 GPU, it is the fastest end-to-end parser at five concurrency levels, improving valid-page throughput by 67.4–118% and reducing P95 latency by 39.2–54.9% versus a same-backbone Sequential SFT baseline.
AI.conclusion: PaDoc demonstrates that layout-grounded factorization with concurrent branch decoding achieves both state-of-the-art accuracy and significant throughput/latency gains over sequential approaches, making it a practical and efficient solution for end-to-end document parsing.

title: HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization
summary: As LLMs are increasingly deployed within agentic systems, their capabilities depend not only on the model weights but also on the harness: the prompts, tools, control flow, memory, and orchestration code surrounding them. This makes automated harness optimization -- the iterative and evaluation-guided improvement of a harness by an AI system -- both an important route to improving AI systems and a demanding capability for AI systems themselves. Yet the community lacks a common protocol for measuring how well frontier LLMs perform at this task. We introduce HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization under expensive and stochastic evaluation. An optimizer, an LLM paired with a coding harness, receives a target agent's seed harness, graded evaluation feedback, and a fixed target-evaluation budget. It edits the harness and nominates a final candidate, which is scored by its normalized gain over the seed on a held-out test partition that remains inaccessible throughout search. A trusted execution environment enforces the evaluation boundary, meters target-agent resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit. We evaluate 5 frontier LLMs as optimizers both under a shared coding harness and under their native harnesses across 4 downstream tasks, over 111 scored runs. Experiment results show that optimizer models separate more than the coding harnesses they act through, native harnesses are not consistently superior, and gains vary substantially across tasks and seed regimes. These results establish harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with large space for improvement.

AI.tldr: HarnessOpt-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating how well frontier LLMs perform automated harness optimization — the iterative improvement of prompts, tools, control flow, memory, and orchestration code — under expensive, stochastic evaluation with a fixed budget. Testing 5 frontier LLMs across 4 tasks over 111 runs, the benchmark reveals that optimizer model quality matters more than the coding harness used, native harnesses offer no consistent advantage, and gains vary substantially across tasks, establishing harness optimization as a measurable, discriminative capability with significant room for improvement.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used in agentic systems, their real-world performance depends critically on the harness (prompts, tools, control flow, memory, orchestration code) surrounding them, not just model weights. Automated harness optimization is thus both a key route to improving AI systems and a demanding capability test for AI systems themselves. However, the community lacks a standardized protocol for measuring how well frontier LLMs perform at this task, motivating the creation of a rigorous benchmark.
AI.method: HarnessOpt-Bench provides an end-to-end optimization framework where an optimizer (an LLM paired with a coding harness) receives a seed harness, graded evaluation feedback, and a fixed target-evaluation budget. The optimizer iteratively edits the harness and nominates a final candidate, which is scored by normalized gain over the seed on a held-out test partition inaccessible during search. A trusted execution environment enforces the evaluation boundary, meters resource usage, and preserves candidate versions for audit. Five frontier LLMs were evaluated both under a shared coding harness and their native harnesses across four downstream tasks.
AI.result: Across 111 scored runs, optimizer models separated more than the coding harnesses they act through, indicating model quality is the primary differentiator. Native harnesses were not consistently superior to the shared harness. Gains varied substantially across tasks and seed regimes, demonstrating that harness optimization is non-trivial and context-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Harness optimization is a measurable and discriminative capability for frontier LLMs, with substantial room for improvement. The benchmark provides a rigorous protocol that the community can adopt to track progress in this important but underexplored dimension of AI system capability.

title: CogVis: Must Open-Vocabulary Change Detection Perceive the Scene Anew for Every Query?
comment: 19 pages, 11 figures, including 3 supplementary figures. Code: https://github.com/KotlinWang/CogVis
summary: Earth-surface monitoring requires change detection models capable of recognizing arbitrary semantic categories. Open-Vocabulary Change Detection (OVCD) addresses this need. However, existing methods often entangle temporal perception, semantic discrimination, and region verification, causing unstable results and redundant computation. Inspired by human visual change perception, we propose CogVis, a cognitive memory-guided framework that reformulates OVCD as a perception-memory-verification paradigm. CogVis first employs a Scene Change Perceptron (SCP) to extract a reusable, category-agnostic change prior from frozen bi-temporal features, thereby decoupling temporal evidence from semantic category decisions. A Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC) then compensates for category-dependent score shifts by dynamically estimating an image-query-specific decision threshold. Finally, an Adaptive Region Filter (ARF) filters connected candidates using learned semantic, temporal, and structural reliability. Experiments on seven benchmarks spanning semantic change detection, binary change localization, and building-damage assessment show that CogVis achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated datasets. By sharing scene-level change perception, CogVis further avoids repeating category-agnostic temporal perception across queries and improves inference throughput by 28.50%.

AI.tldr: CogVis introduces a perception-memory-verification paradigm for open-vocabulary change detection, decoupling temporal change perception from semantic decisions via a Scene Change Perceptron, a Semantic Memory Calibrator, and an Adaptive Region Filter, achieving SOTA across seven benchmarks with 28.5% faster inference.
AI.motivation: Existing OVCD methods entangle temporal perception, semantic discrimination, and region verification, leading to unstable results and redundant computation. The authors draw inspiration from human visual change perception to decouple these processes.
AI.method: CogVis comprises three modules: (1) a Scene Change Perceptron (SCP) that extracts a reusable, category-agnostic change prior from frozen bi-temporal features; (2) a Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC) that dynamically estimates image-query-specific decision thresholds to correct category-dependent score shifts; (3) an Adaptive Region Filter (ARF) that filters connected candidate regions using learned semantic, temporal, and structural reliability. The SCP is shared across queries to avoid redundant computation.
AI.result: CogVis achieves state-of-the-art performance across seven benchmarks covering semantic change detection, binary change localization, and building-damage assessment. Sharing scene-level change perception improves inference throughput by 28.50%.
AI.conclusion: The perception-memory-verification paradigm effectively decouples temporal evidence from semantic decisions, yielding both superior accuracy and computational efficiency for open-vocabulary change detection.

title: iARCS: Iterative Agentic RL for Controllable 3D Scene Generation
summary: Synthetic 3D scene generation is increasingly used as a data source for computer vision and embodied AI, but existing generators often optimize perceptual realism without reliably satisfying task-critical functional constraints. This mismatch limits the usefulness of synthetic data for downstream training, where accessibility, traversability, and spatial rule compliance are often essential. We present iARCS, an iterative agentic reinforcement learning framework that adapts a pretrained scene generator to natural-language task requirements. iARCS uses a two-stage strategy: universal-reward pretraining to improve physical plausibility and layout quality, followed by task-specific fine-tuning with LLM-generated reward programs that are iteratively refined from training feedback. Experiments show improved constraint fidelity on walkability, reachability, and clearance-focused tasks, effective task-specific constraint optimization, and competitive scene diversity. We further show that data generated by iARCS improves a base generator, supporting its value as a practical synthetic data generation tool rather than only a controllable scene editing method.

AI.tldr: iARCS is an iterative agentic RL framework that adapts pretrained 3D scene generators to satisfy natural-language task constraints (e.g., walkability, reachability, clearance). It uses universal-reward pretraining followed by LLM-generated, iteratively refined reward programs for task-specific fine-tuning, producing synthetic scenes with improved functional fidelity while maintaining diversity.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D scene generators optimize perceptual realism but fail to reliably satisfy task-critical functional constraints (accessibility, traversability, spatial rule compliance), limiting the utility of synthetic data for downstream embodied AI training tasks where such constraints are essential.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) Universal-reward pretraining to improve physical plausibility and layout quality; (2) Task-specific fine-tuning using LLM-generated reward programs that are iteratively refined based on training feedback, all within an agentic reinforcement learning loop applied to a pretrained scene generator.
AI.result: Improved constraint fidelity on walkability, reachability, and clearance-focused tasks; effective task-specific constraint optimization; competitive scene diversity. Additionally, data generated by iARCS improves a base generator when used for training.
AI.conclusion: iARCS demonstrates value not only as a controllable scene editing method but also as a practical synthetic data generation tool, bridging the gap between perceptual realism and functional constraint satisfaction in generated 3D scenes.

title: MicroEvo: Knowledge-Guided LLM Sampling for Efficient Microarchitecture Design Space Exploration
summary: Microarchitecture design space exploration suffers from expansive search spaces and expensive PPA evaluation, leaving only a small simulation budget for design decision-making. Existing methods perform blind search without considering microarchitectural dependencies and fail to learn from the iterative search effectively, leading to wasted evaluations and weak Pareto convergence. In this paper, we propose MicroEvo, a knowledge-guided framework that couples off-the-shelf LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for multi-objective microarchitecture optimization. MicroEvo combines LLM-driven evolutionary operators, a Pareto-aware tree policy that balances Pareto contribution and diversity, an active knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts and reuses optimization insights, and state-aware directives that adapt the search behavior online. Experiments show that MicroEvo improves Pareto-front quality by up to 36.2% over NSGA-II and achieves 10.6x higher search efficiency, and also demonstrates strong scalability to a complex industrial-scale core. The code repository is available at: https://github.com/GEAR-SEU/MicroEvo-ICCAD-26.

AI.tldr: MicroEvo combines LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search for multi-objective microarchitecture optimization, using evolutionary operators, Pareto-aware tree policies, and active knowledge accumulation to improve Pareto-front quality by up to 36.2% over NSGA-II with 10.6× higher search efficiency.
AI.motivation: Microarchitecture DSE suffers from vast search spaces and costly PPA evaluations, limiting simulation budgets. Existing methods conduct blind search without leveraging microarchitectural dependencies and fail to learn iteratively, resulting in wasted evaluations and weak Pareto convergence.
AI.method: MicroEvo couples off-the-shelf LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). It integrates four components: (1) LLM-driven evolutionary operators, (2) a Pareto-aware tree policy balancing Pareto contribution and diversity, (3) an active knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts and reuses optimization insights, and (4) state-aware directives that adapt search behavior online.
AI.result: MicroEvo improves Pareto-front quality by up to 36.2% over NSGA-II and achieves 10.6× higher search efficiency. It also demonstrates strong scalability to a complex industrial-scale core.
AI.conclusion: The knowledge-guided LLM+MCTS framework effectively addresses microarchitecture DSE by incorporating domain knowledge and iterative learning, significantly outperforming traditional evolutionary methods in both solution quality and search efficiency.

title: Comparative Approaches to Agent Retrieval over Large Skill Libraries
summary: Agents backed by large skill libraries must decide which skills to load and in what order. Loading the entire library into context is expensive and provides no structure for autonomous sequencing. We study two systems for this problem over a corpus of 690 skills: a hybrid ranker combining lexical and dense-embedding retrieval for sparse, on-demand loading, and a typed knowledge graph encoding workflow relations such as prerequisites, data flow, and ordering. On a set of 117 realistic, non-echoing queries, the hybrid ranker retrieves the correct skill within the top five in 73.5% +/- 8.0 of cases, leaving roughly a quarter of queries unserved. When used as the design intended (substituting graph neighbours for additional ranked results at matched token budget), the graph is significantly worse (-11.2 points, p = 0.0007). Its LLM-generated edge layer adds nothing over neighbours obtained free from a local embedding pass, and 73% of the queries the ranker misses are not reachable through the graph at all. We attribute this to a pre-filter topology bound. Because the graph's candidate edges are drawn from the same embedding neighbourhood the ranker already searches, 98.6% of typed edges connect skills the ranker had already surfaced together. The graph can enrich relation semantics but cannot extend retrieval reach. We further show that evaluating on author-written queries overstates hit@5 by up to 44 points, which would have hidden these results entirely. Our contribution is a mechanistic account of why added structure does not improve retrieval over a strong ranker, and identify the conditions under which adding structural interdependence into the retrieval is optimal.

AI.tldr: A hybrid ranker (lexical + dense embedding) retrieves correct skills within top-5 at 73.5% on 117 queries. Adding a typed knowledge graph of workflow relations does not improve retrieval and significantly degrades performance (-11.2 points, p=0.0007) because 98.6% of graph edges connect skills already co-surfaced by the ranker. The graph enriches relation semantics but cannot extend retrieval reach due to a pre-filter topology bound. Author-written queries inflate hit@5 by up to 44 points.
AI.motivation: Large skill libraries pose a retrieval-and-sequencing problem: loading all skills into context is expensive, and autonomous agents need structured guidance for ordering. The authors investigate whether adding a typed knowledge graph encoding workflow relations (prerequisites, data flow, ordering) improves retrieval beyond a strong hybrid ranker.
AI.method: The authors compare two systems over a corpus of 690 skills: (1) a hybrid ranker combining lexical (sparse) and dense-embedding retrieval for sparse, on-demand skill loading; (2) the same ranker augmented with a typed knowledge graph whose edges encode workflow relations. Graph neighbours substitute for additional ranked results at matched token budget. Edges are derived from an LLM-generated layer and a local embedding pass. Evaluation uses 117 realistic, non-echoing queries.
AI.result: The hybrid ranker achieves hit@5 of 73.5% ± 8.0. The graph-augmented system is significantly worse (-11.2 points, p=0.0007). The LLM-generated edge layer adds nothing over neighbours from a local embedding pass. 73% of queries the ranker misses are not reachable through the graph. 98.6% of typed edges connect skills the ranker had already surfaced together, revealing a pre-filter topology bound: the graph cannot extend retrieval reach, only enrich relation semantics. Author-written queries inflate hit@5 by up to 44 points.
AI.conclusion: Added structural interdependence (knowledge graphs) does not improve retrieval over a strong ranker when both operate over the same embedding neighbourhood. The graph's value is limited to enriching relation semantics. The authors identify the pre-filter topology bound as the mechanistic explanation and specify conditions under which structural interdependence could benefit retrieval: namely, when the graph provides access to candidates outside the ranker's embedding neighbourhood.

title: EnvACE: Internalizing Environment Dynamics via World Rehearsal for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Training large language model agents for long-horizon tool use typically relies on interactions with real or synthesized executable environments, whose construction and verification are costly, or on external simulators that are difficult to ground. We introduce EnvACE, an agentic reinforcement learning method that replaces external environment interaction during training with world rehearsal. The policy alternates between acting and rehearsal: it first generates a tool call, then plays the role of the environment to produce the response induced by that action, and conditions subsequent decisions on the rehearsed response. Both roles are jointly optimized end-to-end using task-success rewards. Through world rehearsal, the policy internalizes the relationship between actions and their environment responses in its parameters, yielding an agent world model that directly supports decision making. Across BFCL-v4, tau^2-Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench, EnvACE achieves strong and transferable performance, outperforming environment-scaling baselines in the overall evaluation. Controlled studies further show that world rehearsal consistently improves policy learning across model scales. At test time, the internalized world model enables private rehearsal before committed execution, yielding further gains under a moderate rehearsal budget without additional external interaction. Our findings establish world rehearsal as a new path toward scaling LLM agent training beyond the constraints of external environments. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Within-yao/EnvACE.

AI.tldr: EnvACE introduces a reinforcement learning method for training LLM agents that replaces external environment interaction with "world rehearsal" — the policy alternates between acting and simulating environment responses, jointly optimizing both roles end-to-end. This internalized world model achieves strong, transferable performance across multiple benchmarks and enables private rehearsal at test time for further gains.
AI.motivation: Training LLM agents for long-horizon tool use typically requires interactions with real or synthesized executable environments, which are costly to construct, verify, and ground. The authors aim to bypass these constraints by having the agent learn an internal world model that replaces external environment dependence during training.
AI.method: EnvACE is an agentic reinforcement learning method based on world rehearsal. The policy alternates between two roles — (1) acting: generating a tool call, and (2) rehearsal: playing the role of the environment to produce the response induced by that action. Subsequent decisions are conditioned on the rehearsed response. Both roles are jointly optimized end-to-end using task-success rewards. This causes the policy to internalize action–environment response relationships in its parameters, forming an agent world model. At test time, the model can perform private rehearsal before committed execution for additional improvement.
AI.result: Across BFCL-v4, tau²-Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench, EnvACE achieves strong and transferable performance, outperforming environment-scaling baselines in overall evaluation. Controlled studies show world rehearsal consistently improves policy learning across model scales. Test-time private rehearsal yields further gains under a moderate rehearsal budget without extra external interaction.
AI.conclusion: World rehearsal offers a new paradigm for scaling LLM agent training beyond the constraints of external environments. The internalized world model supports decision-making directly and enables test-time improvements via private rehearsal.

title: TS-RAG: Retrieval Augmented Generation for Time Series Forecasting
summary: While deep learning models, particularly transformer-based architectures, have shown impressive performance in time series forecasting, the application of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in this domain remains limited. Since RAG has proven effective in enhancing the capabilities of large language models by incorporating relevant external information, retrieving similar time series sequences as references might also improve accuracy in time series forecasting tasks. However, most time series models are constrained by limited training data, smaller parameter scales, and a lack of the extensive generative capabilities found in large language models. Simply concatenating reference sequences into the prompt, as done in language models, may not yield the expected results. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach, TS-RAG, which leverages RAG to enhance forecasting performance. The framework introduces specially designed reference tokens to effectively fuse information from the input sequence with that from retrieved similar sequences, enabling a more robust capture of complex temporal dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that TS-RAG achieves consistent state-of-the-art performance across several real-world forecasting benchmarks.

AI.tldr: TS-RAG proposes a retrieval-augmented generation framework for time series forecasting that uses specially designed reference tokens to fuse input sequences with retrieved similar sequences, achieving state-of-the-art performance on real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: RAG has proven effective in NLP but remains under-explored in time series forecasting. Directly applying language-model-style RAG (e.g., concatenating reference sequences) is ineffective because time series models have limited training data, smaller parameter scales, and lack the generative capabilities of LLMs.
AI.method: TS-RAG introduces specially designed reference tokens that effectively fuse information from the input sequence with retrieved similar sequences, enabling more robust capture of complex temporal dynamics, rather than simply concatenating reference sequences into prompts.
AI.result: TS-RAG achieves consistent state-of-the-art performance across several real-world time series forecasting benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-augmented generation can be effectively adapted to time series forecasting through careful architectural design (reference tokens for information fusion), overcoming the limitations of smaller time series models that cannot benefit from naive prompt concatenation approaches used in LLMs.

title: DASH: Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons for On-Policy Self-Distillation of Reasoning Models
comment: 17 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables. Code at https://github.com/DBtxy/DASH-OPSD
summary:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models using automatically verifiable outcome signals, but these signals are typically sparse and at the sequence-level. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) mitigates this sparsity by querying a privileged teacher at student-visited prefixes and providing dense token-level distributional supervision. Although this dense supervision alleviates signal sparsity, we find that standard OPSD still underexploits the temporal structure of the rollout. It assigns every local divergence the same coefficient, regardless of its position or the divergence sequence in which it occurs. In on-policy autoregressive generation, the same divergence magnitude can follow different discrepancy histories, reflecting different evolutions of the mismatch between the teacher and student. Since the local scalar alone cannot distinguish these temporal contexts, standard OPSD cannot adapt its token-level weights to the realized discrepancy sequence. To address this limitation, we propose Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons (DASH). DASH maps the gap between each local distillation signal and the sequence-level mean to an adaptive propagation gate and then uses these gates to control backward multi-step aggregation. By doing so, DASH adjusts token-level supervision weights according to how local divergences evolve during generation. Experiments on three mathematical reasoning benchmarks across three model scales show that DASH improves over our matched vanilla OPSD reruns on every benchmark at all three scales. DASH reuses the teacher and student distributions that OPSD already computes, so the gains require no additional teacher or student forward pass.
  Code: https://github.com/DBtxy/DASH-OPSD

AI.tldr: DASH improves on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) for RLVR by adaptively weighting token-level supervision based on the temporal evolution of teacher-student divergence during autoregressive generation, rather than treating all local divergences uniformly.
AI.motivation: Standard OPSD assigns uniform coefficients to token-level divergences, ignoring their temporal context. In autoregressive generation, the same divergence magnitude can follow different discrepancy histories, reflecting different mismatch evolutions. OPSD cannot adapt token-level weights to the realized discrepancy sequence, leaving the temporal structure of rollouts underexploited.
AI.method: DASH maps the gap between each local distillation signal and the sequence-level mean to an adaptive propagation gate. These gates control backward multi-step aggregation, adjusting token-level supervision weights according to how local divergences evolve during generation. DASH reuses teacher and student distributions already computed by OPSD, requiring no additional forward passes.
AI.result: Experiments on three mathematical reasoning benchmarks across three model scales show DASH improves over matched vanilla OPSD reruns on every benchmark at all three scales.
AI.conclusion: DASH provides a computationally efficient way to exploit temporal structure in OPSD rollouts, yielding consistent gains across model scales and benchmarks without extra teacher or student forward passes.

title: Improving the Realism of Synthetic Clinical Benchmarks Under Utility Constraints
summary:
Synthetic clinical benchmarks for enterprise AI agents can pass existing utility checks and still remain structurally unrealistic, especially in privacy-sensitive healthcare settings where operational data are hard to access. We study how to improve such benchmarks without breaking the downstream utility checks already used in practice.
  We formulate benchmark revision as utility-constrained realism improvement: dataset changes should increase realism while staying above an operational utility floor. We instantiate this idea on a care-gap benchmark derived from Synthea-generated patients exercised through demonstration electronic health record workflows and then processed by the same downstream pipeline as operational data. Realism is measured through missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment.
  The baseline benchmark is extremely thin: sampled-pair missingness is 79.44%, only 12.75% of rows are actionable, 38.94% of patients have zero actionable measures, and top-three token concentration reaches 100.0%. Two deterministic revisions improve these panels while remaining above the current utility floor, whereas a naive densification control preserves unrealistic templating. We further show that internal benchmark realism and source fidelity to an aggregate operational reference are related but distinct objectives. These results suggest that synthetic benchmark quality should be optimized explicitly, with utility treated as one constraint rather than as sufficient evidence of realism.

AI.tldr: Synthetic clinical benchmarks can pass utility tests yet remain structurally unrealistic. The paper proposes utility-constrained realism improvement — revising benchmarks to increase realism metrics (missingness, simplicity, plausibility, population alignment) while maintaining a utility floor — and demonstrates its effectiveness on a Synthea-derived care-gap benchmark.
AI.motivation: Synthetic clinical benchmarks for enterprise AI agents often pass utility checks but remain structurally unrealistic, especially in privacy-sensitive healthcare settings where operational data are inaccessible. There is a need to improve benchmark realism without breaking existing downstream utility checks.
AI.method: The authors formulate benchmark revision as utility-constrained realism improvement: dataset modifications must increase realism while staying above an operational utility floor. The study uses a care-gap benchmark derived from Synthea-generated patients, exercised through demonstration EHR workflows, and processed by the same downstream pipeline as operational data. Realism is quantified via four metrics: missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment. Two deterministic revision strategies are compared against a naive densification baseline.
AI.result: The baseline benchmark exhibits extreme thinness: sampled-pair missingness at 79.44%, only 12.75% of rows are actionable, 38.94% of patients have zero actionable measures, and top-three token concentration reaches 100.0%. Both deterministic revisions improve all realism panels while staying above the utility floor, whereas naive densification preserves unrealistic templating patterns. Internal benchmark realism and source fidelity to an aggregate operational reference are shown to be related but distinct objectives.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic benchmark quality should be optimized explicitly, with utility treated as a constraint rather than sufficient evidence of realism. Utility-constrained realism improvement offers a principled framework for this optimization.

title: The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use: A Causal Audit of Thinking with Images
summary: The "thinking-with-images" paradigm equips multimodal LLMs with active visual operations such as crop-and-zoom. However, models using these operations often achieve only marginal or negative gains over direct inference at substantially higher token cost. They may also repeatedly crop irrelevant regions and fail on questions that direct inference answers correctly. We ask whether the returned visual evidence causally affects the answer. To answer this question, we formulate visual tool-use as a causal graph that separates observation-mediated paths from action-induced shortcuts. We then audit it through interventions at the three levels: policy (comparing tool-use with direct inference), trajectory (corrupting all observations during rollout), and step (counterfactually replacing one individual observation under a fixed prefix). Our step-level estimand, Visual Evidence Gain, isolates the contribution of each returned observation. Across six representative models and five fine-grained perception benchmarks, we uncover policy miscalibration with two failure modes. In Calling Without Looking, returned observations have no causal effect on the answer. In Looking Without Planning, observations are informative but the call schedule is incoherent. A trajectory-level diagnostic decomposes the policy-level accuracy gain and shows that the gain is concentrated in a Calibrated minority. We term this discrepancy the illusion of visual tool-use: despite aggregate accuracy gains, visual tool-use is not causally effective across a broad range of rollouts. The code is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauAudit.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that visual tool-use (e.g., crop-and-zoom) in multimodal LLMs often creates an "illusion of effectiveness" — aggregate accuracy gains mask the fact that returned visual observations frequently have no causal effect on answers, due to two failure modes: Calling Without Looking and Looking Without Planning.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs equipped with active visual operations (crop-and-zoom) often show marginal or negative gains over direct inference at higher token cost, and may crop irrelevant regions or fail on questions direct inference answers correctly. The authors seek to determine whether returned visual evidence causally affects model answers.
AI.method: The authors formalize visual tool-use as a causal graph separating observation-mediated paths from action-induced shortcuts, then audit via three intervention levels: (1) policy-level — comparing tool-use with direct inference; (2) trajectory-level — corrupting all observations during rollout; (3) step-level — counterfactually replacing one individual observation under a fixed prefix. The key estimand, Visual Evidence Gain (VEG), isolates each observation's causal contribution. A trajectory-level diagnostic decomposes policy-level accuracy gain.
AI.result: Two failure modes are uncovered: Calling Without Looking (returned observations have no causal effect) and Looking Without Planning (informative observations but incoherent call schedules). Policy-level accuracy gain is concentrated in a minority of "Calibrated" trajectories, revealing the illusion of visual tool-use — aggregate gains mask broad causal ineffectiveness across six models and five fine-grained perception benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The illusion of visual tool-use demonstrates that aggregate accuracy gains do not imply genuine causal reliance on visual operations. The proposed causal auditing framework (CauAudit) provides diagnostic tools at multiple granularities to evaluate and improve visual tool-use in multimodal LLMs.

title: QuanTiMedAI: Quantum-Enhanced Time-Series Model guided by Agentic AI for Cardiac Arrest Mortality Prediction
summary: Cardiac arrest remains one of the most lethal conditions encountered in intensive care units. Despite the growing availability of electronic health record data, existing mortality prediction studies in this population largely depend on static summaries derived from early admission. Such approaches ignore the temporal progression of physiological deterioration and recovery that unfolds throughout a patient's ICU stay. To address this limitation, we introduce QuanTiMedAI, a quantum-agentic framework developed for cardiac arrest mortality prediction using agentic AI guided quantum enhancement time series model. The proposed system combines an agentic large language model (LLM) for clinically informed feature discovery with a compact quantum recurrent network for temporality aware mortality prediction. Our findings demonstrate that agentic LLM-guided feature selection consistently outperforms conventional feature selection approaches, and the proposed quantum architecture achieves competitive predictive performance through nonlinear feature enhancement while keeping the number of parameters very low. Through extensive experimentation on a MIMIC-IV cohort of cardiac arrest patients, QuanTiMedAI's quantum-enhanced architecture attains an AUROC of 0.852 using only 605 parameters, an improvement of approximately 2.9\% over a current state-of-the-art baseline for this task. A structured ablation study systematically validates the contribution of each architectural design choice. These results show that quantum-enhanced sequential modeling can exceed classical recurrent networks while using substantially fewer parameters.

AI.tldr: QuanTiMedAI introduces a quantum-agentic framework for cardiac arrest mortality prediction that combines an agentic LLM for feature discovery with a quantum recurrent network. Using only 605 parameters, it achieves an AUROC of 0.852 on MIMIC-IV data, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by ~2.9%.
AI.motivation: Existing cardiac arrest mortality prediction models rely on static, early-admission summaries of EHR data, ignoring the temporal dynamics of physiological deterioration and recovery throughout the ICU stay. This motivates the need for a temporally-aware, computationally efficient model that captures these longitudinal patterns.
AI.method: QuanTiMedAI is a dual-component framework: (1) an agentic LLM performs clinically informed feature discovery and selection, replacing conventional feature engineering; (2) a compact quantum recurrent network provides nonlinear temporal feature enhancement for mortality prediction. The model is evaluated on a MIMIC-IV cardiac arrest cohort and validated through a structured ablation study.
AI.result: Agentic LLM-guided feature selection consistently outperforms conventional methods. The quantum architecture achieves an AUROC of 0.852 with only 605 parameters, a ~2.9% improvement over the state-of-the-art baseline. The ablation study validates each architectural design choice.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-enhanced sequential modeling can surpass classical recurrent networks while using substantially fewer parameters, demonstrating the viability of quantum-agentic frameworks for temporally-aware clinical prediction tasks.

title: Bias Analysis of L2 Speaking Assessment Systems Using Concept Activation Vectors
summary: Automatic speaking assessment systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings to mark second language (L2) learners' speaking tests, making it critical to show that their scores depend on speaking proficiency rather than irrelevant speaker attributes such as first language (L1) or age. Transformer-based foundation models have improved the accuracy of these L2 speaking graders, but their black-box representations make fairness and interpretability analysis more difficult. Building on prior work that used Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to detect bias towards unwanted attributes (`concepts') in feature-based graders, we extend CAV-based analysis to two neural speaking assessment systems: a text-based BERT grader and a speech-and-text multimodal grader based on Whisper. CAVs represent human-interpretable concepts as directions in a model's activation space, allowing us to distinguish between whether a concept is encoded in a model's internal representations and whether it influences the predicted score, the latter quantified using a gradient-based sensitivity metric. Since CAVs rely on linear separability, which is less likely in complex neural embedding spaces, we also investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide cleaner concept directions by learning CAVs in a sparse latent space and mapping them back to activation space. Our analysis shows that concept recoverability depends strongly on the representation and architecture being probed, rather than on the concept alone. Sensitivity to concepts is also architecture-dependent. SAEs make concepts more linearly recoverable, but attenuate the original activation-space sensitivity, especially in low-dimensional layers. These findings highlight the need to distinguish concept recoverability from concept influence when auditing bias in speaking assessment systems.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Concept Activation Vector (CAV) bias analysis to transformer-based L2 speaking assessment systems (BERT and Whisper-based), and investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) improve concept detection. Key finding: concept recoverability and concept influence on scores are distinct, architecture-dependent phenomena that must be disentangled for meaningful fairness audits.
AI.motivation: Automatic L2 speaking assessment systems are used in high-stakes settings, requiring fairness guarantees that scores reflect proficiency, not irrelevant attributes (L1, age). Transformer foundation models improve accuracy but are black-boxes, complicating interpretability and bias auditing. Prior CAV-based bias detection work focused on feature-based graders; this work aims to extend such analysis to neural graders and address limitations in linear separability of concepts in complex embedding spaces.
AI.method: The authors apply Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to two neural speaking assessment systems: a text-based BERT grader and a multimodal (speech+text) Whisper-based grader. CAVs represent interpretable concepts as directions in activation space. They distinguish (1) concept encoding (whether a concept is linearly recoverable from representations) from (2) concept influence (whether it affects the predicted score, measured via gradient-based sensitivity). To address poor linear separability in deep embedding spaces, they also learn CAVs in the sparse latent space of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and map them back to activation space, testing whether SAEs yield cleaner concept directions.
AI.result: Concept recoverability depends heavily on the specific representation and architecture being probed, not solely on the concept itself. Sensitivity to concepts is likewise architecture-dependent. SAEs improve linear recoverability of concepts but attenuate the original activation-space sensitivity, particularly in low-dimensional layers. This reveals a tension: SAEs help surface encoded concepts but may obscure how strongly those concepts influence downstream predictions.
AI.conclusion: Fairness auditing of neural speaking assessment systems must carefully distinguish between concept recoverability (is the concept encoded?) and concept influence (does it affect the score?). These two dimensions are architecture- and representation-dependent. SAEs improve recoverability but dampen measured influence, especially in low-dimensional layers, meaning practitioners should not conflate concept detectability with actual impact on scoring decisions.

title: TRAJDEBUG: Tracing Error Lifecycle to Identify Critical Failures in Long-Horizon Agent Trajectories
summary: LLM-based agentic systems have shown remarkable capabilities in complex domains, while suffering from cascading errors and difficulty in debugging. Critical error detection aims to locate the earliest error step in a failed trajectory that is responsible for the final failure. However, progress faces two main challenges. First, long trajectories make it difficult to identify individual errors, since the evidence for judging a step may be scattered across distant instructions, observations, and prior context. Second, failed trajectories often contain multiple local errors with different downstream effects, only some of which remain responsible for the final failure. In this work, we propose TrajDebug, an error-lifecycle tracing framework that addresses long-trajectory error discovery with multi-granularity history compression and evidence-based error identification, and supports critical attribution by tracing each error's resolution status and terminal impact. We further construct TrajErrBench, a benchmark of 486 manually annotated failed trajectories from Tau2Bench and SWE-Bench Pro, covering realistic tool-use and coding scenarios. Experiments across diverse agent benchmarks show that TrajDebug achieves the best overall performance over existing baselines, and application studies further demonstrate that its diagnoses provide actionable feedback for improving downstream agent success. We will release the codes and data to facilitate further research.

AI.tldr: TrajDebug is an error-lifecycle tracing framework that identifies the earliest critical error in failed LLM-agent trajectories using multi-granularity history compression and evidence-based error identification. It also introduces TrajErrBench, a benchmark of 486 manually annotated failed trajectories.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agentic systems suffer from cascading errors that are hard to debug. Existing critical error detection methods struggle with two challenges: (1) long trajectories scatter evidence across distant instructions and observations, and (2) multiple local errors in a trajectory may have different downstream effects, requiring attribution to the error truly responsible for final failure.
AI.method: TrajDebug uses an error-lifecycle tracing framework with two key components: (1) multi-granularity history compression to handle long trajectories, and (2) evidence-based error identification that traces each error's resolution status and terminal impact to support critical attribution. The authors also built TrajErrBench, a benchmark of 486 manually annotated failed trajectories from Tau2Bench and SWE-Bench Pro.
AI.result: TrajDebug achieves best overall performance over existing baselines across diverse agent benchmarks. Application studies show its diagnoses provide actionable feedback that improves downstream agent success.
AI.conclusion: TrajDebug effectively addresses the challenges of critical error detection in long agent trajectories, and its error diagnoses can be leveraged to improve downstream agent performance. Codes and data will be released.

title: Challenges in Evaluating Explanation Methods for Static and Evolving Data
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure = this paper is a preprint of the workshop [Explainable AI in Space] paper for IJCAI ECAI 2026 conference
summary: This paper addresses the limitations of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) with respect to insufficient evaluation. They are illustrated through the DetoxAI image recognition system for bias detection and concept unlearning. Then, an example of a human-grounded evaluation of methods for explaining image classification is presented. The paper further explores methods for adapting explanations to evolving data streams with concept drift. Experiences with adapting counterfactuals for this problem are discussed. Finally it is related to the challenges of tracking the co-evolution of data, models, and explanations.\footnote{This paper has been accepted for a publication in J.Nalepa (ed) Explainable AI in Space. Proceedings of EASi 2026 Workshop at IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Bremen, Springer CCIS vol 3107 (2016).}

AI.tldr: The paper critiques insufficient evaluation practices in XAI, demonstrates these limitations through a bias detection/unlearning system (DetoxAI), presents a human-grounded evaluation of image classification explanations, and explores adapting explanations (particularly counterfactuals) to evolving data streams with concept drift, linking this to the co-evolution of data, models, and explanations.
AI.motivation: XAI methods suffer from insufficient and inadequate evaluation, limiting their reliability and practical utility. The paper aims to illustrate these evaluation gaps and propose pathways toward more rigorous, human-grounded, and temporally adaptive explanation frameworks.
AI.method: The paper employs DetoxAI—an image recognition system for bias detection and concept unlearning—as a case study to expose evaluation shortcomings. It then conducts a human-grounded evaluation of image classification explanation methods. To address temporal dynamics, it explores adapting counterfactual explanations to data streams exhibiting concept drift, and discusses frameworks for tracking the co-evolution of data, model, and explanations.
AI.result: The DetoxAI case study illustrates concrete XAI evaluation deficiencies. The human-grounded evaluation yields empirical insights into how users interpret and assess explanation methods for image classification. Preliminary experiences indicate that counterfactuals can be adapted to concept drift scenarios, though significant challenges remain in tracking the intertwined evolution of data, models, and explanations over time.
AI.conclusion: XAI requires more rigorous, human-centered evaluation paradigms. Explanation methods must be designed to adapt to dynamic, non-stationary environments where data distributions shift. Tracking the co-evolution of data, models, and explanations emerges as a critical open challenge for deploying trustworthy AI in real-world, evolving contexts such as space applications.

title: The Low Frequency Trap: Video Language Models Fail at Simple Event Bookkeeping
summary: Real-world video benchmarks provide broad coverage, but their fixed clips entangle event count, rate, duration, and visual complexity, making failure modes hard to isolate. While existing programmatic benchmarks offer better control, they score only the final answer rather than auditing reported events against executable ground truth. To bridge this gap, we introduce trace-grounded parametric profiling for event counting in three controlled video tasks: bouncing-ball wall contacts, visual blinks, and categorical state transitions. Across 2,190 videos, we vary event count N and frequency F while holding rendering fixed. Each video includes an executable event trace for capability-surface estimation and timestamp-level evaluation. Our results reveal a staged temporal failure. At an 80% reliability threshold, Gemini 3.6 Flash reliably counts persistent state transitions up to 12 events at 0.5 and 1.0 Hz, yet demonstrates no reliable positive-count region for transient blinking events. Thus, event representation dictates whether a model initially accesses evidence -- a limitation that compounds as count and frequency increase. In the high-count, high-frequency regime, only 0.2% of final counts are correct and the model recovers just 18.1% of true events. To test if visual access is the primary bottleneck, we increase sampling rate. Although this boosts Bounce Ball accuracy from 19.6% to 29.3%, the reported sequence agrees with ground truth only 3.7% of the time. Extra frames can therefore inflate final scores without producing faithful event recovery. Different prompting strategies yield similarly limited gains, and real-world video evaluations show the same concentration of success at low event counts. Ultimately, trace-grounded profiling shifts video evaluation from aggregate accuracy metrics to a detailed diagnostic of where temporal reasoning fails.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces trace-grounded parametric profiling to evaluate video understanding models on event counting. By controlling event count, frequency, and type across 2,190 synthetic videos with executable ground-truth traces, the authors reveal that models fail in staged, predictable ways — succeeding on persistent state transitions at low counts/frequencies but collapsing on transient events, with extra frames inflating accuracy without faithful event recovery.
AI.motivation: Existing video benchmarks have two critical limitations: (1) real-world benchmarks entangle multiple variables (event count, rate, duration, visual complexity) in fixed clips, making failure modes hard to isolate; (2) programmatic benchmarks only score final answers rather than auditing reported events against executable ground truth. The authors aim to bridge this gap with controlled, trace-grounded evaluation that enables fine-grained diagnostic of temporal reasoning failures.
AI.method: The authors design three parametric video tasks — bouncing-ball wall contacts (transient), visual blinks (transient), and categorical state transitions (persistent) — generating 2,190 videos where event count N and frequency F are systematically varied while rendering is held fixed. Each video is paired with an executable event trace that serves as ground truth, enabling both capability-surface estimation (mapping accuracy across N×F parameter space) and timestamp-level evaluation (comparing model-reported event sequences against true traces). They test Gemini 3.6 Flash under varying sampling rates and prompting strategies, and validate findings on real-world videos.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) At 80% reliability, Gemini counts persistent state transitions up to 12 events at 0.5–1.0 Hz, but shows no reliable region for transient blinks. (2) In the high-count, high-frequency regime, only 0.2% of final counts are correct and only 18.1% of true events are recovered. (3) Increasing sampling rate boosts Bounce Ball accuracy from 19.6% to 29.3%, but the reported sequence matches ground truth only 3.7% of the time — extra frames inflate scores without faithful event recovery. (4) Different prompting strategies yield similarly limited gains. (5) Real-world evaluations confirm success concentrates at low event counts.
AI.conclusion: Trace-grounded parametric profiling shifts video evaluation from aggregate accuracy metrics to detailed diagnostics of where temporal reasoning fails. Event representation (transient vs. persistent) fundamentally dictates whether a model can access visual evidence, and this limitation compounds with increasing count and frequency. Higher sampling rates can produce misleadingly improved scores without genuine temporal understanding, underscoring the need for trace-level evaluation in video understanding benchmarks.

title: Tracing the Heart: An Evidence-Linked Pipeline for Heart-Failure Feature Engineering
summary: Electronic health record (EHR) feature engineering is a major bottleneck in clinical research and AI, accounting for 39-45% of data scientists' workload. This is especially pronounced in heart failure, which affects an estimated 6.7 million U.S. adults and requires integrating fragmented EHR data with disease-specific, guideline-based clinical reasoning. Existing rule-based and large language model (LLM)-based approaches offer only partial automation with limited maintainability and evidence traceability. We developed the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), an evidence-linked, rubric-grounded pipeline for automated heart-failure feature engineering, and evaluated it on 500 dummy patient records from nine EHR source tables. nMAS generated 132 structured and 70 rubric-scored aggregated features, verified for structural integrity, rubric compliance, and provenance, and audited by a restricted LLM. Adding the aggregated features improved held-out AUROC from 0.895 to 0.963 for HFrEF and 0.870 to 0.910 for HFpEF phenotyping, and an independent LLM-based rubric assessment of evidence support and methodological soundness scored the features at 81.5% of maximum points. These results demonstrate the feasibility of automated, auditable feature engineering for complex cardiovascular EHR data, though evaluation was limited to a single-institution cohort and external validation is needed.

AI.tldr: nMAS, a multi-agent system, automates heart-failure feature engineering from EHR data, generating auditable, evidence-linked features that significantly improved phenotyping AUROC (HFrEF: 0.895→0.963; HFpEF: 0.870→0.910) with 81.5% rubric-scored quality.
AI.motivation: EHR feature engineering consumes 39-45% of data scientists' time, particularly challenging in heart failure (affecting 6.7M U.S. adults) due to fragmented data and the need for guideline-based clinical reasoning. Existing rule-based and LLM approaches offer only partial automation with poor maintainability and evidence traceability.
AI.method: The authors developed nMAS (Nimblemind Multi-Agent System), an evidence-linked, rubric-grounded automated pipeline. It was evaluated on 500 dummy patient records from nine EHR source tables, generating 132 structured and 70 rubric-scored aggregated features. Features were verified for structural integrity, rubric compliance, and provenance, and audited by a restricted LLM.
AI.result: Adding nMAS-generated aggregated features improved held-out AUROC from 0.895 to 0.963 for HFrEF phenotyping and from 0.870 to 0.910 for HFpEF phenotyping. Independent LLM-based rubric assessment scored evidence support and methodological soundness at 81.5% of maximum points.
AI.conclusion: Automated, auditable feature engineering for complex cardiovascular EHR data is feasible with nMAS, though the study is limited to a single-institution dummy cohort and requires external validation.
